News.title: Cops bash down doors & drag suspects away in cuffs during dramatic raids across tinderbox Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
Next

COPS bashed down doors and dragged suspects away in cuffs during dramatic raids across tinderbox Middlesbrough following the fatal A66 crash.

More than 100 officers swooped on homes across Middlesbrough and Redcar this morning in a major crackdown on suspected organised crime groups.



The raids come amid mounting anger and grief after a horror crash claimed the lives of two police officers and five young men.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died in the devastating collision on the A66 at South Bank in the early hours of Saturday, August 22.



Five others, named as Jakub Matusiak, Makai Saddington, Theo Rae, Michael Robert Cahill and Cole Robert Worthy, also died.

The fatal smash came amid a terrifying wave of violence across the area, including house rammings, fires, a stabbing and vehicle torchings.



Cleveland Police has now launched a major operation to disrupt suspected criminal networks and tackle fears of further violence.

The day-long Operation Artemis raids were supported by officers from the National Crime Agency and the North East Regional Organised Crime Unit.



A 22-year-old woman was arrested at a property on Lancaster Road, Middlesbrough, on suspicion of links to an organised crime group.

Three men and a woman were also arrested at an address on Birchington Avenue, Grangetown, on suspicion of supplying a Class A drug.

Officers targeted properties believed to be connected to organised crime groups, while also tackling off-road bike problems and carrying out public reassurance patrols.

Superintendent Daryll Tomlinson, district commander for Redcar and Cleveland, said the force was determined to take action against criminals operating in the area.

He said: “We are tackling criminals and targeting anti-social behaviour in our hotspot areas.



“Officers from across the region will be joining us to take the fight back to the criminals in this area.

“We executed drugs warrants, arrested people wanted on recall, and sending a clear message out to the community.”

Assistant Chief Constable Mark Hall urged residents to continue sharing information about criminal activity.



He said: “We want to continuously work with the community to understand their concerns and take action.

“For those who are involved in criminality, we will find out and we will take relevant action to disrupt you.

“A number of warrants have been executed. There have been a number of arrests and number of items seized.

“The support from the community has been phenomenal which has been reassuring that we have the vast majority of the public on our side.

“A lot of the activity taking place today is a result of community intelligence.



“We couldn’t do this without the support of the local community. We want to build trust and confidence with the community.”

The fresh crackdown follows a week of turmoil in and around Middlesbrough, with police deploying hundreds of officers to prevent further violence.

The A66 crash occurred after a Volkswagen Passat allegedly being driven on the wrong side of the road collided head-on with a marked police vehicle.



The Passat had reportedly been involved in a police pursuit after a stolen Volvo SUV rammed a house in Acklam.

The five young men inside the Passat and the two officers in the police vehicle were killed in the collision.

The tragedy was followed by a devastating house fire on Birchington Avenue, where seven-year-old Valentina Foster and her aunt Natalie McDonald, 34, died.

A woman was also left critically injured, while three others were hurt in the blaze.

Two men, aged 23 and 31, were arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fire.



A caravan was also set alight nearby, while another house wall was rammed by a car in Steele Crescent, South Bank.

Police subsequently arrested four men after stopping a Mercedes, where a large quantity of drugs and £15,000 in cash were allegedly seized.

The arrests formed part of a wider investigation into suspected organised crime and a series of violent incidents.

Three men were later charged with offences including possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, drug supply and possession of criminal property.

Today’s operation is the latest attempt to disrupt suspected criminal networks and reassure communities left shaken by the events.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The force said its work was being driven in part by information provided by local residents.

Police have not said whether the arrests made during today’s raids are directly connected to the fatal A66 collision.

News.title: Female cop ‘told woman “I know the law” before sexually assaulting her on drunken night out’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

COP 'ABUSE' Female cop ‘told woman “I know the law” before sexually assaulting her on drunken night out’







Next

A FEMALE cop told another woman “I know the law” before allegedly sexually assaulting her, a court heard.

Fiona Anderson allegedly refused to take no for an answer as she kissed and bit the woman while out in Cardiff.



Jurors heard the 33-year-old, who works for Devon and Cornwall Police, performed oral sex on the alleged victim without consent.

Prosecutor Emma Martin said Anderson had been described as “disgustingly drunk” before the incident in 2018.



Bristol Crown Court was told the cop was becoming “rougher” during the encounter and took off the complainant’s underwear.

The alleged victim told her “I don’t want to have sex with you” but Anderson kept persisting, it was said.



Jurors heard she then told the woman: “I know the law, I need you to say yes.”

Ms Martin added: “[The victim] was physically not reciprocating at all.”

The court was told the woman did not consent to Anderson performing the sex act on her.

Ms Martin continued: “[The victim] said no and Fiona just carried on anyway.”



She allegedly felt like “she could not turn to anyone” after the incident because Anderson was a police officer, it was said.

She told police in a video interview that she “struggled to understand” and “get past” what happened to her.

Ms Martin said: “It’s crossed the line from one-sided sexual advance to sexual offending.”

Anderson, who claims her memory of the evening was a “bit fuzzy”, denies two counts of sexual assault.

The trial, listed for four days, continues.

News.title: Driver killed mum and injured girl, 16, in horror 71mph hit-and-run crash after ploughing into her while fleeing cops
News.content:
KILLER JAILED Driver killed mum and injured girl, 16, in horror 71mph hit-and-run crash after ploughing into her while fleeing cops







Next

A MAN has been jailed for killing a mum and seriously injuring her husband and a teen in a hit-and-run while he fled from police.

Lydia la Polla, 47, died minutes after serial offender Michael Connors, 28, was seen behind the wheel of a silver Mercedes driving erratically without a license or insurance.



Driving her Toyota Yaris with her husband, the mum with a “heart of gold” was killed within minutes by Connors’ 63mph crash.

Mrs La Polla’s car was sent “airborne” and rolled over before it smashed into a boundary wall which was demolished due to the force of the crash, and trapped her husband into the car.



Connors appeared before Mold Crown Court today, where he was jailed for 13 years and one month for causing the death of Mrs La Polla, and seriously injuring the other victims.

The criminal was also banned from driving for a further eight years, and told he must serve two thirds of his sentence behind bars.

The collision happened shortly after 9:30pm on March 24, 2025 between Belgrave Road and Percy Road in Hightown, Wrexham, North Wales.

Connors had driven at a speed of at least 71mph in the moments before the crash in a 20mph zone – but had braked shortly before impact reducing the speed to 63mph.

The 16-year-old passenger in Connors’ vehicle feared she had been paralysed when the force of the crash broke her back.



Connors survived the chase and crash unscathed, before he ran from the scene leaving four wraps of cannabis in his Mercedes.

Immediately fleeing to Ireland, he was held in Dublin under an international arrest warrant, and eventually returned to the UK.

Connors of Ballyfermot, Dublin, pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving and two charges of causing serious injury by dangerous driving.

In a victim personal statement Mr La Polla described his wife as his “absolute soulmate”.

He said: “We were connected on a level so profound that I feel half of myself died in that hospital room with her.



“Our close knit family has been shattered into a thousand pieces. To say that I am heartbroken doesn’t touch the surface of this empty, aching, void.”

Jane Miller, defending, said father-of-two Connors would have to live with the consequences of his actions for the rest of his life.

Judge Simon Mills said: “Her excellent life was needlessly cut short at the age of 47, not far from her 25th wedding anniversary.

“Lydia lived a good life devoted to her family and community, her loss has been catastrophic and the harm the defendant did will never be healed.”

He told Connors: “You chose to make off from the scene leaving the people where they were having to be cut out of vehicles or laying on the road in agony.



“You should simply have stopped. Once it became apparent you were being followed by the police you decided to try and escape and you made off at speed.”

At the time of her death, Mrs La Polla’s family said: “Life will never be the same without her.

“Lydia had a true heart of gold and would always be there for others with her selfless acts of kindness.

“She was devoted to her family and friends.

“The night of Monday 24 March has scarred us for the rest of our lives. Life will never be the same without her.”

News.title: ‘Unexploded device’ found in water at UK dockyard as bomb squad descend with homes evacuated & public told ‘stay away’
News.content:
'BOMB' PROBE ‘Unexploded device’ found in water at UK dockyard as bomb squad descend with homes evacuated & public told ‘stay away’







Next

A SUSPECTED unexploded device has been discovered in the water at a dockyard.

Emergency services remain at the scene near Falmouth Dock, Cornwall, as nearby homes are evacuated.



Members of the public are urged to “stay away” and a 150-metre safety cordon has been established covering both land and sea.

The Coastguard are also asking boat users to stay away from area before specialist Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) officers assess the device.



Enquiries remain ongoing as cops work alongside partner agencies including Fire Services, Port Authority and the Harbour Master.

A spokesperson for Devon and Cornwall Police said: “Emergency services are responding following the discovery of a suspected unexploded ordnance device in water near Falmouth Docks.

“The item was located earlier today within the dock area and specialist Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) officers have been contacted and are en-route to assess the device.

“A 150-metre safety cordon has been established around the location, which takes in land and sea, while enquiries and assessment work are carried out. Two homes have also been evacuated.

“Members of the public are asked to avoid the area and follow the advice of emergency services and port officials. The Coastguard are also asking boat users to stay away from area.”

They added: “Officers are working closely with partner agencies, including the Fire Services, Port Authority and the Harbour Master to ensure the safety of the public.



“There is currently no information to suggest any wider risk beyond the established cordon. However, the public is urged not to approach the area or enter any restricted zones.

“Enquiries remain ongoing and updates will be issued when appropriate.”

News.title: Woman, 21, & man, 38, arrested over ‘deliberate’ fire at landmark seafront hotel – after hundreds evacuated
News.content:
BLAZE PROBE Woman, 21, & man, 38, arrested over ‘deliberate’ fire at landmark seafront hotel – after hundreds evacuated







Next

A MAN and a woman have been arrested following an investigation into an allegedly deliberate fire at a landmark seaside hotel.

The Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkstone, Kent, erupted in flames in the early hours of Saturday, September 19.



Police and fire crews were scrambled to the scene to bring the chaotic situation under control with 26 fire engines responding to the call.

Hundreds of people living in nearby homes were evacuated as the inferno tore through the hotel.



Around 280 guests and hotel staff were evacuated with local residents warned to avoid the area and to “close all windows and doors.”

Kent Fire and Rescue Service eventually managed to extinguish the flames with police then launching an investigation.



Local road closures remain in place as police continue to probe the cause of the blaze.

Yesterday, officers confirmed they had arrested a 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman, both from the local area, in connection with the incident.

They have both since been released while enquiries continue.

Kent Police is appealing for anyone with any information that may assist its probe to come forward.

The force said: “Anyone with relevant information to assist officers, including CCTV or dashcam footage, is urged to contact Kent Police on 01622 652006 quoting 46/155727/26.”



Dramatic images show the devastation inflicted on the hotel with charred rubble seen strewn across the floor along with blackened walls and hanging debris.

Burnt out cars were also pictured in the basement and lined up outside the venue after the flames tore through the lower levels of the building.

Kent Fire Service previously said it believed the blaze started in the basement of the property.

Cops said the fire may have been cause “deliberately” as they investigated the cause of the blaze.

The local council was forced to evacuate 90 residents from nearby Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace.



A number of guests were assessed by paramedics at the scene with one taken to hospital with minor injuries – no other injuries have been reported.

It comes after safety inspectors’ concerns that the intensity of the fire at the hotel weakened the building’s structure, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Folkestone’s housing team is working to arrange alternative housing for affected residents while the hotel undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe.

The hotel overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms, according to the Britannia Hotels website.

News.title: Brit dog owners spoil their pets by cooking them bespoke gourmet meals and giving them spa days, poll finds
News.content:
Next

THE extreme lengths paw-rents will go to for their dogs have been revealed – including cooking them bespoke gourmet meals, talking to them as if they were a child, and giving them spa days.

A poll of 1,800 dog owners found other lengths they have gone to included letting them sit in the front seat of the car and purchasing luxury bedding for them.



Typically, owners spend an average of £101 per month looking after their pooch – and are willing to spend £36 on a one-off treat.

A spokesperson for free streaming service, U, which commissioned the research following the launch of its show Wagging Rights, said: “People look after their dog like they’re VIPs, and it’s fascinating to see just how pampered the nation’s pups have become, proving the lengths we would go to for our four-legged friends.



“For many owners, no expense is spared when it comes to keeping their dog happy, healthy and comfortable.

“From luxury dinners to luxury spa days, these findings reveal that Britain’s dogs are truly being treated like members of the family.”

The study found 72 per cent of owners believe their pet is spoilt, while more owners prioritise their pet (27 per cent) over their partner (15 per cent) when considering their needs.

Almost half (44 per cent) have gone as far as putting on a TV show just for their dog, with 12 per cent admitting their furry companion eats better-quality food than they do.

More than a third (36 per cent) of paw-rents allow their companion to sleep in their bed.

And 20 per cent have become ‘helicopter owners’ by installing a pet camera to check in on their dog when they aren’t home.



The OnePoll.com study also found the bond goes much further than just owner and pet, as 49 per cent said their pooch provides them with emotional support.

While 32 per cent believed they can communicate without using a single word.

The U spokesperson added: “What stands out is just how deeply dogs are woven into family life, with many owners putting their pet’s comfort, happiness and wellbeing on a par with, or even ahead of, their own.

“As our celebrities and their dogs take on a series of training challenges, the show celebrates the lovable quirks, unforgettable moments and unbreakable bonds that make dogs such an important part of our lives.”

Wagging Rights is a new six-part entertainment series where celebrities and their pet dogs compete in a range of dog-show challenges, from obedience and agility to scent work, all in a bid to win the Wagging Rights trophy.



Featuring Rhod Gilbert, Harriet Kemsley, Kae Kurd, Sara Pascoe and Vicky Pattison, it is available to stream free on U.

Nigel Reed, celebrity dog behaviourist on the show, said, “For many owners, no expense is spared when it comes to keeping their dog happy, healthy and comfortable.

“From gourmet dinners to luxury spa days, these findings reveal that Britain’s dogs are truly being treated like members of the family.

“What stands out is just how deeply dogs are woven into family life, with many owners putting their pet’s comfort, happiness and wellbeing on a par with, or even ahead of, their own.

“Those extraordinary relationships are at the heart of the show as it celebrates the lovable quirks, memorable moments and unbreakable bonds that make our dogs such an important part of our lives.”

News.title: Liverpool university students top list as the most forgetful, new poll reveals
News.content:
BRAIN FOG Liverpool university students top list as the most forgetful, new poll reveals







Next

A VENDING machine featuring chargers, toothbrushes and nail files has popped up at a Liverpool train station after it was revealed the city is home to the most forgetful university students.

The installation at Liverpool Lime Street also included headphones, slippers and notebooks – all things current undergraduates admitted to forgetting to pack for a new term.



It comes after a poll of 1,300 university students in Britain found 83 per cent have arrived at their halls or shared housing only to realise they’d left an essential back at home.

And with students living an average of 129 miles away from home, many have had to make do, with 43 per cent forced to spend more money than they had originally planned to buy a new item.



Others have had to order a replacement (33 per cent) or lean on their housemates to borrow their stuff (27 per cent).

It also emerged 81 per cent of students have spent an average of £40.56 on replacing items they’d accidentally left at home.

Catherine Lyver for Railcard.co.uk, which was behind the pop up and research, said: “Moving to university can come with a seemingly endless packing list, so it’s no surprise that many students experience that sinking feeling when they realise they’ve left an important item behind.

“Our research suggests that forgetting something is almost a rite of passage when moving to university.



“That’s why we’ve stocked our 16-25 Railcard vending machine with some of the most forgotten items, helping Liverpool students avoid last-minute panic as they settle into the new term.”

The study also found 66 per cent of British students would describe themselves as forgetful, with 48 per cent not realising they’d left something behind until they were unpacking.

Others didn’t realise until they needed to use the item (46 per cent), when their family notified them (18 per cent) and when they were travelling to university (33 per cent).

Interestingly, on the items deemed the most essential, laptops (70 per cent) and chargers (65 per cent) scored higher than underwear (63 per cent).

The OnePoll study also found 57 per cent of students reckon there’s too much to remember when it comes to moving to university.



It also emerged 53 per cent would typically take the train to get to university due to it being the quickest way to travel (24 per cent) and more affordable (17 per cent).

Catherine Lyver from Railcard.co.uk, which offers up to a third off fares for 16-25-year-olds and mature students, added: “Student life often means lots of travelling between home and university, so it’s great to see students choosing to take the train.

“Whether you’re dashing home for a forgotten essential or heading back to uni, the 16-25 Railcard can help keep costs down, so students can make the most of university life.”

News.title: Shocking moment fairground riders are left dangling upside down 50ft in air after ride suddenly stops at Oktoberfest
News.content:
Next

THRILL-SEEKERS were left hanging in mid-air after a fairground ride froze at its highest point.

The terrifying moment happened on the Predator ride at Munich’s Oktoberfest in Bavaria, southern Germany, when it was marking its 191st festival.



The dramatic footage filmed last Saturday showed people suspended on the ride while crowds, dressed in traditional lederhosen and dirndl dresses, congregated below to witness the spectacle.

Workers can be seen carrying a large ladder to the middle of the ride before one manages to climb down.



They also appeared to connect a cable to the machinery before scaling back down the ladder.

Paramedics from Aicher Ambulanz said that those onboard had been hanging upside down for around five minutes.



Emergency services rushed to the scene but passengers had already managed to disembark from the ride.

A handful of people complained of experiencing mild dizziness and circulation issues due to being suspended.

Everyone on the ride was examined briefly and deemed fit before resuming their day of fun at the festival.

What caused the malfunction remains unclear.



But an expert from the local fire department inspected the ride after its technical hiccup and it resumed operation later in the same evening.

The festival’s medical team handled nearly 600 cases on their opening night, with 10 people undergoing CT scans and two others hospitalised, according to reports.

The Predator’s capacity can hold 40 people at once and lifts its gondolas up to around 16 metres.

The platforms rotate in one direction while its gondolas spin in the other, reaching speeds of up to 60km per hour.

It gives those on the ride the same experience “as in a rocket launch”, exerting a force of 30 and 40 metres per second, according to the Oktoberfest website.



They added: “By way of comparison, that’s about ten times the force exerted on a person in a car.”

The German showmen family business, Kaiser, bought the ride between 2013 to 2014, before it underwent a complete redesign.

News.title: Airlines criticise air traffic control as second glitch causes more disruption
News.content:
Airlines have criticised the UK's air traffic control system after a second technical problem in two weeks caused major disruption to UK flights

EasyJet said Monday's incident "once again calls into question the resilience" of how the service works, while Wizz Air said there was a "national confidence crisis" in National Air Traffic Services (Nats), which runs the UK's air traffic.

The technical problem at Prestwick in Ayrshire caused disruption at airports across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England, delaying dozens of flights.

Nats said a "connectivity issue" was to blame for the disruption, and that it had "nothing to do" with a separate software defect at Swanwick that led to the cancellation of 2,000 flights earlier in September.

The underlying issue causing Monday's disruption has since been resolved, with Nats saying it was running at "full capacity" although officials warned of knock-on effects.

A spokesperson said they were now "focused on working with our customers to recover their residual delays and help get their operations back to normal".

According to aviation analytics company Cirium, as of 13:45 BST, at least 200 flights had been cancelled or did not fly on Monday. This includes 100 flights scheduled to arrive in the UK and 99 that were due to depart from the UK.

Easyjet was the worst affected airline, with 47 of its 670 scheduled departures cancelled, while British Airways has seen 11 cancellations from its 513 scheduled departures.

The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers who had flights disrupted were "unlikely" to be entitled to compensation.

It said the technical issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances' under passenger rights rules", meaning that "although passengers should be looked after by airlines, they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident".

Industry representative body Airlines UK said both passengers and airlines "deserve better" service after "yet another Nats failure".

Managing director of Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, called for "urgent reform" of Nats, adding that she did not have confidence in its current leadership.

When asked by BBC Radio 4's World at One programme whether Nats chief Martin Rolfe should resign, Moynihan said: "We need to look at the leadership at the top. But more than that, what are the board of directors doing?"

Jet2 boss Steve Heapy called for "urgent and accountable" action to bolster the UK's air traffic control infrastructure.

Ryanair reiterated its calls for Rolfe to resign, saying he had failed to deliver" either a reliable system or an effective back-up". The latest outage affected 140 of the airline's flights and 25,000 passengers.

British Airways said "yet another technical fault with Nats" was "disappointing".

News.title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
News.content:
As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen.

He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen â one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe â but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in.

In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.

Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised UN-recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

"We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee."

News.title: Young people aren't snowflakes - mental distress is rising, says head of official review
News.content:
Accusations that the young are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has told the BBC.

Prof Peter Fonagy said in an exclusive interview that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.

He said it was "harder to be young" now given the economic and employment uncertainty young people face, coupled with the challenges presented by social media.

His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

Fonagy said he chose to speak to the BBC ahead of the publication, which is expected later this week, because he was concerned the debate around ADHD and autism would "obscure" the wider issue of mental health.

More than 100 experts and families with experience of mental health problems have worked on the review with Fonagy, a clinical psychologist and adviser to NHS England.

He said it will conclude that the rise in mental health problems since the 1990s was real, with about one in four 16 to 24-year-olds now struggling.

The data on this is contested as some sources rely on self-reporting, while sceptics argue greater awareness and reduced stigma around mental health mean more people are coming forward.

Some have also questioned whether society was now over-medicalising distress in people's lives â giving people diagnoses when what they are facing is temporary stress that they should learn to cope with.

Last year, the BBC found that many GPs had concerns about over-diagnosis and felt normal life stresses were being over-medicalised.

NHS figures, external show the number of children and young people in contact with mental health services in England has risen by 50% in the past five years.

News.title: 'I see my abusers in the supermarket' - Oxford grooming gang survivors' ongoing torment
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual violence

Survivors of an Oxford grooming gang say they still see men who sexually abused them, and who have not been brought to justice, walking around the city.

"A shop, a petrol station, a restaurant - everywhere you can imagine - you'll see a man that's done something," one survivor, Sarah, tells BBC Panorama.

Sarah and two other survivors believe "hundreds" of perpetrators are still free. An ex-police detective who led the initial investigation into grooming gangs in Oxford agrees.

It is the first time that Sarah (whose name we have changed) and one of the other women have spoken out publicly about what they were subjected to.

Gangs of men were found to have sexually exploited and abused underage girls in several towns and cities - including Rotherham, Rochdale and Telford, as well as Oxford - between the 1990s and 2010s.

Oxford was one of the places where most of the perpetrators were identified as older men of Pakistani heritage. In some cases, such as in Rotherham, police were accused of hesitating to act out of fear of being seen as racist. But in Oxford a serious case review found no evidence that this had been a factor.

Now, the government has launched a national inquiry to address why vulnerable children were not protected in England and Wales - including whether attitudes to the girls or the ethnicity of the perpetrators contributed to the failings.

News.title: Millions urged to evacuate as powerful Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
News.content:
Almost two million people are under evacuation orders in Japan as Typhoon Dujuan batters a number of the country's prefectures.

Japan's Meteorological Agency had warned of an "imminent threat to life", but several warnings have now been downgraded, with the danger to life warning remaining in place in Oshima Town.

Strong winds caused power cuts for more than 50,000 people, while hundreds of flights have been cancelled and rail services have been suspended.

Dujuan has had sustained winds of 130km/h (80.8mph) and gusts of 194 km/h. It is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El NiÃ±o", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms.

News.title: British Museum bans visitors from photographing Bayeux Tapestry
News.content:
The British Museum has banned visitors from taking photographs of the Bayeux Tapestry over concerns that they were taking too long to view the historic work.

Curators had initially allowed photos to be taken but reversed that decision after long queues delayed ticket-holders from accessing the exhibition.

The medieval embroidery, which is on display in Britain for the first time, depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Visitors are being allowed into the sold-out exhibit in groups every 40 minutes and told to keep moving along the 68m (230ft) work in one direction.

But people stopping to take photographs along the way was restricting that flow and delaying later visitors.

A British Museum spokeswoman said: "There has been enormous interest in viewing the tapestry, and our priority is to ensure that all visitors have the best experience possible.

"In order to do this, we have made the decision to restrict photography while people are moving along the length of the tapestry."

The 11th Century artwork - which is not a tapestry and was actually embroidered in England - is currently on loan from its home in Normandy, France, and will be displayed in London until July 2027.

British Museum bosses decided that the embroidery would be displayed in a single, straight line, unlike the horseshoe-shaped gallery in which it is displayed in Bayeux.

The loan was confirmed following a Franco-British summit in 2025, following years of planning between the two countries.

Under the agreement, the British Museum is funding the costs of move while insurance is provided by the UK government.

The artefact was carefully packed in a climate-controlled crate and was given a police escort along the unprecedented 350-mile (560km) journey from its home to central London.

Some would-be visitors have criticised the high price of tickets - as much as three times what it costs to see the Bayeux Tapestry in France - to cover the museum's expenses.

Tickets for the exhibition are sold out until 31 December but more are expected to go on sale in October.

Alternately, a full-scale replica of the Bayeux Tapestry is available to see for free in Tewkesbury Abbey in Gloucestershire and at Reading Museum.

News.title: Southport killer accused of throwing boiling water mixed with sugar at prison officer
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has appeared in court accused of throwing boiling water mixed with sugar at a prison officer.

The 20-year-old is charged with the attempted grievous bodily harm of a prison officer at HMP Belmarsh, over allegedly throwing the boiling mix through the hatch in his cell door on 8 May last year.

He is also charged with two other assaults of prison officers, as well as possession of a knife or other offensive weapon while in prison.

Rudakubana, who is serving a life sentence for murdering three children at a dance class in Southport in July 2024, appeared via video link at Westminster Magistrates' Court wearing a tracksuit top.

He spoke only to confirm he could hear the chief magistrate, and to give his name and date of birth. He rested his head on his hand during the hearing.

Prosecutor Catherine Pattinson told the court prompt medical attention prevented the prison officer Rudakubana is alleged to have attacked on 8 May from suffering any lasting injury.

The prosecution also accused him of threatening to soak a female officer outside his cell if she did not pass him a newspaper on 6 May 2025, then throwing an "unknown liquid" at her through his door hatch.

Then, on 28 October last year, he allegedly punched a male prison officer in the face. The prosecution said the officer was trying to establish whether Rudakubana had taken his medication at the time.

The offensive weapon charge relates to sharpened stone shards that the prosecution say had seemingly been prised from the floor of the defendant's cell.

They were found stuck to the under side of a shelving unit in his cell. Pattinson told the court that "when questioned by a prison officer, he said that he was keeping them for self-defence".

Rudakubana, who appeared from Broadmoor secure psychiatric hospital, was not asked to enter pleas during the hearing on Monday. He was remanded into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 19 October.

He is serving a life sentence for the murders of nine-year-old Alice da Silva Aguiar, six-year-old Bebe King, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven.

Rudakubana was also convicted of the attempted murder of eight other children and two adults during the attack in July 2024 at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class.

News.title: BBC removes 11 Mitchell and Webb comedy sketches from iPlayer
News.content:
The BBC has removed nearly a dozen comedy sketches from That Mitchell and Webb Look after deciding they no longer "work today".

The Bafta-winning comedy, written by and starring David Mitchell and Robert Webb, originally ran for four seasons between 2006 and 2010.

The show recently returned to the BBC's iPlayer to mark its 20th anniversary. But 11 old sketches, including one that reportedly showed the comedy duo satirising racism while in blackface, have now been cut.

A BBC spokesman said in a statement: "This is a 20-year-old sketch show; in consultation with the programme makers, we have included the ones that still work today and not the ones that don't."

The Times reported, external the removed material included scenes featuring the English comic actors as war re-enactors in blackface, a sketch about a contestant on a makeover show wearing a burka and a "tribe" living in a garden centre.

BBC News has asked Mitchell and Webb - who rose to prominence on the popular Channel 4 sitcom Peep Show - for a comment.

That Mitchell and Webb Look grew out of a similar radio show titled That Mitchell and Webb Sound, which began on Radio 4 in 2003, and went on to win the Bafta for best comedy programme in 2007.

News.title: Specialist courts for rape cases to be rolled out in England and Wales
News.content:
Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, the prime minister has announced.

Each crown court will have at least one courtroom set up to hear such cases, while alleged victims will be able to view proceedings remotely and give evidence from a separate room via video link.

They will also be provided with private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, though this will be dependent on the architecture of each building.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said this was a "significant step forward" that would introduce several reforms it had been requesting for years.

"Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman, said.

Charities have complained that low prosecution rates for sexual offences and delays to court proceedings had disuaded victims from coming forward or pursuing justice.

Just 2.8% of rape offences recorded by police led to prosecutions in the year ending March 2024 and were the crimes that took the longest to investigate.

A prior ONS study, using data from 2017-2020, suggested that only a sixth of the actual number of rape and attempted rape victims had reported their assault to the police, with more than a third saying this was because they felt the police could not help or that the process would be humiliating.

Victims minister Alex Davies-Jones said the new measures were part of efforts to bring down a backlog of Crown Court cases, which stood at 80,098 at the end of March.

Rape Crisis England and Wales said 15,373 of these cases - 19% - related to sexual offences.

Davies-Jones told BBC Breakfast that the introduction of specialist courtrooms "isn't enough on its own" to tackle the backlog and stressed the importance of the Courts and Tribunals Bill to improve "timeliness, effectiveness and also prevention".

The Conservatives say the "long overdue" move should not come with restricting the number of jury trials, which is another provision of the bill.

Under the new measures, expected to cost around Â£23m of the Ministry of Justice's budget, court staff will also be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.

From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Prime Minister Andy Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".

There are 84 crown court buildings across England and Wales, containing around 500 courtrooms, and Davies-Jones said the government was determined that every one of them would have at least one specialist rape and sexual offences courtroom by 2028.

Where architecture might prevent courtroom upgrades, Davies-Jones said staff would be expected to co-ordinate a "trauma informed approach" - for instance by scheduling different arrival times and rooms to give evidence from for victims and defendants.

The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.

Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech in which she described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.

News.title: Helen Jenner unveiled by Nigel Farage as new leader of Reform in Wales
News.content:
Nigel Farage has unveiled Helen Jenner as the newly-elected leader of Reform in Wales, replacing Dan Thomas after his arrest on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.

Speaking on the steps of the Senedd in Cardiff on Monday, Farage said: "I've known Helen for many, many years. She is a determined campaigner."

Farage said he felt sorry about former leader Thomas's "personal difficulties" and that it had been untenable for him to continue, adding: "We could have done without this bump in the road."

Jenner, who served as Thomas's deputy alongside her role as Senedd member for Bangor Conwy MÃ´n, said it was an honour to be elected to the top job.

A leadership vote was held by Reform's 33 Senedd members on Monday morning, and Jenner confirmed that her colleague Jason O'Connell had stood against her.

O'Connell had not been expected to stand, and there had been no vote of the wider party membership.

Speaking to reporters outside the Senedd, Farage said there would be a vote for a new Welsh deputy leader to replace Jenner on Tuesday.

News.title: D-Day veteran who survived capture dies aged 101
News.content:
Normandy veteran Kenneth Hay, who survived being captured just weeks after D-Day and spent years educating children about World War Two, has died aged 101.

Hay, from Upminster in east London, served in the 4th Dorset Infantry Regiment. He was captured a month after the allied invasion of northern France and survived a 1,000-mile (1,609km) forced march in eastern Europe until he was liberated by US forces.

His death was announced on Sunday by the British Normandy Memorial, for which he was an ambassador.

The organisation said he was an "extraordinary gentleman whose remarkable life will never be forgotten".

In its statement on social media, the British Normandy Memorial added: "His passion for education was unwavering.

"The countless schoolchildren whose lives he touched with his stories of courage and resilience nicknamed him 'Grandad Ken'.

"We extend our most sincere condolences to Ken's sons Chris and Jeremy, all the Hay family and his very many friends."

News.title: Two arrested over major fire at Folkestone hotel
News.content:
Two people have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire at a seaside hotel which led to hundreds of people being evacuated.

Kent Police said a 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman were held after the blaze at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone on Saturday.

The fire broke out at the hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours and about 280 people were evacuated from the building.

A total of 90 people were relocated from neighbouring Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors, Folkestone and Hythe District Council said.

The pair who were arrested have been released while inquiries continue, a police spokesperson said.

News.title: Quadruple amputee enters the Big Brother house
News.content:
Charlotte Nott has never let anything hold her back.

The student, from Oxford, is a quadruple amputee, having lost the lower parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was just two years old.

Now 18, Charlotte is a contestant in the latest series of Big Brother, something she has dreamed about for most of her life.

Her dad, Alex, told BBC Radio Oxford he was anxious about her appearance on the show, but said there had never been much point telling his daughter not to do something she had her sights on.

That resilience was on full display within seconds of Charlotte's arrival on the show.

During the launch, her shoe broke as she stepped out to be introduced, and she had to remove her prosthetic legs on stage before entering the house.

"Maybe it was my fate to walk in with no legs," she told the diary room. "Maybe that was just what was meant to happen."

She added that she was used to going without her prosthetics at home.

"When I'm at home, I have my legs off all the time," she said. "When I'm cooking, I have my legs off. I like to be four foot. I like to be tiny, like a little tiny doll."

Alex said the moment had summed up his daughter's unstoppable nature perfectly.

News.title: Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac buy historic Wrexham football pub
News.content:
Wrexham's Hollywood co-owners Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have bought the pub next door to the football club's Racecourse home ground to "protect the future of the club".

Wrexham AFC was founded at the then-named Turf Hotel in October 1864 and is the oldest football club in Wales.

A club statement announcing the purchase from Admiral Taverns said it hoped to "help protect the historic pub" by "incorporating the club, the Racecourse Ground and The Turf under a single ownership".

The pub and its landlord, Wayne Jones, have become regular features on the award-winning "Welcome to Wrexham" Disney documentary series, and Jones described the buy as "great news for all Wrexham fans".

Celebrities have been spotted visiting The Turf since Reynolds and Mac took over the club in 2021, including Paul Rudd, Channing Tatum and Will Ferrell.

Prince William even pulled a pint behind the bar with Mac to mark St David's Day in 2024.

News.title: Union calls for halt to graded Ofsted inspections over health concerns
News.content:
England's biggest school leaders' union has called for a halt to graded Ofsted inspections, saying they could pose a "risk to life" for school staff.

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said the change to inspections, rolled out nationally just under a year ago, had been severely harmful to school leaders' welfare.

It said schools should instead be rated using short narrative reports that set out their strengths and areas they could improve.

Ofsted said it had worked closely with unions and parents to develop the new report card inspection system and that it would continue to grade schools.

Ofsted, England's schools inspectorate, introduced the report card system to replace its previous one or two-word judgements last November, following the death of head teacher Ruth Perry, who took her own life after Ofsted downgraded her school from "outstanding" to "inadequate".

An inquest ruled that an Ofsted inspection had contributed to her death in January 2023.

That led to a change in how Ofsted assessed schools, bringing in report cards designed to grade schools on several areas, rather than focusing on one overall grade.

News.title: 'Other generations just buried it' - Youths share their mental health concerns
News.content:
Accusations that those growing up today are a snowflake generation are wrong, the head of an independent review into mental health, ADHD and autism has said.

Prof Peter Fonagy told the BBC that there had been a real rise in mental distress among children and young people, with anxiety, depression, self-harm and eating disorders the most common.

His review was ordered nine months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

The BBC's Catherine Burns spoke to some young mental health ambassadors who echoed the report's findings and called for an increase in mental health support.

Read more here.

News.title: Crypto ‘Godfather’s’ ex faces prison after hiding $2.6m from IRS
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

An Orange County woman who previously dated a cryptocurrency fraud defendant known as “The Godfather” is scheduled to be sentenced on Monday for failing to report more than $2.6 million obtained through her former partner's criminal operation.

Iris Ramaya Au, 36, of Irvine, entered a guilty plea in a Los Angeles federal court in March 2025 for filing a false tax return.

Her plea agreement indicates that from 2020 through 2024, her ex-boyfriend Adam Iza engaged in a series of crimes.

Iris Ramaya Au, 36, of Irvine, entered a guilty plea in a Los Angeles federal court in March 2025 for filing a false tax return ( Reuters )

These included fraudulently securing access to lines of credit and advertising accounts provided by Facebook Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc., and subsequently selling access to those accounts. Iza generated millions of dollars in unreported income through the scheme.

Iza, 26, previously of Beverly Hills and Newport Beach, pleaded guilty in January 2025 to federal charges of conspiracy, wire fraud, and tax evasion.

He is expected to be sentenced in downtown Los Angeles next month and is currently serving a 15-year prison sentence for his role in an August 2024 attempted Bitcoin robbery and kidnapping in Connecticut.

Following Iza's instructions, Au established shell corporations and opened bank accounts for those entities. Court documents show she then used illicit funds from those accounts to pay roughly $1 million to now-former Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies whom Iza had corrupted.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, the funds were also spent on acquiring or leasing luxury real estate, automobiles, jewelry, and clothing, along with nearly $10 million in recreational activities for herself and Iza. Another $16 million was used to purchase cryptocurrency for Iza.

Au acknowledged in her plea deal that she moved more than $2.6 million from the entity accounts into her personal bank accounts between 2020 and 2023, failing to declare the income on her federal tax returns.

Federal prosecutors said she faces up to three years in federal prison at her hearing.

A group of MPs have warned disability minister Sir Stephen Timms that his review into the Personal Independence Payment (Pip) risks repeating the mistakes of Labour’s ill-fated attempt to cut disability benefits last year.

The Work and Pensions Committee says it is “concerned” about how Sir Stephen’s review is being meaningfully being co-produced with disabled people following a pledge to do so.

This was a key critique made last year when over 100 Labour MPs decided not to back the government’s attempt to cut welfare spending.

While committee chair Debbie Abrahams welcomed the “clear efforts” made by the review to hear from disabled people, she adds that it has not ensured that they have “shared power in decision-making”.

“You know that the Committee has seen co-creation/co-design and co-production as central to the efforts the Department has been making to change the culture within it,” she added.

open image in gallery An update from the Timms review earlier this month said the benefit will continue to “contribute fairly” to extra costs that arise from disability and health conditions ( PA Archive )

Ms Abrahams also urged for more clarity on plans to introduce non-cash awards and services alongside lump payments.

An update from the Timms review earlier this month said the benefit will continue to “contribute fairly” to extra costs that arise from disability and health conditions.

This could mean claimants receive less money in exchange for equipment like walking aids, or transport costs.

But it is unclear from the wording what proportion of costs will be covered by awards, the committee says, and how this will interact with public services.

“For example, the Committee would find it unacceptable for social care charges to be deducted from PIP awards,” Ms Abrahams writes.

Sir Stephen has been asked to respond to the committee by mid-October.

open image in gallery Work and Pensions Committee chair Debbie Abrahams said the group is “concerned” over aspects of the Timms review ( PA Media )

The number of people claiming Pip hit a record high of 4.1 million in July, official figures show, as it continues to be Britain’s most-claimed health benefit.

Sir Stephen’s review into the payment is expected to report in the autumn. Interim findings from the work earlier this year found it is “not fit for purpose,” indicating plans to make major changes to the benefit.

The review was announced last year after ministers backed down on proposals to tweak the Pip assessment criteria to make it effectively harder to claim.

Around £5bn would have been slashed from welfare spending through the plans, with over 100 Labour MPs threatening to rebel against Sir Keir Starmer and his government on the measures.

New prime minister Andy Burnham has committed to reducing Britain’s welfare bill, with spending on health benefits estimated to be £77.1 billion in 2025/26, up from £36 billion in 2019/20.

However, the prime minster’s spokesperson added last week that this “doesn't mean crude cuts that simply push people into crisis and create bigger costs elsewhere.”

Every new digital device in Russia is mandated to come equipped with a messenger app named Max.

But beneath its innocuous white-and-blue logo lies software that experts warn could allow the Kremlin to dramatically expand its capacity to spy on the Russian public.

The app, launched last year by Russian tech company VK, is not only a space for messaging and video calls but serves as a broader information system with the capacity to perform rigid surveillance on citizens.

New research conducted by academics has found tens of millions of people use the platform, which has the potential to serve as a “backdoor” to sweeping invasions of privacy that “undermine the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information”.

The study conducted by academics at the University of Michigan, University of Calgary, Georgia Institute of Technology, and the Indian Institute of Technology, added that the “Android security model does not have any built-in mechanisms to constrain or audit a super-app”.

open image in gallery The logo of the Max messenger app ( Max )

By downloading the app, researchers found that Max can screenshot users’ devices and the contents of mini-apps without their knowledge.

Even more worryingly, the app is also able to impersonate users without them knowing and has access to all information stored in apps including messages and payments.

The app also has the capacity to inject code into the mini-apps, which can be used to launch cyberattacks, one of the academics behind the study, Roya Ensafi, told The Guardian.

“What Max provides is the cleverest and also the scariest tactic by authoritarian governments” to surveil their citizens, she said.

The Independent previously spoke to analysts who predicted the app could work as a “spy programme”, allowing Russia’s FSB security service to establish rigid surveillance and that encrypted messaging apps such as WhatsApp would be banned.

With servers based in Russia, Max is subject to Russian law, which grants the FSB to have access to certain materials.

WhatsApp - the global messenger app used by more than 70 per cent of Russians - was banned in February 2026, pushing people towards using Max.

Telegram has faced a reduction in service, with the Russian government saying it has been used for violations of Russian law.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin maintains a tight control on his citizens ( AFP/Getty )

In June 2025, Max had one million users. By October this had climbed to 50 million, in December it rose to 75 million and by March 2026, this number had skyrocketed to 100 million, although the numbers are released by Max and have not been independently verified.

Russian opposition journalist Andrey Okun said last year that Max would be central to the Kremlin’s dream of constructing a “digital gulag”.

Writing for the Republic website, he said in comments reported by The Times: “This will be a sterile space in which the authorities have complete control over the leisure time, motives and thoughts of citizens.”

Experts on Russian technology and surveillance say that the introduction of the app, which is said to have been developed on Vladimir Putin’s orders, is only the latest step in repeated measures to ramp up its ability to monitor the entire Russian online sphere.

“This is a normalisation of Russia's surveillance of its internet use… it's part of a long, long process,” Keir Giles, author of Russia’s War on Everybody, told The Independent.

“The perceived threat from Western communications technology is not something that's new. It's something that has always been a focus for the Russian security services.”

Moscow’s security industry has for decades been frustrated by Russian citizens using foreign software such as Google, Skype and Hotmail, all of which made it much more difficult to read their messages, Mr Giles explained.

Western communications technologies have always been perceived as a threat by Russian security services. After years of trying to clamp down on services such as WhatsApp, the latest move to push Russians towards Max is “really just tidying up at this point”, he added.

open image in gallery Many Western social media apps have already been banned in Russia ( PA )

Popular apps such as WhatsApp - a messenger owned by Meta, which is designated as an extremist organisation by Russia - have now been banned.

“It would be disruptive and unpopular to [ban it] without having a replacement available,” Mr Giles added.

Mark Galeotti, a veteran observer of Russian security and politics and director of Mayak Intelligence, told The Independent : “The Russian state looks keen to be using sticks rather than carrots... just to kind of drive people towards Max.”

Pushing users towards Max is unlikely to have a significant impact on Russian opposition and activism against the government, Prof Galeotti explained, because they tend to avoid WhatsApp in favour of “more seriously secure” apps such as Proton Mail and Signal.

But it may prompt a significant change in “casual dissent”, he added. “That's where it might have a freezing effect: people who might be under other circumstances willing to send messages with slightly scurrilous content about the Kremlin might think twice.”

Russia previously attempted to block the Telegram messaging app in 2018. But the attempt failed, and did not practically affect the availability of Telegram in Russia, leading it to be officially unblocked two years later. However, it is subject to restrictions.

Max has been contacted for comment.

As Kamala Harris considers whether to seek the presidency once again, she is immersing herself in the midterms by campaigning alongside fellow Democrats, beginning with a Tuesday trip to Michigan on behalf of Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

The stop is a particularly significant choice for the former vice president. Michigan was among seven battleground states she lost to Donald Trump two years ago, and it now stands as one of six states that will initiate the next presidential nominating process for Democrats. Harris also has upcoming rallies set for Nevada and Georgia, two other vital stops on the political landscape.

Her campaign appearances could either solidify or weaken her standing as a prospective Democratic front-runner. Although she remains one of the nation's most recognizable politicians and a pathbreaking figure, others in the party are eager for a fresh chapter after she failed to defeat Trump when she replaced President Joe Biden at the top of the ticket.

"I think she’s run her course," said Barry Goodman, a Michigan Democratic National Committee member who raised funds for Biden and later Harris. "I just don’t think her running again would be the right thing for America moving forward."

A number of Democratic candidates, particularly in regions Donald Trump carried easily, have flatly rejected the prospect of appearing with Harris. "No thanks," Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico. "Let’s move on. We need some new leadership."

open image in gallery Harris is throwing herself into the midterms by campaigning with fellow Democrats, starting with a Tuesday trip to Michigan on behalf of Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed ( Getty Images )

Yet many Democrats, including influential Black women who helped persuade Biden to choose Harris as his running mate in 2020, contend she has earned the right to deliberate over her options without being pushed aside or criticized. Emphasizing her distinct position, California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently told CNN he would not enter the contest if Harris runs.

"Kamala isn’t under any deadline to run for anything," said Donna Brazile, a former Democratic National Committee chair who managed Al Gore’s 2000 presidential bid. Calling it a "waste of time" to dwell on Harris’s shortened 2024 campaign, she suggested other White House contenders "should follow Kamala’s lead and get out there" to assist midterm candidates.

Harris has not announced visits to South Carolina, where Democrats will hold their opening primary. Antjuan Seawright, a political consultant based there, said she could present a compelling case, though a future campaign would need to look and sound different.

"She’s going to have to admit that she was wrong about some things," he said.

Michigan presents risk and opportunity

Harris shares a complicated history in the state, where prominent Arab American communities grew angry over Biden's support for Israeli military actions in Gaza and were disappointed when Harris did not separate her stance from his after becoming the nominee.

El-Sayed, by contrast, is a prominent critic of Israel who has called the war a genocide against Palestinians, a description Israel rejects. He has faced concern from some Jewish voters, which he has tried to navigate by apologizing for past controversial statements.

El-Sayed noted to MSNOW that "there were some hurt feelings" in Michigan following the 2024 election, with some Black voters feeling Arab Americans did not offer enough support to Harris.

With the former vice president visiting, he sees an opportunity "to bring communities together that have often been torn apart by recent events."

The joint appearance will draw intense focus for other reasons as well. Harris maintains a complicated relationship with the party's progressive wing, which includes El-Sayed, while El-Sayed aims to secure establishment backing in his contest against Republican nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman.

"We can build together on the areas of agreement, and we can come to understand each other far better on the areas where we might have seen eye to eye, and I think her coming into town will help us to do that," El-Sayed said.

Harris' travel schedule remains light compared to other prospective candidates like Pete Buttigieg, who ran in 2020 before serving as Biden’s transportation secretary. Buttigieg recently visited South Carolina and has been actively campaigning for midterm Democrats.

Harris visited South Carolina in the spring for smaller party functions, and recently joined an organizing call aimed at registering and mobilizing 1 million Black voters.

open image in gallery Harris' travel schedule remains light compared to other prospective candidates like Pete Buttigieg, who ran in 2020 before serving as Biden’s transportation secretary ( Getty )

"There’s value in doing a lot of stuff behind the scenes instead of being front and center, especially for her," said Bre Maxwell, a Democratic National Committee member from South Carolina. She noted little reason for Harris to step into media cycles knowing "she’s still a target of Donald Trump right now."

Jaime Harrison, a South Carolinian who served as national party chair under the Biden-Harris administration, said her standing gives her a timing advantage other potential candidates lack.

"Many of these folks who do get in quickly would love to have that type of name ID, would love to have that type of network, to have that type of email list," Harrison said.

Harris has stated repeatedly, including in an Associated Press interview last year, that she feels no pressure to decide her plans. "Right now – midterms, midterms, midterms," she told Megan Rapinoe on a recent podcast. Spokesman Eduardo Negrón declined to comment regarding her timeline.

Her other upcoming campaign appearances include events for Nevada’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Aaron Ford, and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is sparking 2028 speculation of his own while running for reelection.

"She is certainly being strategic," said Seawright, the South Carolina consultant.

He pointed out that her book tour for her campaign memoir, "107 Days," visited nearly every major Southern city in states where Black voters carry heavy influence in early primary contests.

Meanwhile, Goodman said he sees no sign that Harris is engaging top party donors, and Harrison noted he has not spoken with her since last December.

Past campaigns offer Harris lessons

Harris first ran for president in the 2020 cycle as a U.S. senator from California, but exited in late 2019 before any votes were cast.

Some progressives viewed the former prosecutor as part of a system that disproportionately imprisons Black men, while some moderates saw her as a typical San Francisco liberal.

Biden selected her as his running mate, making her the first woman and Black person to serve as vice president.

open image in gallery When Biden dropped his reelection bid after a disastrous debate performance, Harris generated visible enthusiasm, drawing crowds that rivaled or exceeded Trump’s. She delivered a convention address and debate performance that most analysts lauded ( Getty Images )

When Biden ended his reelection effort after a poor debate performance, Harris energized voters, generating crowds matching or exceeding Trump’s. Her convention address and debate performance drew praise from many analysts.

However, she struggled to distance herself from Biden on inflation and immigration, famously telling interviewers on "The View" she could not think of anything she would have done differently. Trump targeted her in s focusing on her support for transgender rights, declaring: "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you."

If she runs again, Seawright said she must stress moderate positions and "be willing to say, you know, ‘I’ve rethought some things.’" Voters, he added, "reward that kind of authenticity and humility."

Harrison observed that presenting her own platform would be easier than when "she was a sitting vice president, somebody else’s No. 2." But he warned she must shed the formal trappings of the vice presidency.

"You can’t act like a sitting vice president, standing up on that stage," he said. "I’d tell her she has to run hard, just as hard as everybody else, working every rope line, taking every selfie."

Unlike 2024, Harrison warned, "This is going to be the wild, wild west."

The BBC has announced a brand new Strictly Come Dancing spin-off show set to air alongside the main series and It Takes Two once the live shows restart this weekend.

Fronted by comedian Abi Clarke and Strictly alum Tyler West, who competed in the 2022 series, Strictly: Lights Up will be available on BBC iPlayer after each Sunday’s results show.

Announcing the show on Monday (21 September) afternoon, the BBC said Lights Up will feature “immediate reactions from the night's eliminated couple [and] their dance-off opponents - plus the judges, hosts, other Strictly stars and studio guests”.

The broadcaster also revealed plans for a special “Strictly hub” on iPlayer, where fans will be able to enjoy additional exclusive content.

This will include training room episodes where Clarke visits the couples to see how rehearsals are going. A brand new online-only weekly highlights show will also round up each week’s action.

open image in gallery ‘Strictly’ superfan Abi Clarke and former contestant Tyler West ( BBC/Ray Burmiston/BBC Creative )

It comes after the BBC confirmed West’s fellow Strictly 2022 star Ellie Taylor as the new host of weekday spin-off show It Takes Two.

The comedian replaced Fleur East and Janette Manrara, amid rumours that the entire show is being revamped as a vodcast, meaning episodes will be filmed for viewers and recorded for podcast listeners.

Taylor appeared to confirm the change when her presenting role was announced last month. Appearing on Radio 2, she said It Takes Two will be “the show that everyone knows and loves but refreshed for 2026”.

“We’re gonna be talking to couples but also groups of celeb [contestants] and groups of pros away from their dance partners, for slightly more candid conversation,” she explained.

open image in gallery Taylor was paired with Johannes Radebe when she competed ( BBC/Guy Levy )

Taylor continued: “One thing that we’re really keen to have is more involvement from the viewers at home. You know when you have a WhatsApp chat and you’re gossiping about what’s going on with Strictly? We want it to feel like that. One big, fat celebration of the wonderful world of Strictly.”

This year marks a new era for Strictly Come Dancing.

Following the departure of longtime hosts Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, the show’s new presenters – Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe – made their debut in Saturday night’s prerecorded launch show, which saw this year’s pairings revealed.

open image in gallery The main show’s new hosts made their debut on Saturday ( PA )

While Daly and Winkleman had specific roles on the show, the new hosts are set to take a more chaotic approach and swap around throughout each episode.

Saturday’s launch episode gave viewers a taste of what’s to come – and while Willis in particular was a huge hit, some fans and critics have questioned whether Strictly really needs three presenters.

News.title: Two arrested after fire at Folkestone’s Grand Burstin Hotel
News.content:

Two people have been arrested after an iconic hotel in Folkestone caught fire.

Kent Police were called to the incident at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Marine Parade at around 1.20am on Saturday. About 280 people were evacuated as dramatic pictures showed plumes of smoke billowing over the harbour.

A 38-year-old man and 21-year-old woman, both from the local area, were arrested in connection with the incident on Sunday. They have since been released while enquiries continue.

At least 26 fire engines were called out to the extinguish the fire as Kent Fire and Rescue Service took control of the blaze while police officers attended and moved residents nearby to safety.

No injuries were reported relating to the incident. Kent Police said on Saturday evening that the fire in Folkestone was being treated as suspicious.

Local road closures remain in place for investigation work and police continue to work closely with partner agencies who are supporting those affected by the evacuation.

The force asked that anyone with relevant information, including CCTV or dashcam footage, contact them quoting 46/155727/26.

The Grand Burstin Hotel has since remained closed as a result of the blaze. It has 550 bedrooms and is “renowned as one of the UK’s top entertainment hotels” according to its website.

Guests who were staying in the hotel and have enquiries regarding their belongings were asked to contact the Grand Burstin’s dedicated response team at burstinfireresponse@britanniahotels.com

Nigella Lawson plays around with her new co-stars in a trailer for The Great British Bake Off.

The TV cook, 66, has replaced Dame Prue Leith, who announced in January that she was stepping down after nine series on the show.

In the clip, Lawson, along with fellow judge Paul Hollywood and co-hosts Alison Hammond and Noel Fielding, stand in the Bake Off kitchen pretending to put their forks into something just off camera.

They each take turns individually in front of the camera, with Lawson looking in the lens and saying: "You’re mine, my divine."

Another clip sees Hollywood laughing when someone off camera says: "Can you get on Paul’s shoulders for this one?"

Hammond also interrupts Hollywood and Fielding as she appears on camera and says: "ladies first."

Lawson then manoeuvres her way to the front of the group before a message appears on screen reading: "The bake is back."

The TV star, who is best known for her best-selling cookery books, including How To Be A Domestic Goddess and her Channel 4 show Nigella Bites, says that, as a judge, she likes to look for the positive.

She said: "I always try to look for the positive as well, because you never want criticism to make people feel inadequate, or to be something that pampers them rather than encourages them."

Lawson has also received the blessing of former judge Prue Leith, who believes she is the right person for the job.

Speaking on This Morning in August, she said: "I didn’t have to give her any tips but I did tell her to just enjoy it because she’s so good. She was quite nervous.

"She’s so well qualified and knows exactly what she’s doing and the audience love her."

The Great British Bake Off starts Tuesday at 8pm on Channel 4.
