Sports.title: Ex-Chelsea manager Liam Rosenior sparks heated on-pitch melee after taunting former club Strasbourg as he claims fans 'disrespected my family'
Sports.content:
Paris FC manager Liam Rosenior's exuberant post-match celebrations against former side Strasbourg incited a scuffle between the coach and Strasbourg players.

Rosenior's Paris FC beat Strasbourg 2-1 at home on Saturday. The English coach, who spent 18 months at Strasbourg prior to joining Chelsea last year, could be seen pointing his finger, slapping his chest and raising his arms towards the travelling fans after the final whistle.

Within moments, Strasbourg players walked over to confront Rosenior before members of the Paris FC squad sprinted over to lend support to their manager. A shoving match between the two sets of players ensued, with Rosenior in the middle of the fracas.

After the match, Rosenior said that his enthusiastic celebrations had been a result of being provoked by sections of the Strasbourg fanbase, who he claimed had insulted his family.

The 42-year-old said: '(There was a small part of the Strasbourg) support who disrespected my family. I understand the context of what they were saying. My bench were visibly upset.

'I want to make this very clear: a small section. Strasbourg is a fantastic football club, with great people who work for the club, and great people who support the club.

😳 Scène surréaliste à l’issue de la défaite du Racing à Jean Bouin.



Insulté pendant la rencontre, Liam Rosenior est venu narguer les supporters strasbourgeois. Lucas Hogsberg est venu lui dire d’arrêter avant des échauffourées dans la confusion. #RCSA #LeClubRacing pic.twitter.com/RHE3cQj4e6 — CLUB RACING (@LECLUBRACING) September 19, 2026

The English coach slapped his chest and raised his arms towards the Strasbourg fans after the final whistle

A shoving match between the two sets of players ensued, with Rosenior caught in the middle of the fracas

'For me to celebrate in that way was a message. A message to a group of people who never wanted me to be successful at that club. But I'm not going to say any more than that.'

Rosenior also addressed the incident in a post-match interview with Ligue 1+.

'The people in the club (Strasbourg) who know me know I've always been respectful, I've always wanted the best for that football club,' he said. 'I still do want the best for that football club.

'But when I heard the chants - I understand French, I understand the context, the language - that's a step too far.

'It's a wonderful football club, it's a great city, it's a club with great tradition, I've always protected those traditions.

'So for me to celebrate in the way that I did was for many reasons. Many reasons.'

Paris FC clinched a deserved win at the Stade Jean-Bouin through goals from Ilan Kebbal and Pablo Pagis, despite conceding a late own goal by Moustapha Mbow.

It was another step in a positive start to the season, with Paris FC having won three and drawn two of their opening five matches to sit third in Ligue 1, two points behind table-toppers Monaco.

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Thomas Tuchel is indulging in some elite-level gaslighting by blaming Argentina defeat on his players. No, it was the England manager's first big test - and he blew it spectacularly
Sports.content:
OLIVER HOLT: Thomas Tuchel is indulging in some elite-level gaslighting by blaming Argentina defeat on his players. No, it was the England manager's first big test - and he blew it spectacularly

Thomas Tuchel wants to forget about the recent past. Argentina in the semi-finals of the World Cup just over two months ago? Our best chance to get to the final for 60 years?

Let’s move on, eh? In fact, let’s have a bit of a laugh about it. Tactics? Nobody wants to talk about tactics, Tuchel says.

Only the pesky press want to talk about tactics, Tuchel says, as if that is something the media should be ashamed of. Heaven forfend that some England fans still feel bitter about why the dream died. The real people, Tuchel says, just want to remember Mexico and the glory of the Azteca.

I want to remember Mexico, too. I’ll never forget it. It was one of the greatest football occasions I’ve ever witnessed. I’ll always be grateful to Tuchel for the fact he masterminded that beautiful victory. It was one of England’s greatest performances at a tournament. It was also a last-16 game.

Unfortunately, I’ll never forget the Argentina tie, either. I’ll never forget the missed opportunity. Tuchel and the FA might want to move on to the Nations League campaign stretching ahead of us over the next few weeks and the tie against Spain at Wembley on Saturday but I can’t do it. Not yet.

Tuchel seems flatly unable to accept that he got anything wrong against Argentina. He and those around him are trying to style it out. It’s not him, it’s us. And by ‘us’, I mean English football. We are petty for still dissecting it, apparently.

Thomas Tuchel wants us all to move on from the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina. Well, I'm sorry, I can't do that yet

Tuchel seems flatly unable now and in the immediate aftermath to accept that he got anything wrong in that match

It’s not his fault we blew it against Argentina, he is saying. The fault is in ourselves that we are underlings, he continues to tell us. It’s in our DNA, you see. There’s really absolutely nothing he can do about it.

There is some elite-level gaslighting going on here. Most of us can see through it so let’s be honest about what happened in the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta on July 15: Tuchel faced his first big test as England manager and he blew it. He blew it spectacularly.

He was not hired to get us to the World Cup semi-finals. Gareth Southgate did that. Tuchel was hired to get us beyond the semi-finals. He was hired to coach a talented group of England players to win the World Cup. He was hired, famously, because he would have the ability to get us ‘over the line’.

But when the test came, he wasn’t up to it. That’s the truth. I’ve heard all his excuses and all his deflections. But when the test came, he blew a 1-0 lead against an ordinary Argentina side. He was comprehensively out-coached by Argentina’s Lionel Scaloni. When the heat was on, Tuchel folded.

England always find a way to lose the big games at World Cups and lo and behold we had done it again. Tuchel was being paid the big bucks to fix that glitch in our psyche but he couldn’t do it. When it mattered most, England froze. And he froze with them.

In a weird way, I admire his front. There is something awfully bold about blaming his players and saying there was nothing he could do about their inability to keep the ball. ‘I should be coaching them to keep the ball?’ Tuchel asked on Friday, as if it were an utterly alien idea. ‘That’s my job? I’m not sure that I have the time.’

That’s why many England fans are finding it hard to let the mistakes of the Argentina game go. Because if Tuchel can’t accept that mistakes were made, then how can England move forward? How can we have any confidence at all that the next time we face a critical match, Tuchel does not blow it again?

If I were one of his players, I’d still be thinking about what he said in the aftermath of that Argentina tie. I’d still be thinking about the way he ducked responsibility. I’d still be thinking about what he said about English players and their DNA.

Enzo Fernandez celebrates his goal against England in the World Cup semi-finals

If I were one of Tuchel's players, I’d still be thinking about what he said in the aftermath of that Argentina tie

Put it this way, it wasn’t a surprise to me when the news came through on Monday morning that Cole Palmer had pulled out of the squad for the games against Spain, Czech Republic and Croatia with a ‘small muscle injury’. A few hours later the FA announced that Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Declan Rice and Tino Livramento would also be absent due to 'respective injury issues'.

Palmer didn’t make the World Cup squad, of course. Tuchel discarded him. Mainoo went but he didn’t play a single minute in the USA and Mexico. Tuchel humiliated him. Palmer and Mainoo are two of England’s best players. They are brilliant technical athletes. Of all England’s players, they are two of the best at keeping the ball.

Tuchel chose not to use them at the World Cup. He ignored Trent Alexander-Arnold, too, another of England’s best technical players. And now he has the gall to suggest our players are like neanderthals who can’t keep possession. If you want to keep possession in a World Cup semi-final against Argentina, maybe pick players in the squad who are the best at keeping possession.

It is surely not too great a stretch to suggest that Tuchel’s disdain for the ball-retention abilities of England’s players is not conducive to future harmony in the squad as the country turns its eyes towards a home European Championship in the summer of 2028.

If Tuchel could admit the errors he made in Atlanta, if he could take responsibility for the failure against Argentina, then maybe England could move forward with confidence. But he can’t. The delusion of infallibility has been his downfall before. And so doubt remains.

LIGHT SHONE ON UNITED'S ABSURD RECRUITMENT POLICY

Watching Fulham play Manchester United at Craven Cottage on Sunday afternoon, it was hard not to be reminded once more of the absurdity of United’s stated plan of fixing their team section by section in successive summer transfer windows.

The rationale, apparently, is that they fixed the attack in the summer of 2025, they fixed the midfield this summer and they will turn their attention to the defence next summer.

It is, frankly, bizarre. Football doesn’t work like that. Maybe Matheus Cunha, for example, will want out by next summer. Andrey Santos can’t get a kick at the moment. Football teams are like whack-a-mole: problems crop up everywhere.

And in the meantime, the creaking defence is a liability and another season’s hope of winning the Premier League is over already.

Manchester United's policy of fixing the team section by section is frankly odd. What if Matheus Cunha decides he wants out next summer?

And what of the newly-acquired £50m signing Andrey Santos who cannot get a kick at the moment?

CALLING IT 'THE DOCKERS' DERBY' IS JUST WRONG!

A point of order: a West Ham-supporting friend of mine wishes to advise that the habit of referring to the Championship match between his side and Millwall at the weekend as ‘The Dockers’ Derby’ ground the gears of him and many of his fellow Hammers.

‘West Ham were born from an ironworks yard, not a dockyard,’ he writes. ‘Prior to the advent of people needing to place some corny moniker on every football match, it was never, ever included in the vocabulary of sensible people growing up on the terraces of Upton Park and The Den.’

A fair point, I think. As an adjunct, reports from the aforementioned derby on Saturday, which ended in a 2-2 draw, suggest it was played in a fiercely wonderful atmosphere.

Sports.title: The balance of power in Glasgow has shifted, ignore the league table... Rangers look like the real deal under Derek McInnes: Celtic 0-1 Rangers
Sports.content:
A week after his first victory as a manager in an Old Firm game was greeted with noise to make the eardrums bleed, Derek McInnes was able to savour the sound of silence as he repeated the trick on enemy soil.

Any thought that Rangers’ emphatic triumph at Ibrox was some kind of anomaly can now be dismissed.

Ignore what the league table may say at this early juncture in the season. The balance of power in Glasgow has shifted and it’s done so in what feels like the blink of an eye.

All over the place in the early weeks of the campaign as they stumbled from one horror show to the next, Rangers now look like the real deal under their new manager.

They won the battle here and played football with a fluency and an intelligence which Celtic could only aspire to. How long ago that dismal loss to Jablonec now feels.

On the back of six straight victories, the Ibrox men go into the international break feeling that it’s an interruption they could well live without.

Ryan Naderi scores what proved to be the only goal of the game to silence Celtic Park

Not only have they turned the corner, they’re motoring. If they maintain this rate of travel, Celtic’s slender two-point lead in the title race will be overtaken in short order.

Not only did McInnes have the right game plan to back up the victory in the League Cup, he had all the best players on the field. They had more energy, desire and craft than anyone in the opposing side.

From the instant Ryan Naderi turned home a loose ball with 12 minutes of the first half remaining, the Ibrox men already looked good for the victory.

They dealt with Celtic’s threats – such as they were – with effortless ease. They played with courage and composure. The only thing missing from their display was the second goal which would have removed all doubt long before the final whistle.

All Old Firm games feel hugely significant. This was especially so for McInnes and also for the increasingly forlorn figure of Martin O’Neill.

For the first time as Celtic manager, the Northern Irishman had presided over three straight defeats.

With the capitulation in LASK the catalyst for the debacle at Ibrox and the meek surrender to Ferencvaros, this was a game O’Neill had to win – or at the very least, see some signs of promise from his charges.

It was another pitiful effort from all concerned. In terms of the hierarchy’s unfathomable approach to running a football club, the chickens came home to roost a long time ago.

German forward Naderi slides to his knees in celebration after a week of injury uncertainty

This, though, felt like the day when any hope that O’Neill’s sorcery could keep the whole thing afloat ended.

The veteran should have walked away in the summer on the back of an unlikely Double ahead of a major reset.

He should never have been asked to go again by the club’s powerbroker and he should never have accepted. It all now feels destined to end in tears.

After two dismal performances, O’Neill really had no choice but to change tack. For the first time this season, he switched to a back three. Luke McCowan was the surprise inclusion in a supporting midfield role with Benjamin Nygren also playing off Camilo Duran. It just did not work.

With Naderi passed fit, unsurprisingly, McInnes’ side was unchanged from seven days previously at Ibrox.

Daizen Maeda was back at the place he called home for four years. What O’Neill would have given for his battling qualities in recent times.

McCowan’s first involvement was a slack pass to Naderi. The German threaded the ball through to Djeidi Gassama who took a heavy touch and lost a fine chance to strike first.

Manny Fernandez’s strength eased Duran off the ball in their first joust. In their second, the Colombian’s pace drew a booking for the Rangers defender.

Celtic's beaten players are a picture of frustration at full-time after offering little hope to fans

It was typically feisty. Referee John Beaton next dipped into his pocket to show yellows to McInnes and Celtic coach Mark Fotheringham following a heated verbal exchange.

Celtic did have the ball in the net when Auston Trusty slammed home a volley, although he already knew that Liam Scales was offside.

There was a little more aggression from O’Neill’s players than was witnessed a week ago. That wasn’t difficult. Still, Rangers won the vast majority of the second balls. Naderi’s hold-up play allowed the visitors to gain plenty of territory.

The basics began to look beyond O’Neill’s players, typified by Liam Scales sending one ball straight out of play while under no pressure.

O’Neill was incensed when Dujon Sterling left a bit on Nygren while clearing his lines. Beaton wasn’t interested.

Celtic lacked imagination. The final ball which O’Neill had identified as the missing ingredient in the last two matches was again conspicuous by its absence. The same could be said of composure and bravery on the ball.

Rangers should have been in front before they made it count. Gassama sped away from Colby Donovan and pulled the ball back to the edge of the penalty box. Dan Neil’s shot was weak and easily saved by Viljami Sinisalo. The Finn also easily plucked James Penrice’s header from the sky.

Rangers boss Derek McInnes and Celtic coach Mark Fotheringham tussle on the touchline

Celtic’s most promising moment arrived when they moved the ball from right to left at pace. Nygren found McCowan, who rolled the ball into Tierney’s path. A rising strike slapped the top of the bar. O’Neill would quickly rue that moment.

The manner of Rangers’ opener said everything about the lack of Celtic’s defensive mettle. Penrice’s corner was nodded clear by Scales. Kim Minsu was allowed to shoot from the edge of the box because no one in green and white charged out to meet him.

When Sinisalo dived to his left to palm the shot away, Naderi was first to react. A smart low finish silenced Parkhead.

It could have been worse for the champions at the break. McCowan gave the ball away and watched Gassama take a delightful first touch before clipping the post. Kevin Kelsy’s follow up was blocked.

McCowan was replaced by Kasper Hogh at the break. Celtic restarted positively. Mika Baur’s cross was met at the back post by the head of Donovan. Ivor Pandur pulled off a reflex save.

So fragile were Celtic, though, that a second Rangers goal early in the second half would have sealed it.

Penrice dashed into the box and tried to steer his left foot shot beyond Sinisalo. The Finn did just enough.

When Kim was able to ride three challenges and let fly, O’Neill looked even more exasperated. While the Korean’s shot flew just wide, Celtic were living dangerously.

Kasper Hogh came off the bench for Celtic but got little change out of Olwethu Makhanya

A routine ball over the top exposed Scales. Naderi did Callum McGregor for pace. On the stretch, Kelsy couldn’t convert the cross.

James Forrest replaced the ineffective Nygren. Celtic continued to huff and puff. McGregor, so often the difference in these games, was caught on the ball time and time again and was eventually booked. Tierney, the other mainstay, increasingly looked lost and was subbed.

Olwethu Makhanya found the net after a half-cleared corner only for VAR to spot that his ball juggling on the edge of the box had been a little too literal.

What was striking, although by no means surprising, was how devoid of ideas Celtic looked as the clock ticked down. Sideways passes and aimless crosses were as good as it got. They looked absolutely clueless. It’s a recurring theme.

Sports.title: Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka confesses to faking Covid vaccine while playing for Arsenal - and could face JAIL as he is thrown out of Switzerland's squad
Sports.content:
Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka confesses to faking Covid vaccine while playing for Arsenal - and could face JAIL as he is thrown out of Switzerland's squad

Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka could face a jail sentence after he was axed from the Switzerland squad for admitting he received a forged Covid vaccine certificate.

Swiss authorities are investigating the offence, which could see him slapped with a significant fine or up to five years in prison, with Xhaka expected to provide his account to authorities next month.

He says he had a 'deep distrust' of the vaccine and did not use 'proper channels' to obtain his vaccine certificate in 2022, which was not mandatory for players to play in the Premier League but did reduce their quarantine periods after close contact or travel.

Xhaka, 33, was playing for Arsenal at the time, and has admitted the offence in a statement released on Instagram on Monday morning.

'In recent days, there has been much reporting about a matter from my past,' Xhaka said. 'I would like to address this personally.

'Regarding the Covid-19 vaccination, I was personally very uncertain and had serious concerns at the time.

Granit Xhaka, pictured playing for Sunderland this weekend, will not play for Switzerland after admitting to receiving a fake Covid vaccine certificate

'I felt deep distrust of the vaccine and was plagued by fear and uncertainty.

'In this turbulent emotional state, I obtained a vaccination certificate instead of clarifying my open questions through the proper channels.

'Today I clearly see that this was not the right course of action. It was a mistake. I am sorry.

'I take responsibility for this decision, am committed to investigating the matter, and am fully cooperating with the relevant authorities.'

Xhaka met with Swiss FA chiefs to discuss the matter and they agreed he should sit out their Nations League matches against North Macedonia, Scotland and Slovenia.

'Following his personal statement regarding vaccination confirmation, Granit Xhaka will not take part in the upcoming gathering of the men's national team,' the Swiss FA said. 'This decision was jointly made in a conversation between Xhaka and the SFV association leadership.

'After the conclusion of this international match window, we will re-evaluate the situation together with Granit and discuss the next steps,' added Swiss FA chief Peter Knabel.

Xhaka was playing for Arsenal at the time - and has since returned to the Premier League

Meanwhile, the doctor accused of providing the certificate maintains her innocence after Swiss police seized documents from her clinic in 2023.

The Swiss Authorities told Daily Mail Sport: 'We can confirm the Prosecutor's Office of the Canton of Lucerne has initiated a corresponding investigation against Granit Xhaka.

'The aim is to determine whether there is a behaviour that is legally relevant in connection with a possible forgery of a false notarisation or/and the falsification of documents.

'The person concerned is presumed innocent. The investigation is pending.'

Xhaka is not expected to face any repercussions in English football, as the FA or the Premier League did not mandate vaccines during the pandemic.

Sunderland have declined to comment.

Xhaka left Arsenal in 2023 to move to Bayer Leverkusen in Germany before securing a transfer back to the Premier League with Sunderland, for £17million, in 2025.

In the same year he left Arsenal, Xhaka was cleared of involvement in a possible betting scam following a yellow card he received in a 4-1 win at Leeds United.

The offence carries a potential large fine or imprisonment of up to five years in Switzerland

Multiple investigations into the matter finally concluded there was no case to answer for the Switzerland midfielder.

The FA, Gambling Commission and the National Crime Agency (NCA) all closed their investigations into suspicious betting patterns surrounding the booking, which included one bet of £52,000 being placed on Xhaka to receive a yellow card in the final ten minutes of the game in December 2021.

Mikel Arteta's side were 3-0 up at the time Xhaka was booked by referee Andre Marriner for time-wasting in the 86th minute, with video footage of the incident showing the midfielder standing over the ball deep in his own half for about 20 seconds, delaying taking a free-kick.

Following the FA's own six-month investigation, the matter was passed on to the NCA amid suspicions of involvement from organised crime, but that case was dropped due to a shortage of evidence.

Switzerland, who reached the quarter-finals of the World Cup with Xhaka as captain, travel to face North Macedonia and Scotland before hosting Slovenia and North Macedonia, both in Lucerne, in their Nations League group in the coming weeks.

Xhaka is their all-time record appearance maker, with 152 games for the national team.

Sports.title: England's captain goes German! Harry Kane and wife Kate sip huge beers at Oktoberfest on day out with his Bayern Munich team-mates and their WAGs
Sports.content:
Harry Kane grabbed a few well-earned steins with the Bayern Munich squad at the club's annual day off celebrating the world famous German beer festival Oktoberfest.

England's talisman enjoyed the festivities alongside his wife, and mother to their four children, Kate for the fourth year running, with the pair seen decked out in traditional German clothing.

The England skipper pulled on the lederhosen once again to commemorate the festival and wife Kate opted for a traditional dirndl coloured in the famous red and white of Bayern Munich.

Kane had more reason to celebrate than ever after bringing up a century of Bayern goals in just 98 games, netting his 100th and 101st goals for the German champions in their 7-0 thrashing of Union Berlin last week.

Kane was joined by the rest of the Bayern squad for this traditional afternoon in the sun. Former Crystal Palace talent turned Ballon d'Or candidate Michael Olise was in attendance alongside attacking partner and good friend Jamal Musiala.

The players were met with their usual royal welcome by waves of Bayern fans for a day of drinking, dancing and enjoyment in the world's largest folk festival.

A well deserved rest: Harry Kane and wife Kate holding up their jumbo lagers for the camera

The English couple were decked out in traditional lederhosen and dirndl outfits

Michael Olise (left) and Jamal Musiala (right) captured adding some accessories to traditional lederhosen

Manager Vincent Kompany joined in alongside his wife Carla, looking on at his squad ensuring they didn't lift too many steins throughout the afternoon, as his mind will surely be set on retaining the Bundesliga title for a third year running and finally getting his hands on the Champions League.

Bayern's latest superstar Luis Diaz came for his second taste of the festival with his wife Geraldine Ponce, both in lederhosen and dirndl with the Colombian winger adding some stylish sunnies to the look.

Wonderkid Lennart Karl also earned his first Oktoberfest invitation after becoming old enough to enjoy a drink this February. The 18-year-old had an outstanding breakout campaign with his boyhood club last season and looks to be a serious asset to this star-studded Bayern side.

As is tradition the entire men's team turned up to enjoy the beers and baked food on offer. Nathaniel Brown and Lennart Karl experienced the day for the first time but veterans such as Manuel Neuer and Joshua Kimmich were raising steins and pretzels with team-mates for the 15th and 11th time respectively.

Bayern Munich's annual trip to Oktoberfest is one of the club's longest standing and most important traditions and helps to give players and their WAGs time to relax and get together outside of football. The skipper Harry Kane is a big fan of the event posting to his 20.1million Instagram followers saying: 'Love the Oktoberfest tradition.'

Bayern also posted to their 3.7million followers on X, showing a video of Kane pouring his own Paulaner to set off the festival.

Vincent Kompany and wife Carla embraced a traditional afternoon but the gaffer will have both eyes firmly focused on more silverware this season

Luis Diaz and wife Geraldine Ponce raise a stein together (left) New boy Lennart Karl holding up a traditional pretzel with his girlfriend Zoe Kappele at his first Bayern Oktoberfest

Carla Kompany and Kate Kane led the WAGs of the Bayern Munich stars on their big day out

Harry and Kate, both 33, might be the leaders of the families in England's squad but they appear set to stay in Munich for the foreseeable future.

Kane has been linked with transfer to Barcelona or Saudi Arabia's Al-Hilal but he is in talks over a new contract at Bayern.

Team-mate Diaz today championed the striker as a candidate to be named the world's best footballer in the Ballon d'Or ceremony next month.

'I've noticed that several people have spoken about it, and everyone has their own opinion, right? And that's respectable,' Diaz said in an interview with Sky Germany.

'In my opinion, Harry has to be the winner. Because he's one of the best footballers in the world and has been showing that for a very long time. And the season he had last year was incredible.'

Kane himself told French outlet told TF1: 'Last season will always hold a special place in my heart. Scoring that many goals, important goals for Bayern and England - and it was the season I won the most trophies in my career.

Nothing he can’t do 🫣 pic.twitter.com/XNzO2rt1Ks — FC Bayern (@FCBayernEN) September 19, 2026

Nothing he can’t do 🫣 pic.twitter.com/XNzO2rt1Ks — FC Bayern (@FCBayernEN) September 19, 2026

Nothing he can’t do 🫣 pic.twitter.com/XNzO2rt1Ks — FC Bayern (@FCBayernEN) September 19, 2026

Nothing he can’t do 🫣 pic.twitter.com/XNzO2rt1Ks — FC Bayern (@FCBayernEN) September 19, 2026

'It is a goal to be the best player in the world. That would be a wonderful feeling. It's the greatest individual award; it's something special.

'Mbappe, Dembele, Lamine Yamal, Rodri - all top players. It'll be very exciting, because anything is possible this year. There's also Michael Olise, who has had a fantastic season and a strong World Cup. We'll see. The Ballon d'Or really is something very special.'

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim finally admits he made 'mistakes' at Man United as the AC Milan boss says he needs to be more adaptable in Italy
Sports.content:
Ruben Amorim has admitted he needs to be more adaptable as AC Milan head coach than he was during his time at Manchester United.

Amorim, 41, left United in January after a torrid 14 months in charge of the Red Devils, before taking over at the Rossoneri in June.

One of the issues Amorim repeatedly complained about during his nightmare tenure at Old Trafford was that his players didn't suit his style of play, which relies on a back three. And last week, there were similar problems with the Milan squad as they lost in the Europa League to Benfica.

However, Amorim continued his unbeaten Serie A start on Sunday as Milan dispatched Lecce 3-0 at the San Siro, and showed versatility in his tactics, unlike during his tenure at United.

During the match, it seemed as though Milan's usual back three changed to a back four, with Mario Gila switching roles into the full-back position. It led to a second clean sheet of the season.

'A great victory,' Amorim said. 'I liked the movement, especially the attacking depth. We managed the game and read the opponent well.

Ruben Amorim has admitted he needs to be less rigid in his style while at AC Milan

The former Man United boss said he made 'mistakes' while in the hotseat at Old Trafford

'These are different times, but we're improving. Today the players had more freedom; in recent games we were a bit too static, stuck.

'I can't repeat my mistakes from Manchester. If we don't have the characteristics to play a certain way, we have to adapt.

'We'll go back to building with three, but we'll see. Here in Italy, the coaches are very good, especially at going after other teams one-on-one.'

Amorim has previously been criticised for stating that 2018 Ballon d'Or winner Luka Modric wasn't a fit for his system, given the quality the Croatian still possesses at 41 years of age.

The Portuguese coach still opted to start the midfielder against Lecce, though, and was full of praise for him after the match.

He added: 'With Modric, we need to have the ball for a long time, but he's ready to play every game we need.

'If we only play transition games, it's not good for him, nor for [Ardon] Jashari. In these possession-based games, he's perfect; in the others, we'll see, but he can play every game.'

Sports.title: 'I was shocked and confused. I wondered if life was worth living': Former Bristol star CHRIS VUI on his failed drug test, 'putting my pride aside' to become a truck driver and the 'crazy' fight to clear his name
Sports.content:
'I was shocked and confused. I wondered if life was worth living': Former Bristol star CHRIS VUI on his failed drug test, 'putting my pride aside' to become a truck driver and the 'crazy' fight to clear his name

Chris Vui’s routine is very different these days. Gone are the hourly schedule and healthy salary previously provided to him by Bristol and all the comforts that came with a life in professional rugby.

As captain of Samoa and a lock with more than 100 Bears appearances, Vui was living his dream until his world was turned upside down by a positive drugs test in 2023.

Vui has always denied knowingly taking a prohibited substance. But in July, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) upheld a four-year ban after he appealed against World Rugby’s ruling.

Vui now leads a new life as a truck driver, leaving his house in Bristol at 3.30am each day for a 4am start at the lorry depot. His delivery work takes him all over the country.

‘They are long shifts – 12-hour days,’ Vui says. ‘It’s not the healthiest lifestyle. A truck driver’s diet is all sugar – Coke, pastries, pasties and crisps. I’ve tried to stay disciplined and have taken up running.

‘When you’re a professional athlete, you’re given everything on a plate. It’s a privileged life and when all those privileges are taken away, all of a sudden, you’re in the real world. I’ve had to put my pride aside and find a job to feed my family.’

Former Bristol forward Chris Vui is rebuilding his life after receiving a four-year drugs ban

Vui in action for Bristol before his ban. The lock made more than 100 Bears appearances

For the past three years, legal restrictions have meant Vui has been unable to tell his story. Now, he has explained his disappearance from rugby’s elite level for the first time to Daily Mail Sport.

All was rosy in Vui’s garden at the last World Cup in France in 2023. On the eve of skippering a crunch pool game with Japan, the now 33-year-old was preparing with a traditional loku – a Samoan prayer – when he was called to a meeting by his coach Seilala Mapusua.

‘He told me about the positive test,’ Vui recalls. ‘I was confused, shocked. I thought it was a joke. But his tone got more serious and I realised he was telling the truth. I’d never heard of the drug. I was trying to figure out where the hell it could have come from. My initial thought was there had to have been some sort of mistake. I felt lost immediately.’

Vui speaks softly and with a Kiwi lilt in our hour-long conversation. But he is overcome with emotion as he remembers his feelings in that Toulouse hotel room and has to stop to gather himself. ‘Sorry, man,’ he says. ‘It’s tough to go back to that moment.’ He then insists unequivocally when pressed: ‘I did not take a banned substance.’

Sent back to Bristol the next morning, Vui then began his search for an explanation. ‘No one knew what to do,’ he admits. ‘I was left to figure it out myself. There is no real process to follow when you get notified of a positive drugs test.’

Vui’s positive test dated back to an August training camp in Samoa. A subsequent test taken at the World Cup in France was negative.

‘When I’m in Samoa, I usually do a pescetarian diet because the meat there can be quite fatty and poor quality,’ Vui says. ‘But for that one camp, I got advised that using supplements would help. The drug levels were consistent with supplement cross-contamination because they were small. I believe the positive test came from the supplements.’

Vui tested positive for an indicator for the steroid nandrolone, but he still can't be 100 per cent certain as to the source.

'I had just signed a four-year deal with Bristol and it was the most money I’d been on. All of a sudden, boom. Gone'

Vui was with his Samoa team at the 2023 World Cup in France when he learnt of his failed test

He claims that his case had been prejudiced by delays as he was not notified of his positive test until 57 days after he had provided his urine sample in Samoa. Vui says that meant he was unable to test the supplements he had been using as they were no longer available.

Vui and his lawyers requested a B sample from the August 2023 test and are still unhappy about that process.

Vui is also appealing the CAS verdict. He has already spent hundreds of thousands of pounds on legal fees in a bid to prove his innocence. That process has included a voluntary lie detector test as well as hair and nail sample analysis. None of it has been able to overturn the World Rugby and World Anti-Doping Agency verdict.

Vui remains banned and unable to play rugby until June 2027. ‘I always told myself I was mentally strong. But, man, you’re never prepared for something like that,’ he says. ‘Never in my wildest dreams did I think my career would be put on hold or finished because of a positive drug test. I’d think about it happening due to an injury or maybe even death before that.

‘Sometimes, I wondered whether life was worth living. I can laugh about it now, but there were very dark times.

‘I had just signed a four-year deal with Bristol and it was the most money I’d been on. All of a sudden, boom. Gone. I still had a mortgage, family responsibilities and responsibilities where I come from. Legal fees aren’t cheap. You want to get the best lawyers. There was depression and anxiety in public because no one knew where I was.

‘In my favourite local bakery, people would look at me weirdly and a bit confused. I felt like I was stuck in these four walls.’

Vui credits the support of his wife Karen and Samoan parents Seta and Kay for getting him through. Bristol boss Pat Lam was also a supporter, making regular visits to the Vui family home for dinner. The Rugby Players’ Association arranged for Vui to see a therapist.

‘I believe in clean sport and the fight against doping. There are some who choose to cheat, but I didn’t'

‘When I told my wife on the phone from Toulouse, we ended up crying,’ Vui says. ‘A lot of the things I did in rugby were to make my parents proud. I bought them a house in New Zealand. That was a dream of mine. It was tough for my dad.

‘The first thing he said was: “Did you do it?” I said: “No, Dad. I don’t know where it’s come from. I’ve never heard of it.” He went: “All right. Then don’t act like you did and keep your head high.”

‘I believe in clean sport and the fight against doping. I’d be an idiot if I said I believed all athletes are innocent. There are some who choose to cheat, but I didn’t. It’s crazy. You can always earn more money, but you can’t get the damage to your reputation back.’

Vui holds no grievances with Bristol or Samoa and still loves living in the city he’s made his home since 2017.

The arrival of Vui’s son Cole last year was a moment of light, completing the family of four along with his daughter Kaylen.

Vui is now in a good place and determined to use his experience to help others. He has begun the process of fundraising to produce a film entitled Spiked, which aims to show the dangers for athletes of supplement cross contamination and the fact that not all products are batch tested, as many companies claim.

In Vui’s home, there is no clue as to his former life as a rugby star. The mementos, pictures and shirts have all been taken down. ‘In the past, if I’ve thought too much about where I was and where I am now, it has sent me into a spiral,’ Vui says. ‘If you dwell on those things, it can eat away at you. I’ll always have a bit of regret if my time in rugby doesn’t finish on my terms. I can’t just give up.

‘I know it will be hard as I’ve been out for many years, but I still think I can play at a high level. I miss rugby.’

Vui’s former Bristol team-mates and England internationals Ellis Genge and Kyle Sinckler have been among those to show him support, as have Samoan international brothers Jordan and James Lay.

‘I know it will be hard as I’ve been out for many years, but I still think I can play at a high level. I miss rugby.’

'There should be more awareness around the issues I’ve experienced,’ Vui says. ‘All people read about is my ban, but they don’t read the CAS decision and the finer details'

At his lowest moment, Vui found out who his real friends were. Those who he thought were close to him went quiet. He received help from unexpected places. As our conversation moves to a nearby coffee shop, Vui stresses that any form of cheating is considered abhorrent in Samoan culture.

In the Pacific Islands, pride in your family name is absolute. Vui insists he would never sully his or his father’s reputation.

‘There should be more awareness around the issues I’ve experienced,’ Vui says. ‘All people read about is my ban, but they don’t read the CAS decision and the finer details. There are questions to be asked about rugby’s testing procedures. The most important thing is I’m doing OK now.

‘If you put your mind to it and have the right people around you, you can figure things out and enjoy a great life. Whatever happens. That’s what I’m trying to do. My fight goes on.’

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
