Aside from negative interactions with people-movers, the UN General Assembly has its work cut out for it, and this year’s theme is “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.” The General Assembly also kicks off ahead of Guterres’ own exit from his role at year-end as concerns about emerging AI models hover over the proceedings.

Here’s what to expect as the UNGA’s “General Debate” – where leaders and officials take turns speaking from the organization’s signature stone podium – begins Tuesday.

Dealmaking and meetings

The high density of diplomats and world leaders makes the UNGA a prime spot for meetings on the sidelines of the main event. Trump is scheduled to meet with Gulf leaders on Tuesday to discuss the next phase of the war with Iran, two US officials told CNN.

There will also be a “high-level” briefing for Trump’s Board of Peace during week, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. It’s a notable juxtaposition considering Trump once suggested that the board, meant to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, “might” eventually replace the UN.

Meanwhile, France plans to convene a follow-up meeting this week on the two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, diplomatic sources said. France and several other Western countries announced their recognition of the State of Palestine during the UNGA proceedings last year.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he will hold a meeting with Trump in New York, as he had last year. Such a meeting would come after US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met separately with Zelensky in Kyiv and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier this month. Trump has spoken only with Putin in the weeks since that visit.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said he would meet with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, according to Russian state media.

The General Assembly is also a place where deals are struck or formalized. Months after threatening to annex Greenland by force, Trump is expected to sign an agreement negotiated with Denmark and Greenland that would hand the US “permanent control” over Greenlandic security. It’s unclear how the deal would differ from current arrangements, which grant the US a large military presence on the island.

Who’s speaking?

The speeches delivered from the General Assembly podium often attract attention for the behavior of the audience as much as the speakers themselves. Last year, numerous delegates left the auditorium while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke. In 2018, laughing delegates interrupted Trump’s speech as he outlined his administration’s achievements.

Daniel Forti, head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group, told CNN that the speakers list will set the tenor for this year’s assembly.

“While it seems like we have over 130 heads of state or government coming, it’s actually going to be a much more mixed picture in terms of the signals that world leaders are providing to the UN,” Forti said.

One big question is whether Chinese leader Xi Jinping will make a surprise appearance in New York. Xi is due to appear in Washington for a state visit while the General Assembly is underway.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping is seen on a video screen as he addresses the 76th session of the United Nations General Assembly on September 21, 2021. The virtual address was the last time Xi spoke at the UN General Assembly. Mary Altaffer/Pool/Getty Images

“It’ll be a very difficult split screen for the organization if you have Trump and Xi meeting in Washington, and you don’t have both of the world’s biggest powers engaging in UN diplomacy during High-Level Week,” Forti said.

Asked about Xi’s schedule, Guterres told reporters that while he “would like to have President Xi Jinping with us,” he met with him “twice last month” and is unconcerned about the Chinese leader’s commitment to “a world order based on multilateralism with the UN at its center.”

Other headline speakers include Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who will speak first Tuesday, and Netanyahu, who will speak Thursday, according to a preliminary list.

Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodríguez will make her UN debut on Thursday while her former boss, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, sits in jail mere miles away in Brooklyn. Rodríguez is expected to meet with Trump ahead of her address.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas is slotted for a Thursday speaking time before Netanyahu. However, the Trump administration has again refused Abbas a visa, so he will almost certainly address the chamber via video.

Even as it denies visas to Palestinian officials, the administration will allow Iran’s “core delegation,” which will include President Masoud Pezeshkian, to come to New York.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” a State Department spokesperson said Thursday.

“The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our (sanctions) policy,” they said. “The delegation is smaller than last year.”

Pezeshkian speaking in New York while his country is actively engaged in combat with the United States is virtually unprecedented. The closest international equivalent might be Egyptian President Anwar Sadat’s 1977 visit to Israel while the two countries were technically at war — but even that was part of a larger peace process.

Pezeshkian will travel to New York on Tuesday, a representative from his office said Monday, according to Iranian state media.

Goodbye, UN

There will be a few notable goodbyes at the UN this year: France’s Emmanuel Macron is making his final appearance at the General Assembly, as is Guterres.

The race to replace Guterres before the end of the year will be front of mind for many attendees, Forti said. The current secretary-general is the “last of a previous era of globalist leaders” and spent much of his 10-year tenure focused on development financing, climate change and girding the UN for the rise of artificial intelligence.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres speaks during the United Nations General Assembly at the UN headquarters in New York on September 23, 2025. Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

The last point is especially important to the outgoing leader; Guterres spent more than half of his last press conference speaking about AI.

“Artificial intelligence will certainly be a major topic in my discussions with world leaders next week — and the United Nations will continue to explore practical ideas and approaches in the immediate days ahead,” Guterres told reporters.

After several weeks of apocalyptic warnings about the technology, AI is a top-billed issue for the UNGA this year. On Monday, tech industry figures, diplomats and the actor Joseph Gordon-Levitt are meeting for a conference on “Digital Cooperation.” The Security Council is slotted to meet about AI on Wednesday, and the US is hosting another event the same day.

Guterres has been outspoken on AI since 2021, and his focus on the emerging tech may have come at the expense of his traditional role in promoting UN peacekeeping efforts, Forti said.

“Guterres has certainly been very conservative and cautious on the UN’s role in peace and security,” he said. “He certainly has not made the most of the mandate and legitimacy that the UN carries to try and inject the organization into more peace-making efforts.”

The secretary-general’s last speech is his opportunity to defend his tenure as the UN’s leader, Forti added.

“It may fall on deaf ears,” the analyst said, “but in the long run, there may be more positive reflections on how he fought through a very difficult period.”

An informal UN Security Council straw poll for Guterres’ successor was held Friday, with sources telling Reuters that Costa Rica’s former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan has a narrow lead.

The US has yet to formally back a candidate. However, a State Department spokesperson said candidates must “publicly commit to the changes we require.”

“Any new Secretary General must return the UN to its primary purpose of maintaining peace and security in the world, rather than the absurd, politicized, woke ideology that has undermined the institution’s effectiveness,” they said.

Money, money, money

The 2026 General Assembly finds the UN on firmer financial footing than last year, when it faced a severe budget crisis as the US threatened to cut the organization off entirely.

The Trump administration appears to have reconsidered at least some of its UN skepticism. Ahead of the General Assembly, the US government sent the UN $827 million in dues — a fraction of the approximately $4 billion that the US owes the UN but a not-insignificant amount for a body that in January was facing “imminent financial collapse.”

President Donald Trump speaks during the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 23, 2025. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Yet the UN General Assembly has also increasingly served as a forum for its critics to question whether it matters at all. Last year, Trump asked the assembly point-blank: “What is the purpose of the United Nations?”

“It has such tremendous, tremendous potential, but it’s not even coming close to living up to that potential, for the most part,” Trump said. “At least for now, all they seem to do is write a really strongly worded letter and then never follow that letter up. It’s empty words, and empty words don’t solve war.”

Despite questions about the UN’s legitimacy and its increasing marginalization, Forti insists that the United Nations still matters.

“At this moment in world affairs, where we have more wars than in previous decades … everyone still needs a place to come together, to deconflict, to hash out the rules of the road,” the analyst said. “And quite frankly, the UN is the only organization with the legitimacy, with the legal mandates, the ability to convene every state around the world to actually tackle those things.”

World.title: ‘Voters are like, No thanks’: Trump’s tariffs fall flat with the working class
World.content:
It’s become an article of faith for trade hardliners in both parties that a protectionist agenda is a guaranteed pathway to building support among working-class voters. But now that President Donald Trump is testing that theory in practice, it is largely flopping on the campaign trail.

Trump has pursued the most confrontational trade agenda of any president since at least William McKinley at the end of the 19th century, and by the estimation of some historians, even Thomas Jefferson around its beginning.

But even in heavily blue-collar states and House districts that were long believed to be the most receptive to a protectionist agenda, Democrats almost uniformly have been comfortable this year running against the Trump tariffs, while Republicans have struggled to defend them. Even Democrats who are deeply skeptical of free trade agreements — like Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and Brian Poindexter, the ironworker running against Rep. Max Miller for an Ohio House seat — have been unreserved in condemning the Trump tariffs. Polls by CNN and other media organizations consistently show that far more Americans believe the tariffs have hurt rather than helped their financial bottom line — and that consensus extends even to working-class white voters without a four-year college degree.

All this marks a fundamental shift in the politics of trade that could loosen Trump’s hold on the working-class voters at the core of his coalition — and allow Democrats this fall to recover some of the ground they have lost in blue-collar and rural places. Trump’s skepticism about the North American Free Trade Agreement and other moves to lower trade barriers clearly helped power his historic gains in blue-collar communities during his initial 2016 race and his first presidential term. But his sweeping second-term tariffs — which exceed even the wish lists that other protectionist presidential candidates have put forward since the 1970s — appear to be bleeding Republican support, even in those working-class places. “Everyone else talked about it, but Trump did it,” says Douglas Holtz-Eakin, president of the American Action Forum, a center-right think tank. “And voters are like: ‘no thanks.’”

President Donald Trump walks from the Oval Office to the Rose Garden of the White House on August 24. Win McNamee/Getty Images

The most protectionist president in modern history

For decades, a steady procession of presidential hopefuls in both parties had offered a tough-on-trade message and an assortment of policies to restrict imports. That list extends from Republican John Connally in 1980 to Democrats Walter Mondale and Richard Gephardt in the 1980s to GOP insurgent Patrick J. Buchanan and independent candidate Ross Perot in the 1990s.

But before Trump, none of them won the presidency — and with it the ability to implement a protectionist agenda. Presidents of both parties have often provided some protection to American industries threatened by foreign competitors. But the general pattern since Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1930s has been that Republican and Democratic presidents alike have generally defended free trade, while the protectionist impulse has been confined mostly to Congress, notes Douglas Irwin, an economics professor at Dartmouth College and historian of American trade policy.

Trump’s willingness to impose tariffs on a panoramic list of US trading partners is unmatched since McKinley in the 1890s, says Alan Tonelson, a longtime manufacturing trade policy analyst and advocate for import restrictions. Irwin thinks Trump outmatches even McKinley: He believes Trump is pursuing the most confrontational trade policy since Jefferson imposed an (ultimately disastrous) 1807 embargo on all commerce with both England and Napoleon-era France in protest of their attacks on American shipping during their worldwide conflict. “There’s been no president in modern history who has used the tariff threat nearly as much as Donald Trump,” says Irwin.

Stanley Greenberg, a longtime Democratic pollster who has studied the party’s diminishing support among working-class white voters since the 1980s, says that Trump’s hardline approach on trade contributed to his 2016 breakthroughs against Hillary Clinton in battered blue-collar communities that had, in many cases, previously voted for Barack Obama during his two presidential victories.

“Hillary got hurt and Obama got hurt by not understanding these sentiments in the industrial Midwest,” Greenberg says. “And Trump used that to his advantage to win the election in 2016 and it was a fundamental part of his presidency in the first term, in which the association of him going after bad trade agreements and him championing tariffs” allowed him to present himself as a champion of “forgotten” working-class voters.

In his first term, Trump sharply veered from the preponderantly free trade outlook of his three immediate predecessors: Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton. Trump renegotiated NAFTA, the free trade agreement that Clinton pushed through Congress; scrapped the pan-Asian free trade agreement that Obama had negotiated (but never submitted to Congress for fear of hurting Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election); and imposed tariffs primarily on steel and aluminum imports from many countries as well as a wide array of products from China.

But all that was barely an overture for Trump’s second term. To a far greater extent than in his first term, Trump has levied, withdrawn and reimposed tariffs; brandished threats; and launched investigations in a bewildering blur that has upended the rules of trade with dozens of countries. He has moved as aggressively against allies, such as Canada and the European Union, as against traditional trade adversaries such as China.

Before Trump, Holtz-Eakin notes, many political leaders believed “the politics were good” for protectionism, “but the foreign policy implications were bad.” As a result, “no Republican would go there,” he says. “But Trump didn’t care about the latter. So, we’ve (been able) to see the economics in isolation.” And the reaction has been very different than what Trump — and other trade hawks — expected.

A shopping cart stands in an aisle of a grocery store in New York City, on August 26. Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Tariffs seemed more popular in theory than they are in practice

Since at least the 1970s, the dominant assumption in each party has been that trade issues divided the public along educational lines, with college-educated voters the most likely to favor expanding trade and working-class voters most receptive to a protectionist message of restricting imports to try to protect domestic manufacturing jobs.

That traditional divide persisted even as Trump returned to office. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ annual foreign policy polling, for instance, found that in 2025 nearly two-thirds of whites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that imposed restrictions on imports to protect jobs over an approach that minimized restrictions to lower prices. Whites with a college degree split evenly over which approach they preferred; notably, however, in a sharp departure from their white counterparts, a slight majority of nonwhites without a college degree preferred a trade policy that focused on costs. College-educated nonwhites were the most skeptical of all toward restrictions.

But as Trump has implemented his tariffs, they have proven less attractive for most Americans in practice than in theory. In Pew polling this January, 60% of Americans opposed his tariff increases; more than twice as many said it had affected their family negatively as positively. In a CNN/SSRS poll this April, four times as many Americans said the tariffs had hurt their personal finances as said they’d helped. Recent polls in Wisconsin and Ohio, two heavily working-class, manufacturing-oriented states, both found about 60% of residents opposed the tariffs. Polls released this month have found overwhelming opposition to Trump’s latest trade war against Canada, particularly in states along the border: In CNN surveys, about two-thirds or more of voters in both Michigan and Maine said the new Canadian tariffs were bad for their state.

In many of these surveys, whites without a four-year college degree remained relatively more sympathetic to Trump’s approach than other groups; in January’s Pew survey, for instance, they split evenly on whether they approved of the tariffs.

But even that represents much more resistance than Trump usually faces among a group that supported him by 2:1 margins in all three of his presidential races. And polls consistently find that even most whites without a four-year degree believe the tariffs have hurt their personal bottom line. In the April CNN/SRSS poll, for instance, nearly three times as many non-college whites said the tariffs had hurt as helped their finances. Big majorities of non-college whites opposed the Canada tariffs in both Maine and Michigan.

Other groups were even more lopsided in their opposition. In CNN’s national polling, two-thirds of Black voters and three-fourths of Hispanics said the tariffs had hurt their finances. So did about 7 in 10 college-educated whites. In Maine, college-educated whites opposed the Canada tariffs by more than 11 to 1.

Even supporters like Tonelson agree part of the problem for the tariffs has been the erratic, unpredictable way Trump has imposed, removed and restored them. “It is an unnerving spectacle to a needless extent,” he says.

But many agree the bigger obstacle for the tariffs is that Trump is advancing them at a moment when voters’ top concern is the struggle with persistently high costs. “He’s decided to do these tariffs in such a way that jumped up prices … at a time of unbelievable anger about the high cost of living,” Greenberg says. The receptivity to tough trade measures evident in Trump’s first term, he adds, “has been completely blown away by this new period of inflation.”

Wisconsin-based Republican strategist Mark Graul agrees. The tariff agenda is not working for Trump and the GOP, he says, for a straightforward reason: “because it is being blamed for the higher prices that people are experiencing.”

Shipping containers at the Port of Vancouver in British Columbia, Canada, on July 22, 2026. Paige Taylor White/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Trump’s core problem is a mismatch between losers and winners

Even more than the polls, the actions of politicians capture how the politics of trade have shifted.

It’s probably not a surprise that the tariffs face intense criticism from Josh Turek and Adam Hamilton, the Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa and Kansas, as well as Dan Osborn, the populist independent running in Nebraska. High tariffs have always been unpopular in farm states because of fears of foreign retaliation against agricultural exports.

More revealing is the opposition to the Trump tariffs from Democrats running in burly manufacturing states where many voters have long been skeptical of free trade deals.

In Michigan, for instance, the Democratic nominees for governor (Jocelyn Benson) and Senate (Abdul El-Sayed) have both denounced their Republican opponents for supporting Trump’s tariffs, especially the new levies on Canada. Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, who represents a struggling blue-collar district around Flint, recently blamed Trump’s “chaotic tariff regime” and “reckless” trade policies for the closure of a semiconductor manufacturing plant in her district. “It’s that chaos that causes businesses to close,” she charged.

Poindexter, the ironworker seeking a House seat south of Cleveland, is running a new football-themed ad promising to “block the bad trade deals.” But an in interview, Poindexter said that while he would have voted against NAFTA had he been in Congress at the time, “what we’ve seen with the blanket tariffs is it’s driven up costs on working families.”

“I think tariffs can be very useful in leveling the playing field,” he added. “But it makes no sense to tariff things we don’t produce in America.”

Perhaps most striking has been the reaction from former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is opposing Republican Sen. Jon Husted this year. No Democrat has a longer pedigree of criticizing free trade than Brown. Yet he too says flatly, “These tariffs have clearly not worked. … People everywhere are paying more for everything and this new batch of tariffs against Canada is (taking) a disastrous policy and making even more of a disaster.”

Against this onslaught, hardly any Republicans have broken with Trump (with Sen. Susan Collins’ careful criticism of the Canada tariffs an exception). The vast majority of House and Senate Republicans have repeatedly voted to defend the tariffs. “Look, these tariffs are working,” Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall insisted to loud boos during a raucous debate with Hamilton this month.

Tonelson, too, argues that “from an economic point of view, it’s gone very well.” He points to an increase in total manufacturing output during Trump’s second term. But that level is still lower than at points of Trump’s first term and Barack Obama’s second.

In any case, the more politically relevant measure is how many people are working in manufacturing. And on that front, despite gains in recent months, slightly fewer people are employed in manufacturing now (12.638 million) than when Trump returned to office (12.673 million), according to federal statistics. That’s only about 7.5% of all workers. Manufacturing employment today, in fact, is only slightly higher than when Trump first took office in 2017. “Even people who were saying (at first), ‘I want to give him the benefit of the doubt,’ will say ‘it’s just not paying off,’” says Eva Kemp, director of paid media and partnerships at American Bridge, a Democratic-aligned group that focuses on working-class voters.

Those employment numbers point to a deeper vulnerability. The backlash against Trump’s levies suggests that a protectionist agenda faces a fundamental mismatch between winners and losers. The best-case for Trump’s tariffs is that they might eventually add a few hundred thousand more manufacturing jobs. But the number of people who might get those jobs — someday — will always be dwarfed by the number paying higher prices today. “Even if it’s absolutely the right thing to do, it’s really, really hard to persuade people who are responding to the upfront costs,” says William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and longtime Democratic policy analyst.

Even after Trump, Democrats seem unlikely to return to the Obama/Bill Clinton enthusiasm for free trade agreements. But, as Galston says, on tariffs, the next Democratic president is likely to replace Trump’s “sledgehammer with the scalpel.” The bigger question may be whether the protectionist tide that has been surging in the GOP under Trump starts to recede if his tariffs cost some congressional Republicans their own jobs in November.

World.title: Egypt strongly condemns Israeli official’s incursion into Al-Aqsa Mosque
World.content:
Egypt strongly condemned the storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound by an Israeli official and a group of settlers under the protection of Israeli police.

In an official statement released by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Emigration and Egyptian Expatriates, Cairo denounced the act as a violation of the sanctity of Islamic holy sites and a direct provocation to the sentiments of Muslims worldwide that risks fueling further tension and escalation across the region.

Egypt underscored the critical need to adhere to the established historical and legal status quo of Al-Aqsa Mosque and to respect the Hashemite Custodianship over Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem.

The ministry warned against any attempts to alter the Arab and Islamic identity of the city or impose a new reality on its sacred sites, calling for an immediate halt to unilateral measures that undermine prospects for calm and regional stability.

World.title: Palestinian feature ‘Thirteen in Gaza’ wins NETPAC Award at Toronto International Film Festival
World.content:
The Palestinian film “Thirteen in Gaza” (2026), directed by Hosam Abu Dan, won the prestigious NETPAC Award at the close of the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF).

In its official statement, the NETPAC jury praised the feature for transforming suffering beyond spectacle or mere victimhood, crafting captivating imagery that paints a full picture of life in Gaza.

The jury described the work as a bold, intimate piece that announces an exceptional new cinematic voice.

Written by Khalil Al-Mozian, “Thirteen in Gaza” paints a deeply human portrait of a father and his teenage daughter navigating daily survival within a refugee camp in the Gaza Strip.

The cast includes Nawaf Abu Amra, Feras Al Masri, Ghassan Salem, and Mary Ziyara.

Presented by the Network for the Promotion of Asia Pacific Cinema, the NETPAC Award recognizes outstanding filmmaking from Asia and the Pacific region.

The three-member jury—selected jointly by TIFF and NETPAC—honors the best Asian feature by a first- or second-time director.

The 2026 NETPAC jury was chaired by Mara Matta, alongside fellow jurors Richard Fung and Panos Kotzathanasis.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egyptian Meteorological Authority issues late-month weather forecast and temperature outlook
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) has announced its weather forecast and temperature projections across Cairo and the governorates through the end of September.

Moderate to warm, humid conditions are expected during the early morning hours, transitioning to hot and humid weather during the day across northern Egypt, Greater Cairo, and Northern Upper Egypt.

Extremely hot conditions are forecast for Southern Upper Egypt.

Temperatures along the Northern Coast will range between 28C and 29C, while Greater Cairo and Lower Egypt will record highs between 31C and 32C.

Northern Upper Egypt will experience warmer weather, with highs reaching 33C to 35C, while Southern Upper Egypt will see persistent severe heat, with temperatures hovering between 39C and 40C.

World.title: All options on table to protect Nile rights, Egyptian Water Minister warns over GERD
World.content:
Egyptian Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation Hani Sewilam reaffirmed that his country retains all measures guaranteed under international law to safeguard its water security, stressing that “all legitimate options” remain on Cairo’s table.

Sewilam characterized Egypt as a “strong nation of peace” that upholds international law, but noted it knows precisely when and how to respond appropriately to protect its national interests.

Cairo will not ignore its dependence on the Nile, he stressed, nor will it accept what he called “illusions of control and dominance” over water flows to downstream states.

The minister explained that describing the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) as “unilateral and illegal” reflects a political position rooted in Egypt’s legal view regarding the dam’s solo construction, filling, and operation.

He added that the completion of construction or the passage of time does not imply Egypt’s acceptance of a done deal, nor does it extinguish its rights or legal standing.

The statement comes as Cairo continues to press for a binding legal agreement governing the filling and operation of the GERD amid persistent concerns over downstream impacts.

In July, the Water Ministry disclosed that solo operations had led to fluctuating discharge rates, exacerbated by the absence of clear operational rules and routine data-sharing mechanisms among Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia.

Sewilam warned that uncoordinated operations could trigger sudden discharge shifts—causing either acute spikes, which he termed “artificial floods,” or sharp drops leading to “artificial droughts”—potentially destabilizing water infrastructure and dam management across Egypt and Sudan.

Critique of unilateral control and alternative Nile models

Shifting narratives

Sewilam criticized recent Ethiopian statements regarding the control of downstream water flows, arguing they contradict past assertions that the GERD is merely a hydroelectric project and reveal ambitions to enforce single-handed control over a transboundary river.

Support for equitable development

The minister emphasized that Cairo does not oppose development across the Nile Basin, provided projects align with international law and preserve Egyptian water security.

The Southern Nile Basin model

He highlighted the collaborative approach in the southern Nile Basin—where nations study, notify, and consult on projects prior to funding and execution—noting Egypt actively supports and helps finance development under this framework.

Rejection of fait accompli

Sewilam contrasted this cooperative model with the GERD’s unilateral approach, asserting Cairo will not allow a new fait accompli to be imposed on the Eastern Nile.

World.title: Transport Ministry Breaks Ground For Nimba County Office In Ganta City
World.content:
Ganta, Nimba County — The Ministry of Transport has officially broken ground for a new county office in Ganta City, Nimba County as part of a nationwide decentralization drive to take government services closer to Liberians.

The colorful ceremony on [insert date] brought together national and county officials, local leaders and residents to witness the start of the construction for the Ministry’s Nimba County Office.

The project is one in a series of county and regional offices planned to improve access to transport services and administration outside Monrovia.

Archibald S. Abban, Deputy Minister for Administration and Insurance at the Ministry of Transport, told reporters the ceremony marks progress in the government’s decentralization program.

“We are committed to taking services to the people,” Deputy Minister Abban said. “This new office in Ganta will make it easier for residents of Nimba and neighboring areas to access transport licensing, vehicle registration and other essential services without travelling long distances.”

Ongoing county and regional office projects named by the Ministry include:

Bomi County — Klay

Nimba County — Ganta (current project)

Maryland County — Pleebo

Lofa County — Vonjama

Deputy Minister Abban pledged continued support from the Ministry during construction and after the office becomes operational.

He added that the decentralization effort aims to strengthen local administration, reduce congestion at the capital’s offices and improve transparency and efficiency in service delivery.

Local reactions and expected benefits

Local officials at the ceremony expressed optimism that the Ganta’s Office will spur administrative efficiency and local development.

A county representative said residents will save time and money previously spent travelling to Monrovia for transport services. Traders, drivers and transport unions in the region are expected to benefit from faster processing of permits and clearer regulatory oversight.

Project scope and timeline

Ministry officials said the new facility will include offices for licensing and insurance administration, a public reception area, records storage and parking for service vehicles.

Construction timelines, funding sources and the contractor’s name were not disclosed at the ceremony. Officials said those details would be released as the project moves forward.

Decentralization context

The Ministry’s decentralization program is part of a broader government initiative to expand public services to counties across Liberia. By establishing county-based transport offices, the government seeks to reduce bottlenecks in Monrovia and ensure equitable access to public services.

Looking ahead

Deputy Minister Abban encouraged community cooperation with the project and called on partner agencies and local authorities to support timely completion.

“With the support of county stakeholders and the public, this office will be an important step toward bringing government closer to citizens,” he intimated.

Residents, who attended the groundbreaking, including drivers and local business owners, described the event as a hopeful sign for improved services and local job opportunities during construction and once the office opens.

World.title: Liberia’s Cybercrime Law Faces Its First Real Trial as VP Koung case exposes Liberia’s widening fault lines
World.content:
Monrovia – The arrest of Jerry Nyantee Wrotto, a young man accused of cyberbullying Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung Sr., and the Vice President’s subsequent request for his release have thrust Liberia’s year-old Cybercrime Act into its first major public test, exposing competing views over free speech, criminal prosecution and the limits of executive mercy.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

At the center of the controversy is a question with implications beyond the Vice President’s office: Can an alleged victim withdraw a cybercrime complaint and end a prosecution, or does the state retain the authority to pursue the case in the public interest?

The debate has drawn sharply contrasting responses from Executive Protection Service (EPS) Director Sam Gaye, who defended applying the law to digitally manipulated content, and former Finance Minister Samuel D. Tweah Jr., who argues that Wrotto’s arrest infringes on free expression.

Koung, meanwhile, has called for the suspect’s release, framing his intervention as an expression of tolerance and restraint befitting public office.

“Criminal cases are prosecuted in the name of the Republic, not the complainant,” Garpue K. Wonlue, an Assigned City Solicitor and Prosecutor at the Ministry of Justice, wrote in an open letter challenging the legal effect of the Vice President’s request.

The competing positions have transformed Wrotto’s case into a broader debate over how Liberia should enforce its new cybercrime legislation without undermining constitutional protections for speech and political criticism.

A Law Barely a Year Old, Already Being Tested

Liberia’s Cybercrime Act of 2025 was passed by the Senate in November 2025 and signed into law, filling a gap left by the country’s 1978 Penal Code, which contained no specific cybercrime provisions.

The legislation criminalizes several forms of digital misconduct, including unauthorized computer access, online fraud, identity theft and electronic harassment. Its passage was intended, in part, to strengthen the country’s response to cyber-enabled offenses.

But the Koung controversy is pushing the law into contentious territory involving artificial intelligence, political expression and the boundaries of permissible criticism.

The Act does not explicitly reference artificial intelligence or deepfakes, raising questions about how its provisions should apply to AI-generated material and the circumstances under which such content constitutes a criminal offense.

The controversy also follows an earlier incident involving a manipulated video of the Vice President at Brussels Airport. Wrotto had allegedly posted nude AI-generated photos and video of VP Koung, claiming he was subjected to screening at Brussels Airport.

Before Wrotto’s arrest, EPS Director Sam Gaye publicly defended the police response to the alleged creation of the video, warning that digitally manipulated material intended to humiliate or harass individuals could attract criminal liability under the new law.

“To those making noise about why the police arrested the individual who created the fake, humiliating video footage of the VP at Brussels airport—it is a crime under the new Cybercrime Act of 2025/2026,” Gaye wrote.

He said the law was signed by President Joseph Boakai on August 19, 2026, and criminalizes cyber-harassment and cyberbullying.

“Creating and sharing a fake image to insult, humiliate, or threaten someone constitutes a cybercrime,” Gaye declared, warning that cyber detectives would identify, arrest and prosecute individuals engaged in such conduct.

Gaye’s remarks, made before Wrotto’s arrest, reflected the EPS’s position that the creation and circulation of humiliating AI-generated material could warrant law enforcement intervention.

The Vice President’s subsequent call for Wrotto’s release, however, has raised a separate question: whether the alleged victim’s willingness to forgive should affect the state’s decision to continue a criminal case.

Tweah Challenges Arrest, Calls for Repeal

Former Finance and Development Planning Minister Samuel D. Tweah Jr. has taken a sharply different position, welcoming Koung’s intervention while arguing that the Vice President should never have had to request the release of a citizen accused of online speech-related conduct.

“Mr. Vice President, thanks for calling for the release of the young man Jerry Nyantee Wrotto who was illegally imprisoned for free speech. But the Americans would say No Thanks,” Tweah wrote. “That you have to call for his release is the problem. He should not be behind bars for free speech in the first place.”

Tweah described the cyberbullying law as draconian and predicted that it would be struck down after the Unity Party leaves power. He argued that the legislation conflicts with Liberia’s history of press freedom reforms, including the Kamara Abdullah Kamara (KAK) Act, which decriminalized several speech-related offenses.

He also cited Liberia’s approval of the Table Mountain Declaration under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, presenting the cybercrime legislation as a departure from the country’s previous commitments to press freedom.

“If politicians do not want to be cyber bullied let them leave politics and go to private life,” Tweah wrote, arguing that ordinary Liberians must be able to criticize political leaders.

“The only power ordinary Liberians have is to bully their leaders so that they deliver the desired change.”

Tweah further called on Koung to press President Boakai to repeal the cyberbullying law, while also urging him to address what he characterized as judicial interference and politically motivated pressure on the opposition under the current administration.

He thanked Koung for his intervention on Wrotto’s behalf but maintained that the Vice President’s request for release did not address the underlying problem.

“Thank you for your stand on the jailed political activist, but no thanks sir,” Tweah concluded.

His intervention has broadened the dispute from the circumstances of Wrotto’s arrest to the law’s legitimacy, its potential implications for political discourse and the government’s broader record on civil liberties.

A Deeper Fight: Who Controls Speech Online?

The Koung controversy comes amid a wider debate over the reach of Liberia’s digital laws and the safeguards protecting speech.

The 2019 KAK Act decriminalized speech offenses such as sedition and criminal libel against the President, marking a significant press-freedom reform.

However, a proposed 2026 amendment, the draft Protection from Gender-Based Online Abuse and Harassment Act, has raised concerns among press freedom advocates.

Press Union of Liberia President Julius Kanubah has warned that reopening the KAK Act could erode protections won by journalists and ordinary citizens. The Union has argued that online harassment should be addressed through the Cybercrime Act rather than by revisiting the KAK Act.

The judiciary has also weighed in on the boundaries of online expression. In February 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in the “Prophet Key” contempt case arising from social media commentary directed at the bench that constitutional free speech protections do not extend to vulgar or abusive attacks on individuals.

The ruling adds another dimension to the debate, as authorities and citizens grapple with distinguishing protected criticism from conduct that may lawfully attract criminal sanctions.

For Tweah, the central concern is the potential chilling effect of the cyberbullying law on citizens’ ability to hold public officials accountable. Gaye’s position, by contrast, emphasizes the criminal consequences of creating and distributing digitally manipulated material intended to humiliate or harass another person.

The distinction between political criticism and conduct prohibited by law is likely to remain central to the controversy.

Mercy vs. the Machinery of Prosecution

While Gaye and Tweah have focused on the law’s enforcement and implications for free expression, Wonlue’s intervention centers on the independence of criminal prosecution and whether the Vice President’s request can legally terminate the case.

In his open letter, Wonlue argued that criminal proceedings belong to the Republic of Liberia, not the individual who reports an alleged offense.

“Under Liberian criminal jurisprudence, all crimes are captioned as Republic of Liberia vs. Defendant. The victim — you — is only a witness,” he wrote.

Wonlue contended that the alleged offense is a matter for the state and cannot simply be withdrawn because the complainant has chosen to forgive the accused.

“The Inspector General of Police does not take instructions from a witness on whether to prosecute,” he added, warning that police compliance with the Vice President’s request could amount to interference and an abuse of power.

He also rejected the notion that the case should be treated solely as an issue of personal offense, arguing that the state has a responsibility to protect individuals who may lack the influence or public standing of the Vice President.

“Today it is the Vice President; tomorrow it could be a private citizen who does not have your power to forgive,” Wonlue wrote.

He questioned what message the state would send to ordinary Liberians, particularly women and girls, whose AI-generated intimate images might be circulated online without their consent.

“If the Police release this young man because he targeted a tolerant Vice President, what message do we send to the ordinary Liberian girl in West Point or Sanniquellie whose nude AI images are being shared?” he asked. “That she has no protection?”

Wonlue’s argument underscores the distinction between a complainant’s willingness to forgive and the state’s authority to determine whether a criminal prosecution should proceed.

Yet the competing interventions from Gaye, Tweah and Wonlue expose the unresolved tensions surrounding the law: the need to address online abuse, the protection of political expression and the limits of prosecutorial discretion.

What’s Actually at Stake

The Wrotto case has brought three overlapping issues into sharp focus: the Cybercrime Act’s application to AI-generated content, concerns that expanding online speech restrictions could undermine press freedom, and the question of whether an alleged victim’s request for mercy should influence the state’s prosecution of a criminal case.

For Gaye, the controversy is a reminder that digitally manipulated content can carry legal consequences. For Tweah, it is evidence of a law that threatens political expression and should be repealed. For Wonlue, the central concern is whether the Republic can independently enforce its laws, even when the alleged victim is willing to forgive.

Koung’s intervention has added a human dimension to the dispute, but it has not resolved the legal questions surrounding the prosecution.

Whether Wrotto is released, prosecuted or granted some other legal relief, the case is likely to shape public expectations about how Liberia enforces its cybercrime legislation.

The test is not only whether the law can punish alleged online abuse, but whether its enforcement can withstand scrutiny over due process, free expression and equal protection — particularly when the complainant is one of the country’s most powerful public officials.

World.title: Liberia: LDEA Testing Clears Malaysia Shipment
World.content:
Monrovia — A shipment that triggered alarm this weekend over suspected cocaine and heroin has tested negative for narcotics, the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency says, in a reversal that clears those named in connection with the cargo and instead points to commercial herbal supplements as the likely contents.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The shipment — nine cartons shipped via DHL from Malaysia, declared on their labels as botanical powder, coffee and candy and weighing a combined 202.5 kilograms — had already cleared customs at Roberts International Airport, with $437.65 in duties, levies and GST paid, before it was flagged during a subsequent clearance attempt at a DHL warehouse.

A Favor, and a Shipment

According to a preliminary field report obtained by FrontPageAfrica, the chain of events began with an act of goodwill. Martha Jallah, a 39-year-old Liberian woman residing in Sinkor, Montserrado County, was approached by an acquaintance — identified in the report only as Solange, an Ivorian national employed at the Ivorian Embassy in Monrovia. Solange asked Jallah to help clear the shipment on behalf of one of her countrymen: Tan Makado, a 60-year-old Ivorian national based in Abidjan.

At approximately 12:30 p.m. Saturday, the report states, Jallah went to the DHL warehouse to clear the cartons — the same shipment paperwork elsewhere describes as consigned to a Tan Gouet Gerard at an address on Fiamah Coleman Avenue, Monrovia. LDEA’s RIA Detachment intervened at that point, taking the cartons into custody for testing.

The field report stated that during initial, on-site screening, agents alleged the material tested positive for cocaine and heroin — a finding that prompted Chief Operations Officer Special Agent Milton K. Howard and members of LDEA’s Special Drug Squad, including Special Agent Buster Jolson, to transport the shipment to LDEA headquarters for confirmatory testing.

The Reversal

That confirmatory testing has now come back negative, according to authorities, who say they suspect the shipment instead contained dietary and herbal supplements manufactured in Malaysia — including, officials said, some products marketed for sexual enhancement.

The finding stands in sharp contrast to the initial field-level allegation and underscores the risk of publicizing preliminary results before laboratory confirmation. Individuals named in connection with the shipment — including Jallah, who was asked to help clear the cargo, and Makado, the Ivorian national identified as its intended recipient — appear to have been cleared of any wrongdoing related to narcotics trafficking, pending any further findings from LDEA.

What Was Inside

Photographs of the shipment reviewed by FPA show the cartons — marked with DHL’s “GoGreen Plus” branding and a shipping label citing waybill number 96 5091 8255 — packed with what outwardly resembled ordinary consumer wellness products. One carton examined bore the marking “Piece 3/9,” with an individual weight of 22.5 kg, consistent with the shipment’s total declared weight of 202.5 kg spread across nine separate boxes.

Inside were boxes of “Aceguard” and slim cartons of “Rocenta,” both marketed under the “Dynace” brand by Malaysia-based Dynace Global, alongside foil pouches of “Triple Root Coffee,” an arabica blend infused with ginseng-style root extracts. According to the products’ own labeling and marketing materials, Aceguard is promoted as an immune-support supplement containing plant stem cells and herbal extracts, while Rocenta is marketed as a botanical supplement containing ingredients such as rose placenta extract, bitter melon and ashwagandha. FPA has not independently verified which, if any, of these specific branded products are linked to the sexual-enhancement claims referenced by authorities.

A Possible Ivorian Connection

A separate document obtained by FPA — a Laissez-Passer issued by police in Danané, Côte d’Ivoire, and dated September 9, 2026 — records travel clearance for an Ivorian national identified as “Tan Makado A.,” born in 1964, traveling from Abidjan to Liberia. The name closely mirrors that of the Tan Makado named in the field report as the shipment’s intended beneficiary, though FPA has not independently confirmed the two are the same individual. With the shipment now cleared of narcotics, the significance of this travel document, if any, remains unclear.

Part of a Bigger Pattern

The episode unfolds against the backdrop of a year marked by major narcotics interceptions that have put Liberia at the center of West Africa’s cocaine-trafficking corridor:

• June 8, 2026 — LDEA and joint security intercepted 198 compressed plates of cocaine (about 237.6 kg) hidden in six cargo boxes at RIA, bound for Europe via Brussels Airlines, valued at an estimated US$19.2 million.

• Late June–July — Lawmakers summoned LDEA, immigration, customs and airport officials over the case; five suspects were eventually charged.

• July 22, 2026 — Security forces raided a warehouse in Duazon, Margibi County, detaining two foreign nationals in what was then called the country’s largest cocaine haul.

• July 21–23, 2026 — Police announced an even larger seizure: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317 million.

• August 19, 2026 — Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested and later remanded in custody in connection with what officials called one of the biggest drug busts in Liberia’s history, alongside two Croatian nationals and a Ukrainian national.

Civil society groups have repeatedly flagged Liberia’s growing role as a transit hub for cocaine moving from South America toward European and Middle Eastern markets — and have criticized a pattern in which high-profile seizures generate headlines while prosecutions stall. This weekend’s episode illustrates a related concern: that unconfirmed field allegations can circulate and attach to named individuals before testing is complete.

World.title: Liberia: Jeety Receives “Honorary Fellowship” from Liberia’s Medical Body — As LCPS Cites Decades of Contributions to Health Sector
World.content:
Photo: The leadership of the Liberia College of Physicians and Surgeons conferring upon business tycoon Dr. Upjit Singh Sachdeva, widely known as Jeety, its Honorary Fellowship in Medicine.

CONGO TOWN, Monrovia – The Liberia College of Physicians and Surgeons has conferred its Honorary Fellowship in Medicine on business tycoon, humanitarian and philanthropist Dr. Upjit Singh Sachdeva, widely known as Jeety, recognizing decades of humanitarian service and in particular, his contributions to healthcare, specialist medical services and efforts to extend care to underserved communities in Liberia.

Jeety was admitted as an Honorary Fellow during the 10th Annual General and Scientific Meeting and Convocation Ceremony on September 18 at the Ministerial Complex in Congo Town, outside Monrovia, in a ceremony that brought together medical professionals, government officials, members and fellows of the College, prospective graduates and other guests.

The College, which serves as Liberia’s postgraduate medical training institution, has trained more than 166 Liberian specialists since its establishment.

In a letter dated September 1, the College described Jeety’s record as one marked by humanitarian service, philanthropy and a sustained commitment to the well-being of Liberians, highlighting his support for health initiatives, vulnerable populations, education and community development.

According to the College, Jeety was selected for the honorary fellowship in recognition of his “outstanding humanitarian leadership, extraordinary philanthropy, and invaluable contributions toward the advancement of healthcare and community development in Liberia.”

The certificate formally admits Dr. Upjit Singh Sachdeva as an Honorary Fellow of the Liberia College of Physicians and Surgeons and confers on him the associated rights, honors and privileges enjoyed by the College’s fellows.

For Jeety, however, the honor appeared less as a culmination of his work than as another reason to deepen his involvement in a health system he has supported for years, particularly in the area of eye care, where he has backed the development of the Liberia Eye Center at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center through a partnership with the L.V. Prasad Eye Institute.

Speaking after receiving the fellowship, Jeety reflected on his nearly four decades in Liberia and linked his humanitarian work to the experiences he had witnessed during some of the country’s most difficult periods, including conflict, reconstruction, the Ebola outbreak and the COVID-19 pandemic.

“I have witnessed the courage and resilience of Liberians through conflict, reconstruction, Ebola, COVID-19 and many other challenges. Liberia has given me family, friendship, trust, opportunity and belonging. My service is therefore not charity offered from a distance; it is my duty to a country and people I consider my own,” Jeety said.

It was during the COVID-19 shutdown, he recalled, that his humanitarian response expanded from support for vulnerable families to direct assistance for healthcare workers and institutions. With restrictions affecting movement and livelihoods, Jeety said he began distributing food to people in need while also providing meals to hospitals serving the country’s security personnel.

“From the start of COVID, we were distributing food to the needy because there was a shutdown, and not only to the needy. I used to deliver meals three times a day to the 14 military hospitals and other health facilities for patients, nurses and doctors,” he said. “At the same time, we were feeding vulnerable populations, and by 100 days during COVID lockdown, we had distributed over 110, 000 plates of hot cook meal.”

That experience, Jeety added, gave him a firsthand view of the commitment of Liberian health workers, particularly doctors and other professionals who continued working through extraordinary circumstances.

“I have seen Liberian doctors working very closely with dedication, commitment, sincerity and beyond duty, beyond the call of duty,” he said, before reflecting on the health workers who continued serving patients despite the risks and difficulties surrounding the pandemic.

But it is the expansion of specialist healthcare, particularly ophthalmology that now forms one of the central elements of Jeety’s health-sector contribution. “Healthcare is not only about hospitals and medicine. It is about dignity, livelihood and hope,” he said. “Healthcare has a special place in my heart. For several years, I have been privileged to bring and support the Liberia Eye Centre and its partnership with L.V. Prasad Eye Institute. I remain deeply grateful to the team whose skill and commitment convert that support into healing. The Liberia Eye Centre demonstrates what sustained partnership can achieve.”

Jeety said the experience of supporting eye care in Monrovia also exposed a larger problem: many patients living outside the capital face barriers that have little to do with the medical treatment itself. Transportation, accommodation and the loss of income associated with travelling to Monrovia can make specialist treatment difficult for rural families, even when the treatment itself is available.

That concern has informed the ongoing expansion of the 50-bed health center in Weala, supported by Jeety Rubber LLC and Salala Rubber Corporation, into a surgical facility that Jeety says will include four operating theatres and a dedicated eye unit.

The eye unit is planned to occupy approximately 6,000 square feet and, according to Jeety, will be equipped to manage common eye conditions encountered in Liberia, apart from retinal surgery. The broader facility is intended not simply to create another hospital outside Monrovia, but to establish a platform through which specialist services can be taken closer to communities that have traditionally had limited access to them.

“Bringing patients to Monrovia for surgery and advanced treatments is good, but bringing quality eye care closer to patients is even more practical and sustainable,” Jeety said.

He said the initiative would also include an outreach component, with a mobile eye-care service expected to travel into communities with equipment for screening and examination, while patients requiring surgery or further intervention could then be referred to the Weala facility.

“Our aim is to enable people in rural communities to receive timely, respectful care to see again the things they loved and care about without needing to come to Monrovia,” he said.

The project is also being linked to the return of Dr. Niranjan Pehere, Jeety’s son, to Liberia to lead the eye hospital in Weala. Jeety said Dr. Pehere previously spent years helping develop the Liberia Eye Center at JFK and that his return would create an opportunity to apply that experience to rural populations.

The planned facility, Jeety said, is also intended to support the development of Liberia’s specialist workforce, as he expressed his willingness to work with the Ministry of Health and the Liberia College of Physicians and Surgeons to create opportunities for supervised clinical rotations for medical residents, subject to the College’s accreditation requirements and a formal agreement that would allow trainees to gain practical experience while contributing to the expansion of specialist care beyond Monrovia.

The proposal reflects a wider argument Jeety made in accepting the fellowship: that healthcare infrastructure, specialist training and community investment should develop together rather than separately. For Jeety, that philosophy is also connected to his Sikh faith and the principle of “Vand Chhako,” which he described as sharing what one has with people in need, including wealth, time, opportunity, knowledge and responsibility.

“A business cannot measure success only by production, exports, or profit. It must also ask whether the community around it is healthier, safer, and better prepared for the future,” he said. “This Fellowship strengthens my resolve. I will continue supporting partnerships that expand care, build local capacity, and reach people too often left behind.”

As he concluded his remarks, Jeety spoke about his longstanding ties to Liberia, where he has lived for nearly four decades. “I am Indian by passport, Liberian by heart and blood,” he said, reaffirming his commitment to supporting initiatives to expand access to healthcare and strengthen local capacity.

World.title: Liberia: New Charging Rule Confronts a System the U.S. State Department Has Long Flagged as Broken
World.content:
A new order from the Solicitor General requiring prosecutor sign-off before police can charge a suspect lands against a backdrop the U.S. State Department has documented for years: a justice system where arrests often outrun evidence, and pretrial detainees can wait 180 days or more without ever getting a hearing.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – The State Department’s most recent human rights report on Liberia, released last year, found that although the law provided for a defendant to receive an expeditious trial, lengthy pretrial detention was a serious problem, with the length of detention in some cases equaling or exceeding the maximum sentence for the alleged crime. The report attributed this to a mix of factors, including the use of detention as a punitive measure, delayed indictments, a nonfunctioning bail system, poor court recordkeeping, and a shortage of resources for public defenders.

The numbers behind that finding are stark. Earlier State Department reporting found roughly 60 percent of pretrial detainees, particularly those held on felony charges, spent more than two terms of court — about 180 days — behind bars without ever getting a hearing. Liberian law is explicit that a case should be dismissed if a defendant isn’t tried by the next court term with no cause shown, but the reports found that this rarely happens, making it one of the most frequently violated provisions in the law.

Weak evidence at the point of arrest is part of what feeds that backlog. Earlier State Department findings noted that a shortage of trained prosecutors and public defenders, poor court administration, inadequate police investigation and evidence collection, and judicial corruption all worsened the frequency and length of pretrial detention, and that arrests often were made without judicial authorization, with warrants sometimes issued without sufficient evidence, while police sometimes requested money to carry out arrests for prosecuting authorities.

There is also an implementation question the announcement doesn’t answer: whether Sillah’s office and the City Solicitors nationwide have the staffing to review every police charge in real time without becoming a new bottleneck of their own — trading one delay (weak-evidence arrests) for another (charge-review backlogs). The meeting summary treats the directive as already standing, while a related measure — assigning a Supervisor and Deputy Supervisor to every Magisterial Court — is explicitly described as still needing to be “written as a formal Policy,” suggesting the charging rule itself may also be operating ahead of formal written procedure.

The broader signal

Read against the State Department’s findings, Friday’s meeting reads less as routine internal housekeeping and more as an attempt by the Solicitor General’s office to intervene at the one point in the process — the charging decision — where it has direct authority. Whether it meaningfully reduces wrongful or evidence-free detention will depend on enforcement: whether police actually route charges through prosecutors in practice, and whether the promised written rules and monitoring structure follow the one-week timeline the new committee has been given.

World.title: Liberia: Ex- Foreign Minister Kemayah to Deliver Keynote at International Peace Summit
World.content:
Monrovia – Former Liberian Foreign Affairs Minister Ambassador Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah Sr. has been invited to deliver a special keynote address at the 2026 International Day of Peace conference, bringing him alongside former heads of state, diplomats and other international figures to discuss global conflicts and pathways to peace.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The virtual conference, scheduled for today, Monday, is being organized by the International Human Rights Commission (IHRC) and its affiliated organizations as part of the inaugural International Peace Summit 2026.

According to an invitation addressed to Ambassador Kemayah by the commission, he has been listed among the special guest speakers for the summit, which will convene virtually from Istanbul and Geneva under the theme, “Invest in Peace – For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day.”

The invitation, signed by Ambassador Farshad Haghdadi, Staff Officer to the World Chair of the IHRC, describes the summit as an opportunity for world leaders, diplomats, government officials and civil society representatives to discuss ongoing conflicts and advance recommendations for negotiators, mediators and parties involved in hostilities. The invitation identifies him as one of the personalities selected to contribute to discussions on peace, stability and international cooperation.

To Join Former Presidents, Prime Ministers

The former Liberian Foreign Minister is expected to share the platform with several prominent international figures, including former Pakistani Prime Minister and current Senate Chairman Syed Yousaf Raza Gilani; former Mauritian President Dr. Ameenah Gurib-Fakim; former Ecuadorian President Dr. Rosalia Arteaga Serrano; and former Nepalese Prime Minister Jhala Nath Khanal.

Other invited speakers include former Guinea-Bissau Prime Minister Rui Duarte de Barros and former Maldivian Foreign Minister Dounia Maumoon.

The summit’s agenda also lists Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister Karamoko Jean Marie Traore as a special guest speaker, subject to confirmation.

The gathering is expected to focus on the role of diplomacy, dialogue and sustained investment in human rights in preventing conflict and promoting peaceful coexistence.

Summit Focuses on Diplomacy Amid Global Conflicts

In its invitation, the IHRC said the summit comes at a time of armed conflicts, economic crises and civil wars, emphasizing the need for dialogue and diplomatic engagement to prevent further escalation.

The organizers said the conference would seek to develop recommendations for negotiators and mediators while encouraging parties to ongoing conflicts to pursue peaceful solutions rather than prolong hostilities.

The summit is also tied to the annual International Day of Peace, observed globally on September 21. This year’s theme emphasizes the role of individuals and communities in building peace through everyday actions, cooperation and respect for human dignity.

The conference is scheduled to begin at 8:00 a.m. New York time, 1:00 p.m. in Geneva and 3:00 p.m. in Turkey, with the opening welcome address to be delivered by IHRC World Chairman Ambassador Dr. Muhammad Shahid Amin Khan.

The summit will be moderated by Ms. Emaan Amjid Abbasi, while Ambassador Asra Khan, the commission’s Senior Vice Chairperson, is scheduled to deliver the vote of thanks on behalf of the organizing bodies.

For Kemayah, the invitation places Liberia’s former top diplomat among an international group of political and diplomatic figures being assembled to discuss peace, conflict resolution and the role of diplomacy in addressing global challenges.

World.title: Nimba to Host Youth Peace Conference as Young Leaders Push for Action on National Peace Plan
World.content:
GANTA, Nimba County — Young leaders from across Liberia are set to converge in Ganta City on September 21 for a national conference aimed at pressing for stronger youth leadership and concrete action in implementing Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security.

By Patience M. Jones,[email protected]

The Liberia Youth, Peace and Security Conference 2026, organized by the National Young Women Political Council of Liberia (NYWPCL) in partnership with PeaceGen implementing partners and national stakeholders, will be held under the theme, “Advancing Youth Leadership for Peace: Strengthening the Implementation of Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security.”

The conference comes as stakeholders seek to move Liberia’s Youth, Peace and Security agenda beyond policy commitments and toward practical action in communities, particularly in rural, underserved and conflict-affected areas.

Funded by the European Union and co-funded by the Embassy of Ireland, the PeaceGen Project seeks to strengthen the meaningful participation and leadership of women and young people in peacebuilding, transitional justice, memorialization and accountability processes across Liberia.

“The EU is proud to support the Liberia Youth, Peace and Security Conference through the PeaceGen project. The time has come for young women and men not only to be heard, but to shape decisions and lead action for peace,” said Zoltan Szalai, Chargé d’Affaires of the European Union Delegation to Liberia.

Szalai said the conference could help translate Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security into tangible results, particularly for communities in rural and conflict-affected areas.

For the first time, the conference will be held in Nimba County, bringing together young women, youth representatives, conflict-affected communities, government institutions, civil society organizations and development partners to assess progress and challenges in advancing the national YPS agenda.

Participants from Montserrado, Nimba, Bong, Bomi and Sinoe Counties are expected to engage in discussions on youth leadership, conflict prevention, transitional justice, community peacebuilding and partnerships to advance sustainable peace.

The conference will also examine mechanisms for measuring, documenting and demonstrating the impact of youth participation in peacebuilding and decision-making processes.

Laura Targbeh, President of the National Young Women Political Council of Liberia, described the gathering as an opportunity for young people to take a more direct role in shaping Liberia’s future.

“For too long, young women and youth have watched decisions about our future being made without us in the room. This conference is a turning point—it is our generation stepping forward, not as bystanders, but as leaders in building the peace we all deserve,” Targbeh said.

She added that Nimba’s history provides an important backdrop for discussions about Liberia’s peacebuilding future.

A major outcome of the conference will be the adoption of the Nimba Resolution on Youth, Peace and Security, which will outline collective commitments and recommendations from young people and other stakeholders aimed at strengthening youth leadership and accelerating implementation of Liberia’s national YPS agenda.

Abdullah Oldpa Bility, Co-Chair of the Liberia Coalition on Youth, Peace and Security (LC-YPS), stressed that implementation must receive the same attention as the development and adoption of the national plan.

“I believe the implementation of Liberia’s National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security is as important as the development and adoption of the plan,” Bility said.

He emphasized the need for young people to be empowered to take ownership of the implementation process, arguing that the YPS agenda should produce measurable impact beyond policy documents.

“There is nothing for youth without youth,” Bility said.

The conference will place particular emphasis on groups often underrepresented in national decision-making, including young women, rural youth, persons with disabilities and people from conflict-affected communities.

Esther S. Davis Yango, Executive Director of WONGOSOL, said sustainable peace would remain difficult to achieve without meaningful youth participation and leadership.

“Peace cannot be sustained without the meaningful participation and leadership of young people, particularly young women. We must move beyond recognizing young people as beneficiaries of peacebuilding to fully recognizing them as leaders and partners,” Yango said.

She called for commitments under Liberia’s youth, peace and security agenda to be translated into concrete action, with attention to ensuring that young people are not excluded from peacebuilding processes.

The conference is being organized in collaboration with PeaceGen Liberia partners, including the National Young Women Political Council of Liberia, Liberia Coalition on Youth, Peace and Security, Ministry of Youth and Sports, Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, and Liberia Peacebuilding Office.

As Liberia continues to advance its commitments under the global Youth, Peace and Security agenda, organizers say the conference will provide a platform for young people and stakeholders to strengthen collaboration around reconciliation, conflict prevention, social cohesion and sustainable development.

PeaceGen Project

The PeaceGen Project runs until January 14, 2029, with funding from the European Union and co-funding from the Embassy of Ireland in Liberia. It is implemented by the Kvinna till Kvinna Foundation in partnership with national organizations.

The project focuses on capacity strengthening, dialogue, advocacy, community engagement and awareness initiatives aimed at increasing women’s and youth participation in peacebuilding, promoting awareness of transitional justice and memorialization, and supporting inclusive approaches to reconciliation, accountability and sustainable peace in Liberia.

World.title: Court Sentences Man to Four Years For Theft, Terroristic Threat, Burglary In Maryland County
World.content:
HARPER, Maryland County — The Fourth Judicial Circuit Court in Maryland County has sentenced Lewis Saywon to four years’ imprisonment after he pleaded guilty to charges of Theft of Property, Terroristic Threat and Burglary.

By Peter P. Toe, Jr., [email protected]

The sentence was handed down Wednesday, September 16 during the 32nd day of the August 2026 Term of Court presided over by Assigned Circuit Judge Cllr. George S. Wiles Jr.

The court’s judgment shows that the case initially included a charge of Armed Robbery, but the prosecution later requested that the charge be dropped.

According to the court record, prosecution counsel asked the court to amend the indictment, arguing that the armed robbery charge should be dropped and that the remaining charges should proceed to trial on their merits.

The court granted the application and dismissed the armed robbery charge with prejudice.

The amended charges against Saywon were listed as Theft of Property, Terroristic Threat, and Burglary.

Following the amendment of the indictment, prosecution counsel requested that the Clerk of Court read the charges to Saywon and have him enter his plea.

The court granted the request.

The Clerk subsequently read the indictment to Saywon, after which he pleaded guilty to the charges.

The court then questioned Saywon about whether he understood the indictment and whether his guilty plea was made voluntarily.

According to the judgment, Saywon informed the court that he understood the charges and had entered the guilty plea voluntarily.

The court noted that, under Liberian law and practice, except in capital cases, a trial is no longer necessary when a defendant voluntarily pleads guilty after being properly informed of the charges.

The court, therefore, proceeded to sentencing without a trial.

In its ruling, the court stated that Saywon had admitted to the commission of the crimes of Theft of Property, Terroristic Threat and Burglary.

He was consequently sentenced to a term of imprisonment for four calendar years.

However, the court took into consideration the time Saywon had already spent in detention before the sentencing.

The judgment states that he had been in detention for one year and six months, which was credited toward the four-year sentence.

As a result, Saywon is to serve two additional years and five months in prison, beginning from Wednesday, September 16, according to court records.

The court said the sentence would serve, among other purposes, as a deterrent to other young men from unlawfully taking the belongings of citizens.

Following the sentencing, the court ordered the Clerk of the Fourth Judicial Circuit Court to prepare a Permanent Commitment and place it in the hands of the Sheriff.

The commitment is intended to facilitate Saywon’s detention at Harper Central Prison for the remaining period of his sentence.

The judgment was signed by Cllr. George S. Wiles Jr., Assigned Circuit Judge of the Fourth Judicial Circuit Court, Maryland County, Liberia.

The court record reviewed for this report does not provide details of the specific property allegedly stolen, the circumstances surrounding the terroristic threat or burglary or the identities of any alleged victims.

World.title: Farmers urged to prepare for EL Nino
World.content:
Ngabwe Town Council Chairperson Golden Kalebuka has urged farmers in the district to prepare for El Nino and stock enough maize for consumption.

Speaking when he inspected the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) depot at Chisanga area, Mr Kalebuka said the harvest the district recorded this season is encouraging hence the need for farmers to reserve enough for household food security.

And Ngabwe District Commissioner (DC) Stanley Mwendachabe said efforts are being made to ensure that FRA operations in the district are delinked from Kapiri Mposhi.

Mr Mwendachabe said this will avert the challenges farmers face during the maize purchasing process.

He said the government has transitioned to paying farmers through their mobile money accounts to avoid the security risks of moving with cash.

He stated that efforts are also being made to ensure that more satellite depots are put in place to reduce the congestion during the FRA maize purchasing process.

Farmers that are currently selling maize to the FRA have been complaining of the slow process.

Ngabwe district currently only has three FRA depots.
