"Lioness" season three is officially in the books, and it gave fans a wild surprise at the end.

Season three of Taylor Sheridan's hit CIA/military series focused heavily on the kidnapping of Joe (Zoe Saldaña) and the attempts to rescue her.

LIONESS SEASON 3 EPISODE 7 DELIVERS JOE'S RESCUE IN A GUNFIGHT FANS WON'T STOP TALKING ABOUT

She was eventually rescued in episode seven in a brutally violent and bloody gunfight. That left one major problem unresolved:

Who was the puppet master behind it all?

"Lioness" fans react to shocking finale

Fans were led to believe throughout different parts of the season that it could be the Russians, Ukrainians or the Iranians.

The answer was revealed on Sunday.

Something much more complex and rooted in the history of "Lioness."

It was revealed in the final moments that Aaliyah Amrohi, the daughter of the season one target, was the puppet master who orchestrated the entire operation against Joe as revenge for the killing of her father.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN'S ATTENTION TO WEAPONS HANDLING SETS 'LIONESS' APART FROM OTHER MILITARY DRAMAS

It's also clear that Aaliyah isn't going to stop, and the stage is set for the fourth and likely final season. The season finale – titled "The Unraveling" – also featured an epic restaurant shootout scene when Joe ordered her team to engage the man who kidnapped her. Let's just say things didn't go as planned.

Reactions to the season finale poured in on Reddit. Check out some of the reactions from viewers below:

As soon as the season 1 score started playing at the end, I knew who we were going to see.

I'm not even 10 minutes in and so pissed for Oleksa.

That was a bad call by Joe to engage. Very bad call. Should’ve elected to tail. They were in a crowded restaurant, she should’ve never said to engage.

I knew Aaliyah was behind this.

That episode has such an eerie and suspicious feeling vibe to it very excited to see what happens next season after that ending.

Aaliyah is no longer that bubbly girl. Her demeanor is full of hatred. Hopefully it won't be another 2 years before we get the next season.

NEVER. IN. DOUBT.

But imagine how powerful Aaliyah has become to be able to run such an operation. I am really happy that she is free.

Aaliyah is one of the best female characters Taylor has ever written, in my opinion. I think it’s very symbolic that he brings her back to the fourth season, which will probably be the last. Ending a female protagonist show with a female villain is great.

Congratulations to "Bring Aaliyah Back" crowd. Your efforts were indeed rewarded haha.

I very much enjoyed the dialogue between Joe and Yurimov on the plane. Two equals who respect but would kill the the other. To me that was the highlight of the episode.

Whoa, still shocked. I see things come full circle.

Aaliyah about to get her piece of revenge! So excited for S4!

I knew Aaliyah would be back. Just thought it would be sooner.

Heartbreaking. Heartbreaking. Harrowing. Gonna find out soon what exactly it entails.

Thank you Taylor Sheridan for starting to bring back closure to Aaliyah’s story. So looking forward to season 4!

ZOE SALDAÑA SHARES BEHIND THE SCENES INSTAGRAM POSTS FROM BRUTAL 'LIONESS' TORTURE SCENE

The surprising twist, which I figured out during the interrogation scene, is another example of Sheridan keeping fans on edge and always guessing what's coming next.

A woman shared a photo of herself with Stephanie Nur, the actress who plays Aaliyah, taken when the show was filming in Fort Worth after seeing her at a coffee shop.

It certainly feels like the next season will be the conclusion of the show, and seeing as how so much of Cruz and Joe's arcs are tied back to the actions of season one, it makes perfect sense. While I have no idea what's coming, my guess is many characters won't make it out alive. It wouldn't make any sense if they had happy endings.



It goes against everything the show has given fans through three seasons.

World.title: GOP fiscal hawk sounds alarm on 'out of control' federal spending, saying 'both parties have failed us'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

With the U.S. national debt soaring above $40 trillion and the federal government engaging in massive deficit spending, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. — a fiscal hawk who says the situation is "out of control" and "both parties have failed us" — does not support President Donald Trump's proposal to dole out $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress during the midterms.

The president floated the idea during a speech earlier this month at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, calling it "the Trump dividend."

Asked about the president's proposal during an interview on Thursday, Paul told Fox News Digital that he is not in favor of giving away "dividends when there's a deficit."

"We're running $2 trillion dollars short," he said, noting that he "can't imagine giving out money when you're running a deficit."

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment on Friday.

RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS

America's soaring national debt has surpassed the staggering sum of $40 trillion and shows no signs of stopping.

"And so, the debt is very important. So it's not just important that it might bankrupt us or overwhelm us in some kinda crisis in the future," Paul said, acknowledging that as "a possibility. But every day you're being hurt by it because it's stealing the value" of people's earnings, he indicated.

"So it is literally out of control," Paul said. "And really both parties have failed us because both parties are afraid to tell the American public that some things they like from government would have to be reduced when we cut costs."

Paul has a plan that he says would balance the budget through a series of spending cuts over five years.

GOP LAWMAKERS PUMP BRAKES ON TRUMP'S $5K CHECK PROMISE: 'WHERE ARE YOU GETTING THE MONEY?'

"Now when I first introduced it, it was a 1% cut, or a one-penny plan, and you cut spending 1% a year for five years, and with economic growth increasing revenue, the lines cross at about five years," balancing the budget, he explained. "Well, when COVID came along, both parties frankly started passin' out money like drunken sailors and... the deficit ballooned. Now to balance the budget in five years it's called the six-penny plan cuz it takes about a 6% cut. But it still shows you that we wouldn't have to eliminate everything."

While the cuts under his proposal would not apply to Social Security, they would apply to Medicare, he indicated, though he suggested it could be possible "to cut Medicare 6% without cutting any health benefits," saying that he thinks there is a lot of "waste and fraud in" the program. He also suggested that additional means testing could be used to achieve the Medicare spending cuts.

Paul — who ran for president in 2016 but dropped out after placing fifth in the Iowa GOP presidential caucuses — is considering throwing his hat into the ring again.

"I'd say we're 50-50," he said. "I do think that there should be a candidate on the Republican side, at least, who believes that international trade is good for our country and good for the economy, that believes in free markets, that isn't a big believer in big government coming in and managing contracts and owning parts of countries, that isn't a believer in giving out money we don't have."

RAND PAUL SAYS HE'S '50-50' ON RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028, 'THINKING ABOUT IT'

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Paul said he does not "want there to be a choice of four populists running for president," noting that he wants there to be "at least one free-market candidate. I could be that, or maybe somebody else could be," he said, indicating that he will decide after the midterm elections.

World.title: CHAD WOLF: Congress has a chance to stop China from turning your car into a Chinese spy
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Recent reporting about a British naval drone unknowingly sending data to China offers an urgent warning to policymakers in the United States.

During a routine cybersecurity assessment, the U.K. Ministry of Defence exposed a serious breach. It found that a component in its naval drones was secretly transmitting data to China. The drone was British. The hidden vulnerability was not.

CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'

To be clear, this is part of Beijing’s playbook. It uses intellectual-property theft, cyberespionage and industrial policy to become indispensable to Western supply chains and then exploits that access to collect intelligence and create vulnerabilities it can use against its adversaries.

Our standard response has been to restrict Chinese technology only after the risks become impossible to ignore, often spending billions of dollars to rip and replace equipment already embedded in American networks and infrastructure.

CHINESE ESPIONAGE STEALS $600 BILLION FROM US FIRMS YEARLY. IT’S TIME FOR GOVERNMENT TO ACT

Now, Beijing has its sights on conducting widespread espionage and sabotage in another sector – automobiles. But this time, America has the opportunity to act before it’s too late.

China is now the world’s largest vehicle exporter, and Chinese companies are major players not only in electric vehicles but in the batteries, software, sensors and connected technologies critical to modern cars.

Chinese automakers are using a variety of strategies to enter U.S. markets, and China’s rise as an automotive power presents an obvious challenge for American manufacturers. But as cars become more connected, China’s entry poses severe national security risks.

Modern vehicles are computers on wheels, equipped with cameras, microphones, sensors, GPS systems and internet-connected hardware. They collect enormous amounts of data about their drivers and surroundings, while software increasingly controls critical functions including steering, braking and acceleration.

KARR BLUETOOTH FLAW EXPOSES 2.2M CARS TO THEFT RISK

In the wrong hands, that access could provide a powerful tool for surveillance and espionage or potentially allow an adversary to remotely manipulate or disable vehicles.

Chinese cars on American roads would represent the most direct threat. But Chinese companies don’t need to sell millions of vehicles in America to gain a foothold in the U.S. automotive ecosystem.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

The same risks can be embedded in American, European, Japanese or South Korean vehicles through Chinese-made batteries, software and connected components.

At scale, these technologies could offer Beijing an extraordinary intelligence picture: where Americans live and work, which roads they travel and which vehicles regularly enter military bases, ports, power plants and other sensitive facilities.

In a crisis or conflict, the consequences could extend beyond surveillance. Vulnerabilities in technology embedded across millions of vehicles could potentially provide an adversary a means to disrupt transportation on a massive societal scale.

Chinese automakers are using a variety of strategies to enter U.S. markets, and China’s rise as an automotive power presents an obvious challenge for American manufacturers. But as cars become more connected, China’s entry poses severe national security risks.

Congress has an opportunity to address that threat before it manifests by passing the bipartisan Connected Vehicle Security Act, sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno and Michigan Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin. The legislation builds on the Commerce Department’s connected-vehicle rule, which restricts vehicles, software and connectivity hardware linked to our enemies.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Commerce concluded that foreign-adversary access to these technologies could enable the collection of sensitive data and remote manipulation of vehicles.

That was an important first step, but we must do more. Executive rulemaking can be reversed, but Congress has the chance to make it last. Only an act of Congress can make these national security protections permanent.

CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

The Connected Vehicle Security Act would codify and expand the protections outlined in the Commerce Department’s rulemaking across the supply chain. Critically, it reaches beyond finished Chinese automobiles to the connected technologies inside them, including software, communications equipment and electronics integrated into batteries.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The Senate Commerce Committee advanced it unanimously in July. Congress should pass this legislation and send it to the president’s desk.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

America has repeatedly become dependent on Chinese technology only to later discover how difficult and expensive those dependencies were to unwind. Connected vehicles offer a chance to act before another dependency becomes entrenched.

World.title: NASCAR wives make explosive claims after husbands brawl at Bristol & driver launches water bottle into scrum
World.content:
Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

You see? THIS is why I've always been baffled by NASCAR's decision to move the Bristol night race to September.

We had, easily, the most viral moment of the racing season Saturday night, and it went directly against Ole Miss-LSU. Chase Elliott said it many years ago, and it's still true today ...

STOP COMPETING WITH FOOTBALL.

Phew. OK. I needed to get that off my chest before we dive into the biggest fight this sport has seen since Allison-Yarborough.

NASCAR'S MOST POPULAR DRIVER HAS A TIKTOK GIRLFRIEND THAT'S CAUSING A STIR, AND HE DOESN'T CARE

Fine. That's probably an overreaction. But hey! This Ryan Blaney-Carson Hocevar scrum still a good one!

For Carson, at least. Not sure Blaney got a ton of licks in, but Lordy, he is scrappy. We'll get into it today, obviously. What else are we gonna talk about? Joey Logano winning?

Joey Logano won! There. Happy? Moving on ...

I've also got Blaney's wife, former Hooters girl Gianna Tulio (Blaney), posting some explosive accusations on Instagram about Carson, another NASCAR wife chiming in, NASCAR itself seemingly not doing anything about it, and Ty Gibbs launching a water bottle into the scene of the crime.

That, by the way, may have been the funniest part of the whole thing. You'll see.

Four tires, a couple splashes of that Sunoco racin' fuel, and maybe a raw steak for Blaney's left eye ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'She Said WHAT?' edition — is LIVE!

Blaney hunts down Hocevar after Bristol wreck

No reason to wait around today ... we've had two days to marinate on it. You've all seen the fight by now. We've all seen it.

I know folks despise him, but very few people can make NASCAR trend on X during a college football Saturday night. Carson Hocevar did just that.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

NASCAR needs a villain, and has NEEDED a villain for the longest time. They have one in Carson Hocevar.

Let's dive in:

Goodness gracious. What a fight. What a scene.

Couple things ...

Hard not to give the win to Carson Hocevar here. Fair is fair, and he got in two pretty good licks before Blaney was dragged away. Not sure how Blaney allows that happen, given he was the one came over and started it all. Feels like he needed a better plan. Guy in green was somewhat holding Blaney back. Why? Just let them fight. Seems like he did more harm than good. Blaney breaking containment and forcing his way back to Hocevar was shocking to watch unfold. He's a scrappy little sucker. For those wondering, Hocevar has Blaney beat in just about every metric. It's probably not a fair fight, but Ryan certainly has that DOG in him. I'd love to see it play out further. I have a feeling Blaney's gonna need to put some makeup on that eye before getting to Kansas this weekend. Looks like it's gonna be a pretty decent shiner. Ty Gibbs launching a water bottle into the fight, for no reason whatsoever, was good stuff. Look at this:

Amazing. What's he doing!? No clue. Everyone just hates Hocevar so much, they all wanted a little piece of the action.

Side note: Gibbs finished fifth in Kyle Busch's M&M's paint scheme Saturday night and led 120 laps. Well done, Ty.

Anyway, here's Hocevar after what he called the first fight of his life:

Gianna Blaney stirs the pot, and I'll leave it at that for obvious reasons

"That's the first time I've ever hit anybody," Hocevar said. "It's a cool story at least, to be at Bristol of all places. "I don't know what a decent one (punch) feels like. I've never thrown one."

Hocevar went on to talk about the crash that started all of this, saying he didn't intend to wreck Blaney (duh), and that perhaps the driver of the No. 12 Penske Ford wrecked himself.

Again, I don't want to pick sides here, but ... I think I might be with Carson on this one:

Man, that's a tough one. Hocevar said he was on the brakes pretty hard. I'm not sure I buy that, but I also don't know that he needed to be. It's Bristol. You just made a crossover move, and you have the line.

To me, Blaney went low to try and block the run, and Hocevar's nose was already there. That's just how I see it. I don't think there was any intent.

It didn't matter, though. This was the last straw for Carson. Two weeks ago it was Brad Keselowski, and Saturday night it was Ryan Blaney.

Hocevar, by the way, told me after Daytona that he didn't expect to have any enemies on the track during this 10-race Chase. He said that with a straight face.

Didn't take long!

Those enemies, by the way, ain't just on the track, either:

World.title: Elon Musk is flying under the radar in the Texas Senate race. Republicans like it that way.
World.content:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

Trump boosted Paxton in the primary, even as much of the Republican establishment backed Cornyn. Mark Felix / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”

Talarico had been raising significantly more money than Paxton. Jordan Vonderhaar / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.

So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

World.title: Poll: Most voters say Trump has hurt the economy as competitive midterm election looms
World.content:
“Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates.

Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities.

But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump.

McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf.

“The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said.

Trump’s struggles continue

A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms.

The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%).

And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat.

While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate.

Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely.

A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan.

Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree.

And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran.

Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate.

Democratic opportunities — and challenges

Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall.

Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way.

Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president.

Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust more in dealing with the economy — a result within the poll’s margin of error. It’s the third consecutive NBC News poll with both parties sitting about even on that question. In the same survey just three years ago, Republicans enjoyed a 21-point advantage when it came to handling the economy.

Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents.

The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare.

Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term.

Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party.

The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years.

One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists.

“Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said.

Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates.

Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters.

That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate.

When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely.

Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans.

“This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.”

The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

World.title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
World.content:
Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”

“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said.

“They better behave,” Trump warned.

The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections. He has also said oil prices would not come down until then.

Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Iranian students during an IRGC military parade in Tehran on Friday. Morteza Nikoubazl / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported.

Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when.

“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces.

The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen.

NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday.

He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported.

A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website.

Meanwhile, at least 51 vessels made the crossing along the Bab el Mandeb, with 33 vessels exiting the waterway over the weekend as the Houthis tightened their grip over the strait, the outlet reported. That was down from 57 vessels in the previous weekend.

The Yemeni Health and Environment Ministry accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in the Khabb wa ash-Sha’af district of Al-Jawf Governorate on Sunday that killed four telecommunications workers and injured three others.

“Targeting essential service infrastructure, including telecommunications towers, constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws,” the ministry said in a post on Telegram. “It reveals the aggressor’s determination to disrupt basic services and exacerbate the suffering of the Yemeni people,” it said.

World.title: The Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes look like their old selves, but now with new help
World.content:
The Kansas City Chiefs last season lost more than Patrick Mahomes, their franchise cornerstone player, to a season-ending injury.

Well before the star quarterback injured two ligaments in his left knee last December, the Chiefs had already lost the air of invincibility they’d built while becoming the NFL’s most-feared team in close games.

That quality had earned the Chiefs three Super Bowl titles under coach Andy Reid, and a 17-game winning streak in games decided by 8 points or less. That streak was snapped in last year’s first game, and from there only got worse.

By last season’s end, their record in one-score games was 1-9, a turnaround some attributed to Mahomes’ inconsistent play before his injury, or a supporting cast of receivers and running backs had grown thin. Tight end Travis Kelce, one of the most prolific pass-catchers in the position’s history, was in the middle of one of his worst statistical seasons. On the ground, the Chiefs ranked near the league’s bottom third in yards per carry.

But two games into this new season, Kansas City is 2-0 and again looks like a team that could be feared in the AFC.

Mahomes appears uninhibited by his knee injury, and now has a number of playmakers surrounding him — led by a familiar face, and one new. And in Sunday’s 33-30 overtime win against Indianapolis, the Chiefs showed again they know how to win a close game while overcoming a wild play that might have changed the outcome.

“There was never a doubt that we were going to get that win,” Kelce said.

A walk-off 40-yard field goal as time expired by Harrison Butker gave the Chiefs their eighth consecutive overtime win in the regular season, tying an NFL record also held by San Francisco (2003-10). Mahomes, who threw for 382 yards and three touchdowns, now has 25 career game-winning drives in the fourth quarter or overtime. The Chiefs join Las Vegas, Cincinnati and Buffalo as the only remaining undefeated teams in the AFC.

“That’s what this NFL is about is just finding a way to win games,” Mahomes said on NBC’s “Sunday Night Football.”

Kansas City thought it had the game won with five minutes remaining in overtime.

Tied at 30-30, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones connected with Laquon Treadwell for a 48-yard gain down to Kansas City’s 17-yard line when Treadwell bobbled and recovered the catch while evading one tackle by L’Jarius Sneed. Trying to gain more yardage, Treadwell was then tackled by Chiefs cornerback Nohl Williams, who punched the ball out for a fumble recovered by Kansas City. Under regular-season overtime rules that have been in place since 2025 that allow each team at least one possession each, Kansas City believed it had won the game by forcing a turnover and stopping the Colts short of tying the game on its first overtime drive.

An official review, however, found that Sneed’s left hand grazed the right hip of Treadwell at the same time he secured his bobbled catch — a brush of a few fingers that was barely enough to count Treadwell as down by contact, however slight, at that moment. It negated the fumble that followed. The Colts were still alive.

A touchdown would win the game for Indianapolis, but three plays later it still wasn’t close to the end zone. On fourth and 8, 15 yards from a score, the Colts put their offense on the field and looked ready to snap if they had seen the defense they wanted. When they didn’t, the Colts kicked the field goal for a 30-30 tie. By doing so, Mahomes was left with plenty of time to mount a comeback.

“Had a play called,” Colts coach Shane Steichen said of the fourth-down decision. “Had to love the look to run it there.”

Mahomes jogged into the huddle with 3:06 remaining in overtime knowing the next score would win. He and the Chiefs made it a reality by turning to the franchise’s newest weapon, Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player of last February’s Super Bowl for Seattle who became the team’s prized offseason signing as a free agent.

Walker rushed the ball three times for 18 yards, caught a 22-yard pass from Mahomes, and rushed two more yards to set up Butker’s game-winning kick.

One week after producing a career-high 191 yards from scrimmage during his Chiefs debut in Week 1, a total helped by Walker’s league-best 14 broken tackles, he finished with 117 rushing yards on 24 carries and added 61 yards receiving against the Colts. Walker has looked every bit the missing piece capable of taking pressure off of Mahomes on the ground and opening up the passing game.

“We able to, I guess, freestyle it,” Walker told NBC in a postgame interview of his connection with Mahomes. “If I’m open or if somebody open, play break down, he able to make plays, so it’s great to play with him.”

Even more encouraging for Kansas City was not just how quickly a new addition in Walker has integrated into the offense, but how much Kelce — the record-breaking tight end who helped jump-start the team’s dynasty alongside Mahomes — resembled his old self Sunday.

Kelce has debated whether to retire each of the last two offseasons after producing career-low yardage totals and just eight touchdowns combined in 2024-25. He was targeted on fewer than seven passes per game last season.

On Sunday, a faster, more agile Kelce was targeted 11 times, more than any Chiefs pass-catcher. He caught nine passes for 101 yards including a touchdown that left his pop superstar wife, Taylor Swift, pointing to her wedding ring in a suite in celebration. It was his first game with 100-plus yards and a touchdown since Week 7 of 2023. Kelce now has 128 yards after contact this season, the most in his career through a season’s first two games, per ESPN.

“We’re in a zone right now where everybody’s feeding off each other and it’s only making us better and it’s making us play harder for each other.”

The contributions from Mahomes and his co-stars, and the team’s late-game moxie, have kept the Chiefs undefeated. Still to be seen is whether those factors also can reverse a troubling trend over the course of a long season. Between 2017-22, the Chiefs ranked among the league’s 10 best in scoring every season and led the NFL in points in 2018 and 2022. In the last three years, though, they ranked 15th in both 2023 and 2024 before dropping to 21st last season.

“The parity in this league is crazy,” Chiefs coach Reid said. “You’re going to have some once-score games. You have to bear down, and our guys did that.”

World.title: Home equity loan vs. HELOC: Which option is right for your credit card payoff plan?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

If you're going to pay off credit card debt with home equity, make sure to choose your borrowing option wisely. Pramote Polyamate/Getty Images

Credit card debt has become increasingly expensive to carry over the last few years, and for borrowers who are already struggling to make progress on their balances, today's high interest rates can make the problem even harder to solve. With average credit card rates now hovering above 22%, it's easy for a significant amount of each monthly payment to go toward interest rather than reducing the balance. That can leave borrowers searching for a less expensive way to pay off what they owe.

There are a few different ways to do that, but homeowners, in particular, may have an option that other borrowers don't. Home values have risen considerably over the last several years, allowing many homeowners to build sizable amounts of home equity, even as higher mortgage rates have slowed activity in the housing market. And that equity can be borrowed against, often at rates that are substantially lower than those charged on credit cards, which could make it useful for consolidating high-rate balances.

But while a large portion of homeowners have equity they can tap into, the question is how to access that equity. Two common options are home equity loans and home equity lines of credit (HELOCs), and while both use your home as collateral, the similarities largely end there. The way you receive the funds, how your interest rate works and how you repay what you borrow all differ, so it's important to understand which option is better suited to paying off credit card debt.

Find out how Achieve can help you get rid of your high-rate debt today.

Home equity loan vs. HELOC: Which option is right for your credit card payoff plan?

If you're considering using your home's equity to eliminate credit card debt, it's important to understand that home equity loans and HELOCs work differently. A home equity loan provides a lump-sum loan with a fixed interest rate and predictable monthly payments. A HELOC functions more like a credit line, allowing you to borrow as needed during the draw period, typically with a variable interest rate. The choice often comes down to how much debt you have, whether your balances are still growing and how much payment certainty you want. Here's what to consider when weighing your options:

When a home equity loan is the right credit card payoff option

If your credit card balance is a fixed figure and your main goal is certainty, the home equity loan is usually the better fit. With this route, you borrow the exact amount you need, pay off the card balances and lock in one rate for the life of the loan. Your payment never changes, which keeps budgeting simple.

For example, if you have $40,000 in credit card debt spread across several accounts, a home equity loan allows you to consolidate those balances into one loan with a set repayment schedule. Rather than dealing with fluctuating minimum payments and varying interest rates, you'll know exactly how much you owe each month and have a clear idea of when the debt will be paid off.

And, the fixed-rate nature of home equity loans may be especially appealing in today's environment. While home equity rates remain far below average credit card rates, economic uncertainty and persistent inflation concerns mean interest rate volatility remains a possibility. The Federal Reserve is also signaling the possibility of future rate increases, so locking in a fixed rate can provide peace of mind for borrowers who want certainty.

The tradeoff, though, is flexibility. Once you receive the funds from your home equity loan, you begin repaying the full loan amount immediately, even if you don't end up needing every dollar you borrowed.

Learn more about the debt relief options Achieve can offer you now.

When a HELOC is the right credit card payoff option

On the other hand, a HELOC may be the better option for homeowners who want more borrowing flexibility or who expect their debt repayment strategy to evolve. That's because a HELOC gives you access to a revolving line of credit, and during the draw period, you can borrow what you need, when you need it, up to your approved credit limit.

In turn, this approach can work well if you're paying off credit card balances gradually or you expect more expenses to arise while you're eliminating debt. It can also be a smart move if your goal is more flexibility in terms of borrowing, as the line of credit remains available to draw from for an extended period.

However, that flexibility can come with risks. Most HELOCs have variable rates, meaning borrowing costs can change over time (though there may be fixed options available). If you have a variable-rate HELOC and rates rise, your payments could increase as well, and there's a real likelihood of that happening in today's inflationary environment. Because a HELOC functions like a revolving credit account, some borrowers may be tempted to continue borrowing after paying off their credit cards, potentially creating a new debt cycle.

For homeowners who are highly disciplined and want access to funds without borrowing more than necessary, though, a HELOC can be an effective debt management tool. It just generally requires more financial restraint than a traditional home equity loan.

The bottom line

Both home equity loans and HELOCs can be powerful tools for wiping out high-rate credit card debt, but the right choice hinges on your specific situation. If you have a fixed balance you want to eliminate and value predictable payments, a home equity loan delivers the certainty and built-in discipline that makes consolidation stick. A HELOC, on the other hand, offers flexibility that a lump-sum loan simply can't match — provided you have the restraint to avoid falling back into old habits.

Either way, you'll likely secure a far lower rate than what your credit cards are charging, but it's worth remembering that you're trading unsecured debt for borrowing tied to your home. Before you move forward, weigh your monthly budget, your repayment timeline and your tolerance for rate fluctuations, and consider speaking with a lender or debt relief expert to confirm that tapping your equity is the best path toward becoming debt-free.

World.title: Should you negotiate with debt collectors? 6 tips to improve your chances
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Negotiations tend to go more smoothly when you have accurate information and realistic expectations on hand. Vadishzainer/Getty Images

Keeping up with debt payments has become a tougher task for many households over the last year, as high borrowing costs and elevated everyday expenses are competing for a larger portion of the average borrower's monthly budget. When there isn't enough money to cover everything, even debt that was once manageable can become harder to stay ahead of, and falling behind for long enough can eventually result in the account being turned over to collections.

Reaching the point where your debt goes from overdue to being actively pursued by a debt collector can add another layer of financial pressure to the mix. Collection efforts may start with phone calls and letters but can become more persistent over time, and it can be difficult to find money to resolve that old balance while you're covering your current bills and other debts. The stress associated with those competing demands can be significant, according to a recent Achieve survey, with about half of respondents reporting that money-related stress has caused them to lose sleep.

What many borrowers don't realize, though, is that there can be some flexibility in how certain collection debts are resolved, particularly if you understand what options may be available and how to approach the process. So, before agreeing to a payment or making an offer, it can help to know what could give you a better chance of reaching a workable agreement.

Find out how Achieve can help you find a path to becoming debt-free.

Should you negotiate with debt collectors? 6 tips to improve your chances

If you're facing a legitimate debt you can't pay in full, negotiating is often worth considering. After all, debt collectors are frequently willing to accept less than the full balance to avoid receiving no payment, and a settlement can resolve the account faster than letting it linger. Still, negotiating isn't automatically the right call. If the debt isn't actually yours, is too old to be legally enforceable or is otherwise questionable, negotiating may do more harm than good. The following steps can help you decide which route to take — and improve your odds if you move forward with negotiations:

Verify the debt before you discuss any payments

Don't acknowledge or pay anything until you've confirmed the debt is yours and the details are accurate. To do this, you should request a debt validation letter in writing, which a debt collector is required to provide. This protects you from paying debts you don't owe, balances inflated by improper fees or zombie debts that are past the statute of limitations — where even a small payment or verbal acknowledgment can restart the statute of limitations clock and revive your liability.

Learn about the debt relief options Achieve can offer you today.

Find out who owns the debt

Knowing whether you're dealing with the original creditor or a third-party debt buyer can help shape your leverage. Debt buyers often purchase portfolios for pennies on the dollar, after all, which means they have room to accept far less than the full balance and still turn a profit. Original creditors tend to be less flexible on the number, but may still offer lower settlements or hardship programs worth asking about.

Lead with a realistic lump-sum offer

Debt collectors strongly prefer one lump-sum settlement payment over a drawn-out installment plan, and that preference is leverage. Settlements commonly result in paying 30% to 50% less than the full balance, so opening below that range — while naming a firm ceiling you won't cross — gives you room to negotiate upward if needed.

Stay calm and persistent

Negotiations don't always succeed on the first attempt. Debt collectors may reject an initial offer, propose different terms or ask for additional information. Remaining professional and persistent during this process can help keep discussions productive.

That's especially important because financial stress often affects how people approach debt problems. According to Achieve survey data, 50% of respondents said money issues left them feeling anxious or on edge.

The same study found that many feel overwhelmed by their financial obligations, highlighting the emotional challenges that often accompany collection efforts. Those pressures can make negotiations feel intimidating, but approaching conversations calmly and strategically may lead to better outcomes.

Get every agreement in writing

Never send money on a verbal promise or agreement made with a debt collector; get a written agreement instead. That agreement should spell out the settlement amount, the payment deadline and provide explicit confirmation that the payment satisfies the debt in full. Without it, you risk paying a portion of what's owed and still being pursued for the remaining balance later.

Explore alternatives if negotiations fail

Not every debt collection account can be resolved through direct negotiation. If you're dealing with multiple collection accounts, significant balances or ongoing financial hardship, other forms of debt relief may be worth exploring. For example, debt settlement programs, debt management plans and, in some cases, bankruptcy may provide additional options for resolving your unmanageable debt.

Working with a debt relief company during the settlement process could also help, as these experts negotiate settlement deals routinely and may land better terms than you'd get on your own. Just be sure to weigh the fees against what you'd likely save to ensure it's worth the cost.

The bottom line

Negotiating with debt collectors can be a smart move for borrowers who are struggling to repay delinquent debt. While success isn't guaranteed, debt collectors are often willing to discuss payment arrangements or settlements, particularly when borrowers come prepared with accurate information and realistic expectations.

The key, though, is to verify the debt, understand your financial limits, document any agreements and remain patient throughout the process. And if a negotiated resolution isn't possible, don't assume you're out of options. Exploring your debt relief alternatives may help you regain control of your finances and create a path toward becoming debt-free.

World.title: Iran's early attacks on Bahrain caught Navy families and sailors by surprise
World.content:
On the very first day of the war, Iran targeted the Navy's Middle East headquarters in Bahrain — before the U.S. government had evacuated all the military families based there. Some had to wait about a week or more to reach safety, according to multiple families who spoke to CBS News.

"You're definitely scared," one military spouse said. "As the week goes on, you wake up to ballistic missiles being fired. We went to sleep with the sound of ballistic missiles again."

Iranian missiles and drones targeted Bahrain consistently for several days after the war began, according to another spouse. The scale and duration of those attacks appeared to take the U.S. government by surprise, three sources who were in Bahrain at the time told CBS News, in part because families hadn't been required to evacuate until the war had already begun.

The military had anticipated some retaliation and had even evacuated the headquarters' buildings on the base, but "we weren't expecting that [scale]," one U.S. official said. And there were still several military families living off the base nearby.

One spouse said she could see the contrails of missiles and drones, and another heard explosions from attacks. CBS News granted anonymity to the spouses who feared retaliation for speaking.

No military personnel were killed in the attacks, but images that circulated on social media earlier this year — which sources say are authentic — show extensive damage to the base. One of the images shows an explosion during an attack on the first day of the war that targeted a key radar system.

Pentagon has not released a public estimated cost of damage

The U.S. military has not included the damage to bases in its cost estimates of the war so far because officials say they don't know what will be rebuilt, but acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao in a recent interview with The Epoch Times said Iran's retaliatory attacks "blew the hell out of Bahrain."

Since Naval Support Activity Bahrain officially became the headquarters for the Navy's Fifth Fleet in the '90s, it has served as a logistics hub for ships in the Middle East, including during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. According to the Navy's website, the facility serves approximately 8,300 military personnel, Defense Department civilian employees and their families.

The damage has impacted sailors at sea as well. Earlier this year, the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier faced food shortages as the Navy adjusted resupply routes away from Bahrain. The New York Times reported some supplies had to come through Diego Garcia, an island some 2,200 miles away in the Indian Ocean.

The extended route requires 14- to 18-day logistics cycles to deliver supplies to ships, according to a Pentagon Inspector General report. That's compared to 5 to 7 days from Bahrain, two former officials said. While there are other logistics hubs in the region, Bahrain was a key option before the war began.

Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle, the Navy's top officer, at a town hall last month acknowledged the service has had to restructure how it supplies ships in the Middle East.

"There was some early learning there on getting the logistics process in place that I think now we have in a very good situation," Caudle said.

During the town hall, Caudle told a sailor who was evacuated from Bahrain that officials are working on retrieving belongings that were left behind because the Navy does not have imminent plans to return to the same level of footprint on the base.

"We're not getting back in there anytime soon, I just want to be completely honest with that," he said.

According to a Navy spokesperson, service members in Bahrain can ship their household goods and vehicles in person, and those outside Bahrain can designate a representative to act on their behalf, or coordinate travel back to Bahrain to move household goods and vehicles.

Some military families, service members and civilians in a bind

Since those opening days of the war, the Navy has helped evacuate about 1,450 service members and families from Bahrain. Many are now in a financial bind because they're paying for at least two households — one in Bahrain and another in the U.S.

"We have burned through our savings," one of the spouses told CBS News. "We have started having to take money out of our kids' college funds to pay down all the bills that we're incurring."

The Pentagon is providing benefits to reimburse housing costs in both places, but families told CBS News claims can take weeks to months to process.

In a statement, a Navy spokesperson said, "The Navy remains in close communication with all affected service members, affiliated civilians and families through command channels and continues to provide timely information, individual case management, and relocation support."

The spokesperson said families have until the end of November to transition from a safe haven to an established designated residence to continue receiving housing, relocation and separation entitlements.

Even if some families have not struggled financially through this process, all of them have been uprooted. Many were evacuated to Norfolk, Virginia, which is a Navy hub, or to Tampa, Florida, where U.S. Central Command's headquarters is located.

Blue Star Families, a non-profit that supports military families, provided supplies to evacuees in Tampa, according to Suzy Malloy, the executive director of the chapter in the Tampa Bay region.

"We gave these kids backpacks with school supplies," Malloy told CBS News. "We gave families brand new clothing, we gave them air fryers and crockpots so that they could cook in hotel rooms until they could adjust to something more permanent," like an Airbnb or temporary military housing.

Malloy said the evacuees are still in a bit of limbo but are starting to settle into Tampa.

"My opinion is [U.S. Central Command] and their family readiness program have done a remarkable job keeping the train on the tracks," Malloy said.

None of the families CBS News spoke to blamed the military for their challenges, but are frustrated with the overall situation — the evacuation and the uncertainty that has come after.

"Nobody expected this to go on so long," one of the spouses said.

World.title: Police officer wounded in shooting near synagogue on Yom Kippur
World.content:
A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

The province's Special Investigations Unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.

The synagogue's president, Norman Weddum, told CBC News Network he was ushering people into the sanctuary to begin services when he heard gunfire.

"I could say, 'Oh, this is definitely someone … shooting here,'" he told the outlet. "So that's when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target. And we hit the floor."

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur. He said in a post on social media he was "disgusted by the shooting and that Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear." He called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.

"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow also condemned the violence.

"Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives," she said on social media. "As long as we contend with rising antisemitism and hate, we will spare no expense keeping the community safe."

The Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene. Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.

York Regional Police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday, "Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives."

"Canada's government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law," he said on X.

"My thoughts are with the injured officer and his family, and the entire Jewish community," he added.

Carney previously warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism. He cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

Earlier this month, a Michigan synagogue reopened in time for the Jewish High Holidays, six months after it was targeted in a terror attack. The Detroit-area Temple Israel was attacked on March 12 when a 41-year-old man rammed his truck packed with fireworks and gasoline deep into the building. The FBI called it a "targeted act of violence against the Jewish community."

World.title: Italy's Meloni plans to limit foreign student numbers, ban face coverings in schools
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced plans on Sunday to introduce a legal limit on the number of foreign students allowed in Italian classrooms, as well as a ban on face-covering garments, including the Islamic burqa and niqab, in schools.

Meloni made the announcement during a speech at Fenix, an event organized by Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her conservative Brothers of Italy party.

"If in a classroom there is only one child who doesn't understand Italian, it is possible that that child will manage, with the help of his peers and teachers, to learn the language and integrate fast. But if these children are many, or even the majority, that's not integration anymore, that's abandonment," Meloni said.

She said Italy's government would introduce legislation to legally limit the number of foreign students in individual classrooms to about 30%, adding: "There's no way that in an Italian classroom, the ones who feel marginalized are Italian children because they have become a minority."

According to the ISMU ETS Foundation, an immigration-focused think tank, citing data from the Italian Ministry of Education, students with non-Italian citizenship currently account for about 11.6% of the total school enrollment across the country.

Under Italy's citizenship system, children born in the country to non-Italian parents do not generally acquire Italian citizenship automatically at birth, but only after turning 18 years old, if they have remained in the country.

Meloni also announced plans to prohibit face-covering garments, specifically mentioning the burqas and niqabs worn by some women and girls, in schools.

"At school, you go with your face uncovered, and in Italy no one, in the name of a real or presumed tradition, can decide that a young woman has to hide. Equality between men and women is non-negotiable," Meloni said.

The proposed measure would target only garments that cover the face, not all forms of Islamic head covering.

Meloni said the government would bring the proposed legislation to the Council of Ministers, after which it would require parliamentary approval to become law.

"There are some neighborhoods in more depopulated areas in Italy where the concentration of people coming from a non-Italian background is higher and inevitably creates higher numbers of non-Italian students in classrooms," Mariagrazia Santagati, a professor of sociology at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, in Milan, told CBS News.

Italy would not be the first European country to restrict face coverings in public places. France, Belgium and several other European nations have adopted restrictions on face-covering garments, although the scope and legal basis of those measures vary.

The proposed limit on foreign students in classrooms, however, would represent a first in Europe if it is adopted.

"Italian school is based on inclusion, from children with disabilities to other minorities, everyone attends the same classes. And public school is open to every child to attend, regardless of their juridical status and religion," said Santagati. "It's hard to understand how this would be put into practice. We are for multiculturalism."

The premier's announcements came as Italy looks ahead to next year's general election, with Meloni facing competition from both the left and right of the political spectrum.

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

World leaders convene this week in New York for the United Nations General Assembly. It will be U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres' last General Assembly before his term ends in December. He will open the event on Tuesday morning, followed by Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and then President Trump. Here's what NPR will be watching throughout the high-level event, which runs through Sept. 28.

🎧 Trump has tried to position himself as a peacemaker , but his war against Iran looms over the gathering, NPR's Michele Kelemen tells Up First. Iran's president will speak at the event the day after Trump, though interaction between U.S. and Iranian officials remains uncertain. The U.N. has been somewhat sidelined in the conflict with Iran, but it has offered to monitor civilian shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Kelemen says those efforts haven't gained much traction. Despite Trump's downplaying of artificial intelligence and climate change, these topics are expected to be big topics of discussion at the event.

Trump has announced that he wants his proposed 250-foot arch in Washington, D.C., to function as a military complex that features areas for snipers and weaponry. The president says these military operations are needed to enhance national security. The arch, which would be twice as tall as the Lincoln Memorial, has faced pushback even before the president posted his latest plans on Truth Social. People submitted more than 100,000 comments to the National Park Service, and the arch has also faced legal challenges.



🎧 NPR's Franco Ordoñez says that the president's plan reflects his push for increased executive power. Trump is bypassing traditional processes and Congress to establish a major national monument by broadly interpreting his executive authority, challenging opponents to stop him, Ordoñez adds. Many people fear he will act swiftly on this plan, outpacing any court responses and making it challenging to reverse the project. Some are also concerned that the president's proposal for the arch, along with other projects like the ballroom and threats to demolish the Kennedy Center, could significantly alter Washington's landscape.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is preparing to launch an $875 million AI-powered software overhaul to improve air traffic control efficiency. While regulators and airlines are optimistic about the potential of Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART), critics question its effectiveness.



Sponsor Message

🎧 FAA leaders say that the new tool is not meant to replace human controllers. It aims to help employees by minimizing congestion and potential conflicts in the air before they occur, NPR's Joel Rose says. SMART is supposed to analyze airline schedules, weather patterns, and other factors to optimize flight plans. Rose spoke to former air traffic controller Dave Riley, who wasn't worried that the AI tool would lead to problems because humans would still oversee safety. But Riley says the tool won't address larger issues like the staffing shortage. The FAA still lacks thousands of controllers, leading to mandatory overtime and demanding schedules for those on duty.

The Department of Homeland Security said today that it is investigating a shooting involving a federal immigration agent who shot and injured 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez from Venezuela. DHS says that the shooting of "an illegal alien" happened during an Austin operation on Sunday. The circumstances leading to the shooting remain unclear. DHS says that Rafael Garces Perez is in stable condition and in federal custody pending removal. His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said that Rafael Garces Perez called his wife to say he had been shot while sitting in his car and was yelling in pain. His wife has legal status to be in the U.S.

Basket men, carrying around 35 pounds of fish on their heads, make 40 to 50 trips to the daily auction during long shifts. They're joined by fishermen, auctioneers, fish hawkers and wholesalers, transport workers and ice suppliers. The harbor, originally built for fewer than 600 boats, now serves more than 1,000. World.title: Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on
World.content:
Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on

toggle caption Colin Hubbard/AP

President Trump is still talking about the 2020 election — even as early voting is underway in this midterm cycle and the Republican majorities in Congress are at risk.

And while many Republican candidates, even in some critical tossup races, still back the president's baseless claims about election integrity, some GOP voters say they are ready to move on.

In Georgia, Rep. Mike Collins, the Republican nominee for Senate, launched his first congressional campaign a few months after Trump pressed Georgia's secretary of state to find enough votes to reverse his 2020 loss.

In one campaign ad from that race, Collins falsely claimed that Trump won Georgia and said, "Georgians are tired of weak-kneed, spineless politicians who won't fight for Trump, get to the bottom of 2020 and fix our elections." The spot ended with Collins firing a long gun into a bin with a "voting machine" label.

Sponsor Message

Now as Collins runs for Senate, he has reiterated his position that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. He has also expressed support for compensating some people prosecuted for storming the Capitol on Jan. 6 to disrupt the certification of the 2020 election.

"It bothers me a lot," said Lynn, a lifelong Republican voter in Georgia, who asked NPR to publish only her first name for fear of being ostracized by friends and family for her views. "It worries me for him to get elected. It concerns me any time someone gets pulled into those ridiculous looking-back discussions."

At a farmers market in Alpharetta, a tony suburb outside of Atlanta, Lynn said she could have easily voted for the other two Republicans who ran in the primary. Now she has not ruled out voting for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, in part because of Collins' positions on the 2020 election.

The Collins campaign did not respond to NPR's request for comment.

Finishing a plate of grits at the farmers market, voter Austin Sapp said he regularly votes for Republican candidates, believes election fraud does happen, and supports Trump's push to pass a strict voter ID law through Congress. He also wishes the president would move on from relitigating 2020.

Sponsor Message

"It is what it is," Sapp said. "He lost, then he won [in 2024]. Beating a dead horse serves no purpose. What is your platform? What are you going to do for me?"

"Regular humans have given this up"

Just 1% of voters in a September New York Times-Siena College poll said election integrity is the top issue deciding their vote this November.

"It's really big with the media and the far edges of both parties," said Gabe Sterling, a veteran official with the Georgia secretary of state's office. "Regular humans have given this up a long time ago."

After the 2020 election, Sterling was one of the most visible officials disputing Trump's false claims. Weeks before Jan. 6, he presciently warned people could get hurt. He says that feels far from the climate now.

Sterling says while resurfacing claims about fraud can still be an effective fundraising tool, the 2020 obsession is mostly alive among die-hard activists only.

That is not insignificant though. Some of those activists now hold influential positions on state and local election boards. They also vote reliably in Republican primaries.

Sterling spoke with hundreds of GOP primary voters as he ran for secretary of state this year. He stood firm in his defense of Georgia's elections and felt like he did sway people. It was not enough to win a primary.
