The halved deadline to pay back late rent “just means you can file the paperwork a little sooner at the LTB,” said Kayla Andrade, founder of the landlord advocacy group Ontario Landlords Watch.

“It doesn’t mean that you’re going to get your hearing any faster.”

Kayla Andrade, founder of Ontario Landlords Watch, argues that the only way to speed things up at the LTB is to streamline common applications. (Submitted by Kayla Andrade)

The Small Ownership Landlords of Ontario group has raised similar concerns, arguing that the LTB should allow landlords to skip a hearing altogether for non-payment of rent disputes and instead be able to use a faster-moving mediation process.

Andrade is supportive of the formalizing of the definition of “persistent non-payment of rent,” telling CBC News that previously, “you didn’t know… exactly what the [adjudicator] would consider as persistent late payments. It’s good to have something concrete.”

Tenant advocates call changes a ‘smokescreen’

Tenant organizations have also argued that the RTA updates fail to address the cause of bottlenecks at the LTB.

In a release, the Federation of Metro Tenants' Associations said efficiency was merely a “smokescreen” for “eroding tenants' rights.”

Dania Majid, director of duty counsel for the Advocacy Centre for Tenants Ontario, told CBC News that her legal clinic is deeply concerned that the changes make it easier for tenants to be evicted. But that wouldn't necessarily happen faster, she said.

The switch from 14 to seven days to repay rent will “trigger more hearings. And that’s going to trigger a backlog,” she said.

WATCH | New tenant union launches across Toronto: New tenant union launches across Toronto | Duration closed caption 3:14 Tenants and housing advocates from across Toronto gathered on Saturday to launch a new, city-wide tenant union. Organizers say the goal is to build a collective power to address rising rents and push for stronger protections for renters. CBC’s Naama Weingarten has the story.

Majid says she expects a similar outcome from one of the earlier July 1 RTA updates, which halves the amount of time for tenants and landlords to request a review of an LTB decision.

“If you're not able to provide your materials in time at the LTB to request a review there, people are going to end up at the divisional court and that's going to create a backlog there,” she said.

Then there’s the requirement that tenants pay 50 per cent of the unpaid rent they allegedly owe in order to raise other complaints at their eviction hearing.

“Now the tenant has to file a separate application to raise these issues… when the entire matter could have just been handled at the same hearing,” said Majid

CBC News asked the Ministry of Housing how tenants can recover the money they paid before a hearing if it's found they don’t actually owe it. The ministry did not reply by publication time.

World.title: What could a 'super' El Niño mean for the Prairies?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The much-talked-about El Niño continues to heat up in the Pacific Ocean.

"Every indicator has shown that this [El Niño-Southern Oscillation] is continuing to strengthen," said Lindsey Long, a meteorologist with the ENSO team at the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) in the U.S.

"We're getting [sea surface temperature] anomalies of up to 11 C, so those are extremely warm waters that are helping to fuel this."

El Niño is part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) , which is a fluctuation between warmer sea surface temperature anomalies — El Niño — and colder anomalies — La Niña — in the equatorial region of the Pacific Ocean.

These fluctuations happen in periods of two to seven years.

This illustration shows the El Niño regions in the Pacific Ocean. (NOAA)

During normal conditions, west-blowing trade winds push warm sea surface temperatures from South America toward Asia. However, those winds can break down or reverse direction, allowing that warm water to instead pool near South America.

What does this mean for the Prairies?

This disrupts weather patterns around the world, including a stronger Pacific jet stream and an amplified polar jet stream over western Canada.

As of Sept. 14, a very strong El Niño was being observed in what's called the El Niño 3.4 region in the eastern equatorial Pacific, where average sea surface temperatures were 2 C warmer than normal.

Experts predict the current El Niño to peak during the late fall and winter months.

The last El Niño classified as very strong occurred during the 2015-16 winter. The Prairies also experienced a moderate El Niño during the 2023-24 season. Both brought warmer than normal temperatures to the Prairies.

WATCH | What does a super El Niño mean for the Prairies?: What does a super El Niño mean for the Prairies? | Duration closed caption 2:07 El Niño is back, and it could be record-breaking. CBC Saskatchewan meteorologist Allister Aalders explains what's behind this 'super' El Niño and how it could influence the Prairies during the upcoming winter season.

Research scientist Bill Merryfield with Environment and Climate Change Canada says that could also be the case this winter.

"The odds are certainly tilted in that direction of having a relatively mild winter, possibly by a large margin," he said.

"Some of those temperature differences from normal during past very strong El Niños have been in the range of 5 or 6 degrees averaged over the winter, which is quite substantial.”

Both Long and Merryfield say that El Niño events typically lead to less snowfall in the Rocky Mountains, and that warmer temperatures could mean less snow in the Prairies, but that trends for precipitation are not as strong as with temperature.

Research aims to correlate ENSO, precipitation

With a correlation between precipitation and ENSO on the Prairies unclear, researchers are diving deeper into it.

David Sauchyn, director of the Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative at the University of Regina, says a proxy of soil data across the Prairies has been collected to see years where soil and trees received more or less moisture in a given year.

During a typical El Niño, an amplified polar jet stream often leads to warmer than normal temperatures in much of western Canada during the winter season. (CBC News)

The research is looking into whether drier or wetter periods might correlate with El Niño or La Niña events.

"We can't say exactly if a dry year was an El Niño year, but we get this cycle — this cycle of every two to eight years it's either quite wet or quite dry," he said.

"It's not the direct measurement of sea surface temperature, but we have a proxy record of soil moisture on the Prairies going back 1,000 years."

Cold snaps, snowstorms still likely this winter

The current projection from the CPC has the El Niño continuing into next spring with a 55 per cent chance of a return to neutral conditions in the April-May-June timeframe.

Merryfield is concerned that less snow than normal or a reduced snowpack could create problems with streamflow, drought and wildfires next spring.

"We might expect vegetation to be drier than usual, which could be conducive to drought and wildfire risk if there's not a good amount of rainfall in late spring and summer to offset that," he said.

But Long notes that a warmer or drier winter does not mean classic Prairie cold snaps and blizzards won't appear at all this season.

"Just because overall you might be warmer, you can still have big snow events, big cold snaps, things like that," she said.

World.title: 11 things we learned from the Neil Peart documentary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Drummers often get short shrift. Hidden behind the kit, they remain mysterious, even anonymous.

Not so for Neil Peart, who was a tour-de-force for the Canadian rock band Rush and is widely considered one of the best drummers of all time.

In Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple, co-directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn celebrate Peart's life, extraordinary musicianship and lasting influence through interviews and musical performances.

Bandmates Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, along with Peart’s fellow drummers and friends — including Stewart Copeland of the Police and Chad Smith of Red Hot Chili Peppers — share insights into the wizard behind the kit and perform Rush songs together as a tribute to his enduring legacy. The film debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sept. 16. Here are 11 things we learned:

1. His name is pronounced 'Peert'

"It's not 'Pert' like the shampoo," says Dunn, correcting a mispronunciation that has even appeared in films such as School of Rock and I Love You, Man.

2. He moved to London at 18 to pursue music

After leaving high school, Peart moved from St. Catharines, Ont., to England determined to become a musician. He lived in cheap rooms and shared flats, experiencing what he later described as "anonymity and poverty" — an early test of the focus and stubbornness that would define his career.

3. He was an enthusiastic reader

When his bandmates first met Peart, he was reading "five or six books a day," according to Lee, who said it soon became obvious that their new drummer should also be writing lyrics.

From left, Rush guitarist Alex Lifeson, Peart and lead singer and bassist Geddy Lee perform in 1977. (Fin Costello/Banger Films)

4. He loved The Lord of the Rings

Peart’s imagination was shaped by fantasy, mythology, science fiction, comedy and classical music — influences that found their way into Rush’s songs and lyrics. His love of J.R.R. Tolkien influenced songs such as The Necromancer and Rivendell.

5. He rehearsed before rehearsal

Peart studied, practised and took lessons throughout his career, always approaching the drums as a student.

"I think it matters for me to play better all the time," he says in archival footage, "to play my best all the time, to keep it fresh and changing. It’s kind of my responsibility."

He would rehearse for at least an hour by himself before rehearsing with the rest of the band. As the filmmakers put it, he was continuously trying to get better — even after becoming one of the best in the world.

6. He helped build Rush’s big, theatrical sound

Peart played a major role in shaping Rush’s intricate arrangements and dramatic instrumental passages, which became central to the band’s sound.

His influence is especially evident in 2112, the 20-minute title suite from the band’s 1976 album.



"It was Neil’s idea to do an overture," says Lifeson, to "take all these pieces and put them together in one really cool opening." The movement weaves together themes that return throughout the piece, reflecting Peart’s operatic and orchestral approach to percussion.

WATCH | Rush performs 2112 live:

7. His whisky pours got bigger

During studio mixing sessions, Peart reportedly enjoyed a glass of Macallan whisky at 5 p.m. — a pour of about "two fat fingers," according to Lee. Over their 40-year friendship, Lee jokes, Peart’s "fingers got fatter."

8. He was an air drummer's drummer

Copeland notes Peart’s solos were so intricate, physical and theatrical that audiences didn’t just watch — they played along in the air.

"I asked him one time, how do you get the air drummers? I want that," Copeland said. "It's amazing at a Rush show to see them."

"The middle part of Tom Sawyer is every air drummer’s fantasy section," adds Smith. "If you hear Tom Sawyer, they’re all air drumming."

WATCH | Rush performs Tom Sawyer live:

9. He was intensely private

Peart was uncomfortable with fame and fiercely protective of his personal life.

"If I go off to do my job, I’m a professional," he says in an archival interview. "If I’m not doing my job, then I’m a person, so don’t get that mixed up."

10. He took bikes very seriously

Lee recalls Peart riding his bicycle from Milwaukee to Chicago, some 150 kilometres, on his day off and then performing a three-hour concert.

He later became a devoted motorcyclist, chronicling his travels, which followed devastating personal losses, in his memoir Ghost Rider: Travels on the Healing Road.

11. He nearly retired, but came back for one more tour

After the deaths of his 19-year-old daughter, in a car accident in August 1997, and his wife, from cancer 10 months later, Peart took a five-year hiatus. He returned to make the album Vapor Trails in 2002 and tour.

Following that, Peart took part in the albums and tours for 2004's Feedback, 2007's Snakes & Arrows and 2012's Clockwork Angels.

Although he considered retirement in 2015, he agreed to return for one final tour.

WATCH | Rush red carpet interviews at TIFF: Rush members honour late drummer Neil Peart at TIFF | Duration closed caption 2:18 Filmmakers and Rush members reflect on Neil Peart’s legacy, musical genius and the private, caring person behind the legendary drummer at the premiere of Neil Peart: No One's Disciple.

'Respect the drummer'

"Drummers are the backbone," of bands, Dunn told CBC News, "and Neil was taking drumming to a whole other level."

That appreciation drives the film, which serves as the tribute Peart never received: a proper farewell concert or memorial, made impossible by the pandemic after his death from brain cancer in January 2020.

Instead, Lee and Lifeson reunite with four of Peart’s musical "brothers" for a musical, funny and emotional tribute.

"It’s a very joyous celebration of a complex individual," McFadyen said.

Lee jokes that Peart "would say we were idiots" and might be "a little embarrassed" by the attention. He adds that he remembers him as "a very wise, quick thinker, philosopher" and gifted lyricist.

The film ultimately asks audiences to do exactly what Dunn recommends: "respect the drummer."



Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple will air on CBC’s The Passionate Eye, on Sept. 23 at 8 p.m. (8:30 NT) on CBC and CBC Gem.

World.title: Psychological horror Silent Hill: Townfall ratchets up the scares — and frustrations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Resident Evil and Silent Hill, two foundational series in video game horror that continue to release new games today, both emerged in the late 1990s on the first Sony PlayStation.

But Silent Hill's psychological take on the genre has found a relatively niche audience compared to the crowd-pleasing Resident Evil.

Instead of police officers and secret agents cracking wise in the face of a zombie outbreak, Silent Hill threw civilians into oppressive settings, dripping with unreliable narrators and metaphors for facing past trauma or sins.

Silent Hill: Townfall, published by Konami and developed by Glasgow-based Screen Burn Interactive, has moments that reach the pinnacle of horror in gaming today. But with a grab bag of mechanics that at times seem at odds with one another, it's likely you'll love one part of the experience, but loathe the next.

Welcome to St. Amelia

Townfall's first note is an odd one. The year is 1996, and we see American Simon Ordell (voiced by The Leftovers' Jovan Adepo) wash up ashore in St. Amelia, an abandoned Scottish fishing village, with no idea of how he got there. He's got an IV bag strapped to his arm, its tubing plugged into his left hand.

Protest signs cover the town's square, hinting that a corporation is behind some kind of disaster. Simon answers a ringing payphone and speaks to a man named Richard (Lost's Terry O'Quinn), who tells him to search for a nurse named Zoe Ellis (Kezia Burrows). She knows Simon, though he has no memory of her.

The fishing town, once bustling with everyday folk, is now populated by fleshy, humanoid monsters that moan and growl despite lacking facial features.

The eerie, seemingly abandoned Scottish fishing town of St. Amelia is the setting for Silent Hill: Townfall. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

Key to Simon's survival is the CRTV — a handheld portable television that resembles Sony's Sport Watchman. Tuning the device shows enemies' shivering silhouettes amidst a scratchy red screen, allowing him to hide and skulk past them unscathed.

Cryptic messages come through the fuzzy screen — glimpses of your intended destination like Zoe's house, or clues to help you open a rusty locker in a pharmacy's back room, sometimes with snippets of messages from Zoe or Richard playing through its low-fi speaker.

Your other tools for dealing with enemies are meagre at best: tossing a bottle can distract their attention; a rotting wooden plank can withstand one melee, but cracks in half before long. A handgun is a powerful last resort, but you'll rarely have enough bullets to fill its six chambers.

All of this evokes a feeling of dread and helplessness, forcing you to avoid fights whenever possible.

The CRTV, a portable handheld television device, lets the player find clues around the world and track enemies' movements. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

First-person stumbles

In a series first, Townfall is played entirely in first-person perspective, meaning you see everything through the eyes of Simon (though a few chapters put you in Zoe or Richard's shoes).

Since you can only see what's immediately in front of you, you'll constantly dart your gaze left and right and use sound cues, as well as your CRTV to follow the threats around you.

The player runs into a clinic and locks the door just in time to prevent a gruesome creature from attacking. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

That change has come with some growing pains, though; button prompts will appear when you approach an interactable object or item you can pick up, but the symbols and text that appear onscreen are often too small to read very quickly.

Too often while scrambling to find a closet to hide from a monster's hunt, I lost critical seconds panning around for the "X" button prompt to show up. Sometimes, while trying to avoid an enemy in a cramped hallway, I jammed on the button thinking I was picking up a first-aid item — only to slam a door shut in my face, leading to my demise.

Simon is looking for Zoe Ellis (Kezia Burrows), a nurse who might have answers about why he's found himself in St. Amelia. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

Masters of unlocking

Silent Hill: Townfall is at its best when you're exploring a chunk of the town like it's a giant puzzle box, searching through spooky homes and alleyways to reach the next destination.

You'll consult your paper map, marked in red to denote locked doors and areas you've already searched, planning your next route, making a mental note of enemies and taking a deep breath before setting out for the next trinket or clue. Each step is just close enough that you're compelled to follow the crumb trail for up to hours at a time.

You'll look through old emails and programs on floppy disks using old '90s-era computers in Silent Hill: Townfall. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

You'll also spend a lot of time staring at '90s-era computer screens, checking answering machines for messages next to landline phones or searching for floppy disks and cassette tapes along the way.

This fascination with vintage tech is a signature of developer Screen Burn, formerly known as No Code, who have used the unease you might feel from hearing a monitor's low capacitor hum to great effect in 2017's sleeper hit Stories Untold.

The Weight of it all

Things get really dangerous (and metaphysical) when St. Amelia is plunged into an alternate world, possibly manifesting a part of Simon's psyche. This world is bathed in a blood-red light. Black iron pipes block pathways that were once clear and enemies stalk you in greater numbers.

This is a signature of Silent Hill games, made even more menacing by the introduction of The Weight — a larger grotesque that can kill you the instant it catches you.

The "hide from the big bad" element is common in horror video games, and Screen Burn's team includes people who have worked on Alien: Isolation, one of that subgenre's high points.

Silent Hill: Townfall is at its most dangerous when it throws you into a haunted alternate version of St. Amelia, bathed in blood-red light. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

Here, though, it's an exercise in frustration, as The Weight moves too erratically and can sometimes park itself in front of your hiding spot, leaving you stuck for minutes at a time.

Most frustratingly, if it catches you, the game will often respawn you right where you died — with The Weight still standing in front of you, setting off a frustrating loop of death.

And while the sights in St. Amelia's nightmare version are initially impressive, as time goes on the dreary visuals become tiresome.

It's especially a shame because some parts of "normal" St. Amelia stand out in their novelty. A flat in a block of corporate housing shifts and transforms seemingly at the whim of a series of haunted cassette tapes. Later, Richard attempts to climb an office tower infested with monsters, snatching precious shotgun shells dropped by the bodies of those who unsuccessfully came before him.

Another attempt? For die-hards, maybe

After a gruelling 18-plus hours in Silent Hill: Townfall, I reached the story's conclusion — or one of them, anyways. The game has at least five alternate endings, each (hopefully) shedding light on the tragedy of St. Amelia — and Richard, Zoe and Simon's part in it.

The series is known to focus on vibes more than a coherent plot, but even then I felt frustrated by how few questions were satisfyingly answered — or how many more times I'd have to play it to uncover new details.

A grim situation faces Zoe the nurse in Silent Hill: Townfall. (Screen Burn/Konami Digital Entertainment and Annapurna Interactive)

The excitement I felt exploring the town was at odds with the agony I felt hiding from The Weight — to the point where it might be only the most die-hard Silent Hill fans, or those who truly love every contradictory flavour of horror in video games, who will have the stomach to finish the entire journey once, let alone many times over.

World.title: Identifying unclaimed ashes at N.S. funeral home through DNA ‘very challenging,’ says expert
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While some families in Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley grapple with uncertainty after discovering they may not have buried the actual ashes of their loved ones, an expert in DNA testing says the technology only offers a faint hope of positively identifying the remains.

Several families who used the services of the former Serenity Funeral Home were informed by the home's new owners earlier this month that ashes belonging to their dead loved ones were found in storage.

Michelle Carey had used Serenity when her father, Hendrik (Hank) Sabean, died in 2018. Sabean had specific instructions for his funeral arrangements, including dealing with the funeral home.

Now, having to go through the burial process all over again and being unsure whose remains the family actually buried, Carey said she’s skeptical that they’ll ever be sure of the identity of the remains.

“Well, my sister and I talked and did a little bit of research and it would be very, very difficult to do any sort of DNA testing,” said Carey. “How do we know for sure that what we're going to get is, in fact, our father's remains this time?”

Dean Hildebrand, who manages the forensic DNA laboratory at the British Columbia Institute of Technology, said it’s very challenging to get enough DNA from ashes to make an identification.

“It's not to say that some people or some scientists have reported that you can still find trace amounts of DNA,” he said. “But finding trace amounts of DNA is different from being able to use that [DNA].”

Hildebrand said DNA is surprisingly robust, noting that labs very often get full DNA profiles from human remains that were in car or building fires, despite the damage done.

But the conditions of a crematorium, 900 C for up to three hours, result in a total breakdown of all organic matter.

"[It’s] kind of a worst-case scenario for isolating,” said Hildebrand.

He said throughout his career he’s dealt with identifying remains from ashes mixed up involving other funeral homes. But in this case there are a significant number of remains, according to the new owners of Serenity funeral homes, East Coast Memorial.

While the odds of making an identification are low, Hildebrand said he wouldn’t say it’s impossible.

He said that it’s worth testing in case a fragment of bone could yield useful DNA.

Hendrik (Hank) Sabean was 67 when he died in 2018. He had specific wishes for his funeral arrangements, which included dealing with Serenity Funeral Home for the service and burial of his ashes. (Amanda Sabean)

“I think it's worth the effort,” he said. “But of course, you have to set expectations.”

Carey said she was told the ashes the family buried may contain a small metal disc with an ID number on it, which could lead to identifying the remains.

But the presence of that ID number may be the only way to find out who they originally buried back in 2018.

“I want to believe that what they're telling me is true, that they do in fact have our father's remains,” said Carey. “But it will be very difficult to find out who is the person that was buried.”

The province and Nova Scotia's regulator of funeral directors are investigating.

World.title: It’s showy, it’s insubstantial, but Carney’s EU scheme is slick politics: Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

There’s no such thing as “associate membership” in the European Union and nobody knows what it means, but Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal for it has proven to be a dazzling distraction as he flounders in a trade war with the United States. Brian Lilley talks this week with Anand Menon, an EU studies specialist based in England, and Carlo Dade, international policy director at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy. Menon details the formidable challenges and hazards of Canada trying to displace North American trade with Europe, and why it probably won’t happen, although he says there is room for improved co-operation. And while Carney’s idea is dubious and of questionable benefit, Dade explains why he thinks we might not have much choice but to try it. (Recorded Sept. 17, 2026.)

World.title: Ontario teachers told they serve white supremacist system that must be destroyed
World.content:
Article content

The word from Europe appears to be that “associate membership” status with the European Union isn’t actually a thing, despite the offer of such from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Multiple EU diplomats interviewed by The Telegraph said they still had no idea what the term meant, and were skeptical of member states approving any kind of special relationship with Ottawa. Said one, “she knows full well there will be no associate membership. But she needed a strong headline that goes outside the bubble.” And all this EU talk might be a good time to mention that, to some British eyes, the whole “cozying Canada up to the EU” thing seems to represent a bit of unfinished business for Prime Minister Mark Carney. As governor of the Bank of England, Carney was vocally opposed to Brexit in the lead-up to the U.K.’s 2016 vote on exiting the European Union, a position that led to calls for his resignation. As Conservative MP Jacob Rees-Mogg said at the time, “he has shown himself to be partial in a political debate when the Bank of England needs to be independent.” So, precisely 10 years after his efforts to prevent a British exit from the EU failed, Carney just so happens to be attempting some kind of Canadian entrance to the bloc.

World.title: Andrew Percy: Vancouver’s pro-crack smoking faction is out in force
World.content:
Article content

I lived in London for much of the past 15 years and whilst it has many problems of its own, what we have on the streets of Vancouver is just not seen in London or other cities in the way it is here. Yes, there are terribly sad scenes related to homelessness and addiction in other cities too, but living here now, I have had to become accustomed to people openly injecting or smoking crack pipes in the middle of the day and to that all too regular scene of people bent double and contorted by the cruelty of the substances they’ve consumed. I’ve walked into coffee shop bathrooms to see brown stained tinfoil and the air thick with the aftermath of what was just smoked, open drug use on buses and of course the sad scene of people almost unidentifiable as human-beings comatose in alley ways.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Falklands government extends all offshore oil licences for five years
World.content:
Falklands government extends all offshore oil licences for five years

21st Monday, September 2026 - 12:54 UTC Full article

Portfolio holder for Trade, Industry, and Mineral Resources MLA Cheryl Roberts

The Falkland Islands Government announced on Monday the extension of all existing offshore hydrocarbons production licences, for an initial period of five years with a further two optional years at its discretion, and said the decision has “the full support of the UK Government”.

The licences, all currently in the exploration term, will be subject to satisfactory progress by licensees against their work programmes. The Department of Mineral Resources is now working with holders on enhanced work programmes for the extension period, including commitments to drilling additional appraisal wells. The statement did not specify how many licences are covered or who holds them; registered holders include Rockhopper Exploration, with subsidiaries Falkland Oil & Gas and Desire Petroleum, and Navitas Petroleum Development and Production.

The announcement comes at a moment shaped by the calendar: the PL001 licence was due to expire on December 31 this year, and its partners had been negotiating an extension with the archipelago's government since early 2026.

Separately, the government approved the acquisition by Navitas Petroleum Atlantic Limited of a 65% stake in licence area PL001, a deal announced on March 2 that had been awaiting this authorisation. JHI Associates retains the remaining 35% through its subsidiary JHI Falkland. The block covers some 1,126 square kilometres in around 500 metres of water and borders PL032 to the west, where the Sea Lion project is being developed. JHI estimates its combined prospects at 3.1 billion barrels, with Tyche and Dinlas at around 400 million recoverable barrels each; these are company estimates, not independently verified.

MLA Cheryl Roberts, portfolio holder for Trade, Industry and Mineral Resources, said the extensions “provide security to operators, enabling them to continue to invest and develop their acreage”. She added: “These are our resources to develop, and we will ensure they are developed responsibly, in line with best global practice with regards to environmental and safety standards, in order to deliver long-term benefits to current, and future generations of Falkland Islanders.”

The move comes six days after the Foreign Office published guidance backing companies operating in the archipelago, and three days after Britain's Minister for the Overseas Territories, Uma Kumaran, described Argentine proceedings against those companies as “unacceptable”.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago and maintains that licences granted by the Falkland Islands Government are invalid. It has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied, three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors, and on Thursday sent Congress a bill extending prohibitions to all natural resources on the continental shelf. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: The pending fiscal adjustment dominates the final stretch of Brazil's presidential race
World.content:
The pending fiscal adjustment dominates the final stretch of Brazil's presidential race

21st Monday, September 2026 - 10:42 UTC Full article

According to Brazilian press reports, they pressed the urgency of a fiscal adjustment given rising public debt

Brazil heads into the October 4 general election with a growing economy and unemployment at record lows, but with one debate dominating the campaign's final stretch: the cut in public spending that analysts and business leaders agree will fall to whoever wins, whether President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Brazilians will elect a president, 27 governors, the entire Chamber of Deputies and two thirds of the Senate. If no candidate passes half the valid votes, a runoff follows on October 25. Alongside Lula, running with Geraldo Alckmin, and Bolsonaro, a senator for Rio de Janeiro for the Liberal Party running with Alfredo Gaspar, the field includes Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema.

Recent polls diverge and all fall within their margins of error in a prospective runoff. Quaest, for O Globo, surveyed 2,004 people between September 10 and 13 with a two-point margin: Bolsonaro 42% and Lula 40% in a runoff, and Lula 36% against 31% in the first round. BTG Pactual/Nexus, from September 11 to 13, with 2,003 interviews and the same margin, gave Lula 47% and Bolsonaro 46%. AtlasIntel/Bloomberg, released Thursday with 5,018 cases and a one-point margin, put Bolsonaro at 47.2% and Lula at 46.8%. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 points.

The economic debate was triggered by a dinner Lula hosted in late August at the Alvorada palace for some fifteen business leaders and bankers, including representatives of JBS, BTG Pactual, Itaú and Bradesco. According to Brazilian press reports, they pressed the urgency of a fiscal adjustment given rising public debt. That same day the government presented its 2027 budget bill, aiming for a primary surplus of 0.5% of GDP through, among other measures, cuts to the civil service payroll.

Figures vary by source. Official and private estimates put public debt at around 82% of GDP, while a Trading Economics projection for 2026 places it at 83.5%. The Selic rate remains high, with a BBVA forecast of 13% for this year after 15% in 2025. The Central Bank projects 2% growth for 2026; the IMF estimates 2.4% this year and 2.2% next.

Lula points to unemployment at 5.4% in July, inflation at 4.22% in August, a minimum wage rising above inflation, and the income tax exemption for those earning under 5,000 reais, which reached 15 million taxpayers and was offset by a 10% minimum rate for some 140,000 high earners. Even so, Datafolha measured 50% disapproval against 47% approval.

Two economists consulted share the fiscal criticism. Emerson Marçal, of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation, says growth “is losing momentum” and that “from a fiscal standpoint, Lula's government was extremely profligate.” Otto Nogami, of Insper, says “excess spending is a concern because it is one of the most important factors weighing on investment.” Marçal warns the next government “will have to make a strong fiscal adjustment.” Both candidates promise one, but neither has detailed how it would be financed, and there have been no televised debates between them.

Household debt is at unprecedented levels: 82% of homes owe money and a third have fallen behind on a bill. On Thursday, Lula announced a 15% increase in the Bolsa Família benefit from October, taking it from around 620 to around 715 reais a month for twenty million families; his economic team says it will be funded by cuts elsewhere.

On foreign policy, Lula points to the European Union-Mercosur agreement, though its benefits have been clouded by Brussels' ban on Brazilian beef imports. Washington applied a second round of tariffs, with so many exemptions that the impact is limited; the tension began in 2025, in retaliation for the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez arrives in New York for UN General Assembly, ahead of meeting with Trump
World.content:
Delcy Rodríguez arrives in New York for UN General Assembly, ahead of meeting with Trump

21st Monday, September 2026 - 10:15 UTC Full article

Her address to the General Assembly is scheduled for Thursday, September 24

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, arrived in New York in the early hours of Monday to take part in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, days ahead of a planned meeting with US President Donald Trump on Tuesday.

Rodríguez landed at Teterboro Airport in Bergen County, New Jersey, where she was received by Sectoral Vice President for the Economy Calixto Ortega; First Deputy Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco; and, on the US side, chargé d'affaires John Barrett. “We arrive in New York with the resolve and hope of a people who believe in the encounter and union between nations,” she wrote on X.

Her address to the General Assembly is scheduled for Thursday, September 24. In the UN's official document, Rodríguez is listed as head of state, a protocol designation that formalises her standing with the organisation.

Venezuela's Ministry of Communication and Information had previously released a message describing the occasion as “a pivotal moment” and stating that the country “regains its standing” and “rejoins the world's diplomatic dynamic.” These are the Venezuelan government's own characterizations of what the visit means.

Tuesday's meeting with Trump, confirmed last week by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, will be the first between the two leaders and, as we have previously established, the first between a US president and a Venezuelan leader in more than eleven years, since the brief meeting between Barack Obama and Nicolás Maduro at the Summit of the Americas in Panama in 2015. Maduro, whom Washington describes as an “illegitimate former dictator and drug trafficker,” remains in US custody awaiting trial, following the military operation that led to his capture in January.

World.title: US investigates ICE shooting of Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin
World.content:
US investigates ICE shooting of Venezuelan delivery driver in Austin

21st Monday, September 2026 - 09:44 UTC Full article

An ICE agent got out of an unmarked truck, rammed Garcés Pérez's vehicle, then exited and fired at least five times

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded a Venezuelan man on Sunday in Austin, Texas, while he was making a delivery for DoorDash, in an incident the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) confirmed it is investigating alongside the FBI and which prompted calls for an independent investigation from local officials.

The wounded man was identified by his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, as Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28. The shooting occurred around 1 p.m. near the intersection of U.S. Highway 183 and Anderson Square, in North Austin. According to Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz, the man was shot in the torso and was transported in serious but stable condition. His lawyer, by contrast, placed the wound “in the back, below the neck,” and a witness who asked to be identified only as “Juan” said he saw two bullet wounds in the man's back after approaching the vehicle. DoorDash confirmed Garcés Pérez was working as a delivery driver at the time and said it was investigating.

Accounts of how the incident began also diverge.
