Austin City Council member Mike Siegel, who arrived at the scene, said an ICE agent got out of an unmarked truck, rammed Garcés Pérez's vehicle, then exited and fired at least five times. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said a foot pursuit may have preceded the shooting, though she described the information as preliminary. The Texas Department of Public Safety confirmed it had received a request for assistance from ICE over a vehicle pursuit involving Garcés Pérez's car.

Accounts of the wounded man's immigration status conflict. A DHS spokesperson said Garcés Pérez “entered illegally” under the Biden administration and had a final removal order. His lawyer, Lincoln-Goldfinch, said that, based on the information available to her team, he had entered the country lawfully and had previously held a valid work permit; his wife said she was unaware of any removal order and believed he was still in immigration proceedings. Neither account has been independently confirmed.

Garcés Pérez was discharged from Dell Seton Medical Center around 4:30 p.m. and transferred to ICE custody, a hospital attorney told Lincoln-Goldfinch. His family had not been able to reach him or obtain information about his condition. Austin's Democratic mayor, Kirk Watson, condemned the incident and said local police, who were not involved in the operation, would carry out an independent investigation alongside the Texas Rangers. The DHS spokesperson said the Homeland Security Investigations office is leading the inquiry into the agent who fired.

Austin Congressman Greg Casar warned on X that if Garcés Pérez is deported, “the key witness to the shooting disappears,” and sent a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding an investigation and the preservation of evidence, including the man's continued presence in the country. Congressman Joaquín Castro called for the release of the agents' body-camera footage.

The incident comes just over two months after ICE shot and killed Mexican immigrant Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, in an operation in which he was not the person being sought, as DHS itself acknowledged; that case is under review by a grand jury. According to a Washington Post report published in July, at least six drivers have died and eleven more have been wounded by gunfire from federal immigration agents since Trump returned to the White House. In January, two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were shot and killed during an ICE operation in Minneapolis.

World.title: Canada invites the UK to join its economic alliance with the European Union
World.content:
Canada invites the UK to join its economic alliance with the European Union

21st Monday, September 2026 - 09:31 UTC Full article

“Why don't we team up?” the minister said, adding that “the world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change.”

Canada's Finance Minister, François-Philippe Champagne, has proposed that the United Kingdom join the economic alliance Ottawa is negotiating with the European Union, in comments to the BBC. “We are independent and sovereign, but we are stronger together,” he said. The British government has not publicly responded to the proposal.

“We need to look at partnership in a different way and the great thing is that when you look at Canada - and I would say the United Kingdom - we share the same values. We are very aligned in our vision of the world. Why don't we team up?” the minister said, adding that “the world has changed. America has changed. So we need to change.”

The remarks follow European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to “open the door” to Canada becoming the bloc's first associate member, a status not provided for in the EU treaties and whose details have yet to be formalised. Champagne described Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's trip to Strasbourg as an effort “to build the alliance of the future”. Carney, a former Bank of England governor, has previously floated an alliance of “middle powers” working together on economic growth, resilience and security.

Trump responded by threatening further tariffs on the European Union if the associate membership plan proved “hostile” to the United States. He called the idea laughable and described Canada as a “terrible trading partner”.

Canada has been in a trade war with the United States since talks collapsed at the last moment in August and both sides imposed tit-for-tat tariffs. Champagne said the conflict was not one his country chose: “We responded because at some stage you have to say 'enough is enough'. No one can infringe on our economic sovereignty.” He described Canada's response as “measured, targeted and strategic”, “dollar-for-dollar, tariff-for-tariff”, said Ottawa is not seeking escalation and would “re-engage at the right time” with Washington. He added that affected industries would be supported “as long as it takes” and that the dispute offers a “golden opportunity” to diversify markets.

The invitation places the United Kingdom in a delicate position: it renegotiated its own trade deal with the United States in June last year, and the Canadian initiative raises questions about its post-Brexit positioning towards Europe. Carney met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool during last week's European trip, and Champagne attended a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday alongside Chancellor John Healey. Burnham will meet Trump for the first time this week, at the UN General Assembly in New York.

Among the specific elements Carney has raised are Canadian participation in European university, scientific research, artificial intelligence and defence funding schemes, mobility for young people on both sides of the Atlantic to study and live, Canadian supply of critical minerals and gas, and access to European advanced technologies.

Both Ottawa and Brussels see the mechanism as potentially serving other like-minded countries that would never become full members, with Australia cited as an example.

World.title: Bachelet withdraws her UN bid after the third Security Council straw poll
World.content:
Bachelet withdraws her UN bid after the third Security Council straw poll

21st Monday, September 2026 - 04:36 UTC Full article

“I am convinced that leadership is not only knowing when to move forward. It is also knowing when to step aside,” she said in a video posted on her social media accounts

Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet announced on Saturday that she is withdrawing her candidacy for United Nations Secretary-General, a day after the third informal Security Council consultation, in which she lost ground compared with earlier rounds.

“I am convinced that leadership is not only knowing when to move forward. It is also knowing when to step aside so the process can run its course. The results of the Security Council straw polls tell me that moment has come,” she said in a video posted on her social media accounts. She attributed the adverse context to “strong winds blowing against principles such as multilateralism, against international law that is permanently transgressed,” and added: “I do not regret having taken on this great challenge. We contributed to placing on the global agenda that the next Secretary-General should be a woman from Latin America.”

The consultations are informal, non-binding and secret, held among the Security Council's fifteen members with three options: encourage, discourage or no opinion. Their results tend to leak to the press. According to preliminary figures published by PassBlue, an outlet specialising in UN coverage, Bachelet received one “encourage,” eleven “discourage” and three “no opinion” in Friday's round, the highest level of discouragement she recorded during the process; in July she had placed fourth. After these consultations, the five permanent members — the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom — must agree on a recommendation to the General Assembly, and each holds a veto. António Guterres completes his second term at the end of 2026.

Bachelet, 74, was president of Chile from 2006 to 2010 and from 2014 to 2018, was the first director of UN Women between 2011 and 2013, and headed the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights from September 2018 to June 2022. Her candidacy, presented in February by then president Gabriel Boric, sought to make her the first woman to lead the organisation and the second person from Latin America to hold the post, after Peru's Javier Pérez de Cuéllar.

On March 24, José Antonio Kast's government withdrew Chile's sponsorship, after assessing “the dispersion of candidates in the region and its impact on the chances of success.” Chile's foreign ministry said the country backs none of the remaining options and reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and to reform of the UN system. Interior Minister and spokesman Claudio Alvarado said the government had warned, even before taking office, that this was “a candidacy for which no solid base of support was apparent.” Bachelet retained the backing of Mexico and Brazil; she thanked Claudia Sheinbaum and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by name.

Boric responded on Sunday on X that “the dignity and consistency” with which she approached the bid “will be an example that endures in history,” and said that “even if there is a temporary defeat, that defeat will become a seed for the future.” Mexico's foreign ministry said Bachelet holds “unquestionable credentials.” In Chile, the withdrawal triggered mutual recriminations: figures close to Boric blamed Kast for dropping state support, while the opposition argued the outgoing government had failed to secure international backing before launching the bid.

Before the withdrawal, the race comprised five women and three men. Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of UNCTAD, and Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, a former foreign minister, lead the consultations. Argentina's Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, also lost support in Friday's round.

World.title: Super Bowl 2027: NFL confirms SoFi Stadium host, eyes on a Rams home game
World.content:
Super Bowl 2027: NFL confirms SoFi Stadium host, eyes on a Rams home game

21st Monday, September 2026 - 00:56 UTC Full article

The NFL has officially announced Sunday, February 14, 2027 as the date and location for Super Bowl LXI: SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. The date is based on the traditional calendar of the league, having the championship game on the second Sunday in February. The timing also makes it a unique sporting event as the largest game in American football will be coming on Valentine's Day.

The announcement has stirred up the Superbowl 2027 Rams rumors, as fans envision the Los Angeles Rams winning another Superbowl in their home stadium. Anyone who has been on the edge of the conversation and the futures markets in the early days of the championships can also check out resources like best bookmaker bonuses, as they watch expectations evolve ahead of the start of the 2027 season.

A familiar story: The Rams' historic Super Bowl LVI win at SoFi Stadium

SoFi Stadium is already a place of special significance in Rams history. The Los Angeles Rams were the only team in NFL history to win the Super Bowl at home when they defeated the Cincinnati Bengals 23-20 in Super Bowl LVI in February 2022. The win gave the franchise their second Super Bowl championship and made the stadium in Inglewood a significant place for the franchise.

Head coach Sean McVay and quarterback Matthew Stafford were the orchestrators of this famous win. Stafford, the No. 1 overall pick by the Detroit Lions back in 2009, was traded to the Rams ahead of the 2021 season and delivered several clutch fourth-quarter plays during that postseason run, including the go-ahead touchdown pass to Cooper Kupp in the Super Bowl LVI win itself, and McVay was one of the youngest coaches to win the Lombardi Trophy. The partnership was a reflection of the Rams' strategy of pairing trusted stars with fresh ideas.

That history has created the 2027 event with an obvious story line. The Rams would have the once-in-a-while opportunity to have a Super Bowl in the home stadium again in five years.

The road to 2027: Can the Rams make it to the big game at home?

Any analysis of the Rams making the playoffs to Super Bowl LXI is still in the world of possibility. The NFL is constantly evolving and a lot of things come into play when it comes to success, such as player health, draft development, salary-cap figures, free agents, and coaching stability. The NFC is still very competitive, and even the better teams will have a hard time getting through the regular season and playoffs.

The Rams have been a team that has always had a clear plan and that plan has been to maximize elite quarterback play, develop young talent and have a strong coaching staff. That's going to be crucial if they want to transform their Super Bowl '27 host into a real home-field advantage.

Key personal and team statuses

At the helm of the Rams' football operation is Sean McVay. Since taking over as head coach in 2017, his creativity and ability to change his game has defined the team. The team's solid foundation with McVay will give it continuity, but the future of the team will be determined by the quality of the coaching staff's development of the next generation of players.

Matthew Stafford enters 2026 as the reigning NFL MVP, fresh off a career year at age 38 in which he threw a career-high 46 touchdown passes against just eight interceptions and led the league with more than 4,700 passing yards, powering the NFL's highest-scoring offense. That performance, paired with an aggressive offseason that brought in Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and lured Aaron Donald out of retirement, made the Rams the consensus favorites to reach Super Bowl LXI on their own turf. The start to the season has complicated that story, however: LA was upset 27-7 by the rival San Francisco 49ers in a season-opening trip to Melbourne, Australia, with Stafford managing just 155 yards and an interception before being pulled late in the fourth quarter. Head coach Sean McVay has already spoken publicly about how difficult that result was to swallow, and turning that result into a distant memory quickly is now the team's most immediate challenge before the Rams can even think about a home Super Bowl.

Beyond Stafford, the Rams enter 2026 with arguably the deepest roster of the McVay era. Wide receivers Puka Nacua (an NFL-best 129 catches for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns in 2025) and Davante Adams (the league leader in touchdown catches) give Stafford two elite targets, while running back Kyren Williams has rushed for more than 1,100 yards in three straight seasons. On defense, the additions of Garrett and a returning Donald joined a unit that already ranked ninth in the league and added 47 sacks last season, alongside cornerback Trent McDuffie to shore up a secondary that had been the roster's clearest weakness. The lingering questions are age and durability: Stafford is 38, Donald is 35 and has not played in two and a half years, and the offensive line lost longtime right tackle Rob Havenstein to retirement, leaving significant responsibility on unproven replacements.

Early projections and expert opinions

Entering the season, most analysts rated the Rams as the outright favorite in the NFC, if not the entire league, given the scale of their offseason investment. The New York Post's own roster breakdown graded the offense A-, the defense A, and the coaching staff A, concluding that anything short of a deep playoff run would be considered a disappointment given the talent assembled. The Week 1 defeat in Australia has not erased that outlook, but it has introduced early uncertainty about execution, special teams reliability (an area that contributed to their NFC Championship loss the previous season), and offensive line depth, three factors that will likely define whether the preseason hype translates into a home Super Bowl appearance. Meanwhile, experts understand that a lot can shift between now and the 2027 season.

If you're going to have a Super Bowl run, it takes a long time. Injuries, new NFC threats, and offseason decisions can change the landscape of the league. Therefore, the Rams Super Bowl prospects will continue to develop as the team nears championship.

Planning your Super Bowl LXI experience: tickets and viewing

Super Bowl LXI fans should keep in mind that official general ticket availability and pricing information is released closer to the Super Bowl. Access options include NFL distribution programs, team-related channels, corporate allocations, hospitality packages, and verified secondary marketplaces.

Tickets for a Super Bowl are typically one of the most expensive sporting events anywhere in the world, particularly in the big, entertainment markets like Los Angeles. Premiums are expected on this game as it's around SoFi Stadium, and potentially a game at the home of the Rams.

Super Bowl LXI should be widely viewed around the world via ESPN and ABC coverage, according to those who are viewing remotely. The broadcast will further the NFL's legacy of making the game look like a big entertainment affair with football, music and cultural programming.

The Super Bowl 2027 location gives Los Angeles another opportunity to showcase its ability to host the NFL's biggest occasion. Whether the Rams can turn a roster built for exactly this moment into a home-field Super Bowl appearance remains to be seen, especially after a humbling season-opening defeat exposed real questions about execution and depth. But with an MVP quarterback, a retooled defense anchored by two of the league's most dominant pass rushers, and a fanbase that has already seen this story end in triumph once before, the Superbowl 2027 Rams conversation will remain one of the defining storylines of the NFL season.

World.title: British columnist proposes London take half of Falklands oil revenues
World.content:
British columnist proposes London take half of Falklands oil revenues

20th Sunday, September 2026 - 00:25 UTC Full article

The column describes the Argentine campaign in terms of bullying and calls the sovereignty claim spurious

A column published on Saturday in the British newspaper The Telegraph proposed that the UK Treasury take half of the tax revenues generated by the Falklands oil industry, in exchange for increased defense spending in the South Atlantic and a diplomatic push against Argentina.

The proposal, by economics columnist Matthew Lynn, would alter the existing arrangement under which the archipelago retains all of its energy revenues, on the basis that it is a territory required to be self-financing apart from defense costs. Lynn argues that this arrangement “clearly cannot hold” in the face of Argentina's hardened position, and contends that a territory of a few thousand people would scarcely know what to do with the full revenues the industry could generate.

The column appeared three days after federal judge Mariel Borruto, of the Río Grande court in Tierra del Fuego, issued an injunction ordering Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum to refrain from drilling, installing infrastructure or beginning hydrocarbon extraction at Sea Lion. The measure stands until an environmental impact assessment is completed before the Argentine authority, and requires the companies to report within ten days on the project's status, its contractors, financial backers and insurers.

The suit was filed in early September by the La Plata-based Centre of Former Combatants of the Malvinas Islands and an association of environmental lawyers, on environmental, sovereignty and procedural grounds. London does not recognize the jurisdiction of Argentine courts over the archipelago, which limits the ruling's practical reach. In 2015 a court in the same province ordered the seizure of some US$156 million, which was never enforced.

Rockhopper and Navitas said in a joint statement that their licenses were lawfully granted by the Falklands government and that they do not anticipate any material effect on the project or its timetable, with drilling due in early 2027 and first oil in 2028.

Lynn puts Sea Lion's reserves at 900 million barrels and their value at between £5 billion and £6 billion, adding that initial estimates for developments of this kind typically multiply. The column does not identify a source for those figures. The most recent independent report on the project, by Netherland, Sewell & Associates, works from a long-term Brent assumption of US$76 per barrel and puts the capacity of the first two phases at 55,000 barrels per day, with a further 125,000 to be added by a second FPSO.

The column describes the Argentine campaign in terms of bullying and calls the sovereignty claim spurious.

World.title: Inside ‘Facing El Chapo’: An interview with screenwriter Bernardo Esquinca
World.content:
Netflix’s “Facing El Chapo” (originally titled “La Captura”) has established itself as a true milestone for Mexican cinema. Directed by Chava Cartas, the film racked up more than 18 million views in its first weekend.

What’s truly surprising is that, without a massive advertising campaign and driven primarily by word-of-mouth, this police drama managed to claim the No. 1 spot on the global Top 10 chart, officially crowning itself as the streaming service’s most successful non-English-language debut of the year.

Inspired by the real-world events of the January 2016 military operation “Cisne Negro” and the journalistic chronicles of Héctor de Mauleón, the plot reconstructs the third and final arrest of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera.

However, the story does not focus on the drug trafficker or his head of security, Jorge Iván “El Cholo” Gastelum. Instead, the film portrays the suffocating ordeal of two police officers — portrayed by Alfonso Herrera and Noé Hernández — who, by a twist of fate, arrest the drug lord during a routine traffic stop on a highway in Los Mochis, Sinaloa, and must temporarily guard him before criminal cells locate their position. Of course, complications soon pile up as the officers struggle to maintain control of the situation and resist both Guzmán’s attempts to bribe them and the external siege.

La captura | Tráiler oficial | Netflix

Watch this video on YouTube

Although rooted in a criminal environment, “Facing El Chapo” distances itself from glorifying crime or illicit opulence. Instead, it weaves together a buddy cop drama, psychological suspense and a modern western to tell a story where the dramatic tension stems from resisting crime rather than participating in it.

To understand how this Mexican streaming phenomenon came to be, we spoke exclusively with its screenwriter, Bernardo Esquinca, a renowned master of horror and crime fiction, as well as the creator of the celebrated “Casasola” series.

The official secrecy and the challenge of the screenplay

While writing “Facing El Chapo,” Esquinca faced a major challenge: the official secrecy surrounding the case.

Beyond the widely known events that took place at the motel — where the officers were locked in while the drug lord tried to bribe them — the specific details of the operation were, and remain, scarce. Furthermore, the identities of the real police officers are under strict protection, and the production team had no contact with them.

Faced with this lack of information, the author used Héctor de Mauleón’s journalistic chronicles — “Cómo atrapamos al Chapo” and “Veinte minutos a solas con ‘El Chapo’” — as a roadmap, taking creative liberties to develop the characters, expand on the situations and craft a solid plot.

“The screenplay presented several challenges, as does any story that needs to be adapted for the big screen,” Esquinca tells me. “But for me, the main (challenge) was addressing the fact that most of the action (in the early drafts) took place on the highway. Precisely because so little is actually known about it.”

With this in mind, the screenwriter explains that his priority was to prevent the narrative from becoming monotonous if it were confined to the road trip. After extensive research, he decided to expand the dramatic universe by devising narrative detours, such as a sudden lack of gas or an unexpected encounter with local criminals (there are many other surprises, but I don’t want to give too much away).

A true story that steals the spotlight from drug trafficking

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bernardo Esquinca (@bernardo.esquinca)

It’s no secret that, over the past few decades, narco-genre productions have increased dramatically in Latin America, especially in Mexico. This narrative usually humanizes or glorifies the drug lord by portraying his lavish lifestyle, his unlimited power and an almost religious aura. “Facing El Chapo,” however, subverts this tendency by shifting the spotlight entirely to two honest and dedicated Federal Police officers.

The plot centers on the officers’ experiences and the enormous moral dilemma they face in balancing their institutional duty against the potentially deadly consequences of holding one of the world’s most dangerous criminals in custody.

The author explains it clearly: “It’s not the typical drug trafficking story that focuses on the bad guys — the drug traffickers, the villains — but rather on the police officers who capture El Chapo and do the right thing.”

Without a doubt, this shift in focus is the story’s main appeal: taking the spotlight away from drug trafficking and placing it on ordinary citizens who, despite the violence in the country, continue to strive to do their best.

Esquinca believes that the resounding success of “Facing El Chapo” offers important lessons that should not be overlooked. For the industry, the message is “that stories about the good guys can be told successfully.” At the same time, the message the audience is sending “is that we do want stories like this.”

The rescue of the Mexican hero

Much like the film “Counterstrike” (2025), “Facing El Chapo” continues the artistic vision of Mexican filmmaker Chava Cartas, who has embarked on a crusade to restore the image of the national hero. His primary goal has been to challenge the cultural prejudice that almost relentlessly brands the authorities of Mexico as incompetent or corrupt.

In this project, it’s a great move for Cartas and Esquinca to steer clear of the superhuman, nearly indestructible action hero of commercial cinema. The story instead focuses on flesh-and-blood characters who feel fear, struggle to get by and have a family to protect, defining heroism as their ability to maintain moral integrity in the face of extreme danger.

Thus, we meet Arturo Carmona (Herrera), overwhelmed by financial pressures as he prepares for the arrival of a new child, and Héctor Rosales (Hernández), recently transferred to the police station and facing the vulnerability that comes with retirement.

“This film precisely offers many reflections, but the main takeaway is that there really are good people out there,” Esquinca says. “And those good people can succeed, and their adventures can be very exciting and keep you on the edge of your seat.”

Beyond the bullets

Although the production features scenes of armed confrontations, tactical operations and highway chases, the true dramatic power of “Facing El Chapo” lies in the way the events are told. Beginning with the accidental arrest, Esquinca opts for an almost claustrophobic psychological suspense that transforms the story into an intense survival thriller.

In this story, Carmona and Rosales are partners who have recently been assigned to work together, so neither of them trusts the other very much. In their unexpected situation with Guzmán and his lieutenant, the tension grows palpable, as the officers don’t know each other well and aren’t sure who to rely on while their surroundings become increasingly dangerous.

When asked about the emotional suffocation that defines the plot, Esquinca explains that the main driving force behind his writing was to put the viewer in the officers’ shoes.

“The viewer should feel as if they were there, as if they had to make the choice,” he says. “So the guiding principle was basically: What would you do? That’s what we’re trying to convey to the viewer the whole time. What would you do if you were in their place? Would you take the money or resist?”

The high cost of doing the right thing

With no complacent endings or filters to gloss over the country’s harsh social reality, “Facing El Chapo” highlights the true value of everyday heroes. A very human lesson that, to be fair, is always worth revisiting.

Esquinca notes that, although both the historical events and the film demonstrate that good can triumph over evil, it’s clear that doing the right thing can come at a significant cost.

“That ending also tells us that this (being a hero) comes at a cost, and they had to pay a price,” Esquinca says. “They had to change their lives and go into hiding … because there is a danger — a sword of Damocles, as they say — hanging over them.”

Almost a month after its release, this 91-minute film remains a strong contender on global charts. If you haven’t seen “Facing El Chapo” yet, there’s still time to discover it. If you have, it’s worth returning to it with a fresh perspective.

Carolina Alvarado is a Venezuelan journalist who has devoted much of her career to creative writing, university teaching and social work. She has been published in Lady Science, Latina Media, Global Comment, Psiquide, Cinetopic, Get Me Giddy and Reader’s Digest, among others.

World.title: Why pozole is more than just a Mexican stew
World.content:
No state in Mexico has raised pozole to the level of culinary art quite like Guerrero. Of course, that’s only appropriate. Pozole is a stew (excepting pozole seco) whose main ingredient is corn — nixtamalized maize, to be exact, or hominy in English — and Guerrero is where corn was first created, 9,000 years ago.

Originally domesticated in the Balsas River Basin in Guerrero from a species of teosinte called parviglumis, corn was a wonder of the ancient world. It took over 1200 years to spread as far as Panama and 2300 to reach Peru, but corn eventually became one of the most consumed foods on the planet. In its birthplace of Mexico, where there are now at least 59 varieties, it has always been assumed that pozole was a natural evolution from this invention.

The origins of pozole

However, the origins of pozole are shrouded in controversy and contention. For instance, one of the most commonly shared stories about pozole is that the Mexica (Aztec) elites ate pozole with human flesh; essentially, committing cannibalism. This may or may not be true, but it must be noted that the oft-cited source, Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, never mentions pozole by name.

In fact, Alberto Peralta de Legarreta, who wrote the book on pre-Columbian food in Mexico (literally: “Cultura gastronómica en la Mesoamérica prehispánica”), insists that the word pozole was never used once in any pre-Hispanic text. He also explains that the Spanish authors who shaped our perception of this era, like Sahagún and Fray Diego Durán, didn’t use it either. They mention dishes of cooked corn, which may or may not have been pozole. After all, there are lots of corn dishes in Mexico.

The birth of pozole blanco, rojo and verde variations

That doesn’t mean pozole didn’t exist in pre-Columbian Mexico. It’s almost certainly a staple from great antiquity. But we don’t know much about its origins, only how it’s made — and even that is controversial. The first cookbook recipe Peralta could find for pozole is from 1937, a year before the Mexican president of the time, Lázaro Cárdenas, took control of the oil industry by expropriating wells from foreign owners.

This period of patriotic fervor was profound for Mexican cuisine, particularly with dishes that mimic the colors of the Mexican flag, like the rojo, blanco and verde variations of pozole. One of them, pozole verde, my favorite, certainly originated in Guerrero, and pozole blanco, the original form of the dish, is sometimes credited to the state, too.

However, the latter statement, like all those dealing with the early history of pozole, is unprovable. Nevertheless, Guerrero is famous for pozole verde and pozole blanco, just as Jalisco and Michoacán are hailed for their pozole rojo, and Colima for pozole seco.

How pozole is made in Guerrero

Corn is nixtamalized for pozole via several methods — typically by boiling it in an alkaline solution. Afterward, the kernels are left to steep overnight before being washed to remove the outer shell. Notably, this is the prelude to grinding to make nixtamalized tortillas. However, for those who don’t want to go through the traditional effort of making pozole from scratch, nixtamalized corn in a can may be found at almost any grocery.

The corn used as the base for pozole varies from state to state. In Guerrero, they use the ancho variety, not cacahuazintle, a more generically acceptable type. This is the first of many ways the state distinguishes its pozoles. Pork is the protein of choice in Guerrero and for pozole verde, for instance, tomatillo is used to color and flavor the sauce, as are herbs like hoja santa and epazote.

To make pozole blanco, the pork-and-corn-simmering-broth acquires seasoning via ingredients like onion, garlic, bay leaf, salt, pepper and oregano. It’s simple and delicious, with chilies added as preferred. Of course, depending upon what part of the state of Guerrero one resides in — coast, mountains or plateau — some regionally specific ingredients like eggs, chicharrón and sardines may be added to both pozole blanco and pozole verde.

In rare pozole verde recipes, chicken may be substituted for pork. This exception is observable nationwide, although pork is easily the most common meat in Guerrero and elsewhere. Then there are the fixings, added afterward — but more on that subject later.

Always on Thursday — the creation of jueves pozolero

The practice of serving pozole every Thursday, which originated in Guerrero and has now been picked up by restaurants in many states in Mexico, can be traced back to the 19th century in Iguala, where local families made it a custom. That’s one theory, anyway. Of course, many theories for how “jueves pozolero” began have been posited.

An earlier tale links the birth of jueves pozolero to a crucial event in Mexican history: namely, the Embrace of Acatempan, an 1821 agreement between military leaders Agustín de Iturbide and Vicente Guerrero in the town of that name, Teloloapan municipality, in Guerrero — yes, it was named for him — that paved the way for Mexico’s independence from Spain. After the Thursday rapprochement, the two generals declared a feast, with a pig roasted for pozole served in clay pots.

Another theory claims the practice arose near a famous nightclub in Acapulco in the 1980s — News Disco & Concert Hall or Baby’O, perhaps — where the music scene was especially popular on Wednesday nights. Thus, hungover patrons needed their pozole verde or blanco to cure the condition on Thursdays, and there was always a vendor nearby to assist.

But who knows? Almost nothing about pozole is known with certainty. There are only legends and lore, so why not embrace them like Iturbide embraced Guerrero?

Building the perfect pozole

There’s a process to taking all the fixings home and arranging them in the bowl. That’s part of the pleasure. The stew with pork and hominy is packaged in a large styrofoam cup and poured straight into the bowl. Then come the fixings.

Oregano, onion and dried chili powder are rolled up in small foil balls and added as desired … as are the chicharrón — which I crumble — radish, avocado and lime; squeezed in the soup only.

Lettuce or the alternative cabbage is optional, at least in my opinion. And, like all lovers of Guerrero-style pozole, I have developed strong opinions.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Guest who said ‘bueno, ya me voy’ at 9:14 p.m. reaches front gate at 1:37 a.m.
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Local resident Eduardo Ramírez made significant progress toward departing a dinner party Thursday night, successfully reaching the host’s iron front gate at 1:37 a.m., roughly four hours and 23 minutes after executing his opening farewell statement at 9:14 p.m.

According to witnesses, Ramírez, 34, began the departure protocol by standing up, patting his knees, and uttering the traditional phrase “bueno, ya me voy.” The action immediately triggered a standard defensive maneuver from the host, who insisted that leaving before sampling a freshly brewed pot of café de olla and a final slice of flan would constitute a breach of basic hospitality.

“I made the tactical error of standing up while still within three meters of the dining table,” Ramírez later explained, noting he had then been trapped in a deep conversation regarding a distant cousin’s apartment renovation. “Once the host offered the second coffee, I knew my projected arrival at home was no longer possible.”

Ramírez’s exit operation hit several predictable logistical bottlenecks. Between 10:15 p.m. and 11:30 p.m., for example, he entered the mandatory individual farewell round, which required separate physical goodbyes, three distinct inquiries into the health of extended family members, and a full exchange of local news with each of the 12 attendees.

The situation further stalled at 12:45 a.m. near the hallway mirror, when a chance comment about upcoming weekend plans prompted a 45-minute debate on optimal driving routes.

Ramírez was last observed with his hand on the front door handle, locked in a crucial discussion about a reliable mechanic while his host held open the front gate to ensure he did not leave without taking some leftovers.

World.title: Mexico City’s invisible recyclers fight for rights — and a share of the profits
World.content:
“Living from garbage doesn’t mean we become part of the garbage,” Soledad Mella told a packed auditorium in Iztapalapa, the Mexico City borough most burdened with the megacity’s massive waste stream. “We must dignify and defend our work. But above all, we must organize.”

The energetic grassroots recycler — referred to here in Mexico as a pepenadora — had carried her message all the way from Chile on an international tour through the region. She has carried that message from the streets and landfills of Santiago to international climate conferences and United Nations negotiations.

At Iztapalapa’s Forum on Inclusive Circular Economy, she spoke directly to Mexican pepenadores confronting a pivotal question: Will the country’s new circular economy become a route out of invisibility, or another lucrative industry that leaves them behind?

A push for legal recognition

Mexico is estimated to have some 400,000 pepenadores separating waste in landfills and open-air dumps, according to the forum’s organizers, and more than 2 million people working throughout the informal recycling economy. Many labor in precarious conditions without Social Security, stable wages or legal recognition.

The Sept. 10 forum brought grassroots recyclers together with industry representatives, officials, academics and environmentalists at the Centro Cultural Iztapalapa. The crowd filled the auditorium and spilled into the lobby, where participants exchanged contacts and examined products made from recovered materials.

The event was organized by the alcaldía, or borough, of Iztapalapa and environmental activist Arnold Ricalde, an adviser to Iztapalapa Mayor Aleida Alavez Ruiz. The goal was to shape how Mexico’s new General Circular Economy Law is put into practice — and ensure that grassroots recyclers are not once again left on the margins.

The law, published Jan. 19, seeks to extend the useful life of products, recover and reuse materials and establish “extended producer responsibility,” requiring manufacturers to take greater responsibility for what happens to their products after use.

It also creates a National Circular Economy System charged with developing a national program and coordinating government agencies. Crucially for Soledad’s colleagues, the law formally defines both grassroots recyclers and “inclusive recycling.”

Translating law into action

Much of the practical work remains unresolved, however. The law’s regulations have yet to be published, and questions remain about how recyclers will be registered, gain access to Social Security, form cooperatives and sell materials directly to industry.

René Sánchez Galindo, the Environment Ministry’s director general of legal affairs, said the regulations must balance sharply different interests as rules are developed for each type of product.

“We have to ensure that the measures are viable for everyone: industry, consumers and grassroots recyclers,” he said. “There must be what we call economic viability.”

“We want to help bring these concepts down to earth and bring the spirit of Iztapalapa to the law,” Alavez said. “A law that people don’t know how to use is not operative.”

Iztapalapa as a living laboratory

Iztapalapa has reason to position itself as a laboratory for inclusive recycling. The borough of 1.8 million people is one of the country’s most important centers for the recovery, repair and resale of discarded materials. It also collects roughly 2,200 metric tons of waste every day.

Alfonso González May, the borough’s director general of urban services, said only 2% to 3% of that waste was being separated when the current administration took office. The share has since risen to 8%, with separation taking place along 37 collection routes.

“This 8% has been achieved little by little, through different strategies,” González said. “We don’t want to give the mayor impressive numbers that have nothing to do with reality.”

The borough has expanded a once-weekly collection program for unwanted furniture, appliances and household debris into six weekly “junk days.” The program is intended to prevent residents from hiring informal haulers who may later abandon the items in vacant lots or on street corners.

Local initiatives and youth programs

Another initiative will collect used cooking oil at public markets and government offices. Residents will be encouraged to store the oil in bottles and deliver it separately to municipal collection crews. The oil will then be transferred to a private company for conversion into energy instead of being poured into drains, where it contributes to clogs and flooding.

The borough’s sustainable development office has identified more than 500 local circular-economy enterprises, ranging from cellphone, appliance and shoe repair shops to upholstery businesses and artisans working with discarded cardboard, textiles, wood and plastic.

Its “Soldando Iztapalapa” program trains young people to repair damaged metal furniture. Participants have restored more than 10,000 school desks that otherwise would have entered the waste stream, said Adriana Bustamante Castellanos, Iztapalapa’s director general of sustainable development.

“That means 10,000 objects that are not becoming waste,” she said, “and young people who have acquired knowledge, experience and a sense of service to their community.”

Other initiatives include a public recycling point outside the cultural center, neighborhood composting workshops and an ecocanje program that exchanges recyclable plastics for basic food products and vegetables grown in local greenhouses and community gardens.

National waste challenges

The borough is also developing a composting plant that will use black soldier fly larvae to process organic waste from markets, businesses, child development centers and community facilities.

Those local advances remain small compared with the national scale of the waste problem. Mexico generates more than 139,000 metric tons of urban solid waste daily, according to the federal Environment Ministry’s 2026 national assessment.

Only 5% receives any form of treatment, while 72% undergoes no recovery or valorization process. Of the country’s 2,250 final-disposal sites, just 52 operate as sanitary landfills meeting adequate standards.

Mella came to Mexico with a warning drawn from Chile’s experience. When that country adopted its extended producer responsibility law, she said, grassroots recyclers were initially excluded. They fought their way into the system through political pressure and organization.

Organizing against corporate interests

Mella distilled their demands into three points: formal recognition of recycling as work; dignified conditions supported by equipment, infrastructure and social protections; and payment for the service recyclers provide, rather than compensation based solely on the fluctuating value of the materials they collect.

“The garbage and recycling sector is a business model,” she said. “There are many interests that want to take what belongs to us and remove us from that space.”

Without a just transition that allows grassroots recyclers to compete, she added, “the sharks — the large companies — are going to eat us.”

Abel Balderas, who began working as a pepenador at age 8 and now leads Mexico’s National Recyclers Movement, echoed Mella’s call for organization and recognition.

“We are the experts,” he said. “You are the ones who can teach what can be recycled, what cannot, which material works and which doesn’t.”

Breaking down barriers

Following the presentations, participants divided into five dialogue groups focused on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), other plastics, paper and cardboard, metals and electronics. Each table included recyclers, companies, government officials, academics and civil society organizations.

They were asked to develop recommendations around four central issues: Social Security, tax-system inclusion, training and direct purchases of materials by industry.

At most tables, participants with sharply different interests managed to identify common barriers — particularly the bureaucracy involved in permits and formalization — and develop preliminary proposals.

The metals table proved the most contentious. Facilitator Adelita San Vicente, best known for her decades defending Mexico’s native corn and seeds, struggled as automotive industry representatives, the primary buyer of these materials, raised one objection after another while calling for a zero tax rate.

“Sharks,” she called them afterward, echoing Mella’s warning.

For Mella, legislation alone will not prevent that outcome. Grassroots recyclers must have seats at the tables where regulations and product-specific rules are written.

“If we are not actors and protagonists in this history,” she said, “once again we will be left out of the process.”

Her movement’s slogan reduces that argument to but a few words:

“Recycling without recyclers is garbage.”

Tracy L. Barnett is a Guadalajara-based freelance writer and the founder of The Esperanza Project.

World.title: In photos: The spirit of Mexican independence comes alive in Vienna
World.content:
The little boy, perhaps 3 years old, had everyone’s attention, dancing unrestrained and joyous with his little Mexican flag.

For that moment, he had traded schnitzel for tacos.

Mexico’s Independence Day was celebrated Sept. 12 in Vienna, Austria, for the city’s few but proud Mexican residents in a place appropriately called Mexikoplatz.

The square’s name recognizes a little-known act of courage when, in 1938, Mexico became the only country to lodge an official complaint with the League of Nations against Adolf Hitler’s annexation of Austria.

A Grito de Independencia fit for Vienna

According to Javier Basulto, a minister at the Mexican Embassy in Vienna, there are roughly 2,500 Mexicans living in all of Austria. The embassy, which also represents Mexico in Slovakia and Slovenia, coordinated the celebration alongside the Mexico-Austria Association.

The event showcased traditional dancers, food stands, a cumbia band and even a Grito de Independencia performed by the ambassador himself, José Antonio Zabalgoitia Trejo.

While dancers in Oaxacan dresses warmed up the gathering crowd, it was the Grito de Independencia that officially started the party.

While the ambassador didn’t have a roaring crowd of 300,000 and extravagant fireworks displays, like in Mexico City’s Zócalo, the roughly 500 people in attendance cheered with no less fervor.

Mexico and Austria’s shared history

Despite the jubilant atmosphere, there’s an irony to the whole thing.

In 1864, Habsburg dynasty Emperor Maximilian, younger brother of Austrian Emperor Franz Joseph, was installed as emperor of Mexico, with the backing of Napoleon III of France and Mexico’s conservative faction at the time.

He and his wife, Carlota, transformed Chapultepec Castle, formerly a military college, into a European-style imperial residence that reflected the Habsburg world Maximilian had left behind.

However, it was all for naught. After France withdrew its troops, Benito Juárez’s Republican forces closed in on the crumbling empire. Maximilian was captured at Querétaro in 1867 and executed by firing squad, effectively restoring the Mexican Republic.

But who thinks about executions when a cumbia band is playing, right?

Enter Los Nopaleros, a Vienna-based cumbia and psychedelic Latin-rock band whose members hail from Mexico, Argentina, Colombia and Austria.

The buoyant mood saw kids and the elderly dancing arm-in-arm, as the ambassador was showered with compliments and congratulations.

The wholesome Vienna celebrations were a far cry from the boozy Cinco de Mayo activities that often make headlines in the U.S., and which many mistakenly believe honor Mexican independence

Two distinct cultures, one shared spirit

It’s easy to write events like the one in Austria off as quaint, but they are undoubtedly significant for small communities.

The cultures of Mexico and Austria could hardly be more different. Just compare cumbia to waltzing. The contrasting styles need little explanation.

But small communities all over the world keep themselves alive in much the same way: with food, music, stories and the occasional excuse to crowd together in a public square.

Somewhere in that crowd, the little boy was still dancing, tiny Mexican flag in hand.

For a few hours in Vienna, Mexico was not 6,000 miles away. Its spirit could be felt right there in Mexikoplatz.

Jimmy Monack is a teacher, photographer and award-winning writer. He profiles interesting people all around the world as well as writing about and photographing rock concerts. He lives in Mexico City. www.jimmymonack.com

World.title: From the archive: How do I know it’s a ‘no’? A comprehensive guide for foreigners
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in November 2024 — is a humorous look at why Mexicans won’t say “no,” and how to know when they’re telling you “no” without actually saying it.

Mexicans are famous for their polite social graces and good humor. Unfortunately, they’re also known for a strong aversion to saying “no” or saying anything negative at all.

But what one sees as polite omission, another might take as flat-out lying. Being polite while also communicating what you mean can be a tricky balancing act; it’s true. And for those of us from more direct cultures, it’s downright opaque. Why would someone just not say what they mean?

Nothing is as simple as it seems, I suppose. Still, there are plenty of recognizable broad strokes we can examine here.

A lesson in keeping the negative to yourself

An impressive example of this tendency came years ago when I lived in Querétaro. I’d been working at a language school then — the kind that says they’ll help with immigration papers but never do. It was someone’s birthday, and teachers and students alike all went out to a bar to celebrate. It was a good time!

The next day, the director of the school told us teachers that one of the students wouldn’t be coming to class that day; there’d been an issue with his car. What was the issue? Someone had broken into it and stolen his car radio and CD player!

And when had this happened? It wasn’t when we were inside the bar, no. It happened at the school before we all left. He’d given some of us a ride, even, and had said nothing about his missing equipment.

It’s been almost 20 years, and I’m still shocked he kept that in.

He didn’t want to say anything about it because he didn’t want to ruin the evening before it had even begun. I myself would have been physically incapable of not saying anything. Just, wow.

Now that I’ve been here a while longer, I’ve seen more examples. People simply seem loath to talk about things that will make people gloomy. What for? We can get sad all on our own, after all.

So the first rule of communication, then, is to not disappoint. That is, of course, if you want the person you’re talking to to feel good. I’d personally rather be momentarily disappointed than later be sitting around like a dummy waiting for someone who’s not going to show, but that’s on me, I guess.

So knowing that “no” is a “no-no word” here, how might you decipher what people mean when they give you an answer?

Words that actually mean ‘no’: a guide for foreigners

Well, that’s just what I’m here to help you with! Below is a list of “actually, that might mean ‘no'” words and phrases.

‘Gracias’

This one is tricky. I sometimes have to stop myself from pedantically saying, “Um, that’s not one of the options for a yes or no question.” I can tell you from experience that challenging someone’s politeness in this way makes you look like an ass.

The way I’ve personally gotten around this is to pause comically and ask, “¿Gracias ‘sí’ o gracias ‘no’?” That will usually get a grin and an actual answer, which, by the way, is almost always “Gracias, no.” Remember that you can use it, too! It’s especially helpful when you’re wandering through a market and merchants are offering their wares. It also usually works if the “market” is coming to you in the form of individual sellers! An emphatic “muchas gracias” will usually transmit the idea that, while you are very grateful for the offer, you will not be purchasing a bottle of perfume on that particular day.

‘A lo mejor sí’

“A lo mejor” is a phrase that means “probably” or “likely.” It’s important to note, then, that all interpretations leave some wiggle room for it maybe not working out. If it doesn’t actually work out, well, they haven’t lied! There was always a chance.

This is, to me, one of the more dismissive ways to say no, a kind of “uh-huh, sure” version. In Mexico, this kind of dismissive “doing what you can to leave the conversation already” is called “dar el avión” (to … give the plane?). And when you “das el avión,” it’s often detectable. There are two likely outcomes of this, then. One is that the other person sighs, gives up and goes on their way. Another is that they get frustrated: “¡No me des el avión!” If that happens, you’d better think of a better, more convincing way to say “no.”

‘Déjame ver/checar’

This one is similar to “a lo mejor sí” in that it’s very likely to be an actual “no.” It means “Let me see” and “Let me check.” Spoiler alert: they will likely conclude, and may or may not tell you, that the result of the seeing/checking was negative.

‘Ahorita’

This is one that my kid uses on me all the time, and it drives me crazy. We speak in English together, so her version is “in a minute.” “Ahorita” could be when someone will definitely do something right then. Or it could mean anywhere from right that moment to when hell freezes over.

In my experience, it’s typically the latter, or after the person’s finally been worn down from enough nagging about it. So beware, people. If you’re hearing “ahorita” from your partner frequently and it’s not turning out to be “right now for real” kind, there will probably be some frustration in your future.

‘Estamos en contacto’

This one is kind of fun because it sounds so official and business-like. “We’ll be in touch.” Oh, will we? Most people don’t intend for this to be a lie; it’s just nicer to say than, “We may never see each other again, I don’t know, but you’re pleasant enough.”

Alas, this is a short list. I’ve got a word limit! But I’d love to hear more examples of “This is what they actually meant” in the comments. Consider this your official call for stories!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: FIDAE 2026 Brings Performing Arts to Three Cities in Uruguay
World.content:
URUGUAY · THEATRE

Key Facts — What The Festival Internacional de Artes Escénicas, or International Festival of Performing Arts, in its tenth edition.

— When 9 to 18 October 2026. The Paysandú leg runs from 11 to 18 October.

— Where Montevideo, Paysandú and San José, using theatres, galleries and cultural centres in each city.

— Who runs it The Instituto Nacional de Artes Escénicas, a body inside Uruguay’s Ministry of Education and Culture.

— Practical Every show in Paysandú is free. Ticket terms for the other cities had not been published on the festival site.

FIDAE 2026 is the tenth edition of Uruguay’s international performing arts festival, and it spreads ten days of theatre, dance and circus across three cities.

Montevideo. The city carries the largest share of the FIDAE 2026 programme in October.

What FIDAE Is and When It Runs

FIDAE runs from 9 to 18 October 2026 in Uruguay. The letters stand for Festival Internacional de Artes Escénicas, which translates as International Festival of Performing Arts.

This is the tenth edition. The festival is not held in one place, and it spreads across Montevideo, Paysandú and San José, three cities in different parts of the country.

The Instituto Nacional de Artes Escénicas organises it. That body sits inside the Ministry of Education and Culture, and it works with the local governments of the host departments.

The theme of this edition is Lo grande y lo pequeño, which means the big and the small. It points to a programme that places large productions and small, intimate pieces side by side.

Where the Shows Happen

Montevideo carries the largest share of the programme. Listed venues include the Teatro Solís, the Sala Verdi, the Auditorio Nacional del Sodre and the Auditorio Nelly Goitiño.

Independent houses take part as well. The Teatro Circular, the Teatro Victoria, the Teatro Alianza and the two halls of El Galpón all appear in the Montevideo listings.

Spaces outside the theatre world are also in use. The Espacio de Arte Contemporáneo, the Fundación Mario Benedetti, the Subte gallery and the Centro Cultural de España each host part of the programme.

Paysandú hosts its leg from 11 to 18 October. Shows there run at the Teatro Florencio Sánchez, the Casa de Cultura and the Espacio Imagina.

The Programme and the Countries Involved

Work from nine countries is on the bill, according to the Uruguayan magazine Revista CERO. Companies from France, Chile, Spain and Italy are among those travelling to the festival.

Uruguayan work is the backbone of the edition. The Comedia Nacional, the state theatre company, appears in the programme, and so does Edipo en Ezeiza, a Florencio prize winner from 2025.

The disciplines go beyond spoken theatre. The listings include dance, circus and puppetry, which lowers the language barrier for a good part of the audience.

Paysandú alone carries close to 17 productions. The local government says every show in that city is free to attend, and training sessions run alongside the performances.

What Is Not Yet Published

Ticket arrangements for the whole festival were still incomplete at the time of writing. The festival’s own ticket page carried a note saying the content would be updated shortly.

That gap matters for planning. The free entry confirmed for Paysandú does not automatically apply to the Montevideo venues, which have their own box offices.

Start times for individual shows sit in the downloadable programme rather than on one summary page. Readers should treat the festival site as the reference and check it close to the date.

Venue capacity is another open point. Several of the listed rooms are small, and the festival had not said how many seats each production would offer.

Why This Edition Is Worth Noting for Residents

Uruguay concentrates most of its cultural activity in Montevideo. A festival that also books San José and Paysandú is a deliberate step against that pattern.

Paysandú lies on the Uruguay River in the north-west of the country. It is several hours by road from the capital, and San José de Mayo is much closer to Montevideo.

For foreign residents, the practical value is simple. Ten days of programming in one country makes it possible to see companies from several continents without long travel.

The festival has also built a steady rhythm. Ten editions mean it is no longer an experiment, and the October slot in the calendar has become predictable.

There is a wider point about access. Touring work rarely reaches the interior of Uruguay, so a festival week in Paysandú changes what is available there for the rest of the year.

Public money pays for most of this. The festival is run by a state institute. Its choices are therefore a matter of public record rather than private taste.

October is a reasonable month to travel inside Uruguay. Spring weather is mild, the summer coast crowds have not arrived, and bus fares are lower than in January.

The festival also runs training work. Workshops sit alongside the performances in Paysandú, which matters for local companies that rarely meet visiting directors.

None of this guarantees a full house. Uruguay has a small population, and a ten-day festival spread over three cities depends on local audiences turning up.

Sources

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

What does FIDAE stand for?

FIDAE is short for Festival Internacional de Artes Escénicas. In English that is the International Festival of Performing Arts. It is organised by Uruguay’s Instituto Nacional de Artes Escénicas.

When and where is FIDAE 2026?

It runs from 9 to 18 October 2026. Three cities take part, namely Montevideo, Paysandú and San José. The Paysandú leg runs from 11 to 18 October.

Are FIDAE 2026 shows free?

Every show in Paysandú is free, according to the city government. Arrangements for Montevideo and San José had not been published on the festival ticket page. Readers should check that page before making plans.

Do I need Spanish to enjoy the festival?

Not for every show. The programme includes dance, circus and puppetry, which carry across languages. Spoken theatre is mostly in Spanish, with visiting companies from France, Italy and Spain.

World.title: Nass El Ghiwane Casablanca Concert Set for 26 September 2026 in Morocco
World.content:
MOROCCO · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — What Nass El Ghiwane perform at the Théâtre L’Hermitage in Casablanca.

— When Saturday, 26 September 2026, at 20:00 Morocco time, which is one hour ahead of UTC.

— Where The Théâtre L’Hermitage, on avenue de Nador in Casablanca.

— Tickets 250 to 550 Moroccan dirhams, or about US$26 to US$58, across four seating categories.

— Who they are A Moroccan group formed in Casablanca around 1970, known for chaabi songs built on older North African poetry.

The Nass El Ghiwane Casablanca date returns the group to the city where it formed, in a 600-seat public theatre that opened only in May 2026.

Casablanca. Nass El Ghiwane play the Théâtre L’Hermitage on 26 September 2026.

What Is Happening in Casablanca on 26 September

Nass El Ghiwane play the Théâtre L’Hermitage in Casablanca on Saturday, 26 September 2026. Casablanca is the largest city in Morocco, and the concert starts at 20:00 local time. The country keeps UTC plus one hour in September.

The theatre stands on avenue de Nador. It is a public venue rather than a commercial hall, and it opened to audiences in May 2026.

Tickets are priced from 250 to 550 Moroccan dirhams. At 9.4966 dirhams to the US dollar, that is about US$26 to US$58. Four seating categories are listed.

The evening is promoted by a private events company. The set list, the running time and any support act had not been published at the time of writing.

Who Nass El Ghiwane Are

The group formed in Casablanca around 1970. Its first members came out of the city’s experimental theatre scene rather than out of a conservatory.

Their music is rooted in chaabi, the popular music of Moroccan streets and weddings. They set it against older material, including Sufi poetry from North Africa.

The sound leans on percussion and on the banjo, an instrument the group helped bring into Moroccan popular music. There is no orchestra and no large arrangement behind the singers.

The words carried weight from the start. The songs deal with hardship, memory and society, and they were read politically in the 1970s.

Their reach went well beyond Morocco. The American director Martin Scorsese called them the Rolling Stones of Africa, and used their track Ya Sah in The Last Temptation of Christ.

Founding members have died, and the line-up has changed several times. The group that tours today includes musicians who joined in the 1990s and 2000s.

The Hermitage Theatre and Why the Room Matters

The Hermitage theatre is new. It opened in May 2026 after a long build, with a first programme of drama and Moroccan music.

The hall seats about 600 people. That is small next to the arena shows Casablanca usually hosts, and it puts the audience close to the stage.

The building is more than a stage. The complex also holds a music institute, a library and an art gallery, and it houses regional cultural offices.

It is run through a partnership between the national culture ministry and the city of Casablanca. The venue is therefore part of public cultural policy rather than a private business.

The district around it has its own artistic record. Moroccan coverage of the opening described the neighbourhood as one with a long cultural history.

What This Means for Residents and Visitors

For foreign residents in Casablanca, this is a direct route into Moroccan popular culture. Few groups are as widely known across age groups.

The lyrics are in Moroccan Arabic, and much of the meaning sits in the words. Readers who do not follow the language will still get the rhythm and the response of the room.

A 600-seat hall fills faster than an arena. Anyone who wants a particular seat should buy early rather than at the door.

Prices are moderate for a named act. The lowest category costs about US$26, and the highest about US$58, at the rate used in this article.

Some practical detail is missing. We could not find published guidance on parking, accessibility or the time the doors open.

The Wider Picture for Live Music in Morocco

The Moroccan venue map changed quickly in 2026. The Hermitage opened in May, and the much larger royal theatre in Rabat opened to the public in April.

Both are public buildings. That matters, because Moroccan live music has long leaned on festivals and on private promoters hiring sports halls.

A permanent hall allows a regular calendar. Moroccan listings for this autumn show concerts spread across several weeks rather than packed into festival dates.

For investors, the signal is in the supporting spaces. A music institute and a library beside a stage point at training and audience-building, not only at one-off events.

For residents, the change is easier to feel than to measure. There are more evenings out that need neither a festival ticket nor a trip to another city.

The direction is gradual rather than sudden. Casablanca still holds most of the country’s large commercial dates, and the new public halls are small by comparison.

Sources

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Nass El Ghiwane concert in Casablanca?

It takes place on Saturday, 26 September 2026, at 20:00 local time. The venue is the Théâtre L’Hermitage on avenue de Nador. Morocco keeps UTC plus one hour in September.

How much are tickets?

Tickets are listed from 250 to 550 Moroccan dirhams across four seating categories. At 9.4966 dirhams to the US dollar, that is about US$26 to US$58. The hall seats about 600 people.

Who are Nass El Ghiwane?

They are a Moroccan group formed in Casablanca around 1970, out of the city’s experimental theatre scene. Their songs combine chaabi, the popular music of streets and weddings, with older North African poetry. Martin Scorsese once called them the Rolling Stones of Africa.

What is the Théâtre L’Hermitage?

It is a public theatre in Casablanca that opened in May 2026. The complex holds a hall of about 600 seats, a music institute, a library and an art gallery. It is run by the national culture ministry together with the city.

World.title: Swartland Olive Festival Runs 25 to 27 September 2026 in South Africa
World.content:
SOUTH AFRICA · FOOD AND FARMING

Key Facts — What A three-day olive and wine event in the Riebeek Valley, in the Western Cape province.

— When Friday 25 to Sunday 27 September 2026. Friday 16:00 to 22:00, Saturday 10:00 to 21:00, Sunday 10:00 to 17:00, South African Standard Time.

— Where Riebeek Kasteel Town Square and Plein Street, about 86 kilometres north-east of Cape Town.

— Tickets Weekend passes run from R150 to R500, or about US$9 to US$31, sold through Webtickets.

— Who runs it Swartland Tourism, in partnership with the SA Olive Industry Association.

The Swartland Olive Festival fills the town square of Riebeek Kasteel for three days, with olive oil and wine tastings, an artisan market and live music.

Riebeek Kasteel. The village hosts the Swartland Olive Festival from 25 to 27 September 2026.

What Happens in Riebeek Kasteel in Late September

The Swartland Olive Festival runs from Friday 25 to Sunday 27 September 2026 in Riebeek Kasteel, South Africa. The village lies in the Riebeek Valley, inside the Swartland wine and olive region of the Western Cape. The festival is centred on the town square.

The organiser has published the opening hours. Friday runs from 16:00 to 22:00. Saturday runs from 10:00 to 21:00. Sunday runs from 10:00 to 17:00. All times are South African Standard Time, which is two hours ahead of UTC.

Tickets are sold through Webtickets, a South African ticketing platform. The all-weekend pass is listed at R150 to R500. At 16.267 rand to the US dollar, that is roughly US$9 to US$31.

Single-day passes are also on sale. The Friday street party pass is R200, or about US$12. The Saturday pass runs from R100 to R350, and the Sunday pass from R100 to R200. In dollars, that is about US$6 to US$22 on Saturday, and about US$6 to US$12 on Sunday.

Children under eight enter free when they come with a ticket-holding adult. Children aged eight to sixteen can buy discounted general access tickets. Local residents can buy an all-weekend ticket at R350, about US$22, from the Swartland Tourism office, and that rate is not sold online.

Where the Swartland Is, and Why Olives Grow There

The Swartland begins about 50 kilometres north of Cape Town and runs inland. Its name comes from an old Dutch phrase for the black land. It refers to the dark renosterbos shrub that covers the hills after winter rain.

Riebeek Kasteel sits in the Riebeek Valley, about 86 kilometres north-east of Cape Town by the N7 road. The valley holds four small settlements: Riebeek West, Riebeek Kasteel, Riebeeksrivier and Hermon.

For most of its recorded history the Swartland was wheat country. It is still described as the bread basket of Cape Town. Wine came later, and the region is now one of the better known wine areas in the country.

Vines here are mostly grown without irrigation. That method is called dryland farming, and olives suit the same conditions. The Western Cape holds about 95 percent of South African olive plantings, on figures published by the SA Olive Industry Association.

An olive festival has run in this valley since 2000, according to the regional tourism route West Coast Way. The present event carries the Swartland name.

What Is on the Programme, and What Is Not Published

The core of the weekend is tasting. Visitors can sample extra virgin olive oils, table olives and tapenades from Western Cape producers, alongside Swartland wines and craft beers.

Extra virgin is the top grade of olive oil. It is pressed without heat or chemical treatment, and it must pass a sensory test. Tapenade is a spread made from crushed olives.

Around the tastings there are chef demonstrations, food trucks and a market of olive products and handmade goods. A children’s zone offers magic shows and jumping castles, and Sunday is set up as the family day.

The weekend opens on Friday evening with a street party in Plein Street. The organiser lists food vendors, long-table dining, street performers and a DJ set.

Live music runs across all three days. The organiser names the folk duo RAAF on Saturday and the singer Robin Auld on Sunday. A full stage schedule with set times has not been published.

Some practical detail is also missing at the time of writing. We could not find a published list of every participating producer, or a parking plan for the village.

What This Means for Residents and Visitors

For foreign residents in Cape Town, this is a short drive rather than a trip. The village is about 86 kilometres away, and the route runs north on the N7 before turning east into the valley.

Late September is early spring in the Western Cape. The region has winter rainfall, so the hills are green at this time of year rather than dry and brown.

Riebeek Kasteel is a small village. It is home to the Royal Hotel, which is described as the oldest hotel in the country. Visitors who want to stay overnight should plan ahead.

Prices are modest by European or North American standards. A full weekend at the top rate costs about US$31, and a single Sunday ticket can cost about US$6.

The Wider Picture for Olive Farming in the Western Cape

The South African olive sector is small in world terms. The SA Olive Industry Association puts national output at roughly 1.5 to 2 million litres of olive oil a year.

More than 90 percent of that oil is consumed inside the country, on the same figures. Export volumes are therefore low, and most of what is poured in Cape Town kitchens is local.

The association also reports that growers are mostly small. About half of the registered growers farm less than five hectares each.

These numbers come from an industry factsheet and are several years old. A more recent national count was not available at the time of writing.

For investors, the read is modest but steady. Olive planting has grown from a low base, and the crop suits the dry, hot summers that the Swartland has.

For residents, the read is simpler. A weekend festival is a cheap way to meet the producers whose oil sits on supermarket shelves across the Western Cape.

Sources

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Swartland Olive Festival 2026?

It runs from Friday 25 to Sunday 27 September 2026. Friday opens at 16:00 and closes at 22:00. Saturday runs from 10:00 to 21:00, and Sunday from 10:00 to 17:00.

How much do tickets cost?

The all-weekend pass is listed from R150 to R500 on Webtickets, which is about US$9 to US$31. Day passes are cheaper, starting at R100, or about US$6. Local residents can buy a discounted weekend ticket at the Swartland Tourism office.

Where is Riebeek Kasteel?

It is a village in the Riebeek Valley, about 86 kilometres north-east of Cape Town. The valley sits inside the Swartland, the farming region that begins around 50 kilometres north of the city. The drive runs north on the N7.

Is the festival suitable for children?

Yes. Children under eight enter free when they come with a ticket-holding adult, and those aged eight to sixteen pay a discounted rate. Sunday is set up as the family day, with magic shows and jumping castles.

World.title: Los Pericos Gran Rex Concert Set for 22 October 2026 in Argentina
World.content:
ARGENTINA · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — What Los Pericos present Inmortal, a ten track studio album released in 2026.

— When Thursday 22 October 2026. The start time had not been confirmed.

— Where Teatro Gran Rex, Avenida Corrientes 857, central Buenos Aires.

— Who they are An Argentine reggae band formed in 1986, with roughly four decades of touring behind it.

— Tickets Sold through TuEntrada. Prices differ by section and no single headline figure was published.

The Los Pericos Gran Rex date brings the Argentine reggae band back to Avenida Corrientes with Inmortal, the studio album it released in 2026.

Buenos Aires. The Teatro Gran Rex on Avenida Corrientes hosts Los Pericos on 22 October 2026.
