The Gran Rex Date

Los Pericos play the Teatro Gran Rex in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Thursday 22 October 2026. The band is presenting Inmortal, a ten track studio album released in 2026.

The start time had not been confirmed at the time of writing. Published listings give different figures, so readers should follow the time printed on their own ticket.

Tickets are sold through TuEntrada, the theatre’s ticketing partner. Prices differ by section, and the promoter had not published a single headline figure.

The platform also lists a meet and greet option. Buyers of that extra still need a normal show ticket to enter the auditorium.

About the Teatro Gran Rex

The Gran Rex stands at Avenida Corrientes 857, in the centre of Buenos Aires. It opened on 8 July 1937 and was designed by the architect Alberto Prebisch.

The building is an Art Deco cinema that became a concert hall. It seats about 3,300 people, which places it between a theatre and a small arena.

Avenida Corrientes is the city’s theatre street. The Gran Rex sits within walking distance of the Obelisco and of several subway lines.

The room is used mainly for concerts and musicals now. Argentine and international acts book it for single nights rather than long runs.

Who Los Pericos Are

Los Pericos are an Argentine reggae band formed in 1986. They were among the first groups to make reggae sung in Spanish a mainstream sound in South America.

Their debut album, El ritual de la banana, appeared in 1988 and sold strongly. Later records include Big Yuyo in 1993, Pampas Reggae in 1994 and Yerba Buena in 1996.

The line-up changed in 2004. Juanchi Baleirón moved from lead guitar to lead vocals after the departure of the singer known as Bahiano.

The band works well beyond Argentina. During 2026 it toured Colombia, Mexico and Honduras before turning back towards Buenos Aires.

Reggae sung in Spanish was not an obvious idea in the 1980s. Argentine radio was built around rock, and a band playing Jamaican rhythms in Buenos Aires was an outlier.

The group outlasted many of its peers from that decade. Four decades of touring have given it audiences in Mexico, Colombia and the United States as well.

What the New Album Changes

Inmortal is the reason for the date. The band describes it as a record about its own history, identity and memory, made after nearly four decades of touring.

The release came with side projects. Sesiones Inmortales is a set of acoustic video sessions, and Cápsulas del Tiempo places markers at sites that matter in the band’s history.

A Gran Rex night is a specific kind of show in Buenos Aires. It is seated, it is indoors, and it usually means a longer set than a festival slot allows.

The band had not published a set list. Nor had it said which guests, if any, would appear, and that detail often arrives only in the final week.

Practical Notes for Visitors

Concerts in Buenos Aires start late by European standards. A weekday show in this part of the city commonly begins well after 20:00 local time.

Argentina runs three hours behind UTC and does not change its clocks. Visitors arriving from Europe should plan for a late finish and a late return.

The area around Corrientes stays busy after a show. Cafes and pizzerias on the avenue serve late, and taxis are easy to find on the main street.

Ticket prices in Argentina move with inflation. A figure quoted months ahead may not match the price on sale, which is one reason to buy from the official platform.

One more caution. Resale sites list Gran Rex dates at a markup, and TuEntrada is the only sales route the promoter names.

Buenos Aires is an easy city for a concert trip. The theatre district sits close to hotels, and the subway runs until late on weekday evenings.

Bring identification if you buy online. Argentine venues often ask to see the card used for the purchase, or a document matching the name on the ticket.

Prices for the same show can differ widely. Stalls seats at the Gran Rex cost considerably more than the upper level, and the cheaper tiers sell out first.

The theatre is listed by Argentina’s national monuments commission. Its Art Deco interior is worth arriving early for, even if the concert is the reason for the visit.

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Los Pericos play the Gran Rex?

The date is Thursday 22 October 2026 at the Teatro Gran Rex in Buenos Aires. The start time had not been confirmed, because published listings disagree. The time printed on the ticket is the one to follow.

Where is the Teatro Gran Rex?

It is at Avenida Corrientes 857, in central Buenos Aires. The theatre opened in 1937 and seats about 3,300 people. Several subway lines stop within a short walk.

What are Los Pericos presenting?

They are presenting Inmortal, a ten track studio album released in 2026. The band describes the record as a look at its own history. The show is expected to mix new songs with older material.

Where can I buy tickets?

Tickets are sold through TuEntrada, the theatre’s ticketing partner. Prices differ by section and no single headline price has been published. Resale sites list the date at a markup.

World.title: Milongas Extremas Zitarrosa Tribute Set for 22 October 2026 in Uruguay
World.content:
URUGUAY · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts — What Zitarrosa desde el fondo del tiempo, a tribute concert by the group Milongas Extremas.

— When Thursday 22 October 2026. Doors at 19:30 and the show at 21:00, Uruguay time.

— Where Antel Arena, Avenida Dámaso Antonio Larrañaga 4001, central Montevideo.

— Tickets UYU 1,200 to UYU 2,600, or roughly US$30 to US$65 at 40.27 pesos to the dollar.

— Who he was Alfredo Zitarrosa, the Uruguayan singer and composer who died in 1989.

The Milongas Extremas Zitarrosa tribute closes a two-year run at the Antel Arena, with a rock-weighted reading of the songs that shaped Uruguayan popular music.

Montevideo. The Antel Arena hosts the Milongas Extremas tribute to Zitarrosa on 22 October 2026.

The Concert at the Antel Arena

Milongas Extremas plays the Antel Arena in Montevideo, Uruguay, on Thursday 22 October 2026. The show is a tribute to Alfredo Zitarrosa and carries the title Zitarrosa desde el fondo del tiempo.

That title translates as Zitarrosa from the depths of time. The venue lists doors at 19:30 and the performance at 21:00, in Uruguay time, which is three hours behind UTC.

Tickets run from UYU 1,200 to UYU 2,600. At 40.27 Uruguayan pesos to the United States dollar, that is roughly US$30 to US$65.

All three levels of the arena are seated for this date. Tickantel handles the sale, and the company Piano Piano is credited as the producer.

Who Alfredo Zitarrosa Was

Zitarrosa was born in Montevideo on 10 March 1936. He died in the same city on 17 January 1989, at the age of 52.

He wrote and sang milongas, a song form from the River Plate region. His arrangements leaned on guitars and the guitarrón, a large bass guitar used in folk trios and quartets.

His best known songs include Doña Soledad, El violín de Becho, Adagio a mi país and Crece desde el pie. Several of them are still taught in Uruguayan schools.

He spent eight years in exile, from 1976 to 1984. He lived in Argentina, Spain and Mexico, and his records were banned in Argentina, Chile and Uruguay during that period.

Why the Date Matters

The concert falls in the year that marks 90 years since Zitarrosa was born. The venue describes the show as a contemporary reading of his work rather than a copy of his recordings.

Milongas Extremas is a five-piece group. It mixes River Plate folk roots with the volume and drive of a rock band, which is an unusual setting for this repertoire.

The Antel Arena date closes a run that began earlier. The venue says seven tribute performances were given between 2024 and 2025, mostly in smaller rooms.

Archive material is part of the production. The venue says the show uses images and recordings from the Zitarrosa archive, shown alongside the live performance.

Getting to the Arena

The Antel Arena stands at Avenida Dámaso Antonio Larrañaga 4001, at the corner of Avenida José Pedro Varela. It sits on a nine hectare site in central Montevideo.

Many city bus lines stop at the door. The venue lists routes 71, 79, 144, 174, 180, 192, 328, 330 and 538, among others.

Drivers have about 1,200 car spaces and 120 spaces for motorbikes and bicycles. Parking can be booked online in advance, or paid at the José Pedro Varela entrance.

Street parking on the central medians of both avenues is not allowed. Taxi ranks sit on both streets, and ride apps use a pick-up point on Larrañaga.

What Is and Is Not Known

The date, the venue, the times and the price range come from the arena’s own event page. Those are the firmest details available at the time of writing.

The set list had not been published. The group has said it will play well known songs alongside less familiar material, but no running order exists in public.

Guest performers are another open question. Tribute shows of this kind often add singers for one or two songs, and none had been announced.

For a newcomer to Uruguayan music, the evening is a reasonable entry point. The songs are slow enough to follow, and the words matter more than the volume.

The Antel Arena is a large room for this repertoire. Zitarrosa wrote for small halls and radio studios, not for a hall that seats several thousand people.

That gap is part of the point. The group has said it wants the material heard by people who were not born when the original records came out.

Tickets sell through one platform only. Tickantel is the arena’s own system, and buyers need a payment method that the platform accepts.

There is an easy way to prepare. Listening to two or three of the best known songs beforehand makes the evening far easier to follow for a newcomer.

A last practical note. October evenings in Montevideo can turn cold, and the walk from the arena to the bus stops on Larrañaga is short but open to the wind.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Milongas Extremas Zitarrosa concert?

It takes place on Thursday 22 October 2026 at the Antel Arena in Montevideo. The venue lists doors at 19:30 and the show at 21:00. Those are Uruguay times, three hours behind UTC.

How much do tickets cost?

Prices run from UYU 1,200 to UYU 2,600. At 40.27 pesos to the United States dollar, that is about US$30 to US$65. Tickantel handles the sale.

Who was Alfredo Zitarrosa?

He was a Uruguayan singer and composer, born in Montevideo in 1936, who died there in 1989. He is best known for milongas such as Doña Soledad and El violín de Becho. He spent eight years in exile between 1976 and 1984.

How do I get to the Antel Arena?

The arena is at Avenida Dámaso Antonio Larrañaga 4001, in central Montevideo. Around ten city bus lines stop nearby. The site also has about 1,200 car parking spaces.

World.title: Quito Book Fair Runs 30 September to 4 October 2026 in Ecuador
World.content:
ECUADOR · BOOKS

Key Facts — What The Feria Internacional del Libro de Quito, Ecuador’s largest book fair.

— When 30 September to 4 October 2026, open daily from 10:00 to 20:00 local time.

— Where Centro de Exposiciones Quito, Avenida Amazonas N34-332 and Atahualpa, in northern Quito.

— Who runs it The Ministry of Education, Sport and Culture, the Cámara Ecuatoriana del Libro and the Biblioteca Nacional del Ecuador Eugenio Espejo.

— Practical Entry is free. The Quito metro stops at Iñaquito nearby, and the venue has its own parking.

The Quito book fair returns for five days at the Centro de Exposiciones Quito, with free entry, an international guest list and a programme built around readings and launches.

Quito. The Centro de Exposiciones Quito hosts the book fair from 30 September to 4 October 2026.

What Is Happening at the Centro de Exposiciones Quito

The Feria Internacional del Libro de Quito opens on 30 September 2026 and runs to 4 October. It takes place at the Centro de Exposiciones Quito, in the north of Ecuador’s capital city.

The venue stands at Avenida Amazonas N34-332 and Atahualpa. It is a multi-pavilion site, and the fair uses the Pabellón Simón Bolívar along with the Las Caras auditorium and several smaller halls.

Doors open at 10:00 and close at 20:00 each day. Those are Ecuador times, five hours behind UTC. The organisers expect around 45,000 visitors across the five days.

Three institutions are running the fair together. They are the Ministry of Education, Sport and Culture, the Cámara Ecuatoriana del Libro, and the Biblioteca Nacional del Ecuador Eugenio Espejo.

How the 2026 Fair Came Together

This year’s fair has a different organiser than in past years. The Quito city government stepped back from the event in March 2026, saying legal limits stopped it from taking the lead.

The national government then picked the event up. That is why the Ministry of Education, Sport and Culture appears on the announcements, alongside the national library and the publishers’ chamber.

The handover also changed the timetable. Dates were confirmed only in April 2026, which is later than a fair of this size would normally announce them.

Exhibitor terms were published at the same time. Publishers receive a nine square metre stand at no cost, and pay only if they want a larger space.

Who Is Coming, and What Is Still Open

The guest list mixes Ecuadorian writers with names from across the region. Guillermo Arriaga of Mexico and Carmen Posadas of Spain are among the confirmed international guests.

Writers from Argentina, Peru and Colombia are also listed. On the Ecuadorian side the programme includes Juan Luque, Valeria Coronel, Gabriela Franco and Yana Lema, among others.

The published programme covers book launches, panel discussions, academic round tables and reading club meetings. A separate strand is aimed at children and teenagers.

Several details had not been published at the time of writing. There is no announced guest country of honour, no final count of participating publishers, and no full hour-by-hour schedule.

What It Means for Foreign Residents in Quito

A free book fair is an easy first outing for someone new to the city. There is no ticket to buy and no fixed start time to catch.

Most of the programme is in Spanish. Readers with limited Spanish can still use the stands, because publishers bring translated titles and imported editions that are hard to find in Quito bookshops.

Prices at the stands are in United States dollars. Ecuador has used the dollar as its currency since 2000, so visitors from abroad do not need to convert anything.

The site is easy to reach without a car. The Quito metro stops at Iñaquito nearby, several bus lines serve the avenue, and the venue has its own parking.

Practical Notes for the Five Days

Weekdays are quieter than the weekend. The fair opens on a Wednesday, and the first two days usually leave more room to browse and to talk to publishers.

Quito sits at about 2,850 metres above sea level. Visitors arriving from the coast often feel the altitude on a long day of walking, so a slow morning helps.

The building is indoors, which matters in October. Quito afternoons often bring rain at this time of year, and the exhibition halls stay dry.

One caution applies to any programme this large. Times and guests can change, and the organisers publish those changes through their own channels rather than through listings sites.

The fair is one part of a wider calendar. Quito also hosts smaller literary events through the year, and several of them run in the same northern districts.

Cash is still useful in Ecuador. Some stands take cards, but small publishers often prefer notes, and the United States dollar is the only currency in use.

Books are heavy, which sounds obvious until the walk back. A cloth bag and a short list of targets make a first visit far more useful.

Children are welcome throughout. The fair sets aside a strand of activities for them, and school groups usually fill the morning hours on weekdays.

Expect a crowd at the entrance on Saturday. Free entry removes the ticket queue but not the pressure, and the busiest hours run from the middle of the afternoon.

It runs from 30 September to 4 October 2026. The halls open at 10:00 and close at 20:00 each day. Those are local Ecuador times, five hours behind UTC.

Entry is free, according to the Ecuadorian daily Expreso. An earlier announcement in April had mentioned a charge of one dollar. Readers should check the organisers’ own channels before they travel.

Where is the Centro de Exposiciones Quito?

It stands on Avenida Amazonas at Atahualpa, in the north of Quito. The metro station at Iñaquito is close by. Several bus lines also serve the avenue.

Who organises the fair this year?

Three institutions share the work. They are the Ministry of Education, Sport and Culture, the Cámara Ecuatoriana del Libro and the Biblioteca Nacional del Ecuador Eugenio Espejo. The Quito city government stepped back in March 2026.

World.title: Swan Lake Lima Season Runs to 3 October 2026 in Peru
World.content:
PERU · STAGE

Key Facts — What Ballet Municipal de Lima performs Swan Lake, after the Petipa and Ivanov choreography, staged by Carlos Valcárcel.

— When The season runs to Saturday, 3 October 2026. Four performances have a live orchestra: 26 and 27 September at 6:00 pm, 1 and 2 October at 8:00 pm, Peru time.

— Where Teatro Municipal de Lima, Jirón Ica 377, in the historic centre.

— Who plays The Orquesta Sinfónica del Teatro Municipal de Lima, conducted by Carlos Calleja, in the four orchestra performances.

— Tickets Sold by Teleticket and the theatre box office. Orchestra performances run from 32 to 500 soles, about 9 to 148 US dollars.

The Swan Lake Lima season closes on 3 October 2026, and four of its performances are played with a live orchestra rather than recorded music.

Lima. The Teatro Municipal is the home of the Ballet Municipal de Lima.

What Is on Stage at the Teatro Municipal de Lima

The Ballet Municipal de Lima is performing Swan Lake at the Teatro Municipal de Lima, in Peru, until Saturday, 3 October 2026. The season opened on 11 September 2026. Sixteen performances are scheduled in total.

Four of those performances are played with a live orchestra. The Orquesta Sinfónica del Teatro Municipal de Lima takes the pit on 26 and 27 September at 6:00 pm, and on 1 and 2 October at 8:00 pm.

The remaining performances use a recorded score. That is the usual arrangement for a long ballet run, because an orchestra adds substantial cost to every date.

Carlos Calleja conducts the orchestra performances. The staging is by Carlos Valcárcel, working from the nineteenth-century choreography of Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov.

The Work and the Company

Swan Lake is a four-act ballet with music by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, first staged in Moscow in 1877. The version most companies dance today follows the 1895 revival in St Petersburg.

The story concerns Prince Siegfried and Odette, a young woman held under a spell in the form of a swan. A deception involving her double, Odile, drives the second half.

The Ballet Municipal de Lima is the resident company of the theatre. This production is a joint effort between the company and the city government of Lima.

A guest dancer appears in four of the sixteen performances. The theatre describes him as an artist with experience at San Francisco Ballet and the Royal New Zealand Ballet.

The running time is about two hours, according to the ticketing listing. That figure normally includes an interval, although the theatre has not broken the timing down.

Tickets and Prices

Teleticket and the theatre box office sell the tickets. Prices depend on the seating area and on whether the performance has an orchestra.

For performances without an orchestra, the listed range runs from 16 to 450 soles. That is roughly 5 to 133 US dollars at 3.3757 soles to the dollar.

For the four orchestra performances, the range runs from 32 to 500 soles, or about 9 to 148 dollars. The premium reflects the cost of the players in the pit.

Those lower figures are real rather than symbolic. A seat in the upper gallery at this theatre costs less than a cinema ticket in much of Lima.

The range is wide because the theatre has several levels. A seat in the stalls and a seat in the top gallery are priced very differently for the same performance.

What This Means If You Live in Lima

Ballet with a live orchestra is not a weekly event in Lima. Four dates in one season is a narrow window, and two of them fall in the closing week.

The theatre is in the historic centre, at Jirón Ica 377. That places it within walking distance of the Plaza Mayor and the main museums of the old city.

Evening visits to the centre need a little planning. Many residents take a taxi or ride app back rather than walking, and the streets quiet down quickly after the theatres empty.

For families, the work is an accessible entry point. There is no spoken text, the story is carried by movement, and language is therefore not an obstacle for children or for new arrivals.

Booking ahead matters more for the orchestra dates than for the rest. Those four performances carry the higher price and the narrower supply, and two of them close the season.

The Wider Picture for Stage Work in Peru

Lima’s publicly funded companies carry much of the city’s classical programming. The ballet, the choir and the symphony orchestra all sit under municipal or national structures.

That model keeps prices low. Entry seats in the range of five dollars exist because the productions are subsidised, not because demand is weak.

It also shapes the calendar. Seasons cluster into blocks of a few weeks, rather than running continuously as they do in cities with larger commercial theatre markets.

For residents deciding how much cultural life Lima offers, the honest answer is uneven but real. The peaks are strong and cheap, and the quieter months between them are genuinely quiet.

The building itself is part of the appeal. The Teatro Municipal is a traditional tiered theatre in the old city, and its scale suits a nineteenth-century ballet better than a modern hall would.

The season closes on Saturday, 3 October 2026. It opened on 11 September 2026 and covers sixteen performances in total. Four of those are played with a live orchestra.

Four dates do: 26 and 27 September at 6:00 pm, and 1 and 2 October at 8:00 pm, Peru time. The Orquesta Sinfónica del Teatro Municipal de Lima plays, conducted by Carlos Calleja. The other performances use a recorded score.

How much do tickets cost?

Orchestra performances are listed from 32 to 500 soles, about 9 to 148 US dollars at 3.3757 soles to the dollar. Performances without an orchestra run from 16 to 450 soles. Teleticket and the theatre box office sell them.

It is at Jirón Ica 377, in the historic centre of Lima. The theatre is within walking distance of the Plaza Mayor. It is the home of the Ballet Municipal de Lima.

World.title: New Costa Rica Law Requires Wildlife Crossings on Public Infrastructure
World.content:
Costa Rica now has a law requiring wildlife crossings on public infrastructure projects, but the regulation that will actually put it into practice could take more than two years to arrive. The rule requires new road, bridge and other infrastructure projects to incorporate mechanisms allowing wild species to move safely across routes that would otherwise fragment their habitat, but before any of that happens the National System of Conservation Areas and the Ministry of Public Works and Transport still have to jointly write the technical regulation defining procedures, responsibilities and criteria for applying it.

Once that regulation takes effect, the conservation agency will then have up to 24 months just to identify the natural corridors wildlife use and the most vulnerable points on existing roads, meaning construction itself is still years away. The law took a long road to get here. It was filed in the legislature back in 2022 by then deputy Ariel Robles Barrantes and spent four years moving slowly enough that it nearly expired under the four year shelf life Costa Rican bills carry before automatic archiving.

Lawmakers voted 53 to 0 in June to extend it just before that deadline, and the bill finally cleared final approval in August with unanimous support. That gap between broad political agreement and years of inaction is a pattern environmentalists and officials both recognize. An environmentalist inside MOPT itself, Andrea Ávila, who runs the ministry’s transportation infrastructure project, has been candid about the reason nothing moved for years before the law passed.

She said every wildlife protection measure taken until now came from individual institutional initiative rather than obligation, and did not rule out a lack of political interest, since no law required new construction projects to include such measures. She specifically pointed to Lanamme, the University of Costa Rica’s highway research institute, saying it makes recommendations nobody follows because they carry no legal weight.

A wildlife biologist from the National University’s conservation institute made a similar point, saying the missing piece was never a shortage of impact studies but a legal framework forcing institutions to act on them. That track record matters because it suggests the coming regulatory delay has less to do with a lack of technical groundwork and more to do with institutional follow through. Much of the mapping work the new law assigns SINAC up to 24 months to complete already exists in some form.

A group tied to Universidad Latina compiled more than 19000 roadkill records dating back to 1996, and one 20-kilometer stretch of route 253 in Guanacaste alone was estimated to see around 7000 roadkill incidents annually as of 2019. Panthera, the University of Costa Rica and the Las Pumas rescue center separately tracked wild cat deaths and found 676 felines, jaguars, pumas, ocelots and margays among them, killed on Costa Rican roads between 2012 and 2025, with more than 4200 animals of all kinds struck between 2013 and the present.

Lanamme has also already developed and field tested a methodology for identifying exactly the kind of crossing points the new regulation calls for. Researchers working along the Barbilla Destierro biological subcorridor as part of the Jaguar Corridor Initiative compared roadkill and wildlife sighting data between a paved and an unpaved section of the same road as far back as 2015, documenting jaguar and margay crossings and raccoons using existing culverts.

A separate scientific guide on wildlife friendly roads, developed jointly by conservation and transportation researchers, has been informing individual projects like the route 32 expansion to Limon since 2014, where aerial rope crossings for monkeys and underground tunnels were installed based on monitoring data from that period. Follow up monitoring across existing structures has recorded 59 wildlife species safely using them, though researchers note some sensitive species such as the margay and spider monkey still show limited evidence the current designs work well for them.

None of that existing work resolves the underlying question of how quickly MOPT and SINAC will move once the regulation is actually written, but it does complicate the idea that a two year timeline for identifying priority corridors reflects how much work remains. Much of the mapping this law calls for has already been done piecemeal by university researchers and conservation groups over more than a decade, without a legal mandate forcing anyone to act on it. Whether the regulation leans on that existing research or starts largely from scratch may end up determining whether the two year estimate holds or stretches further.

World.title: Jacó Beach Is Changing as New Residents and Major Brands Move In
World.content:
For decades, Jacó’s economy has revolved around the beach. Surfing, hotels, restaurants, nightlife and weekend visitors from San José helped turn the Central Pacific town into one of Costa Rica’s best-known tourist destinations. Tourism is still central to Jacó, but something else is happening. More people are living there year-round, residential construction is growing, and national chains are investing in businesses meant to serve customers every day rather than relying only on tourists during weekends and high season.

McDonald’s is preparing to open a restaurant along Avenida Amapola on Route 34 near the Costa Nera shopping center. The company has already held two job fairs in Jacó as it recruits workers for the new location. As of September 20, the restaurant had been announced but its opening date had not been made public.

Fresh Market has already opened at Plaza Comercial Costa Nera, marking part of the supermarket chain’s push beyond the Greater Metropolitan Area. The company’s own store directory now lists the Jacó location as operating seven days a week. KFC, meanwhile, is not new to Jacó, but the chain recently moved its existing restaurant to a larger location closer to the highway. KFC said the new restaurant involved an investment of about $500,000 and was designed to better serve residents, tourists and people traveling through the Central Pacific. The operation employs about 25 people.

Coffee and bakery chain Mocapan has also chosen Jacó for its first location outside the Greater Metropolitan Area (GMA). The company invested about $200,000 in its Costa Nera restaurant, creating 16 jobs. Little Caesars is another national chain already operating in the same commercial area.

Taken individually, a hamburger restaurant, supermarket or coffee shop does not change a town. Together, however, the investments point toward something larger: companies increasingly see Jacó as a place with enough permanent customers to support businesses throughout the year. Residential construction helps explain why.

Garabito, the area that includes Jacó, recorded 106,875 square meters, or about 1.15 million square feet, of new residential construction in 2024, according to Costa Rica’s National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). That was the second-highest total of any municipality in the country, behind only Santa Cruz in Guanacaste.

The population has also risen sharply. Garabito had 17,229 residents in the 2011 census. By the government’s 2022 population estimate, that number had climbed to 26,672, an increase of roughly 55% in just over a decade. Jacó’s location gives it an advantage that many other Costa Rican beach communities do not have.

It is close enough to San José and the Central Valley for residents to travel back and forth regularly, particularly people who work remotely or only need to be in the capital several days a week. It also offers supermarkets, banks, restaurants, medical services, schools and other basic services that are harder to find in some smaller beach communities.

That combination has helped create a different type of real estate market. Jacó still attracts foreign buyers, vacation-home owners and investors looking for short-term rental properties, but developers are increasingly building apartments and condominiums aimed at people who expect to spend much more of the year at the coast.

INEC’s construction figures provide some of the clearest evidence that the trend extends beyond tourism. While residential construction nationally declined in 2024, Garabito remained one of Costa Rica’s largest markets for new housing. The change does not mean Jacó is about to stop being a tourist town. Visitors remain essential to hotels, restaurants, tour operators, surf businesses and nightlife.

Instead, Jacó appears to be developing two economies at the same time: the traditional tourism economy and a growing residential economy built around people who actually live there. That shift creates opportunities, but it also places more pressure on infrastructure and public services.

Garabito ranked last among Costa Rica’s 82 municipalities in the 2025 National Competitiveness Index, with security identified as a major factor holding the area back. The same report warned nationally that weaknesses in security, infrastructure and workforce skills could limit economic growth.

Jacó will therefore have to keep pace with its own expansion as more residents mean greater demand for water, roads, health care, education, public transportation, policing and reliable internet, while rapid development brings the risk of congestion and poorly planned growth.

For now, however, the commercial signs are difficult to miss. McDonald’s is preparing to open. Fresh Market is operating and KFC has invested in a larger restaurant. Mocapan has chosen Jacó for its first move outside the Central Valley. Those companies are not abandoning tourists, but they are betting that Jacó now has enough people who stay after the weekend is over.

World.title: Heavy Rains Hamper Access to Irazú Volcano and Costa Rica’s Caribbean
World.content:
Heavy rains have disrupted travel to two of Costa Rica’s most important tourism areas after a landslide affected the road toward Irazú Volcano and falling debris forced the closure of Route 32, the main highway connecting San José with the Caribbean. The most serious incident was reported last night on National Route 219 in Oreamuno, Cartago, where a large landslide blocked part of the road leading toward Irazú Volcano following hours of heavy rain.

An initial emergency report indicated that around 30 people may have been left isolated by the landslide, prompting the Costa Rican Red Cross to send rescue crews and basic emergency units to the area. However, by late Saturday night authorities had not confirmed that anyone needed to be evacuated, and there were no reports of injuries connected to the incident.

Emergency officials activated the Municipal Emergency Committee in Oreamuno, while the National Road Council, police and rescue personnel were sent to evaluate conditions and determine what would be needed to clear the road. As of this morning, authorities had not publicly confirmed whether Route 219 had been completely reopened or whether all of the people initially reported as isolated had been able to leave the area.

The uncertainty is important for anyone using Route 219 as its the main road used to reach Irazú Volcano National Park from Cartago, as well as communities including Cot, Tierra Blanca and Potrero Cerrado. The road had already experienced problems earlier in September because of heavy rain, making the latest landslide another reminder of how quickly conditions can change on Costa Rica’s mountain routes during the rainy season.

The problems were not limited to Cartago. Route 32, the main highway between San José and Limón, was also closed last night after heavy rain caused material to fall onto the road in the mountainous section of the highway. The closure was announced shortly before 7 p.m., and drivers were advised to use alternate routes, including Route 10 through Turrialba, Route 126 through Vara Blanca or the Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta de Kopper connection.

Route 32 is one of our most important transportation corridors, taking drivers between the Central Valley and Caribbean destinations such as Puerto Viejo, Cahuita and Tortuguero, while also serving as the principal land connection to the Caribbean ports.

The highway has suffered repeated closures this rainy season because of landslides, falling rocks and saturated hillsides, particularly through the mountainous section near Braulio Carrillo National Park. Last night’s problems followed the passage of Tropical Wave 45, which brought heavy showers and thunderstorms to several parts of Costa Rica while being influenced by the Intertropical Convergence Zone.

Although the tropical wave has moved through by now, unstable weather is expected to continue today, with more afternoon showers and thunderstorms possible in the Central Valley and other parts of Costa Rica. That means travelers heading toward Irazú Volcano, the Caribbean or other mountainous areas should check road conditions before leaving and be prepared for sudden closures if heavy rain causes additional landslides.

For anyone planning to go to Irazú Volcano National Park today, the main issue is the condition of Route 219 rather than volcanic activity, and you should confirm that the road is passable before making the drive from Cartago. The same applies to anyone traveling between San José and the Caribbean, where Route 32 can reopen quickly after crews remove debris but can also close again if rain destabilizes surrounding slopes.

Costa Rica is in one of the wettest times of its rainy season, and saturated ground makes steep mountain roads especially vulnerable to landslides even after the heaviest rain has ended. Authorities are continuing to monitor conditions, and further road restrictions remain possible if strong afternoon storms return.

World.title: Why Experts Say Costa Rica Is the Best Wellness Trip After 50
World.content:
Costa Rica keeps turning up at the top of lists aimed at older travelers and retirees. The latest comes from Travel + Leisure, which interviewed more than half a dozen travel, retirement and wellness experts about the best wellness destination for senior travelers and found them all pointing to the same country.

The magazine’s August feature starts from a shift in how older travelers think about wellness. Fewer are chasing spa days or demanding fitness regimens. More want to lower their stress, spend time in nature and with local communities, and stay active without feeling rushed.

Leigh Barnes, president of Intrepid Travel, North America, said Costa Rica gets people “to slow down without feeling like they’re missing out.” He told the magazine that travelers over 50 can stay active every day, walking in rainforests, watching wildlife and soaking in hot springs, while setting their own pace.

Nature is the core of the argument. The magazine notes that Costa Rica holds about 6% of the world’s biodiversity across 12 distinct climatic zones, from jungle and cloud forest to beaches on both the Caribbean and the Pacific. Other experts in the piece made similar points. Simon Jones, CEO of tour company Trafalgar, highlighted natural hot springs, flat and well-kept walking trails, and wildlife outings such as boat tours and guided rainforest walks that require no strenuous hiking.

Arnaud Dieuteguard, spa and wellness director at Four Seasons Resort Costa Rica at Peninsula Papagayo in Guanacaste, said being surrounded by nature takes away some of the pressure people associate with wellness. Exercise becomes a walk, a swim or a surf lesson rather than another obligation.

Food and culture also feature. The magazine points to tours that include a home-cooked meal with a local family in Santa Cruz, visits to a family-run heart of palm plantation, coffee estates and chocolate experiences. It also mentions the Camino de Costa Rica, a coast-to-coast trek of about 280 kilometers (174 miles), as a draw for more adventurous hikers.

The recognition builds on earlier nods from the same publication. In July, Travel + Leisure’s World’s Best Awards placed two Costa Rican properties among the top five international wellness retreats of 2026: Surf Synergy in Jacó and Tabacón Thermal Resort & Spa in La Fortuna.

Retirement rankings have been telling a similar story. Costa Rica placed third among 24 countries in the 2026 Annual Global Retirement Index, behind Greece and Panama and ahead of Portugal, Mexico, Italy, France and Spain. The index weighs cost of living, access to health care, climate, visa options, housing, infrastructure and overall quality of life.

Forbes also included Costa Rica among its 24 best places to retire abroad in 2026, chosen from 96 destinations on five continents. The magazine pointed prospective retirees toward San José, the Central Valley, Atenas and Santa Cruz. It highlighted a cost of living well below the U.S. average and good-quality medical care in the larger cities.

Forbes noted that foreigners who obtain residency can join the public health system run by the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS). It estimated the cost for retired residents at around $150 a month, though actual contributions are set according to declared income and vary from person to person.

Costa Rica has also collected tourism awards this year. According to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), these include Best Nature Destination at the Forbes Travel Awards 2026. The run of accolades arrives at a mixed moment for the tourism sector. ICT figures show that arrivals of U.S. travelers by air fell 13.9% in August compared with the same month last year.

The institute links the slowdown largely to the bankruptcy of Spirit Airlines and to flight cuts by JetBlue, Volaris and Avianca, while arrivals from Canada and Europe have grown over the same period. For Costa Rica, whose economy leans heavily on visitors, and on the people who choose to settle here, rankings like these carry weight beyond bragging rights. Whether they translate into more arrivals in the coming high season remains to be seen.

World.title: Guinea Grass man charged with theft after failing to return bicycle and medication money
World.content:
Guinea Grass man charged with theft after failing to return bicycle and medication money

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Guinea Grass Village man has been charged with theft after an elderly woman reported that he failed to return with her bicycle and money she had given him to purchase medication.

According to police information, the 78 year old woman reported that on September 8, a man she had known for many years visited her home in Guinea Grass Village.

During their conversation, she reportedly told him that she was ill and needed medication.

The woman said she gave him $20 and asked him to go to a pharmacy on her behalf.

Because he was on foot, she also allowed him to use her black 26 inch gents beach cruiser, valued at $435, so he could return more quickly.

Police say the man allegedly failed to return with either the medication, the money or the bicycle.

The woman later requested court action.

Police identified the accused as Andres Batun, a labourer of Guinea Grass Village.

He was detained and later formally arrested and charged with theft.

The total value of the allegedly stolen property and cash is $455.

Minister Fonseca outlined the State of Belize’s foreign policy, emphasising our pragmatic and principled stance on international issues, our pursuit of deeper cooperation for Belize’s development, commitment to multilateralism, Belize-Guatemala relations and the case before the ICJ and our willingness to advance global priorities on climate change and sustainable development.

The Foreign Minister was joined by Ambassador Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer for Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Ambassador Alfonso Gahona, Ambassador Ayesha Borland and Director General for Foreign Trade Andy Sutherland.

World.title: Fisherman says gunmen opened fire on pickup near Trinidad Village
World.content:
Fisherman says gunmen opened fire on pickup near Trinidad Village

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police in Orange Walk are investigating a shooting incident after a 22 year old fisherman reported that several armed men opened fire on his pickup truck near Trinidad Village.

According to police information, the fisherman had gone on a fishing trip with two friends in a remote river area near Trinidad Village early on September 17.

He reportedly left his friends near the river and drove back toward the village to buy beer and additional fishing line.

While travelling along a dirt road near cane fields, he said his headlights illuminated a man dressed in a blue uniform resembling that of a Customs officer.

The fisherman told police he then saw two additional men wearing camouflage clothing resembling police uniforms, one of whom was holding a black rifle.

He said none of the men signalled him to stop or spoke to him, and because the area was dark and isolated, he became frightened and continued driving.

As he passed the man in the blue uniform, the fisherman alleged that the individual pointed a black handgun at the pickup and fired about six shots.

He said he felt a burning sensation in his left foot and accelerated away from the area.

After reaching a safer location, he reportedly found that both front tires were flat and later observed several bullet holes in the pickup.

Police and Scenes of Crime personnel visited the area and recovered five expended Aguila brand shell casings.

The pickup was also processed, and police reportedly observed bullet holes in the rear windshield, driver’s door and passenger door.

The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: Driver charged after police say he refused specimen request in Orange Walk
World.content:
Driver charged after police say he refused specimen request in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police in Orange Walk have charged a 24 year old man after he allegedly refused to provide a specimen during a traffic investigation early Saturday morning.

The incident unfolded at around 1:30 a.m. as officers were patrolling near the Phillip Goldson Highway.

Police say they stopped to check a yellow Chevrolet Colorado pickup that had pulled off the road.

The driver reportedly exited the vehicle while staggering, and officers say they detected a strong aroma of alcohol while speaking with him.

Checks also allegedly showed that his driver’s licence had expired.

The man, identified as Erick Ryan Santos, was taken into custody and escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police say Santos was repeatedly asked to provide a urine specimen but declined.

He was later taken to the Northern Regional Hospital, where he was again asked to provide either urine or blood for analysis and allegedly refused.

Police subsequently charged him with failing to provide a specimen and driving without a valid driver’s licence.

World.title: Belize to the World: How Belizeans share our culture through food, music and tradition
World.content:
Belize to the World: How Belizeans share our culture through food, music and tradition

By Zoila Palma: From the familiar taste of rice and beans with stew chicken to the rhythms of Belizean music, Belizeans across the world are carrying the country’s culture beyond its borders. Whether through education, professional training, travel, or artistic expression, Belizeans are introducing people from different countries to the traditions, flavors, and identity that make Belize unique.

Food remains one of the most powerful ways Belizeans share their heritage.

Belizeans living, studying, or traveling abroad prepare and introduce dishes such as barbecue, relleno, escabeche, sere, hudut, tamales and garnaches, offering others an opportunity to experience the country’s diverse culinary traditions. Each dish tells a story of Belize’s multicultural identity, bringing together influences that have shaped generations of Belizean families.

Belizean students studying in Taiwan and other countries, along with those pursuing education in the United States, become cultural ambassadors in their everyday interactions.

By preparing local meals, sharing stories about Belize, and participating in cultural activities, they help international friends and communities learn more about the country’s traditions.

Similarly, journalists and public officers who travel overseas for training and professional development represent Belize beyond their workplaces, carrying with them the customs, experiences, and cultural identity of home.

Music is another powerful bridge between Belize and the world. Belizean artists, including “The General” Supa G and many other talented musicians, continue to share the country’s sounds and creative expression with audiences beyond its borders. Through music, Belize’s unique cultural influences, languages, and experiences reach listeners in different countries, demonstrating how a small nation can make its presence felt on the international stage.

Even a bottle of Marie Sharp’s pepper sauce discovered in a store or restaurant abroad can create a sense of home for Belizeans and introduce foreigners to a beloved Belizean brand. These everyday connections, from food and music to language and traditions, highlight the ways Belizeans represent their country wherever they go.

From Belize to the world, Belizeans are sharing more than products and performances—they are sharing a culture, a heritage, and an identity that remains uniquely Belizean.

World.title: International military leaders join Belize for 45th Independence flag raising ceremony
World.content:
International military leaders join Belize for 45th Independence flag raising ceremony

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Senior military officials from across the Caribbean and beyond joined Belize in celebrating its 45th anniversary of Independence with a flag raising ceremony at Memorial Park in Belize City.

The ceremony formed part of a series of activities organized by the Belize Defence Force involving visiting military partners and invited guests.

Among the international representatives participating in the Independence celebrations were Brigadier Carlos A. R. Lovell, Chief of Staff of the Barbados Defence Force, and Warrant Officer Class One Leroy Chase, Force Sergeant Major of the Barbados Defence Force.

The delegation also included Brigadier General Miguel Maldonado Castro of the Honduran Army, Brigadier Mahatma Williams and Captain David Hutchinson of the Jamaica Defence Force, and Colonel Donald Henley, Canadian Defence Attaché in Mexico.

The Belize Defence Force said the raising of the Belizean flag represents the country’s sovereignty, national identity and journey since attaining Independence in 1981.

The wider programme began Friday with a welcome reception in Belize City, followed Saturday by the graduation of the Jungle Warfare Instructors Course 01/2026.

Visiting military representatives also travelled to Caye Caulker for a cultural and heritage experience that included an excursion along Belize’s reef.

The BDF said the activities provide an opportunity to celebrate Independence while strengthening relationships and military cooperation with Belize’s international partners.

World.title: Look at me, I am Belize at 45!
World.content:
Look at me, I am Belize at 45!

By Zoila Palma: Belizeans around the country and in the diaspora are today celebrating the 45th Anniversary of Belize’s Independence.

On that fateful night, September 21, 1981 when the Union Jack was lowered and the red, white and blue Belize flag was lifted signaling a nation, proud, free, independent and sovereign.

Across Belize, Belizeans will gather at their respective municipalities for today’s Independence Day parade.

Ceremonies feature speeches on the journey to Independence by our Mayors, our Area Representatives, and a reminder of Belize’s journey from British Honduras to Belize.

As Belize celebrates the 45th Anniversary of Independence under theme “Look at me, I am Belize at 45”, may we always be reminded of the legacy of Father of the Nation George Cadle Price, the journey to Independence and the principles of social justice, service to country and people and the unique cultural history that makes us Belize.

Happy Independence Day Belize!

World.title: Hague relief
World.content:
Minister without portfolio in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development, with responsibility for land titling and settlements, Robert Montague (right) hugs a resident in Cooper’s Pen on Saturday.

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — With residents whose houses remain standing facing a November 30 deadline to vacate the privately owned Cooper’s Pen property, the Government has begun subdividing lands at nearby Hague to create lots for those who qualify for longer-term relocation.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development Arlene Williams, addressing residents in the community on Saturday, said work had started on the Hague property, and that Government was actively preparing the site for eligible Cooper’s Pen residents.

“We have identified lands very near to here in Hague that we are actively subdividing so that persons who are there longer term will get [their] title,” Williams said.

She stressed, however, that the Hague lots would not be given away.

“Nothing is coming free, as the prime minister would have said to you,” Williams emphasised to residents, explaining that those who are employed and able to do so would be expected to purchase their lots.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness had previously told Cooper’s Pen residents that Government assistance would help qualified residents transition to a properly planned settlement, but that they would ultimately have to pay for the land and associated services.

The Hague arrangement applies to residents whose homes have not been demolished but who occupy the privately owned property and will have to relocate.

Meanwhile, the families whose homes were demolished on August 11 by the private owners of the property, and who have since been living in tents on the property, are being dealt with separately. They had been given until September 19 to vacate the land.

Sunday, the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development announced that cheques had been delivered to these displaced residents as the ministry with responsibility for housing — following directives by Holness during his visit to Cooper’s Pen last month — was coordinating a whole-of-Government intervention to assist members of the community to relocate.

Minister with responsibility for land titling and settlements, Robert Montague, alongside Williams, issued 19 humanitarian grants, valued at $9.9 million, to assist vulnerable citizens who were displaced in the eviction exercise.

The grants, ranging from $200,000 to $800,000 per family, are being provided to some of the most vulnerable residents, many of whom have been living under tents provided by the Government as emergency shelter since August 12, 2026, the ministry said.

At the handover, officials outlined the Government’s position on the relocation exercise and reiterated the November 30, 2026 deadline for the full evacuation of the site. Montague emphasised that the emergency assistance is being funded by Jamaican taxpayers.

“The cheque is not a Government cheque. It is the taxpayers of Jamaica’s cheque,” he said. “You who pay your taxes, and taxpayers from all over the country, have provided this assistance.”

Williams also reiterated that the Government is not the owner of the property and was not responsible for the demolition or displacement of the occupants.

Under legitimate terms issued by the property owners, residents remaining on the site are required to leave by November 30, 2026, while those currently occupying tents were required to relocate immediately.

Extensive work was done in engaging the occupants, the ministry said. A multi-sector team comprising representatives from Jamaica Defence Force, Jamaica Constabulary Force, HEART/NSTA Trust, the Social Development Commission (SDC), and others, provided social support to the displaced occupants including formalisation of their tax registration and national identification documents. The ministry said many households and displaced occupants had no formal identification documents or bank accounts, therefore a three-day facility was arranged with a commercial bank to allow beneficiaries to cash their cheques.

The ministry and the SDC are scheduled to return next week to assess the remaining residents and support the finalisation of the resettlement process ahead of the November 30 deadline.

Meanwhile, some of the displaced families have also been offered the option of temporary accommodation at a site prepared at Salt Marsh for two weeks.

Williams said the immediate assistance was only part of a broader Government intervention, with several agencies working together to determine the appropriate support for affected households.

She said the Government is working with residents to facilitate an orderly transition while preparations continue at Hague, underscoring that the State does not own the Cooper’s Pen property and therefore cannot permit residents to remain there beyond the period agreed with the owners.

Montague said the circumstances of residents vary, and that Government therefore had to hear their individual concerns rather than assume that one solution would meet everyone’s needs.

World.title: ‘People first’ on the agenda at 88th PNP National Conference
World.content:
Comrades gather at the 88th PNP National Conference at Independence Park in Westmoreland Sunday. (Anthony Lewis)

PEOPLE’S National Party (PNP) leader Mark Golding pledged a message of ‘people first’ at the PNP’s 88th anniversary conference public session at Independence Park in Westmoreland, Sunday.

Telling officers of the party, members of Parliament and senators, regional chairs, mayors and councillors, delegates and hundreds of Comrades what his vision is for Jamaica, Golding also thanked people of Westmoreland and all of western Jamaica for welcoming the party and standing strong through one of the hardest periods the region has ever faced.

Golding said the party didn’t gather in the traditional way at the National Arena in Kingston but came to the west, “because this is where the pain has been greatest, where the recovery has been slowest, and where the need for determined leadership is most urgent” following Hurricane Melissa last October.

He said the decision to come to the west was also strengthened by the fact that the Government’s response to the Hurricane Melissa disaster has been an “abject failure of the people”.

“There has been no coherent recovery plan, and the people have largely been abandoned,” Golding said.

“The many thousands who lost their roofs and suffered other damage have faced delayed and inadequate assistance to repair their homes, and those whose houses and businesses were destroyed have been left to fend for themselves.”

He continued, highlighting that there has been no programme to cushion rising food prices for hurricane victims, and well into the new school year the vast majority of damaged schools remain unrepaired.

“There has been no programme to support small business operators and help them get back on their feet,” he lamented, adding, “We did not come here merely to describe your suffering. We came to say what must now be done.”

Citing the need for a recovery road map for western Jamaica, Golding said Jamaica needs a public reconstruction dashboard showing every damaged school, health facility, road and public building, the money allocated, the contractor responsible, and the deadline for completion.

“The people must be able to see where the money is going and whether the work is being done,” he said.

“Second, we need a properly funded recovery facility for farmers, fisherfolk and small businesses. Assistance must reach people quickly and on reasonable terms so they can replace equipment, restore production, rehire workers, and earn again.”

He said reconstruction must make the west stronger than it was before — more resilient roofs and public buildings, better drainage, stronger electricity and water systems, and construction standards fit for a country exposed to more powerful storms.

“What has happened in the west reflects a wider national problem. Too many Jamaicans are left to struggle alone against the raging tide of high prices, unreliable public services, insecure housing, inadequate health care, and an economy in which work does not deliver a better life for the people,” Golding said.

“Jamaica does not lack talent. We do not lack hard-working people. We do not lack ideas. What we lack is governance and policies that put the people first.”

Golding said his vision for Jamaica is anchored in the core principles of the PNP. “Our policies must always seek to benefit the majority of the people; that is what putting people first means. We pursue social justice because we know that the way things are is not how they are meant to be, and better must come because positive change is not beyond us.”

At the conference Golding listed party promises, including ownership for more Jamaicans, making the country not a Jamaica of “permanent tenants and insecure occupants” but one of owners. He also promised a better life for working people — making life easier for those who work for a living by, among other things, introducing a liveable wage that takes the working poor out of poverty and is adjusted annually for inflation.

A third promise of a strong economy that builds and grows wealth and reduces inequality, was followed by public services that works for ordinary people, an honest government, and equal justice under the law.

“Last year the people made the PNP a much stronger Opposition, but they did not yet give us the Government,” he told delegates. “We must reflect and learn from both parts of that verdict.”

He added: ”We must be humble and ask why some Jamaicans who wanted change were not yet ready to place the full responsibility of government in our hands. We have listened. We are learning. And we are changing.”

World.title: Johnson Smith leading Jamaica’s delegation to 81st session of United Nations General Assembly
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, shakes hands with United Nations Secretary General António Guterres on the margins of the 78th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York in 2023.

MINISTER of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith is leading Jamaica’s delegation to the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81) where Jamaica will join international partners in advancing cooperation on development financing, peace and security, climate resilience, and reform of the multilateral system while deepening partnerships that support national and regional goals.

“Jamaica remains firmly committed to principled and effective multilateralism, because the challenges before us are shared and so too must be the solutions. At UNGA81, we will work with partners across regions to advance cooperation on peace and security, financing for development, climate resilience, and reform of the international system. We will seek to strengthen partnerships that support our efforts at sustainable and inclusive development, including building resilience. Jamaica will bring its experiences and perspectives to the table, working in a spirit of mutual respect and shared responsibility to help shape outcomes that benefit our region and other developing countries,” Johnson Smith said.

The minister’s emphasis on effective multilateralism speaks directly to the theme the Assembly has set for the 81st session, ‘Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All’. Jamaica is contributing directly to that effort through its co-chairmanship of the General Assembly’s Ad Hoc Working Group on Mandate Implementation Review, held jointly with Norway by Jamaica’s permanent representative to the United Nations (UN), Ambassador Brian Wallace, helping to reshape how UN decisions are designed, implemented, and assessed.

The ministry said matters relating to financing development will remain central to Jamaica’s advocacy. The country continues to press for international financial arrangements that better recognise the unique challenges facing countries like Jamaica and provide developing states with affordable resources to invest in resilience, infrastructure, and sustainable growth. Jamaica’s experience with increasingly severe climate shocks further underscores the case for adaptation and loss-and-damage financing accessible to vulnerable countries before development gains are reversed.

Jamaica will also continue building international cooperation against transnational organised crime, gangs, and illicit weapons flows, while maintaining its strong advocacy for sustained international support for peace, stability, and development in countries like Haiti.

Throughout the high-level week, scheduled for September 21 to 28, Johnson Smith will also hold bilateral talks with other foreign ministers and heads of international organisations to strengthen existing partnerships and pursue new opportunities in trade, investment, and for technical cooperation.

World.title: Suspense means business
World.content:
Suspense

Suspense is no longer waiting for the music industry to figure out what to do with her. Nine years after winning Magnum Kings and Queens of Dancehall, the entertainer is approaching her career with a different mindset — one built as much on strategy, branding, and business as it is on talent.

At the start of 2026 the Jamaica Observer named Suspense among its artistes to watch for the year. Months later she believes she has made good on some of that promise, but she is nowhere near ready to declare the mission accomplished.

“Since the beginning of the year I’ve been putting in the work — creating new music, developing my image, connecting with my audience, and making sure people understand who Suspense is as an artiste,” she said. “I’m proud of how far I’ve come so far this year, but I wouldn’t say I’m satisfied yet.”

That hunger is central to what Suspense previously described as her “rebirth” — a period that saw her reassessing not only her music, but the way she conducts her career.

“When I said this chapter was a rebirth I really meant that I was becoming a new version of myself — not just as an artiste, but as a woman,” she explained. “Over the past eight months, I’ve been learning to trust myself more, be more intentional about the moves I make, and understand the kind of artiste and brand I want Suspense to represent.”

That has meant refusing to be confined to one sound. Suspense has experimented with reggae, rap, and house music, while maintaining her dancehall foundation. She has also taken her act beyond Jamaica, completing three tours this year — two in Canada and one in England.

“I’m not trying to fit into a box or follow what everybody else is doing,” she said. “I’m learning what works for me and building from there.”

There have been signs that the approach is paying off.

Suspense points to Too Bad, her collaboration with Nhance, as one of the year’s major wins. According to the artiste, the track has surpassed five million views on YouTube and inspired more than 42,000 uses on TikTok. She’s now banking on her follow-up single to keep that momentum going.

The track, Female Boss, produced by Countree Hype, deliberately presents a different Suspense — less aggressive than the sound on which she initially built her name, but no less confident. She says the response so far is proving that exploring her versatility is invaluable.

“The response to Female Boss has shown me that my audience wants music that feels empowering, relatable, and authentic,” she said. “It’s different and it’s proving that switching things up has its rewards. Listeners are taking on well to my new calm sound.”

World.title: ‘I have to sue schools’
World.content:
A copy of an industrial techniques textbook that was published by Everett Fraser which is being reprographed by educators.

AN educational author said he is considering taking legal action against more than 80 schools over breaches of the Copyright Act by teachers and other school administrators.

The author, Everett Fraser, said he has spent more than a decade gathering material to produce text and workbooks for students, spending millions of dollars to publish his work. However, he said he is not seeing the rewards of his labour as many teachers at several institutions are photocopying, scanning, or taking pictures of the entirety of his publications to share with their students instead of purchasing the material or adding it to the book list.

An educator himself, Fraser said the revelation came through his own investigations at some institutions, and interactions with teachers who became hostile when confronted about their actions. He called a meeting with the Ministry of Education to discuss the matter, stressing the need for teachers to be sensitised.

According to the Copyright Act of Jamaica, making unauthorised photocopies of entire books or substantial parts of them is illegal. While Section 59 of the Act states that copies of passages from published literary, dramatic or musical works can be made by or on behalf of an educational establishment for educational purposes, the law states that no more than five per cent of the material may be copied.

However, Fraser said many educators are not aware of the law.

“What I realise is that teachers are not aware of the Copyright Act, and when I tell the schools, it is a challenge; they are usually hostile. According to the Copyright Act, there are rules that govern how schools can use the material, and often, teachers, once they have purchased a book, they feel like they are entitled to do whatever they want with it, which is not the case,” said the frustrated author.

Fraser said his published works cater to students at the early childhood level, with a focus on teaching them how to read. He added that he has also published textbooks and workbooks designed to prepare students for technical subjects, including industrial technology, at the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) level.

“You find cases where they are ‘reprographing’ the entire book, or they might scan the book and share it with students. When this is done, it affects me tremendously. I’ve spent millions of dollars and years of research, travelling to different countries to get material. I’ve volunteered to work in particular fields, and I’ve gone into schools to volunteer to work to get the experience to write these books. I even pay for students to do CSEC just to get people to learn, and I’m not making anything. It’s a real struggle,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“It is affecting me tremendously because what you find is that students do not buy books because they see that they can get the material for free, and those who buy the books, for example half of the class buys the books, you find that the teacher will take pictures or share it in their private

WhatsApp groups or on their various school platforms,” he said.

The author said he understands that books can be expensive and that not every parent can afford to purchase a textbook or workbook for their child. In response, he said he heavily discounted the materials and even provided more than $80,000 worth of free copies to less fortunate students. However, those efforts have done little to address the problem.

“I remember I went to this school to introduce a book to the students, and when I stepped into the class I realised that they were doing

AutoCAD. I used a book I wrote to demonstrate some techniques, and I realised that the students knew every little. This book was being sold for $650; it was a massive reduction because the books were sitting there not selling, so I said, ‘Let me just sell them out cheap since they are not going,’ ” he recalled.

“…After showing the students the books they said they wanted some to buy. I went outside to get some more books, and by the time I stepped back into the classroom the teacher allowed the students to have their phones out, taking pictures of my book,” he told the Observer.

Fraser said at that same institution he had previously sent some books over to be sold that never were. He said further checks with a teacher at the institution revealed that the teacher had photocopied the entire book and was sharing it with students.

“I really have to act. I have a list of about 80 schools that are reprographing my work. Some schools, I try to go in and talk to them and try to at least get some change but they are not listening,” he shared.

“I love teaching, and I have a lot of knowledge. I want to give back what I have to education — and I think the way to give back to education is to share my knowledge with others by writing books — but it has reached a point now where I have decided that I’m going to have to sue schools. If I can’t make money from my work I have to sue schools and the ministry, because the ministry has failed its statutory duty to protect our intellectual property,” he reasoned.

Fraser said the problem became so bad that he pulled his books from book stores. He said he also has more than 10 books he recently completed that he refuses to publish out of fear they will also be photocopied and shared illegally.

“I think if authors were taking action we would see changes. I think we all have just accepted it, but I have decided that I am going to take action. If it means that I am only going to sell the books to 10 schools or parents, I am going to take action because this is damaging education,” he said.

World.title: TOP-SIX PUSH
World.content:
Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz footballers train at Sabina Park in Kingston in September 2025. (Photo: JFF)

INTERIM head coach Rudolph Speid says Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz cannot afford any slip-ups in the upcoming Concacaf Nations League games as they look to put themselves in a strong position for the start of the 2030 Concacaf World Cup Qualifiers.

Jamaica begin their 2026/2027 Nations League A group stage campaign this week at the National Stadium, starting with Guatemala on Friday and Honduras next Monday. They will then travel to El Salvador next Friday before ending action on October 5 away to Honduras.

It will be the national men’s first competitive fixture since the Inter-Confederation Playoffs in March which saw them miss out on this summer’s FIFA World Cup in the United States, Mexico and Canada.

The Reggae Boyz will need to finish top two in their group to advance to the quarter-finals where they will play one of Concacaf’s top four nations, Mexico, USA, Canada or Panama, which were pre-seeded.

Speid says the team is taking the Nations League seriously, knowing the results could have major implications for their route to the 2030 FIFA World Cup. Unlike this year when they earned automatic qualification as co-hosts, Mexico, USA and Canada will have to go through the qualifying process this time around.

“At this particular time, if you look on all the teams, we are currently seventh in Concacaf, but we need to be in the top six by the end of the year to prepare for the seedings for the World Cup qualifiers in 2030,” he said.

“So it is important that we do well in this competition because it actually decides if we get a seeded spot in the World Cup Qualifiers for 2030. If we’re not seeded, then we could go against some difficult teams.”

Speid named his 24-man squad last Friday, with the majority set to report to camp today and the others arriving by Tuesday.

A total of 14 players from Jamaica’s World Cup play-off squad in March have been retained, with the remainder made up of under-23 players, debutant centre back Miguel Freckleton and players earning recalls, including striker Javon East and full back Tayvon Gray.

Speid believes the team is strong enough to make a deep run in the competition.

“If you look at the squad, it still boasts a lot of players from March but clearly, at some point, we had to retool, so it’s a balancing act,” he said.

“But we still expect to do well because we know what we have to achieve by the end of the year. It’s a balancing act but a lot of these players are on form, doing extremely well at their club, and we think they can get us over the line.”

Questions have been raised about the absence of several players, including winger Kaheem Parris, who recently made his UEFA Champions League debut for Azerbaijan’s Sabah FK against Manchester United; and Coventry City duo Ethan Pinnock and Ephron Mason-Clarke.

There have also been questions about the number of locally based players in the squad, with only Mount Pleasant FA goalkeeper Shaquan Davis and Cavalier FC defender Christopher Ainsworth selected.

However, Speid says the door remains open to players from across the country and overseas, after scouting more than 70 players ahead of the upcoming four games.

“We’re still on the lookout for talented players, [and] I hope some come to fruition. What is most important for us is for Jamaica to really field a competitive team all the time and give players who deserve it opportunities.”

SQUAD

Goalkeepers — Andre Blake, Amal Knight, Shaquan Davis

Defenders — Damion Lowe, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Joel Latibeaudiere, Christopher Ainsworth, Tayvon Gray, Miguel Freckleton

Midfielders — Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer, Dwayne Atkinson, Karoy Anderson, Brandon Cover, Courtney Clarke

Forwards — Leon Bailey, Renaldo Cephas, Kaheim Dixon, Bailey Cadamarteri, Rumarn Burrell, Tyreece Campbell, Andre Brooks, Javon East

World.title: $500-m investment for Queen Heights water system
World.content:
Samuda says the project will be implemented by the National Water Commission, with plans to advance it to the procurement stage next year.

MORE than $500 million is expected to be invested in the development of the Queen Heights water system in St Ann North Western as part of efforts to address water supply challenges across the constituency.

Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda said the project will be implemented by the National Water Commission (NWC), with plans to advance it to the procurement stage next year.

He made the announcement while addressing the commissioning ceremony for the Discovery Point to Mount Boon pipeline project in Discovery Point, St Ann, on Friday.

Samuda said the project must undergo several processes before implementation, noting that significant work remains before it reaches the construction stage.

He, however, gave the assurance that the Government is committed to advancing the project, “[and] getting it done as soon as it’s possible”.

Samuda said the Queen Heights development forms part of a broader programme of water infrastructure upgrades in St Ann North Western where addressing the constituency’s various water supply challenges is expected to cost more than $2 billion.

He noted that the scale of the required investment reflects the varying infrastructure needs across the constituency.

The minister explained that some communities require new systems to provide residents with a reliable water supply for the first time, while others need ageing infrastructure to be replaced.

He noted that infrastructure in some areas already served by the NWC has aged and deteriorated over time.

“So, we have to both be building new systems to give many people reliable water supply for the first time while also replacing existing systems that, in many cases, have outlived their useful life,” he said.

Samuda acknowledged that residents awaiting improvements can become frustrated, noting that their assessment of progress ultimately depends on whether water is reaching their homes.

He further outlined that the scale of the challenge will require continued investment in new and replacement infrastructure to gradually improve water services across the constituency.

World.title: Meet Susan Peterkin: The hairstylist changing the conversation about black hair loss
World.content:
.

FROM Kingston to the United States, Susan Peterkin has spent more than 40 years building a career around natural hair, professional education and, increasingly, the health of the scalp and hair.
