When she left Jamaica at 16, she did not expect hair to become the focus of her professional life. She arrived in 1981 with ambitions that had little to do with the beauty industry, imagining that she might eventually work in marketing for one of the major hair companies whose products were familiar to black women at the time. Instead, she found herself drawn to the relationship between a cosmetologist and her clients, beginning a career that would span more than four decades.

“There was something about the immediate gratification of being able to make a difference in someone’s life and see that difference right in front of you,” Peterkin recalled. “I loved the relationships I built, the trust clients placed in me and, quite frankly, I also realised that I could build a very good living doing work that I enjoyed.”

Today, Peterkin is based in Maryland and is the co-founder of PeterKINdred Hair & Scalp Wellness Center and S.T.R.A.N.D. (Stylists Training, Researching, and Networking with Dermatologists), an initiative that educates cosmetologists about hair and scalp concerns and strengthens collaboration between hair professionals and dermatologists.

Her path to this work began in the salon. Peterkin opened Jaha Hair Studio in 1996, building a natural hair business that eventually grew to a team of 10 stylists and served more than 20,000 clients. In 2003, she founded Jaha Natural Hair Academy to provide professional education in natural hair care.

Her work expanded into consumer education and industry advocacy, including creating My Hair, My Way and co-founding the Natural Hair Industry Convention.

But her own experience with hair loss changed the direction of her career.

Peterkin began noticing her own changes while also encountering scalp and hair loss concerns among her clients. Despite decades of experience, she recognised that there were things she was observing that she did not fully understand from a medical perspective.

“Looking back, that experience is important to me because it reminds me what it’s like to be a very experienced cosmetologist and still not have the education to understand everything you’re observing on the scalp,” she said.

Her search for answers led to a professional relationship with dermatologist Dr Chesahna Kindred. Peterkin eventually became Kindred’s patient and was diagnosed with central centrifugal cicatricial alopaecia (CCCA) and female pattern hair loss. The experience changed how she approached her clients.

“As I started seeing results and learning from her during treatment, I became much more confident talking to my own clients,” she said. “I understood more of the language. I understood more of what I was observing. I better understood when a scalp concern required a referral to a dermatologist.”

That relationship eventually led to PeterKINdred Hair & Scalp Wellness Center, bringing natural hair care and dermatological expertise together.

The idea came from a problem Peterkin and Kindred were seeing from different sides.

“Dr Kindred would talk about patients sometimes falling through the cracks after leaving the dermatologist’s office because they didn’t know where to go for knowledgeable and appropriate hair care,” Peterkin explained. “And on my side, I knew hair professionals were seeing things every day that they didn’t necessarily understand required medical attention.”

The answer was collaboration. “Neither profession needed to become the other,” Peterkin said. “We simply needed to learn how to work together.”

That philosophy became the foundation for S.T.R.A.N.D., which Peterkin and Kindred co-founded in 2024.

The initiative provides cosmetologists with education about hair and scalp disorders, alopecia, medical treatments and when a client should be referred to a dermatologist. S.T.R.A.N.D. has trained and certified more than 100 cosmetologists and developed relationships with more than 20 dermatologists.

Peterkin believes hairstylists can play an important role in early recognition because of the relationships they develop with their clients.

“If I’ve cared for someone’s hair for five, ten or fifteen years, I know her baseline,” she said. “I know what her density normally looks like. I know her hairline. I know her crown. I know how her scalp typically looks. I may recognise that something has changed before she does.”

She is equally clear about where a stylist’s responsibility ends.

“We don’t need hair professionals diagnosing medical conditions,” Peterkin said. “We need them educated enough to recognise change, understand when something is outside their scope, document what they’re seeing and make responsible referrals.”

For black women, that awareness can be particularly important. Hair loss can have multiple causes, including traction from repeated tension, scarring conditions such as CCCA and female pattern hair loss. Early recognition can make a difference, particularly with conditions that can cause permanent follicular damage.

Peterkin’s own experience has also shaped the way she talks about styling. She does not believe women need to abandon braids, wigs, extensions or other styles. Instead, she wants them to become more attentive to what is happening underneath.

“I don’t believe we have to reject wigs, braids or extensions to love our natural hair,” she said. “But I do believe every woman should have an opportunity to know, understand and appreciate the hair that grows from her own scalp.”

Peterkin urges black women to learn what is normal for your own hair so that you can recognise when something changes.

“You simply need to know what normal looks like for you,” Peterkin said. “Because when you know your baseline, you’re much more likely to recognise change early.”

More than 40 years after leaving Kingston, Peterkin is still working with hair, but her focus has expanded from styling to education, early recognition and collaboration between two professions that have traditionally operated separately.

“I want to leave this industry better educated than I found it,” she said. “I want hair professionals to understand that their eyes have value, their relationships with clients have value and their observations can have value — when they’re supported by education and respect for professional boundaries.”

World.title: Spanish PM’s wife to face trial over influence peddling, embezzlement allegations
World.content:
The proceedings are the latest in a scandal-riddled year for Socialist leader Sánchez. Former Prime Minister José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero recently faced questions over a €53-million pandemic bailout, while Socialist heavyweight Santos Cerdán was investigated in a public-contract kickback probe involving former minister José Luis Ábalos. Both men deny wrongdoing.

Gómez’s case will now go to a higher court, which must set a hearing date. Spain’s public prosecutor, which says the evidence does not establish a criminal offense, and the defense teams are seeking acquittals. Hazte Oír, an ultra-Catholic group acting as a private prosecutor, is seeking 13 years in prison for Gómez.

Her lawyer, Jaime Campaner, has argued that Hazte Oír’s indictment contains “serious technical defects” that are incompatible with the law and “irremediable” at this stage. He has called for the case to be closed.

World.title: Merz pledges reset as he admits German conservatives don’t have the ‘answers’
World.content:
Party officials had warned that an outcome below 5% for the CDU in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania would unleash a storm of criticism and renew calls for a change in leadership, or Kanzlertausch.

But Merz is clinging to power — for now.

Unless he steps aside voluntarily, forcing a leadership change risks triggering a snap election at a time when polls show the far right to be the country’s most popular party — making such a move unlikely for the time being. That could quickly change if party members begin speaking out against him.

That’s why Merz has vowed to chart a new course for the CDU, announcing consultations in the coming days to unite the party’s rank and file behind him.

The chancellor said he would engage in “intensive deliberations” with his party’s leadership to work out how they could remain a people’s party that attracts large and diverse swathes of the electorate.

“We will discuss the party’s work and structure, our platform, and the CDU’s public image,” he said. “To be frank, we no longer have satisfactory answers to too many questions. And that is something we will and must change.”

“We know that the federal government and the states must stand together and join forces,” he added. “We must — and we will — find a new way of working together, and to that end, we will hold discussions with the state premiers very soon regarding the course of action and the process for the coming weeks,” he said.

After deliberations at the CDU headquarters on Sunday evening, the party’s state premiers met secretly in Berlin without the chancellor, according to media reports. That meeting fueled renewed speculation about their weakening support for Merz. On Monday, however, the chancellor said he enjoyed the full backing of his party’s leadership.

World.title: EU deadlocked over France’s bid to take Russian tycoon off sanctions list
World.content:
Around 3,000 listings, including Usmanov’s, are at risk of expiring Tuesday after Paris withheld its support for the renewal. Three diplomats, all of whom were granted anonymity to describe the private discussions, said capitals remained deeply divided, despite France’s pledge to establish guardrails to assuage concerns that the move could undermine the sanctions regime more broadly.

Two other diplomats said EU capitals were likely to agree to extend the sanctions — for a period as long as 36 months — as part of a compromise with countries seeking delisting.

Envoys are due to meet again Monday afternoon after consulting their capitals. A decision to remove Usmanov — whose business empire spans mining, telecommunications and media — from the list could allow him to move money in and out of the EU, do business with European firms and potentially travel to the bloc.

Luxembourg has continued to call for the delisting of Ukrainian-born, Russian-Israeli tycoon Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.

At a meeting last week that ended in stalemate, capitals expressed concern that removing one prominent billionaire from the list would set a dangerous precedent.

France has declined to explain its motivations publicly or privately. Diplomats said only that the move relates to “a specific national security issue” and that Paris “wishes to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.” The Financial Times reported that his delisting could form part of a deal under which Azerbaijan would release detained French nationals.

Brussels imposed financial and travel restrictions on Usmanov in 2022 as it unveiled sanctions on businesspeople and politicians involved in “undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine,” citing his alleged material support for Russia’s war. Usmanov rejects those charges along with his depiction as an oligarch, and has campaigned to be removed from the list.

World.title: Former Romanian presidential candidate Georgescu detained on suspicion of fraud
World.content:
The ultranationalist politician, who was accused of fomenting a violent coup in Bucharest, is facing a battery of criminal cases.

Former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu was detained Monday on suspicion of fraud by Romanian police and the Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT).

The ultranationalist politician shot to prominence when he unexpectedly won the first round of the November 2024 presidential election, snapping up 23% of the vote. But the Constitutional Court annulled the election in December that year and barred Georgescu from running again due to his campaign’s links to a Russian influence operation.

Romanian authorities are investigating Georgescu for committing fraud and forming an organized criminal group that prosecutors say defrauded a Romanian businessman by promising access to multimillion-euro foreign bank financing in exchange for cash guarantees.

World.title: EU pressures Big Tech to go green with new data center sustainability label
World.content:
The new label is optional for smaller data centers, “but later we are also going to introduce minimum performance standards which, of course, will put more pressure on those who may not voluntarily wish to be as sustainable as we want them to,” he added.

While Australia and Singapore already have schemes rating the energy efficiency of data centers, the Commission's new label would be the most comprehensive worldwide — asking tech companies to be transparent not only about their power use but also their impact on the local and global environment via information on how much water they consume, how clean their electricity is, whether they reuse the heat they generate and more.

The EU executive's performance standards, which the Commission wants to present in spring 2027, are expected to tighten the screws by setting mandatory sustainability thresholds for newly built or retrofitted data centers.

Those two initiatives are an attempt at ensuring the European Union can compete in the artificial intelligence race without sacrificing its commitment to climate neutrality in 2050, Jørgensen said.

“We need to deal with this in a way that data centers in the future are not something that will hurt our energy systems, and thereby our competitiveness and capabilities of decarbonizing and making sure we have security of supply for our citizens,” he said.

“If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets,” Jørgensen warned. Data centers are already hoovering up 2.5% of the bloc’s electricity use, a share expected to double in the coming years, he noted. “We’re looking at a huge change.”

World.title: Putin’s party dominates in Russia’s sham elections
World.content:
“I have proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories,” she added. Residents of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — regions that the Kremlin unlawfully occupied after the 2022 assault started — also took part in the vote, with some reportedly coerced into doing so.

The war in Ukraine featured heavily in the elections, which were marked by severe repression. Dissenting voices were all but silenced, and Yabloko — the country’s only openly anti-war party — was banned from fielding a national list of candidates in the State Duma.

“A party that has not been represented in the country’s parliament for 23 years [would have] secured second place in the polls, given the conditions in which we operate,” said Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov following the elections. “And the authorities could do nothing about it other than remove the party from the election.”

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said of the results: “The citizens of our country maintain their trust in our leading political force [Putin’s party] and consider it appropriate to continue entrusting it with governance at various levels of state authority.”

World.title: Google hit with €403M privacy fine over handling of user location data
World.content:
Google infringed the General Data Protection Regulation, the EU’s landmark laws, on four counts, said Ireland’s three privacy commissioners Des Hogan, Dale Sunderland and Niamh Sweeney. The issues concerned how Google processed and retained location data in its Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy functions, as well as transparency.

The complaints from consumer groups alleged that Google had used dark patterns and unfair practices to incite users to enable features that shared their location data.

The Irish DPC has three other ongoing large-scale investigations against Google. Those are examining data processing by Google’s PaLM2 AI model, the company’s personalized advertising system, and Google’s account sign-up process.

Google spokesperson Mathilde Méchin said in a comment: "This case centers around historical policies that have since been updated. From 2019 onward, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”

Agustín Reyna, director general of BEUC, said in a comment: “The decision is good news for consumers, as it holds Google accountable and confirms the illegality of the way the tech giant obtained consent to use peoples’ location data. However, the time needed to come to this conclusion is disproportionate with the seriousness of the infringement ... Consumers’ fundamental rights need to be upheld faster and better."

This article was updated to include comments from Google and BEUC.

World.title: How can leaders on the ropes bounce back?
World.content:
Can the Liberal Democrats withstand the political turbulence around them?

As delegates gather in Brighton for their party conference, Sam Coates gauges the pressure on Sir Ed Davey’s party as it faces a squeeze from the Greens and the Andy Burnham bounce.

Elsewhere, the prime minister prepares to go to New York for the UN General Assembly, the duo look ahead to his first meeting with Donald Trump – can they find any common ground?

Plus, Anne McElvoy – who’s in Germany – reports on a disastrous set of regional elections for Friedrich Merz – but is he in a similar position to Sir Keir Starmer post-elections in May 2026?

World.title: How fake Naxos potatoes and modern ambitions are threatening the future of a world-renowned crop
World.content:
Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades and its eponymous variety of potatoes has been grown here since the late 18th century. Sold all over Europe, the crop is an important part of the local economy. Sowing and harvesting takes place twice a year with the second time happening every September. Euronews went to meet Naxos potato farmers and learn more about a crop under threat.

 

Potato planting in Naxos Euronews

We meet Stelios Vathrakokoilis, one of the biggest potato growers on Naxos and President of the Galanado Agricultural Cooperative, and ask him what makes the island’s potatoes so special. "First of all, we have abundant sunshine almost all year round," he says. "Second, we have the sea all around us, at a distance of three to four kilometres. Third, we use cow manure on our fields, as much as we judge necessary, and the fourth and most important factor is that our subsoil lacks certain elements. That element is calcium. If, in these areas, you grow tomatoes or vegetables without adding fertilisers, they will start rotting on the back side of the fruit. That means a lack of calcium. Potatoes are not bothered by this. So it is the absence of calcium from our soils that gives the potato about 80 per cent of its distinctive flavour."

Young people don't want to farm potatoes anymore

In the 1980s, annual production of Naxos potatoes reached 15,000 tonnes. Every member of a family worked on the crop. Families today are smaller and children follow other career paths. Some 300 families on the Cycladic island are involved in potato farming today and production has dropped to a mere 5,000 tonnes.

Potato planting in Naxos Euronews

What is a fake Naxos potato?

In 2010, the Naxos potato was granted protected status. This means that potatoes must be given the seal of approval before being able to be sold under the Naxos potato label.

Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis explains that some package up potatoes as Naxos when they are, in fact, inferior varieties.

"We started marketing Naxos potatoes first through the AB Vassilopoulos supermarket chain. A year later, Sklavenitis came in very strongly, followed by all the chains, so that all this product was going straight onto supermarket shelves."

"But even there, some fraud takes place. I don’t know who, but certain people buy potatoes from other regions, even other continents, especially Egypt. They take them into their packing plants, package them and sell them as Naxos potatoes."

"This happens even more in the street markets. If you walk into a market with 20 or 30 stalls, you will see all of them claiming to sell Naxos potatoes. They are not from Naxos. Out of forty stalls, perhaps one or two sell the real thing. Everyone calls their potatoes Naxos because the price is higher and the taste better. The upshot is that consumers can find genuine Naxos potatoes in 99 per cent of cases only on supermarket shelves. Only there will they find them."

Potato planting Euronews

Water and labour shortages threaten the future of Naxos potatoes

The shortage of labour has become acute in recent years and is a serious concern for farmers - it is very difficult to find workers with the legal right to work.

Water shortages are also an issue. More residents and tourists on the island along with prolonged drought means water resources are spread much more thin.

Farmers have to buy expensive water from the municipality, supplied from desalination plants.

Farmer Stelios Vathrakokoilis is sounding the alarm for the future, seeing production shrink and problems multiply:

"The basic precondition for having production is manpower. A second point, and what I see when I look ahead over the next five to ten years, is that we will be searching with binoculars to find a farmer, not only on Naxos but across Greece."

"It makes no sense for one 'stremma' of land to leave €1,500 in a Dutch farmer’s pocket, €1,200 for an Israeli farmer and €50 for a Greek farmer. It can not go on like this! Clearly we are doing something wrong. We are still using traditional methods, techniques from decades ago, and we are not moving towards something different, such as hydroponics or similar systems, with smaller areas, better working conditions and more income."

Potato planting in Naxos Euronews

"What I see is that in 5–10 years there will be no Greek farmers left anywhere in the country. And I think this is broadly a European issue as well, as we can see from the protests farmers are staging in France and Germany."

"It is not sustainable to pay €2.5 per litre for diesel fuel, to have fertiliser prices through the roof, seed prices through the roof and monthly wages of around €2,500. If you try to farm under these conditions, you will end up completely in the red," stresses Stelios Vathrakokoilis.

The local farmers union is trying to help

This year the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos marks a century of activity. It stands by the producers and works to solve the many challenges facing the island’s agricultural and livestock sectors. The Union’s goal is to support both the product and the people who grow it:

"Naxos potatoes are not just another product. They are the history of the place, its production, its economy. They are the wealth of the farmer and the livestock breeder," Dimitris Kapounis, President of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos, tells Euronews.

"Potatoes arrived on Naxos before the time of Kapodistrias, so you can see the passion, the love, the genuine cultivation of the land in this chapter we call Naxos potatoes," he says.

17th Potato Festival in Naxos Euronews

Every year the island hosts a major festival celebrating the potato. The 17th Potato Festival was held on 12 September at the port of Naxos. The centenary of the founding of the Union of Agricultural Cooperatives of Naxos was celebrated at the same time.

More than 3,000 people took part in the event in Nikiforos Mandilaras Square, alongside local organisations and representatives of the farming community. Residents and visitors sampled different recipes in which Naxos potatoes took centre stage, and enjoyed performances by musicians and dance groups.

World.title: Ireland backs 'ambitious' new EU taxes as budget talks intensify
World.content:
The forthcoming draft of the EU’s long-term budget will include an “ambitious” proposal on new EU taxes, known as own resources, Irish Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne told journalists on Monday.

 

The European Union is currently negotiating its long-term budget for 2028–2034, with the Irish government chairing the talks. EU institutions aim to reach a deal by the end of the year, with the package expected to include new taxes for the first time in the bloc’s history.

The draft text is expected to be presented before mid-October, ahead of the European Council meeting in Brussels. It will serve as a basis for further discussions among EU leaders during the summit.

"The Irish Presidency is confident to deliver a good own resources package," the minister said, specifying that all own resources proposed by the European Commission and the European Parliament are still on the table.

"We don't rule out any own resource," Byrne told journalists.

The own resources under consideration include the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a parcel handling fee, an online gambling tax, tobacco excise duties, the Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE), non-collected e-waste, the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), a digital levy, and a tax on crypto assets.

Opposing camps

In July 2025, the European Commission proposed a €2 trillion EU budget, which is now being negotiated by the bloc’s 27 member states. The negotiations have since divided countries into two main camps.

The “Friends of Cohesion” group is seeking to protect funding for agriculture, fisheries and regional development, which would be reduced under the Commission’s proposal compared with the current budget. The group comprises 17 member states, including Spain, Italy, Poland, Hungary and Portugal.

The “frugal” camp, composed of German, Finland, Austria and Denmark wants to significantly reduce the overall budget and redirect spending towards priorities such as competitiveness and defence. They have increasingly portrayed themselves as the “modernisers” and have also expressed strong reservations about the proposed own resources, arguing that they would become net contributors under the new system.

In June, Cyprus, which was then chairing the member states’ discussions, proposed a compromise involving a €32.8 billion cut, focused on programmes favoured by the modernisers.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has repeatedly said that the budget still requires significant cuts and has expressed skepticism about the proposed own resources.

"Own resources are part of the solution," Byrne said, arguing that a deal on the whole budget must be reached by the end of the year.

"If we don't have a agreement by the end of the year, that would be disappointing for the beneficiaries in 2028," the minister said, pointing out that a deal missed by December would "undermine Europe's credibility."

To reach a deal, all 27 member states must approve the text, while the European Parliament must also give its consent to the proposal.

World.title: More flight disruption in UK after second air traffic control glitch this month
World.content:
Passengers travelling to and from the UK on Monday were faced with delays and cancellations to flights after air traffic control systems suffered a "technical issue" for the second time this month.

 

Air traffic control operator NATS announced that it had discovered a "connectivity issue with part of our systems network" at its Prestwick centre in Scotland early on Monday morning, adding that it had "nothing to do with the problem we had earlier this month."

NATS said at around 11 am local time that the issue had been "fixed" and that it was working with airlines and airports to remove air traffic restrictions.

"We apologise to passengers for the disruption and thank them for their patience," it added in a post on social media.

Data from flight-tracking site Flightradar24 shows "major problems" at Scotland's Edinburgh and Glasgow airports as well as Newcastle airport in northeastern England on Monday. Flights have also been disrupted at Manchester, Birmingham, Belfast, London Luton, and London Gatwick airports, as well as Dublin airport in Ireland.

In a statement, Glasgow airport warned that delays and disruption could continue despite the fix "due to the knock-on impact across the network."

Manchester airport added that operations were "returning to normal" but also said further disruption was possible.

Airports are advising passengers to check with airlines for the latest updates before travelling.

Earlier this month, airports across the UK and Ireland were hit with severe disruption after NATS reported a problem with its flight processing system.

In a statement at the time, NATS described it as a "very complex recovery" that had "created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover."

UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said then that she was "seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job."

On Monday, Irish budget carrier Ryanair called on NATS CEO Martin Rolfe to resign following the latest glitch.

"UK passengers cannot continue to suffer repeated disruption because of system failures, inadequate back-up procedures and failed management," the airline said in a statement on its website.

World.title: Former enemies form alliance to overthrow Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed
World.content:
Forces that fought on opposing sides in Ethiopia's Tigray war have joined a seven-group military alliance to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and install a transitional administration, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) said on Sunday.

 

Both the government and the TPLF have massed troops along the border of the northern state in recent months, according to the African Union, fuelling fears of a return to the war that killed up to 600,000 people.

"We just formed an alliance, we are collaborating with several groups and our objectives are to remove the regime and facilitating a transitional government," said TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa.

The groups in the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival include Tigrayan forces, Amhara nationalist Fano militias, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), along with four groups from three other regions, making up half of the country's 12 regional states.

"We think we will be successful, we have been talking with each other for more than a year," said Amanuel. Fano leader Zemene Kasse will chair the alliance, he added.

Abiy, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 partly for brokering a peace agreement with neighbouring Eritrea, has faced mounting armed opposition since 2023 as the post-war settlement unravelled.

Future unclear

The Tigray war began in November 2020 when federal forces moved against the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for three decades before Abiy came to power in 2018.

The two sides signed the Pretoria Agreement in November 2022 to end the two-year war.

According to the deal, the TPLF was to demobilise its forces and refrain from military mobilisation.

The TPLF did not demobilise. It also unilaterally reinstated its pre-war regional council in May of this year, effectively voiding the agreement.

Kjetil Tronvoll, professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New University College in Norway, cast doubt on the alliance's effort to overthrow the federal government, which possesses numerous drones.

"I am not sure they will be able to sustain such a war," Tronvoll said.

"If they coordinate as a military command, it may make a difference, it is a potential four to five fronts that the government will have to deal with, it might be a challenge," he added.

Ethiopia has been plagued by armed conflicts in its two most populous regions, Oromia and Amhara.

Federal forces have been fighting the OLA, which the government has designated a "terrorist organisation", since 2018 in central Oromia.

The Fano, "self-defence" militias of the Amhara ethnic group, took up arms against the government in April 2023 after federal authorities moved to disarm them.

Despite Sunday's announcement, doubts remain over an alliance between groups that espouse different ideologies and have clashed in the past. Fano fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces during the Tigray war.

The groups also have territorial disputes. Amhara nationalists have administered Western Tigray, a contested area between Amhara and Tigray, since the end of the war.

"We will sit at the table later to solve our problems peacefully," Amanuel said.

Further violence hits Gambella region

Meanwhile, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) announced that at least 12 people have been killed and dozens injured as a result of a separate conflict in western Ethiopia near the border with South Sudan.

Clashes are frequent in the Gambella region, home to more than 400,000 refugees, most of them South Sudanese who have fled violence in the world's youngest country.

"MSF teams at Kule health centre in Ethiopia's Gambella region have been responding to an influx of wounded patients following violence in Itang Special Woreda on 18 September," the medical charity said in a statement on Sunday.

MSF said it had received 88 patients from Friday's clashes, including eight who were already dead and four who died upon arrival.

"We call on all those involved to exercise restraint and protect civilians from further violence," said MSF's operations manager in Ethiopia, Gul Badshah.

It is not clear who was responsible for the clashes.

A 2025 Rift Valley Institute report attributed the rise in conflict in Gambella to economic crisis and an influx of refugees.

World.title: 13 EU countries call for 'deep cleaning' of European laws
World.content:
Thirteen member states are calling on Brussels to systematically design new EU legislation as pro-innovation and assess whether the current laws are still fit for purpose, as part of a broader push to cut red tape and make the bloc more business-friendly.

 

Austria, Czechia, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia and Slovakia signed a non-paper calling for "an exercise in legislative deep-cleaning" to determine, sector by sector, whether existing rules are still needed, need updating, or impose burdens without added value.

"EU legislation cannot be an end in itself. Therefore, regulatory restraint to avoid over-regulation and the introduction of new administrative burdens is a condition for sound EU law-making," reads the Austrian-led paper, obtained by Euronews.

The non-paper was circulated ahead of the launch of a new Alliance for the Reduction of the Bureaucratic Burden expected on Monday, meant to establish a permanent network of EU countries committed to regulatory simplification at the national and European levels.

Regulatory simplification has dominated the EU agenda during Ursula von der Leyen's second term as European Commission President, driven by both member states and the centre-right European People's Party.

As a result of this simplification drive, the Commission has proposed a series of "omnibus" packages, spamming from AI rules to climate-related obligations, to reduce and streamline the current EU regulatory patchwork.

The 13 signatories want to go one step further by asking that new EU laws systematically assessed for their impact on economic competitiveness, and only pursued at EU level where objectives cannot be sufficiently achieved nationally, in line with the treaties' principles of subsidiarity and proportionality.

The document also calls for a "European Implementation and Consolidation Year, primarily focusing on implementation of existing legislation, simplification, interoperability, evaluation of cumulative burden, enforcement convergence, reduction of duplicative reporting obligations, and indispensable legislative amendments."

The goal, as they put it, is better regulation: EU-level legislation enacted only where Union action is necessary and adds value, designed to be proportionate, coherent, legally predictable and supportive of a business environment where European companies can invest, innovate and grow.

The signatories want the EU to prioritise high-quality, enforceable and predictable legislation over "regulatory density," while maintaining current protections for health, safety and labour.

"Every major new reporting or compliance obligation should be preceded by a review of existing obligations in the same policy field with a view to consolidation, simplification or repeal," the paper continues.

Legislation would be judged on whether it is implementable, predictable, coherent with other laws, evidence-based, robust, competitiveness-enhancing and respectful of the split in competences between EU and national levels.

New regulation would also require a mandatory review clause at least every five years, to check whether it has met its objectives.

"It is of the utmost importance to avoid cumulative complexity that risks weakening the effectiveness and as a result the legitimacy of EU action while also reducing the attractiveness of the EU Single Market as a place to do business and invest," the paper says.

World.title: ECB launches 'Pontes' to settle tokenised assets in central bank money
World.content:
Europe's central banks now have a working bridge into tokenised markets.

 

Launched on Monday, Pontes lets wholesale transactions in tokenised assets, meaning stocks, bonds and other instruments recorded as digital tokens on distributed ledgers, to settle in the safest form of money available — reserves held at the central bank itself.

It matters because the absence of a risk-free settlement asset has been one of the main barriers holding blockchain technology back. Without it, tokenised trades have typically settled in commercial bank money or stablecoins, carrying credit risk that large institutions are reluctant to accept.

"The Eurosystem is working to enable a more integrated, innovative and resilient European financial market in the digital age," said ECB President Christine Lagarde.

Thirteen institutions have completed onboarding and are ready to use the system immediately, including Deutsche Bank, Santander, Société Générale, KfW and the European Investment Bank, alongside four ledger operators including Clearstream.

The ECB also intends to become a user itself.

In a separate announcement, it said it has begun preparatory work to invest a small portion of its own funds in tokenised securities, with purchases settled through Pontes.

The initial focus will be euro-denominated debt issued by euro area governments, regional authorities, agencies and European supranational institutions.

The own-funds portfolio sits outside monetary policy and generates income to cover the bank's running costs. No amount was specified, and the Executive Board will decide on timing once the groundwork is done.

"Pontes brings tokenised markets another step closer to the core of the euro area's financial infrastructure," said Richard Baker, founder and CEO of Tokenovate, which builds technology to help financial institutions automate post-trade processing, collateral management and tokenised settlement.

Baker noted the service will initially run within existing market hours, but that "the longer-term opportunity is to support more continuous, potentially 24/7, settlement."

That gap is where Europe is playing catch-up.

American markets have moved faster as the New York Stock Exchange is building a blockchain-based venue for trading tokenised shares and funds around the clock, and BlackRock has run a tokenised money market fund since 2024.

Pontes itself will only reach full capability, with longer operating hours and enhanced features, by 2028.

The two sides are also taking different routes.

Washington, under US President Donald Trump, abandoned plans for a Federal Reserve digital currency and backed privately issued stablecoins instead. On the other hand, Frankfurt is betting that public central bank money should sit at the centre.

Where the digital euro stands

Pontes is aimed at banks and markets, not consumers. The retail equivalent, the digital euro, would let the public make everyday payments directly in central bank money.

That project is further from reality.

The European Parliament's economic committee approved its position in June, opening negotiations with member states, and final legislation is targeted for the end of this year.

If that holds, a pilot involving 36 payment providers will begin in September 2027, with first issuance possible in 2029.

World.title: 2026 Michelin Key hotels: All the new three key properties in Europe
World.content:
If you’re looking for a truly exceptional hotel stay, a five-star rating isn’t enough. You need to look to the big guns: The Michelin Guide.

 

The tyre company is well known for its reviews of restaurants and associated Michelin stars, but in 2024, it began awarding “keys” to properties around the globe.

One Key means a “very special” stay, while Two Keys means it will be "exceptional".

But Three Keys? A Three Key hotel offers something next level. According to Michelin: “It is one of the world's most remarkable and extraordinary stays and a destination for the trip of a lifetime.”

Sounds good to us.

According to the 2026 Michelin Key selection, which was unveiled last week, there are just 155 Three Key hotels around the globe – including eight new additions in Europe for this year.

Here, we take a look at what makes them worthy of the distinction.

All of the new Michelin Three Key hotels in Europe

Venice’s Airelles Palladio doesn’t only boast Three Keys – it was also just named Michelin’s Opening of the Year.

Located on Giudecca Island opposite St. Mark’s Square, the property offers all of the charm of Venice without the chaos of the city streets.

Made up of four heritage buildings, the hotel has something for those looking to relax, with the largest spa in Venice and three swimming pools to choose from; something for culture vultures, with experiences offered including an exclusive visit to the Doges Palace and traditional Venetian rowing lessons; and something for foodies, with restaurants from Nobu Matsuhisa, Norbert Niederkofler and Cedric Grolet.

Airelles Palladio is one of just two hotels that debuted on the Michelin Key guide with Three Keys, the other being Soneva Secret in the Maldives.

Seven hotels in Europe were upgraded from Two Keys to Three this year – three in Italy, and two each in both France and Switzerland.

In Florence, Collegio alla Querce, Auberge Collection – which was named Esquire’s best new hotel earlier this year – offers a Three Key stay thanks to its historic location within a former 16th-century villa that was then used as a college.

Guests here will love the nods to its former life, including a bar in the former headmaster’s office with dishes that draw on the tales of famous explorers once studied here, as well as the gorgeous outdoor pool.

Borgo Santandrea on the Amalfi Coast, found within a sixties modernist structure, is “ultra-chic and ultra-luxe”, and the terrace restaurant in particular is something to shout about thanks to its grand vistas.

Kulm Hotel St. Moritz “is as fine an Alpine five-star gets”, according to Michelin Leading Hotels of the World (LW)

The last property to be upgraded in Italy is Splendido, A Belmond Hotel, in Portofino. The fabulous hotel has just 53 rooms, a gorgeous outdoor pool, and the world’s first Dior Spa.

Over in France, Château de la Chèvre d'Or earned its place thanks to its spectacular location in the medieval village of Èze, which it takes full advantage of from its two outdoor pools as well as its Michelin two-starred restaurant, La Chèvre d’Or.

The 17th-century convert turned wellness retreat Le Couvent des Minimes was also upgraded this year, with Michelin’s reviewers praising its 2,500 sq m Spa L’Occitane en Provence as well as its one-starred restaurant, Le Feuillée

Beau-Rivage Palace, described by Michelin as “one of the last of Europe’s traditional grand hotels”, was also awarded Three Keys.

The property on the shores of Lake Geneva was recently renovated, and boasts everything from an extensive spa to tennis and padel courts as well as a golf driving range.

Kulm Hotel St. Moritz “is as fine an Alpine five-star gets”, with an incredible view over the lake, a 2,000 sq m spa, an outdoor pool overlooking the slopes, and exceptional restaurants.

World.title: 'Be realistic, demand the impossible': Portugal's MUZEU wants visitors to think and reflect
World.content:
A rally for revolution is the inspiration behind MUZEU, the new contemporary art museum in the Portuguese city of Braga.

 

Its motto “Be realistic, demand the impossible“ is taken directly from the famous photograph shot by Gérard-Aimé during the civil unrest of May 1968 in Paris, capturing graffiti on the Pont de Neuilly bearing the phrase “Soyez réalistes, demandez l’impossible”.

"Be realistic, demand the impossible" sign at MUZEU, 16 September 2026, Braga, Portugal. Euronews

“May of 1968 was a time of liberation within a country that sought a freedom of movement, not really political, but a freedom to break the social and moral walls of the time that existed“ - founder of MUZEU, José Teixeira, told Euronews Culture.

“Nowadays we are living a new version of May 1968 - morally, socially and ethically. A liberation that opens ourselves and opens the community to the communities and to a communal life. Because today, in the moment we live, especially in Portugal, we value meritocracy, individualism. There is a need for a new debate about the communities and how comprehension and compassion should be brought to the table as a means to solve that as well".

MUZEU, Project by Carvalho Araújo, Braga, Portugal. Manuel R. Costa

Moder interior of MUZEU, Braga, 2026. Hugo Delgado

100 artworks by 84 artists on 5 floors

José Teixeira, the founder of MUZEU is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of dstgroup, one of Portugal's leading industrial companies. He's also the 35th richest person in Portugal according to Forbes.

Spanning five floors and an exhibition area of ​​approximately 3,000 square meters, his collection brings together more than a hundred artworks by 84 artists - 45 from Portugal and 39 from abroad. A total of 16 countries are represented - comprising 57 men and 27 women.

Among many others Teixiera's collection features the work of Pablo Picasso, Alex Katz, Artur Lescher, Candida Höfer, Nan Goldin, and Eduardo Batarda.

A dedicated gallery has been set aside for the work of Anselm Kiefer.

"SOL INVICTUS Helioglobal", Anselm Kiefer (2023), MUZEU, Braga, Portugal, April 2026. Hugo Delgado

MUZEU, April 2026. Hugo Delgado

Photography holds a uniquely important place in the collection, reflecting one of the Teixeira's great passions as he believes: "photography captures the moment without taking it away".

To read, to think and to live in a community

A keen collector over four decades, Teixeira's company's campus in Braga is full of large scale works of art, libraries, and sporting equipment for his staff to take advantage of.

“The Project #2“ by Pedro Cabrita Reis, dstgroup campus, 16 September 2026, Braga, portugal. Euronews

Despite his immense wealth and the privilege it provides, Teixeira describes himself as a working man who wants to lead by example.

“Simone Weil is a French philosopher that lived in France during the Nazi occupation of France. She wanted to write about work, so she stopped lecturing classes and sent an application to Renault and worked there as a press operator and milling machine operator," says Teixeira.

"Later, after working, she wrote a book about it. So if you want to speak about work, you need to know how to do it and do it like Simone Weil - ask the real questions. This is the true importance of literature, poetry, arts, and everything that I spoke about. Poets speak through metaphors, I speak through art works I collect.“

"Painting Sem título", André Butzer (2018), MUZEU, Braga, Portugal, 2026. Hugo Delgado

Teixeira likes to think about himself as the signal man, pointing the direction for people working with him and for him - to read, to go to museums, to reflect and think about how to live in a community.

As fragile as people killed by it

A significant element in the new exhibition at MUZEU which opened last Thursday is Handle with care by Lebanese-Canadian artist Elias Nafaa. It comprises of 300 hand-cast glass replicas of weapons used in contemporary conflicts, presented for the first time this year at The Québec City Biennial.

For Nafaa, Handle with care transforms instruments of destruction into delicate objects of contemplation: “I want to make them [weapons] out of a very fragile material so that they are as fragile as what they're destroying," he tells Euronews Culture.

"I wanted to reverse the power dynamics, so instead of them looking down on me, I would look down on them, and I wanted to scale them down so they don't feel as strong or powerful as they are or destructive as they are. This became the start of the work that you see here,“ adds Nafaa.

Elias Nafaa, MUZEU in Braga, 17 September 2026. MUZEU

“18,000 weapons were used by the end of 2025 and I think now it's over 20,000 that were used on Lebanon by the Israeli army. And what you see here is 300 pieces. I have six models that I researched and identified that were used more commonly.

"The frequency of its use in this space is proportional to its use like in real life so for example the smaller ones which are used mostly you will see more of them in the place the bigger ones which I use a bit less you'll see less of in this space."

"Handle with Care" by Elias Nafaa, Braga, Portugal, 17 September 2026. MUZEU

Visitors should be aware of the difficulties Nafaa had in getting his work exhibited as it was kept in custody for more than two weeks until the eve of the exhibition opening.

Ironically, Nafaa says that while real weapon travel the world mostly fast and freely - legally and illegally - his artwork was being held for a much longer time.

“Handle with Care“ is part of MUZEU’s inaugural programme titled Abrir Abril and is open until 31 October 2026.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
World.content:
Rising electricity demand, shocks in energy security and climate commitments are reviving long-stalled plans for nuclear power across Southeast Asia. But proponents of nuclear energy still face formidable obstacles.

Southeast Asian governments are revisiting nuclear power as electricity consumption raises, exposing the region's dependence on fossil fuels.

The rise is largely driven by new factories, electric vehicles and the region's rush to host data centers against the backdrop of countries trying to reduce carbon emissions.

No Southeast Asian nation currently operates a commercial nuclear power plant, but several are now placing their bets on nuclear energy and reviving plans that had been stalled for years.

On September 8, Vietnam's state-owned Petrovietnam and South Korea's KEPCO agreed to deepen cooperation on the planned Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear plant. Six days later, Singapore's government said it was studying nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs)with an "open mind", though it stressed that it had not made a decision.

Vietnam also wants to bring its two Ninh Thuan plants into operation by 2035 and pursue at least one SMR project.

Indonesia plans an initial 500 megawatts of nuclear capacity, with units targeted to begin operating in 2032, while the Philippines is working towards its first 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity from the same year.

Thailand's latest draft power plan proposes its first SMR in 2037, while Malaysia and Singapore remain at the study stage.

Can nuclear power cover AI's energy demands? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Energy shocks vs. the shadow of Fukushima

The renewed interest marks a sharp reversal from the caution that followed Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011.

The incident stalled several Southeast Asian countries' plans to pursue nuclear energy, Alvin Chew, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told DW.

But a string of geopolitical shocks in recent years has changed the energy debate.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Southeast Asia's electricity generation has risen by around 60% since 2015, but coal supplied most of that increase, pushing its share of regional generation from 37% to 47%.

The war in Ukraine and the current Middle East crisis have heightened energy-security concerns for developing countries, even as most Southeast Asian governments have committed to net-zero emissions by 2050 or 2060, Chew said.

The region's electricity demand is forecast to grow by an average of 5.3% a year between 2026 and 2030.

"Nuclear energy is deemed to be the viable solution to address both challenges of climate and energy security," Chew said.

Middle East conflict is firing up China's electric future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Appeal of modular reactors

One reason governments are reconsidering nuclear power is that today's technology is starkly different from what was used 15 years ago in Fukushima.

SMRs have broadened the range of possible projects. Unlike conventional reactors, SMRs are designed as smaller units that can potentially be added in stages.

"In the past, deploying nuclear energy generally meant building very large conventional reactors, involving long construction periods, enormous upfront investments and requiring electricity grids capable of absorbing very large generating units," Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, assistant professor and director at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, told DW.

"SMRs have changed the nuclear conversation in Southeast Asia because they potentially make nuclear compatible with smaller grids, smaller countries and more incremental investment," he added.

China has started implementing SMRs Image: Zhang Boqun/Xinhua/picture alliance

That does not mean SMRs will solve nuclear power's economics. Many designs remain at an early stage of deployment, meaning promises of cheaper construction through mass production have yet to be demonstrated on a broad commercial scale.

Another force pushing nuclear energy back onto the agenda is the rapid expansion of data centers, which require large quantities of reliable electricity, Julius Cesar Trajano, a research fellow with the Centre for Non-Traditional Security Studies at RSIS, told DW.

The IEA expects electricity consumption from Southeast Asian data centers to more than double by 2030.

More than 70% of existing regional data-center capacity is concentrated in Singapore and Johor in southern Malaysia.

"Countries are therefore approaching nuclear energy with greater emphasis on governance and regulatory capacity than during earlier attempts," said Trajano.

Building a nuclear safety net

The hardest problems, however, remain much the same. Nuclear plants, even SMRs, still require a lot of time and money, and newcomer countries must establish independent regulators, train specialist workforces and develop credible systems for radioactive waste and emergency response.

Geography adds another layer of difficulty. Parts of Southeast Asia are vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis, making site selection and emergency planning particularly sensitive.

Nuclear power also places unusually heavy demands on state institutions, Tan-Soo said. Governments need institutions that take a long time to establish and must remain reliable for decades.

"For countries developing nuclear power for the first time, building this ecosystem can take as much effort as building the plant itself," he added.

Does nuclear energy make financial sense? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Long road to wielding nuclear power

Public support is another matter. A Philippine government survey released last year found that more than 70% of respondents supported nuclear energy's potential role in providing electricity.

By contrast, the Indonesia Energy Transition Outlook 2026 reported that 78% of respondents placed nuclear as their least-preferred energy source.

"The biggest obstacle is the political will to proceed with adoption of nuclear energy, which, to a certain extent, is dependent on public perception," said Chew.

Southeast Asia's highly varied national capacities and electricity systems also make a common pathway unlikely, Trajano said.

Vietnam has revived plans for large conventional plants, Indonesia and Thailand are giving greater attention to SMRs, while Singapore is still building the expertise needed to determine whether nuclear power is suitable at all.

"There is clearly much more political momentum behind nuclear power in Southeast Asia today than there was a decade ago, and I think some countries could ultimately deploy it," Tan-Soo said.

"But moving from announcing a nuclear ambition to financing, licensing, constructing and safely operating a reactor is an enormous step."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
World.content:
A series of killings in South Africa has renewed scrutiny of efforts to combat violence against women. Activists say laws alone are not enough without effective implementation.

On Thursday, police in South Africa found the pattially naked body of Dineo M. The 38-year-old had been beaten and stabbed to death in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city.

This is one of a series of killings of women in their 20s and 30s in Ekurhuleni over the past two months.

But for Dineo's sister, Carol, this is much more than another statistic in a country where gender-based violence (GBV) was declared a national disaster in 2025.

"We sit here today and we will never see her walk through the door. Her 2-year-old has no idea what is going on," Carol told DW. "How do you explain to her [...] your mother was brutally murdered, dumped behind shrubs, left unrecognizable? [...] That is why you don't have a mother today."

A community on edge

Authorities said it was not yet clear whether the killings were linked. However, they said they have identified similarities, and have issued an alert for women in Ekurhuleni to take precautions.

Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said on Sunday that so far there was no conclusive evidence that the killings were carried out by a serial killer, "but nothing has yet been excluded while investigations continue."

For families and communities, the deaths have raised fresh questions about whether existing measures are enough to protect women.

South African Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Sindisiwe Chikunga said at a protest march in Johannesburg that violence against women often starts behind closed doors.

"Please, stop it. Stop raping women. Stop insulting women. Stop financially abusing women," she said, warning that verbal abuse can escalate. "They start with insults. They proceed to assault and then to murder. It cannot be."

Why laws fall short

For Naledi Masipa, campaigns manager at Gender Links, an NGO promoting gender justice across Southern Africa, the problem encompasses all of society.

"Having laws and policies does not automatically change what happens in communities and households," she told DW, adding that the entire support system must work, from reporting and policing to health services, psychosocial support and legal assistance.

If one part fails, she said, women continue to carry the burden. "The real test is whether a woman in an ordinary community feels safer."

Amnesty International South Africa said the response to the crimes must recognize the gendered nature of killings.

"Femicide itself is not recognized as a crime. It's just seen as another murder," said Tegan Snyman, a research assistant at the international non-governmental organization, pointing out that South Africa had declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis . She argued that more resources were necessary as well as a sense of urgency.

A regional challenge

The neighboring country of Botswana also struggles with high levels of gender-based violence.

Natasha Rampa, a permanent secretary in Botswana's Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, said that "at least 37% of women in Botswana have experienced violence in their lifetimes."

In June, Botswana and the United Nations launched a joint program focused on prevention, survivor-centered services and stronger institutions.

"Violence is unacceptable, and we must work together as a society to address this issue," Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs Lesego Chombo told parliament. He said that tackling gender-based violence (GBV) requires action beyond government.

Turning policy into protection

Zambia also faces persistent gender-based violence — despite laws and national programs aimed at tackling it.

Why are women still unsafe in South Africa? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anne Mbewe-Anamela, the executive director of the Non-Governmental Coordinating Council, an umbrella organization in the country that champions gender equality, said the response must put survivors at the center.

"GBV is deeply rooted in power, inequality, and social expectations," she told DW. "We can have strong laws, but if communities still believe violence is a private matter or a normal part of marriage, then survivors remain silent and trapped."

For activists across the region, the challenge is, therefore, not simply creating more policies. It is making protection, support and justice work in practice. And for families like Dineo's, that difference is painfully personal. Carol knows her sister will never walk through the door again.

She wants Dineo's daughter to grow up understanding that what happened to her mother was not normal and that women deserve to be safe.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: As US and China talk, middle powers jostle for position
World.content:
China's Xi Jinping is traveling to Washington this week. Regardless of what comes from his talks with US President Trump, the EU will likely remain stuck between erratic US trade policy and Beijing's export machine.

Last week, German and Chinese business leaders met in the German city of Düsseldorf for an economic dialogue. Although the panel focused on trade, and investment between China and Europe, ongoing US-China rivalry was the elephant in the room.

As Xi Jinping and Donald Trump sit down in the US capital Washington this week, there is some hope that talks will show progress on alleviating the ongoing trade war launched by the US president. The last time the two leaders met at a Beijing summit in May did not yield any tangible results.

"The assumption in Beijing, and that's the way they're operating, is that China and the US will hold each other in check for the foreseeable future," Mikko Huotari, director of the Berlin-based China think tank MERICS, told a policy briefing last week.

"Xi really doesn't need a breakthrough in Washington. He needs more time. And the same is true for Washington. So we have this strategic stalemate situation, which I think is the best description of what we see currently."

A deal could benefit Trump's Republican Party ahead of the important US midterm elections in November, but that outcome remains far from certain.

"We will discuss everything,"Trump said about Xi's visit to the White House.

Cooperation on AI?

Beijing and Washington are competing on multiple levels, and nowhere is this rivalry more consequential than with artificial intelligence (AI).

The US government prohibits the export of high-performance chips to China. Beijing, in turn, restricts the export of rare earth elements, which are indispensable for semiconductor production.

And amid concerns about the dangers of unregulated AI, there is some expectation that Xi and Trump will discuss AI guardrails during their talks. Xi has called for international cooperation on AI development, while Trump sees its regulation as a threat to the US' leadership in the field.

After meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that US and Chinese officials have already discussed creating a "notification mechanism" to share information about AI-related security incidents.

AI's expanding power alarms China's intelligence agency To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Europe's 'China shock'

From a European perspective, both China and the US are currently considered difficult partners.

The second "China shock … is already here" in Europe, said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her 2026 State of the Union address last week.

The first "China shock" came 25 years ago, triggered by China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), when inexpensive "Made in China" products began to flood the global markets.

The second one stems from Chinas technological progress in industries such as battery technology, green energy and mobility.

"It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. It leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable," von der Leyen said in her address.

The EU is aiming for a rapid transition to e-mobility and wants to drastically reduce CO2 emissions from road traffic. At the same time, Brussels is calling for additional tariffs on low-cost electric cars from China, as China enjoys competitive advantages with cheaper cars and high government subsidies.

China denies having an unfair advantage, and German automakers VW and BMW also oppose punitive tariffs due to potential revenue losses resulting from Chinese retaliatory measures.

What new alliances will reshape the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A Chinese participant at the Düsseldorf economic dialogue told DW anonymously that China's domestic consumption cannot absorb manufacturing.

"China's economy is weak. Companies are worried about their business and urgently need to tap into foreign markets," said the Chinese executive, who headed the European branch of a Chinese state-owned enterprise in Düsseldorf for decades.

Trump pressuring EU over China, but also on trade, security

"Against the backdrop of the ongoing escalation of strategic rivalry between the US and China, the US is constantly urging its allies to tighten restrictions on China in the areas of technology, supply chains, and security," said Yang Xiepu, director of the Center for Sino-German Cooperation at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).

Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, Trump frequently threatens the EU with tariffs while injecting instability into the strategic NATO alliance. When the EU offered Canada "associate membership" last week, Trump floated the possibility of new punitive measures from the US.

While Carney expressed interest , Trump called the idea "ridiculous."

"If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said, without specifying what he considers about EU-Canada ties to be "hostile."

Copying Canada's 'middle' approach

Facing Trump administration's tariff upsets and caustic rhetoric, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is openly hedging his bets on the world stage.

"We know the old order is not coming back. We shouldn't mourn it," he declared at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos in January, with the US allies rattled by Trump threatening to annex Greenland from Denmark.

Carney said that great powers can "afford for now to go it alone" but middle powers need to work better together.

"When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what's offered. We compete with each other to be the most accommodating. This is not sovereignty," Carney told the forum.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he emphasized.

In early 2026, Carney visited China and agreed to a "new-era strategic partnership." Ottawa subsequently lowered import tariffs on Chinese electric cars from 100% to 6.1%. The quota stands at 49,000 vehicles per year.

Separately, China has launched a charm offensive toward US allies, "more specifically, the fragile allies," according to MERICS Director Mikko Huotari.

For example, Xi attended the BRICS summit in India in September despite the rocky relationship with New Delhi. He also attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan. In November, China will host the G-20 summit.

Carney has described this new form of diplomacy as "variable geometry" — different alliances for different issues based on common values and interests. In November, he will travel to Shenzhen for the APECE summit. He will also be at the table there — and hopefully not on the menu.
