World.title: India's road rage: When cars become weapons
World.content:
Road disputes are turning violent across India, raising questions about status and impunity behind the wheel for drivers of expensive cars.

A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car.

The two sides gave differing accounts of the initial dispute, with the car driver telling Indian media that the group of bikers overtook his car and slowed down in front of it.

In turn, the motorcycle rider, Shivani Chauhan, said the car was following her and the argument started when she asked the people inside to keep a safe distance.

Chauhan's motorcycle-mounted camera shows the car hitting her from the side and them speeding away as she falls and rolls on the road.

"I could have suffered serious fractures or internal injuries and even died. Due to such people, the roads of Gurugram and Delhi feel unsafe," Chauhan was quoted as saying by Indian news outlets.

According to reports, the driver claims that he lost control of his vehicle and left the scene because he feared reprisals from the biker group. Police have since arrested the driver on charges including attempted murder and stalking.

Road rage escalates to violence, shootouts

The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent.

In March in Hassan, in the southern Karnataka state, young men reportedly shouted at the driver of a Toyota Fortuner SUV to slow down.

Police said the driver turned the vehicle around and rammed the group, killing one man and seriously injuring three others.

In the northern city of Dehradun that month, an argument over giving way between two SUVs, a Toyota Fortuner and a Mahindra Scorpio, escalated into a chase and gunfire.

The altercation cost the life of one man, a retired Army brigadier Mukesh Joshi, who was not involved in the initial dispute.

"The occupants of the Scorpio waited outside the club till early morning and then chased the Fortuner. During the firing, the brigadier, who was out on a morning walk, was hit by a bullet in the chest," said senior superintendent of police Pramendra Dobhal.

Concerns over road safety prompted the administration of Daman, a small coastal town north of Mumbai, to take an unusual step. On September 9, officials gathered owners of Mahindra Thar and Toyota Fortuner SUVs and made them take a public road safety pledge.

District Collector Saurabh Mishra, the district's top administrator, warned that these kinds of larger vehicles should not be used to intimidate others or display power.

More cars, less space on Indian roads

India's roads are notoriously dangerous, with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network.

Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not necessarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation.

"For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW.

"One drives with impunity to make an impression on smaller vehicles," said Azad.

He called for tougher policing using new technology, rigorous punishment and a nationwide programme to promote safer driving.

"Hitting a smaller vehicle intentionally is not rash driving. It is a measure of criminal intent," he said.

'SUV drivers have a beast in their hands'

Road safety expert Prince Singhal, founder of the Community Against Drunken Driving, sees both vehicles and drivers as parts of the problem.

"The issue of terror behind SUVs is not just a traffic challenge but also a behavioral issue," Singhal told DW.

"The SUV drivers have a beast in their hands and it's their mindset which decides the outcome."

How a start-up in India is turning old cars into EVs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Singhal notes that SUVs are a practical choice for bad roads and long journeys, but also points to issues in their design.

"High bonnets and elevated bumper heights increased the risk of fatal head and chest injuries for pedestrians, children, and cyclists and all other road users compared to traditional lower cars," added Singhal.

With an SUV at hand, drivers often experience "a psychological sense of invincibility," which can lead to hostile behavior, road bullying and rule violations, he said.

Are drivers taking traffic too personally?

Psychiatrist Ravi Prakash, who studies traffic behavior at Veditha Mind Care Clinic in Bengaluru, agrees that the driver "feels both powerful and protected inside a large, sturdy vehicle."

He also warned that there are other mechanisms at play.

"There is a psychological phenomenon called 'personalization,' where people interpret an ordinary act by a stranger as something personally directed at them," he told DW.

Someone cutting across a lane may be in a hurry. But the other driver may see it as an attempt to assert superiority. A perceived insult can then threaten a person's identity and trigger a spike of anger.

"Usually, hitting the other person is not the goal initially," Prakash said.

The driver first tries to assert superiority through speeding, honking, gestures or shouting. When that fails, a desire to punish can emerge, what Prakash calls an "illusion of retributive justice."

'Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture'

Sociologist Dipankar Gupta says road rage happens "because traffic rules are not strictly enforced," with the problem in no way limited to SUV drivers.

"Even motorcyclists get into road rage," he told DW.

"It's like a child who is not disciplined and throws a tantrum," Gupta said of the wider breakdown in road discipline. When rules are routinely ignored and people do not want to face the consequences, he added, it becomes similar to "a punch up" in school.

Why India will shape the car of the future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With cameras everywhere, however, such behavior has become harder to ignore.

"The anger is not new. What has changed is that everyone has a camera now, whether it is a dashcam, a helmet camera or a mobile phone," Deepanshu Gupta, cofounder of CrashFree India, a road safety nonprofit, told DW.

He warns that recording an incident is not the same as preventing it.

"Every driver knows that the odds of facing any real consequence are very low," he said.

"Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture. Aggressive driving is normalized here, but culture responds to enforcement," Deepanshu Gupta said.

He also noted that road rage is not a specifically defined offense in India, leaving police to choose between rash driving and far more serious charges such as attempted murder. "There is very little in between," he said.

In such conditions, responsibility rests on the drivers, particularly when a large vehicle is in a confrontation with a more vulnerable road user.

"The bigger the vehicle you bring onto the road, the greater your duty of care has to be," he said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Russia: Putin party retains majority in controlled parliamentary vote
World.content:
Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of Chechnya.

Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that the ruling United Russia party has won the parliamentary election.

It's the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin has cast it as a referendum of support for what is termed in Russia, the "special military operation."

Parties that support Putin and the Kremlin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition was barred from taking part.

The polls took place amid rising prices, a crackdown on political opponents and the internet, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.



War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the Russian election results?

The Central Election Commission said that with 95% of ballots counted, the party of Russian President Vladimir Putin won 57.83% of the vote.

Commission chair Ella Pamfilova said that according to the preliminary results, United Russia would get 355 seats in the 450-seat Duma, giving the party around 20 more seats than it currently holds and marking the strongest result in its history.

The parliamentary vote was also the first to include residents of four regions in Ukraine — those being Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia — that were occupied and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.

Voting was also held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.



Record Ukrainian attack leaves Moscow ablaze on election day To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chechen ally receives nearly 100% of vote

Russia's electoral commission also announced that close Putin ally, Ramzan ​Kadyrov, has been re-elected to a fifth term as leader of Chechnya, a Russian republic in the North Caucasus region.

Electoral officials said he achieved 99.85% of the vote, a slight improvement from the 99.73% garnered in 2021.

International observers have previously severely criticised electoral processes in the small region.

Kadyrov's government has been accused of widespread rights violations by human rights organizations, including targeting journalists and homosexuals, something he denies.

Ramzan Kadyrov's forces have been part of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP

World.title: Germany news: Trial starts of ex-Transport Minister Scheuer
World.content:
09/21/2026 September 21, 2026 Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis

VW workers are seen here protesting in Zwickau Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

Protesters from Germany's automotive industry have called for action from the government and company managements to save their jobs and factories as the country's car production sector faces a growing crisis.

Tens of thousands of people are expected to take part in rallies, which, according to the IG Metall union — Europe and Germany's largest — will take place at more than 280 sites.

Car industry being driven 'into a brick wall'

Speaking at carmaker Volkswagen's Wolfsburg factory, IG Metall's chairwoman, Christiane Benner, who is also a member of VW's supervisory board, said: "Things have really hit the fan."

"Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality," she said.

"Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall."

Benner called on the government to bring down energy costs, give financial help to suppliers to help them adjust to new challenges and use "Made in EU" rules to bolster domestic production.

Massive job cuts underway

Many observers put the blame for the current crisis on companies having started too late with the shift to electric vehicles, while others say China's government support for its own producers has led to an unequal playing field in the sector.

US tariffs have also done their bit to damage what is one of Germany's key industries, while domestic demand has weakened.

VW itself plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what would be the biggest ever restructuring in global automotive history, while Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also reducing their workforces.

World.title: Pakistan says strikes in Afghanistan killed '28 terrorists'
World.content:
The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were struck overnight. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, Afghanistan said three civilians died. This follows soon after an attack on police in Kohat, Pakistan.

Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistan's Ministry of Information described as suicide bomber training facilities.

It was the first Pakistani strike of its kind on Afghan territory since June, and followed soon after an attack targeting Pakistani police across the border in Kohat.

The uneasy neighbors reported seemingly conflicting casualty tolls.

What were the conflicting accounts on the strikes?

Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting claimed online that the attacks had targeted terrorist training sites in Afghanistan with "precision and accuracy."

"Three targets were destroyed with precision including a Suicide Bombers training markaz [station], killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. Large quantities of weapons and ammunition ... were also destroyed," the Ministry said.

The Taliban government in Kabul, meanwhile, claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes."

Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.

He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.

Neither side's assertions on the details of and casualties from the strikes could be immediately verified.



The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm Image: Shafiullah Kakar/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.

At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.

Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.

The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.

Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.

Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.

Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.

Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.

Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.

The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.

World.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
World.content:
German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.

Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.

Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.

The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.

"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.

Labor costs too high in Germany?

Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.

Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a report published by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.

To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.

The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.

It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."

Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.

IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.

VW is bringing out the axe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can longer working hours save jobs?

The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.

The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.

"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.

On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.

"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.

How can Germany's auto industry recover?

Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.

"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.

"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.

At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.

Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.

"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.

And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

World.title: El juez Peinado abre juicio con jurado a Begoña Gómez por delitos de tráfico de influencias y malversación
World.content:
El magistrado envía al banquillo a la esposa del presidente del Gobierno tras rehacer el final de su instrucción por las correcciones de la Audiencia de Madrid

El magistrado Juan Carlos Peinado ha mantenido el guion marcado y, tras volver de unos días de vacaciones, ha comunicado que ha decidido enviar al banquillo a Begoña Gómez y a su asistente en La Moncloa, Cristina Álvarez. Tras conseguir el pasado julio el aval de la Audiencia Provincial de Madrid para procesar a la esposa de Pedro Sánchez por delitos de tráfico de influencias y malversación, el juez instructor ha firmado este septiembre la resolución de apertura de juicio oral con jurado contra la pareja del presidente del Gobierno y su ayudante. El sumario pasará ahora al tribunal superior para que pueda fijar fecha para celebrar la vista. La Fiscalía y las defensas reclaman la absolución. La acusación popular liderada por la asociación ultracatólica Hazte Oír exige 13 años de prisión para Gómez.

Peinado pone así punto y final a una cuestionada instrucción de más de dos años. En abril de 2024, aceptó una denuncia del pseudosindicato Manos Limpias y emprendió entonces una expansiva investigación. Decenas de testigos (incluido el propio Sánchez y Félix Bolaños, ministro de Presidencia, Justicia y Relaciones con las Cortes) han declarado en este tiempo ante el juez, que llegó a atribuir hasta cinco delitos a la esposa del líder socialista. De hecho, en junio de este año, el magistrado abrió juicio oral a Gómez por cuatro de ellos (malversación, tráfico de influencias, corrupción en los negocios y apropiación indebida); pero la Audiencia invalidó ese paso al anular en julio esos dos últimos delitos.

Esa rectificación obligó a Peinado a rehacer la fase final de su instrucción y ha tenido que volver a convocar la audiencia preliminar prevista en la ley como paso previo necesario para poder abrir juicio oral con jurado. En ese acto, celebrado el 8 de septiembre, las partes quedaron a la espera de conocer la decisión comunicada este lunes por el juez, al que reiteraron de nuevo sus posiciones: las defensas y la Fiscalía reclamaron el archivo del sumario; y la acusación popular, que se abriera juicio oral. Además, el nuevo abogado de Gómez, Jaime Campaner, expuso que el escrito de acusación de Hazte Oír contenía “graves defectos” técnicos, incompatibles con la ley e “insubsanables” a estas alturas del procedimiento; por lo que, según añadió, no podía aceptarse y, como no existe otra acusación, debía darse carpetazo definitivo al sumario.

El juez Peinado, en diciembre de 2025 en Madrid. Andrea Comas

Sin embargo, el magistrado no acepta la pretensión del letrado: “Se desestima la alegación de ineficacia del escrito de conclusiones provisionales de la acusación popular”, escribe Peinado, que se jubila esta misma semana —cumple 72 años el próximo domingo 27 de septiembre, la edad máxima prevista en la ley para ejercer—. En esa línea, desde el verano, las defensas daban por hecho que Peinado pisaría el acelerador para enviar al banquillo a Gómez antes de dejar la carrera.

Más información El juez Peinado encamina a Begoña Gómez hacia el banquillo antes de irse unos días de vacaciones

La tesis que el magistrado lleva a juicio es que Begoña Gómez se aprovechó de su condición de esposa del presidente para extender una red de influencias para proyectar su carrera profesional en la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM), donde codirigió una cátedra extraordinaria —en cuyo seno se desarrolló un software gracias al apoyo de empresas como Google e Indra—. Además, según el magistrado, la pareja de Sánchez se valió del apoyo de su asistente en La Moncloa, que la ayudó con sus trabajos privados: “Cristina Álvarez no actuaba como mera acompañante ocasional, sino como asistente y apoyo logístico permanente de la actividad profesional y académica de Gómez, pese a tratarse de actuaciones completamente ajenas a las funciones institucionales de la Presidencia del Gobierno, que era quien abonaba su sueldo”.

A lo largo de su resolución, de 67 páginas y fechada este lunes, Peinado expone su teoría y repite frases calcadas de dictámenes anteriores. Entre ellas, la que asegura que no se puede encontrar una supuesta trama de corrupción como esta desde “el reinado de Fernando VII”. “Las conductas que provienen de palacios presidenciales, como este supuesto, parecen más propias de regímenes absolutistas, por suerte, ya olvidados en el tiempo en nuestro Estado”, asevera el magistrado. E incide: “Tras la investidura de Pedro Sánchez se produce un cambio radical en la trayectoria de Begoña Gómez”.

“Una instrucción arbitraria”

Tras conocerse este último paso de Peinado —que las partes ya esperaban—, el Gobierno ha cargado de nuevo contra el magistrado. Fuentes de La Moncloa han “condenado” la decisión de abrir juicio oral a Gómez. “Durante toda la instrucción, ha quedado clara y demostrada su inocencia y estamos seguros de que así quedará también demostrado en el juicio. Mantenemos nuestra plena confianza en que el jurado será ecuánime e impartirá justicia”, han expuesto estas fuentes, que remachan: “Denunciamos que se trata de una instrucción arbitraria e injusta, que solo responde a la persecución judicial contra Begoña Gómez por el hecho de ser la mujer del presidente del Gobierno”.

Por su parte, el PP ha arremetido contra la pareja del líder socialista. “La hora de las responsabilidades se acerca”, ha comentado Alicia García, portavoz de los populares en el Senado. Miguel Tellado, secretario general de los conservadores, ha apuntado en la misma dirección: “Señores socialistas, los jueces no son fachas ni persiguen al Gobierno. Hacen su trabajo y aplican la ley. Y sí, la mujer del presidente puede trabajar; lo que no puede es aprovecharse de su condición para medrar y conseguir lo que nunca obtendría por méritos propios”.

Contra la decisión de Peinado de este lunes no cabe recurso y, de no producirse un sorpresivo giro de última hora, Begoña Gómez se convertirá en la primera esposa de un presidente del Gobierno en sentarse en el banquillo de los acusados. En su escrito de defensa, su abogado sostiene que ella no se aprovechó de su condición de pareja del jefe del Ejecutivo; ni influyó en los cargos de la universidad, en autoridad o funcionario alguno para conseguir la creación de la cátedra bajo sospecha; ni obtuvo ningún beneficio económico.

Pero el propio Peinado utiliza este nuevo dictamen para responder a las explicaciones de la imputada. “En esta fase del procedimiento no puede darse verosimilitud a las tesis de la defensa de la acusada”, argumenta el instructor, que parafrasea a la Audiencia de Madrid: “Está fuera de toda duda el beneficio que la creación de la cátedra y su nombramiento como directora (luego codirectora) le comportó: prestigio personal o reputacional de su carrera académica con acceso a múltiples recursos y eventos, relanzamiento de los propios másteres insertos en la cátedra, lo que disparó sus ingresos por ese concepto de forma exponencial”. Aunque el propio tribunal provincial admitió en julio que, como máximo, Gómez cobró 14.900 euros en un curso académico (el 2021/2022) por su labor docente en los másteres, y en alguno no llegó ni a los 800. Y la Fiscalía apostilló que percibió “cero euros” por la cátedra.

Fianza descartada

Paralelamente, Juan Carlos Peinado ha rechazado imponer una fianza a Gómez y Álvarez antes de la futura vista oral con jurado, como así solicitó Hazte Oír. En cambio, el magistrado sí acepta que se recaben las “cinco últimas declaraciones del Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas” (IRPF) de la esposa del presidente, con el objetivo de “averiguar” su “capacidad económica” de cara al cálculo de posibles sanciones económicas que le pueda imponer el tribunal que la enjuicie —de considerarla culpable—.

La Universidad Complutense de Madrid, que está personada como perjudicada, reclama 113.000 euros.

World.title: CaixaBank, Bankinter y Unicaja aceleran el despliegue de Bizum en comercios: ya alcanza a 20 millones de usuarios
World.content:
La banca española acelera el despliegue para pagar con Bizum en los comercios físicos. CaixaBank, Bankinter y Unicaja han ampliado este lunes el acceso de sus clientes a Bizum Pay, la cartera digital que permite abonar las compras con el móvil directamente desde la cuenta bancaria vinculada a Bizum. El movimiento eleva a casi 20 millones el número de usuarios que ya tienen disponible el pago presencial, alrededor del 60% del total de clientes de la plataforma en España, según los datos facilitados por la compañía.

El avance supone un cambio de ritmo respecto al estreno del servicio. Bizum puso en marcha oficialmente el pago en comercios físicos el pasado 18 de mayo, pero lo hizo con un despliegue muy limitado: solo algunos clientes de determinadas entidades podían utilizarlo y todavía eran pocos los terminales preparados para aceptarlo. Después de cuatro meses incorporando progresivamente bancos, usuarios y comercios, septiembre estaba señalado en el sector como el momento de acelerar su implantación. CaixaBank ha abierto ahora Bizum Pay al 100% de sus clientes y asegura tener habilitados más de 517.000 terminales de pagoen comercios. Bankinter también ha extendido desde este lunes el servicio a toda su clientela, mientras que Unicaja lo ha activado para los usuarios que ya tengan Bizum. A ellas se suman Banco Sabadell, Abanca y entidades de Caja Rural, que ya ofrecían la cartera digital. El objetivo de Bizum es que a finales de año prácticamente todos sus usuarios puedan pagar de esta forma.

La extensión entre los comercios también ha avanzado desde mayo. Bizum cifra en más de 1,6 millones los establecimientos que ya pueden aceptar el nuevo medio de pago, aproximadamente tres de cada cuatro terminales bancarios (el 75%). A ellos se suman los terminales de más de 25 grandes cadenas que se encuentran en distintas fases de implantación. En general, no es necesario sustituir el datáfono. El establecimiento debe solicitar la activación del servicio a su banco o proveedor de pagos y puede continuar utilizando el mismo terminal.

El despliegue no significa que cualquier cliente de Bizum pueda pagar desde hoy en cualquier comercio. La disponibilidad depende de que el banco del cliente le haya habilitado el pago presencial. Y además, el terminal del comercio debe estar preparado para aceptarlo. Esa doble dependencia explica que el número de usuarios y el de datáfonos compatibles hayan avanzado a ritmos diferentes durante los primeros meses.

El salto al comercio físico supone un cambio importante para una herramienta que durante buena parte de su primera década estuvo asociada sobre todo a enviar dinero entre amigos y familiares. Después llegaron las donaciones y el comercio electrónico. El siguiente objetivo de la banca es trasladar esos pagos a la caja de un supermercado, un restaurante o una tienda y convertir Bizum en un medio de pago cotidiano y que pueda competir con Apple Pay o Google Pay.

La experiencia para el usuario se parece a la de cualquiera de las otras billeteras digitales. Basta con desbloquear el teléfono y acercarlo al datáfono mediante tecnología NFC para realizar la compra. La principal diferencia es que cuando se selecciona Bizum como medio de pago, el dinero sale directamente de la cuenta bancaria y se transfiere a la del comercio mediante una transferencia inmediata, en lugar de utilizar los raíles de una tarjeta. Según Bizum, los fondos se transfieren en cuestión de segundos.

Bizum Pay también permite incorporar tarjetas de débito o crédito. De esta forma, el usuario puede reunir en una misma aplicación el pago desde su cuenta y sus tarjetas. Además, puede seleccionar un método de respaldo. Si intenta utilizar Bizum en un establecimiento que todavía no lo acepta, la compra se realiza con ese segundo método establecido sin tener que abandonar la cartera digital ni reiniciar el proceso.

Más allá de la ampliación de los servicios financieros para los clientes, la entrada en el comercio físico tiene una dimensión económica para los bancos. Bizum es propiedad de una treintena de entidades financieras españolas y su expansión a las tiendas les permite competir en un negocio dominado durante décadas por las redes internacionales de tarjetas. Para el usuario que paga el servicio es gratuito, pero al establecimiento se le descuenta una pequeña comisión (igual que sucede con las tarjetas), por lo que Bizum es a partir de ahora una fuente de ingresos más para los bancos.

La prueba ahora será comprobar si la disponibilidad se traduce en uso. Bizum asegura que los usuarios que ya pagan presencialmente con el servicio realizan una media de tres operaciones semanales, aunque no ha facilitado el volumen total de compras realizadas desde mayo. CaixaBank sí ofrece una primera referencia y ha anunciado que, desde el inicio de su fase piloto, a mediados de julio, sus clientes han realizado cerca de 25.000 pagos por un importe superior a 400.000 euros, unos 16 euros de media por operación. Son todavía cifras reducidas frente al volumen del mercado de tarjetas, pero corresponden a una fase en la que el servicio solo estaba disponible para una parte muy limitda de sus clientes.

La ambición de Bizum tampoco termina en España. La plataforma participa en una alianza europea que busca conectar distintos sistemas nacionales de pagos europeos. Los usuarios españoles ya pueden enviar y recibir dinero de forma inmediata con usuarios de soluciones equivalentes de Italia, Portugal y Andorra. El siguiente paso será llevar esa interoperabilidad a más mercados y a las compras presenciales. La hoja de ruta contempla extender en 2027 la interoperabilidad al comercio electrónico y a los pagos en establecimientos físicos, lo que abriría la puerta a que un usuario español pudiera utilizar Bizum para pagar en otros países europeos a través de Bizum.

World.title: Council of State: freeze “disproportionate” traffic fines
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Council of State has urged the cabinet to rethink its decision to raise traffic fines amid concerns that the penalties have increased out of proportion to other offences.

Justice minister David van Weel wants to raise fines across the board by 2.7% next year, in line with inflation.

If approved, the new fines would include €130 for parking without authorisation, €330 for running red lights and €450 for using a mobile phone at the wheel.

Speeding fines depend on the actual speed, ranging from €33 for going 4km/h over the limit to €424 for exceeding the limit by 30km/h. But fines are higher in built-up areas and 30km zones: driving 50km/h in a 30km/h limit will cost €351.

The Council of State, which issues non-binding advice on all government bills and decisions, queried if the raise was “necessary, fair and proportionate”, echoing criticism from other legal bodies in recent years.

They include the prosecution service (Openbare Ministerie), judges and the agency that collects the fines, the CJI, which said there was “imbalance” with fines for other offences such as common assault, which typically carries a penalty of €400.

Debt problems

Traffic fines have increased cumulatively by 220% in the last 30 years, while in 2024 127,000 families had problems with debt caused by outstanding traffic penalties.

The Council of State said freezing the fines rather than allowing them to rise with inflation was a “first obvious step” towards rebalancing the penalties.

It said the reason given by ministers – that the income from fines was needed to meet the justice ministry’s costs – was not a valid legal argument.

“The aim of these fines is to sanction behaviour that breaks the rules and improve road safety,” it said in a written advisory. “Raising the tariffs for traffic fines should relate to serving that purpose.”

World.title: Urgent help needed for children in emergency asylum shelters
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Children in emergency shelters are living in unsafe and dangerous conditions that violate international law, according to a two-year investigation by the Dutch Safety Board.

The organisation has been looking into the living situation for some 7,000 children who are currently living in crisis accommodations while awaiting the outcome of their asylum claims.

Children experience constant noise and a total lack of privacy in these shelters as well as a high risk of physical and sexual violence, the report found.

The safety board wants the immigration ministry to make sweeping reforms in the next six months.

“Emergency shelter is not normal. It was initially intended for a short period, but by now, children sometimes live in emergency shelters for years,” the organisation’s chairperson Chris van Dam said in a statement.

More than 60% of asylum seekers are now being housed in “emergency” shelters, like vacant offices, ships, event halls, and temporary container homes.

The safety board wants a structural solution to the shelter problems as well as improvements in emergency shelters, including setting a maximum length of stay and enforcing quality standards.

World.title: Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Maastricht has limited how Pierre Rieu can decorate his hotel in the city center, telling the son of famous musician André Rieu that his current proposal is too extravagant.

Rieu had proposed to turn the historic building into a life-sized Christmas gift, with string lights and an illuminated bow.

The 4-star Hotel Derlon dates from 1870 and was bought by Rieu in 2025.

He had done up the hotel in the same manner last year, but the city’s Planning and Monuments Commission found the decorations to be excessive, according to local news outlet L1.

The hotelier was told he needed to choose between the bow and the string lights to allow the building’s architecture to be visible.

Rieu told regional broadcaster 1Zuid he was irritated with the decision. “We’re talking about Christmas lights. I don’t think anyone is bothered by that,” he said.

World.title: More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice
World.content:
More Dutch students are spending part of their degree abroad, but the proportion is still below pre-pandemic levels, according to latest official figures.

Some 24% of students who graduated from universities and vocational colleges in 2025 went abroad for part of their studies, with one in six (17%) staying for three months or longer.

Five years ago, during the most restricted phase of the coronavirus pandemic, just 16% of all students had spent time outside the Netherlands, the government statistics agency CBS said.

Spain was the most popular destination for students who took part in the Erasmus+ exchange programme between 2014 and 2024, accounting 16.9% of the total, followed by Germany (9.7%) and the UK (8.9%).

The last figure is noteworthy because Britain left the Erasmus+ scheme in 2020 as part of the Brexit agreement, though it is rejoining from next year.

Students who went abroad for their entire degree were most likely to go to Belgium, followed by the UK and the United States.

Online decline

One in seven students took part in online lessons or projects hosted by foreign colleges and universities, but here there was a declining trend, particularly among university students.

Just 10% of the latter group followed an online course, down from 14% in 2021, while for vocational students the proportion slipped from 19% to 18%.

More than one-third (36%) of recent graduates who spent time abroad also included an online element.

World.title: LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious
World.content:
Less than a quarter of schoolboys in the Netherlands have a positive view of homosexuality, almost half the proportion of four years ago, according to a Europe-wide survey.

The HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children) poll found that just 22% of boys aged 12 to 16 had a positive view of homosexuality, compared to 40% the last time the survey was carried out in 2021.

Gonneke Stevens, professor of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University, said there was a “worrying turn in the trend” after decades of growing acceptance of same-sex relationships.

“In recent years sexual diversity has been increasingly questioned by leading figures in society, including politicians,” said Stevens, who led the Dutch research team in collaboration with the Trimbos mental health institute.

The COC, which campaigns for LGBGTI rights in the Netherlands, described the findings as a “frightening development.” Director Marie Ricardo said: “We badly need the young generation for a free country in which everyone can be themselves.”

The survey found girls were still more accepting of homosexuality than boys, but the proportion had fallen from 78% to just over half (51%) since 2021.

Manosphere

Stevens said there was a clear link between deepening intolerance and the rise of trends on social media such as the “manosphere”, which provides a platform for aggressive and discriminatory messages about women and gays.

“The fact is that in recent years young people have been exposed to these views and that in the same period they have taken a more negative view of homosexuality.”

Prime minister Rob Jetten, who is due to marry his male partner Nicolás Keenan next year, said the figures were “shocking”.

“The influence of social media as huge and the cabinet will look at how we can put pressure on the social media companies to take action if a lot of content is appearing online that has a bad influence on young people,” he told RTL Nieuws.

Hardline conservative organisations have also pushed back against efforts to teach children about tolerance by promoting spurious links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

In 2023 children’s writer Pim Lammers had to go into hiding after receiving death threats when his novel De Boer en de Dierenarts (“The farmer and the vet”), about a same-sex relationship, was targeted by the radical Catholic organisation Civitas Christiana after he was asked to write a poem for children’s book week.

The sex education institute Rutgers, which organises the annual “Week van de Lentekriebels” (Spring Fever Week), won a court case against Civitas Christiana banning it from making false statements or publishing its “black book”, listing people and organisations that it accuses of “sexualising” children. The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal in May.

The Netherlands will see a mix of sun and clouds in the coming days, with a bit of rain midweek, but warm temperatures and sunshine are predicted for the weekend.

The Dutch meteorological institute KNMI says Monday will mostly be cloudy and dry, with highs ranging from from 17°C in the north to 21°C in the southeast.

Tuesday will be cloudy, with a chance of light rain, with highs of 16°C to 21°C across the country.

The weekend is likely to be warm, with highs on Sunday reaching 23°C.

World.title: Meerdink and Til added to Oranje Nations League squad
World.content:
AZ Alkmaar striker Mexx Meerdink and PSV’s Guus Til have been called up as late replacements to Xavi Hernandez’ Netherlands men’s football squad for this week’s Nations League clash with Germany.

They replace Bournemouth striker Justin Kluivert and AS Roma forward Donyell Malen, who withdrew at the weekend with injuries.

Til, 28, has won eight caps in as many years and was part of Ronald Koeman’s World Cup squad in the summer, marked his recall by scoring twice for his club away to Twente Enschede at the weekend, but PSV still lost 3-2.

Meerdink, 23, who is hiping to win his first cap, scored AZ’s only goal against Telstar as they leapfrogged PSV at the top of the table.

The inclusion of the pair brings the number of Eredivisie players in Xavi’s 26-man squad to five. Thursday’s match against Germany in Amsterdam is the Spaniard’s first as head coach since he was appointed as Koeman’s successor last month.

World.title: Jetten condemns second year of far-right riots in The Hague
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Prime minister Rob Jetten has condemned rioters who clashed with police for the second year in a row at a demonstration in The Hague organised by the far right.

Police broke up the gathering of around 300 people on the Malieveld on Saturday afternoon on the orders of acting mayor Richard de Mos.

Altogether 24 people were arrested for ignoring an emergency order to disperse and carrying weapons. All of them were released on Sunday pending further inquiries.

“They thew fireworks at police, committed vandalism and wore face-covering clothing, despite an agreement with the organisers that they would not,” a spokesman said.

Jetten said in a post on X that the rioters had “deliberately sought to confront police”. He added that they “used excessive violence against police, chanted repulsive extreme-right and anti-Semitic slogans and made Nazi salutes”.

March cancelled

A far-right group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”) organised Saturday’s demonstration against immigration. The violence was less extreme than a year ago, when 1,000 rioters set fire to police cars, blockaded the A12 motorway and smashed windows at the offices of Jetten’s party D66.

Op het Malieveld is vandaag door relschoppers bewust de confrontatie gezocht met de politie. Er is excessief geweld tegen de politie gebruikt, er zijn weerzinwekkende extreemrechtse en antisemitische uitingen gescandeerd en Hitlergroeten gebracht. Veel waardering voor het… — Rob Jetten (@MinPres) September 19, 2026

Originally the group was due to march through the city, but De Mos cancelled the march after some members refused to remove face masks.

“That is why we cancelled the march and only allowed a demonstration on the Malieveld,” the acting mayor said. “When the violence continued, it was necessary to put an end to it.”

Photographer in water

A Spanish photographer who was covering the demonstration filed an official complaint against police after he was allegedly pushed into a canal by an officer.

Nacho Calogne, who works as a freelance correspondent, told NOS his accreditation was clearly visible. “Not one police officer came over afterwards to help me or check if I was OK,” he said. “Other photographers pulled me out.”

Police said they had made contact with the photographer and the Dutch journalists’ union NVJ to discuss possible compensation.

Three other journalists reported they were intimidated and attacked during the demonstration, according to PersVeilig, which campaigns for the safety of reporters.

World.title: Poland’s Catholic church recruits priests from Africa and Asia to stave off vocations crisis
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Marcin Choduń (published in cooperation with Tygodnik Powszechny) With the number of Poles training to be priests falling steadily, Catholic parishes are increasingly looking beyond Europe to fill the gaps. Father Fransiskus Laka will never forget his first day in Poland. When he stepped out of the arrivals hall at Warsaw’s Okęcie (now Chopin) airport in October 1999, he thought he would not last long. Why? The bitter chill in the air. “It was only seven degrees,” he laughs. It is not surprising that the young man from Indonesia was having second thoughts. At home, a cool day meant 25°C. Now, though, having spent 27 years in Poland, no weather fazes him. In the middle of winter, he will sometimes even go out in just a T-shirt to shovel snow or bring wood for the stove. Father Fransiskus has settled in the village of Brzegi, near Zakopane in southern Poland, where he has been parish priest for the last two years. And the mountainous Podhale region it is part of still has long, cold and snowy winters. Father Fransiskus, a Verbite, is not the only foreign Roman Catholic priest working in Poland, where around 70% of the population is Catholic. Their numbers are growing every year in response to the rising shortage of Polish priests. Polish dioceses are increasingly keen to invite young foreigners to study at their seminaries. Poland’s shortage of priests Most of those invited are from Africa. In Kielce, for example, there are currently two seminarians from the Central African Republic and seven from Angola. The Tarnów seminary also trained a priest from the Central African Republic in recent years (ordained as a deacon in the nearby village of Szynwałd in 2024). In the diocese of Ełk, Bishop Jerzy Mazur announced in a letter read out in churches in 2023 that he would be combating the shortage of priests by inviting clergy from Africa to the diocesan seminary. In return for receiving training in Poland, the newly ordained priests were to spend at least a few years working in the region. Previously, the support of retired priests had been sufficient. But, as the shortage grew, the curia even considered reducing the number of services or merging parishes. That was when the idea of seeking help from abroad came about. Just one new priest was ordained in Łódź, Poland's fourth largest city, this year – the lowest figure ever recorded One church figure admits there has been a “dramatic decline” in interest in the priesthood while the head of a seminary calls it a “crisis” https://t.co/QuwKsoPSg3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 13, 2023 “Priests from Poland increasingly work for as long as their health permits,” says Andrzej Kobyliński, a priest and ethicist from Cardinal Stefan Wyszynski University in Warsaw. “However, that doesn’t change the fact that, in a few years’ time, we’ll have a staffing shortfall, because Polish seminaries are more and more deserted.” In recent years, a lack of recruits has led to several seminaries merging or closing down. The Wrocław, Legnica and Świdnica seminaries have been combined into one institution – which in reality means the two smaller schools being transferred to the big city. Clerical students in Kalisz have met a similar fate, having to go to Częstochowa to study, while seminarians from Elbląg have been sent to Olsztyn. The seminaries in Łowicz and Bydgoszcz have closed, and education in Drohiczyn and Sandomierz has been suspended. “The changes are happening at such an alarming rate that at present over a dozen seminaries will need to be closed,” says Kobyliński. “Let’s take the Płock diocese. You could say that the students in the seminary there are being put through a mental ordeal.” “Since there are currently 13 seminarians studying in seven year groups, that means that some years are empty or only have one or two people. That causes terrible loneliness. Because how can you survive seven years on your own?” For Kobyliński, the Ełk diocese is a symbol of the changes that are coming. This year, it only ordained one deacon – from Togo, West Africa. A new home in Poland The deacon’s name is Roger and he arrived in Poland a few years ago, along with another prospective priest from Togo who decided to return home for personal reasons. “There are currently seven people studying in our seminary, three of them from Africa. Apart from Roger, we have two more, from Ghana,” says Marcin Maczan, chancellor of the Ełk curia. According to him, however, the presence of African seminarians in Ełk is not only a response to the shortage of priests. “Bishop Jerzy Mazur, who himself spent several years working in Ghana and in the past was the head of the missions committee of the Polish Episcopal Conference, is familiar with the realities of mission dioceses. He knows very well that they can always use help in training priests.” “So these two ideas were combined: training a priest for his home diocese in Africa and his ministry in Poland for eight to ten years after ordination. All in line with the terms of the agreements that the bishop of Ełk made with bishops in Africa,” Maczan says. These agreements vary. Some priests return to their home dioceses shortly after ordination – seminarians from Kielce, for instance. Others remain for many years, such as Father Fransiskus Laka, whose stay in Poland is prolonged by the congregation’s provincial superior every three years. Poland was not his first choice. Shortly before being ordained, each of the clerical students in Fransiskus’s seminary, the Divine Word Missionaries in Pieniężno, northeastern Poland, was supposed to name three countries where they wished to serve. He chose Ecuador, Nicaragua and, in last place, Poland. Usually, one of the first two options is selected, but the provincial superior suggested otherwise. A surprised Fransiskus agreed, and he has never regretted his decision. After spending the first four years in the parish in Pieniężno, he returned to the seminary to become a prefect, responsible for keeping order. In this period, he travelled the length and breadth of Poland to lead retreats in parishes. He then spent seven years as a curate in Chludów, near Poznań, before in 2024 becoming the priest of the parish of St Anthony in Brzegi in the Podhale region. “I arrived on 8 December – so almost immediately I had Christmas pastoral visits to make to parishioners’ homes,” says Father Fransiskus. “They really welcomed me very warmly. They often help me – show me how to light the stove, or leave food outside my door. I learn hard work, humility, patience and faith from them. The mountains are tough terrain – you really need grit to survive.” Poland became home. Fransiskus feels safe here – despite growing hostility towards foreigners, which is particularly visible in the public and online space (foreign ministry statistics confirm that in 2024-2025 the total number of hate crimes reported in Poland increased by more than 50% – from 760 to almost 1,200 cases). “I’ve never yet encountered any hostile behaviour towards me,” says Fransiskus. Although he regularly visits his home island of Lembata, there are many things in Indonesia that he can no longer accept. The organisation of mass, for example: if it is supposed to begin, say, at 7 a.m., worshippers turn up just before 9. They don’t understand why Fransiskus sees this as a problem. Or a bus journey – when the driver passes his house, he’ll usually take a break to have lunch and play with his children. “The passengers wait patiently and no one thinks anything of it,” laughs Fransiskus. The Togolese footballing priest Father Romuald Mawakina Tchilabalo Mozou, from Togo (pictured top), is a newer arrival in Poland. His stay in the country is on the same basis as Fransiskus – an interdiocesan agreement extended every three years. Romuald has only been here seven years, but already speaks impeccable Polish, with barely a trace of a foreign accent. Upon arriving in Poland, he learned the language intensively – for seven months, from Monday to Saturday, seven hours a day. “I knew from the outset that if I couldn’t communicate well with the faithful, I wouldn’t build any relationship with them,” he says. Romuald was born in the village of Kaza, near Sotouboua. His father was a French teacher in the local primary school. And so his first language was French – he only learned Kabije, the ethnic language in northern Togo, in later years. His family is Catholic. And their neighbours? A mixture, just like everywhere else in Togo: the majority are Muslims, but there are also some Catholics and followers of traditional faiths. The proportion of people in Poland who are religious non-believers has risen to a record 14% while those who attend Sunday mass have fallen to a low of 34%. But a large majority of Poles still identify as believers and Catholics https://t.co/2yqrLePAsw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 23, 2024 The Mozou family are very religious. As a young boy, Romuald and his family would pray together daily, and this was what first brought him into indirect contact with Poland: every evening, along with his parents, two sisters and two brothers, he recited Saint Faustina Kowalska’s Chaplet of the Divine Mercy. He also associated Poland with John Paul II – to date the only pope to have visited Togo. Romuald’s great passion has always been football. His dream of a professional career led him to neglect his studies, until his father made things clear: first school, then football. While at high school, however, Romuald started to consider the priesthood. After taking his exams, he began studying in a seminary in Lomé, the Togolese capital. Three years in, the bishop proposed that he go to Poland to study at the seminary in Opole. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 As a dean, Father Romuald gained hands-on experience in Krapkowice. After his ordination in May 2024, he became a curate in Opole (and from August this year he will be based in nearby Ujazd). I ask him how the new parishioners responded to him. “Well, to be honest, they were a little surprised at first,” he laughed. “But that’s hardly surprising – after all, I’m the first priest from Africa to serve in the Opole diocese. They gave me a very warm welcome, though – I’ve never encountered any unfriendly gestures or words from them.” In Poland, Romuald’s childhood passion has been rekindled: he’s playing football again. First for Maciowakrze, a club playing in Klasa B (the eighth tier of the Polish league system), then in Żywocice, in Klasa A. He now plays as a striker for GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory. “I don’t know if I’ll return to my homeland – everything is possible,” Romuald says. “I feel good in both Poland and Togo.” Polish dioceses recruiting in Africa In 2026, 196 priests are to be ordained in Poland – 12 fewer than last year and some 205 down on the figure from 2013. The number of dioceses in which no ordinations took place because of a lack of candidates is growing – seven this year, compared to six in 2025. “We actually have a vocations crisis everywhere in Europe, so we will be looking for priests in other parts of the world,” says Andrzej Kobyliński. “Essentially, we have two areas where we can recruit candidates for the priesthood. Mainly Africa, and possibly India, but the experiences of German and Italian dioceses show that priests from India find it harder to settle in Europe.” “Latin America is not an option, as the Catholic church there is facing its own crisis of a mass exodus to Pentecostal churches,” he adds. “So in the future we will definitely be working intensively with African dioceses. This is an enormous historical change, because it was once Poland and Europe that sent missionaries to Africa.” One of the lads Przywory, a village near Opole, the GKS Piomar Tarnów Opolski-Przywory home pitch. Seven p.m. Training has started. Father Romuald Mozou is a little late, so he rushes into the dressing room. “Romek, you’re doing push-ups as punishment,” laugh his teammates when he appears on the pitch. Everyone calls him by this Polish diminutive – Romek. The team’s coach, Marcin Chudala, admits that the players like to have a laugh at the footballing priest’s expense. “Sometimes we joke when he’s sitting on the bench staring at his phone: ‘What are you doing, Romek – confessing?’ The banter can be cruel,” says the coach. But he also admits that Romek’s presence has left its mark on the team. Less swearing, for example. Even if there is nothing to suggest that Romek is a priest. “We treat him just like one of the lads from the playground,” Chudala says. The original version of this interview can be seen here. Translated by Ben Koschalka. Marcin Choduń is a journalist and translator of German and English. He publishes his articles mainly in Tygodnik Powszechny and Duży Format, a supplement of Gazeta Wyborcza. In 2012, he was nominated for the Grand Press Award in the reportage category for his article “The Blood of a Skinhead, the Blood of a Jew”. Poland plans to have more than 1,000 warning sirens in the eastern Lublin province by the end of the year in response to increased Russian attacks in Ukraine near the Polish border, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński has announced. The Polish government is also working on an application that would use Cell Broadcast technology to turn mobile phones into warning devices, allowing them to function like sirens in a crisis, the minister added. Minister @MKierwinski w Lublinie:💬Budujemy system ochrony ludności niemal od podstaw. W województwie lubelskim na początku 2024 roku było około 30 syren, które można było uruchomić zdalnie. Dziś jest ich prawie 350, a do końca tego roku będzie ich ponad tysiąc. To pokazuje, jak… pic.twitter.com/6uWAgcNrJh — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) September 19, 2026 Speaking in Lublin on Saturday, Kierwiński said that the region now has almost 350 automatic sirens, compared to just 30 at the start of 2024. The number is expected to triple to over 1,000 by the end of this year. “Jet-powered drones and missiles are increasingly flying near the Polish border” and Poland is therefore “turning to tools designed to counter the associated threats,” Kierwiński said, quoted by news website OKO Press, adding that the government had to build Poland’s civil protection system “almost from scratch”. As part of these efforts, Poland’s fire service, working with the Lublin governor, is now rolling out a project to identify and mark the province’s nearly 3,500 shelters. Last year, Poland launched a mobile application and website that allows people to find their nearest shelter in the case of an emergency. By the end of the year, Poland also wants to introduce an application that would allow it to “take over” residents’ phones “to function like a siren”, Kierwiński added, without providing any further details. Residents in areas close to the Ukrainian border have heard warning sirens during Russian attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks and received alerts through the state warning system. The opposition has criticised the alerts for not giving residents clear instructions on what to do when the sirens sound. In response, the ministry has stepped up its public information campaign, including a television and social media campaign on emergency preparedness. Additionally, more than 500 fire stations in the eastern Lublin and Subcarpathian provinces held training over the weekend on how to respond to emergency alerts. The sessions were part of a wider campaign that has already involved 630,000 people across Poland. Poland’s interior ministry has launched a TV campaign, including spots on public broadcaster TVP’s flagship morning show, aimed at educating the public about how to respond to emergency situations such as natural disasters and security threats https://t.co/MS0APufAmq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Poland has stepped up preparations along its eastern border following a series of Russian attacks in western Ukraine, including a drone strike on a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw about 2 km from the Polish border. The recent escalation follows a number of incidents in recent years involving violations of Polish airspace, including the entry of around 20 Russian drones on one night last year, as well as the explosion of a Russian missile in a field in eastern Poland earlier this year. Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski described the attacks in the border area as “another escalation” by Russia, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s further plans could include attacks designed to test NATO’s response. During his visit to Ukraine last week, Tusk announced that Poland had joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries working together to develop an integrated air defence system for the continent. World.title: Moody’s cuts Poland’s credit rating to lowest level since 2002
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later. Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday. “Large fiscal deficits persist, leading to a material increase in public debt and, together with rising interest costs, weaken debt affordability metrics,” added the agency. It also warned that “fiscal policy effectiveness has weakened”, including a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”. “Political constraints, including the continued standoff between the government and the president and the proximity of the November 2027 parliamentary elections, also limit the scope for meaningful fiscal consolidation,” concluded Moody’s, pointing to Poland’s high social and defence spending. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. However, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, blamed the situation on the government. “They steal, they lie and they burden our homeland with debt,” he wrote on social media. “Unfortunately, we Poles will have to pay for it all.” Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led both Fitch and Moody’s to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Standard & Poor’s, meanwhile, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on the Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. Powodem jest plan budżetu bez żadnej przewidywanej redukcji deficytu fiskalnego państwa w relacji do PKB. World.title: Poland joins European Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. We are launching a new format – “C8,” the Carpathian Eight – bringing together us and our… pic.twitter.com/tcIupMsBBK — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 18, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
