World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds was designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colours offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems. The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymyr Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly. “Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk. “The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw launches patrols to crack down on improperly parked electric scooters
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. World.title: Crowdfunding Campaign Launches for Book Tracing the History of Prague’s Roxy Club
World.content:
A new book documenting the history of Prague’s Roxy club and the alternative cultural scene that grew around it is seeking public support ahead of its planned publication this autumn.

Titled Kopneš do plechovky a dva dny se tančí (“Kick a Can and Dance for Two Days”), the book looks at Roxy’s development from its beginnings in the early 1990s to its current role in Prague’s music scene.



A crowdfunding campaign to finance the publication has been launched on Donio.cz.

Rather than focusing solely on the history of one nightclub, the project examines the people, artists and cultural movements connected with the venue.

More than 40 musicians, promoters, artists and other figures associated with Roxy contribute their memories and perspectives.

Roxy opened in 1992 and quickly became an important venue for alternative music in Prague. Over the years, its programme has covered genres including hardcore, house, trip-hop, hip-hop and drum’n’bass.

The book is the result of almost five years of research by cultural journalist Ondřej Horák. He examined thousands of archival documents, located previously unpublished photographs and interviewed nearly 50 people connected with Roxy and its history.

The campaign will also feature newly created artwork. Graphic designer and typographer Jozef Ondrík has produced a series of three screen-printed posters based on visual elements from Roxy’s history.

The design draws on three pages from the original handover document for the non-residential premises at Dlouhá 33, which were transferred to the Linhart Foundation.

Large-format photographs and works by artists connected with Roxy and the NoD Gallery are also expected to be among the campaign rewards.

World.title: Prague and the 15-Minute City? Only for One in Seven Residents
World.content:
In the first year of the Friendly City Index, Prague ranked second among Central and Eastern European metropolises.

Yet only 13.82% of residents can reach most daily destinations – work, schools, shops, or healthcare – within 15 minutes. The best metropolises in the region remain closer to “30-minute cities.”



Young Czechs are closest to the ideal: 34% of those aged 18–24 said they can reach everyday destinations within 15 minutes. Middle-aged people, especially 45–54, scored the worst at 14.7%.

Smaller Czech cities outperform Prague. Olomouc (36%), Ostrava (29.7%), and Brno (21.8%) all ranked better in their categories. Compact urban structures and shorter distances explain much of this advantage. Polish cities also dominated the rankings, including Krakow, Szczecin, and Lublin.

Among metropolises, Warsaw leads with 15.9%. In other categories: Krakow (30.3%), Split (44%), Rijeka (53.3%), and Zadar (53.6%). Riga ranked worst at 9.8%, while Zagreb scored only 20%.

The smaller the city, the better the accessibility

Around 10–15% in metropolises, 30% in large cities, 40%+ in medium-sized cities, and over 50% in small cities. Even cities with metro systems like Prague or Bucharest show little improvement, confirming that compactness and urban structure matter more than infrastructure alone.

Transport habits

In Central and Eastern Europe, 46% rely on cars and 27% on public transport. In Czechia, the split is nearly even: 42.6% drive, 42.4% use public transport. Among 18–24-year-olds, more than half (51.1%) rely on public transport. Alternative mobility options such as bikes, scooters, and carsharing remain marginal.

Urban planner Peter Bednár explains: “The point is not that all journeys must be short, but that most daily activities can be done without a car. Achieving this requires higher density and a mix of functions. Without enough services and destinations nearby, the most practical walk still leads to the parked car.”

About the index

The Friendly City Index is an international survey on quality of life and urban development. In 2025, it covered 54 cities in nine countries with 4,500 respondents, including 500 in Czechia. The study was carried out by Syno International in partnership with Bolt.

World.title: Where to See Prague’s Best Autumn Colors Without Leaving the City
World.content:
Autumn in Prague does not have to mean a crowded walk across Petřín or a stroll through Stromovka.

Beyond the city’s best-known parks, forests, valleys and protected natural areas offer quieter routes where the changing season can be enjoyed without leaving Prague.

Many of these places are also surprisingly easy to reach. A tram, bus or train can take you close to the starting point, making it possible to plan a two- or three-hour walk without a car or a full-day trip.



Vinoř Park and the Satalice Pheasantry

In northeastern Prague, a marked trail links Vinoř Park with the Satalice Pheasantry through a narrow wooded valley.

The landscape is shaped by the Vinořský Stream, sandstone formations and small springs. Along the route, walkers can also come across traces of the area’s history, including rock carvings, the remains of an old hillfort and the entrance to a water cave.

The area is especially attractive in autumn, when old oaks and other trees turn yellow and brown. A long avenue between Vinoř and Satalice adds another distinctive feature to the route.

The official educational trail is about 3.5 kilometers long and takes roughly two hours. It starts near the Malá Obůrka pond and finishes close to the Chapel of St. Anne in Satalice. From there, buses and trains provide connections back into Prague.

Hvězda offers more than its main avenue

Hvězda Game Reserve is one of Prague’s better-known green spaces, but many visitors stay on the central avenue leading from Vypich to the white Renaissance summer palace.

The quieter parts begin once you leave the main route and head into the surrounding woodland.

Oaks, beeches and hornbeams dominate the reserve. According to Prague’s records, more than half of its forest stands are over 150 years old. Several notable beech trees date from plantings carried out after 1763, including a tree recognized as the oldest and largest beech in Prague.

A loop through the reserve can lead from the summer palace toward the pond and Světlička wetland meadow before returning along one of the smaller paths.

Dalejské Valley offers a different side of Prague

Prokopské Valley is familiar to many Prague residents, but the landscape continues west toward Řeporyje in the quieter Dalejské Valley.

Here, limestone cliffs, former quarries, open slopes and the Dalejský Stream create a landscape that changes frequently along the trail.

One option is to follow the green-marked hiking route from Řeporyje toward Hlubočepy. Rather than forming one continuous wall of autumn foliage, the valley combines yellow trees with exposed rock and brownish grass-covered slopes.

The area forms part of the northeastern section of the Bohemian Karst and is recognized for its geological features. Prague’s Nature Portal recommends following the valley along the stream.

Hostivař Forest Park changes after summer

Hostivař is closely associated with its reservoir and summer swimming, but the area takes on a different character once the bathing season ends.

The woods surrounding the water offer numerous walking routes, with more than 35 kilometers of paths and trails running through the forest park.

A shorter walk can follow the reservoir, while longer routes continue through woodland and meadows and pass the animal enclosure near the gamekeeper’s lodge. The Botič Stream Basin educational trail also crosses the area.

Autumn brings changing colors to the oak and larch trees, while the reservoir provides views that are particularly noticeable on cooler mornings.

World.title: New Dog Playground Opens in Central Prague with Agility Course
World.content:
Prague 1 now has its first public dog playground, giving dog owners in the city center a dedicated space for exercise and training.

The new facility is located on Ludvík Svobody Embankment, next to the Ministry of Transport’s traffic playground and close to Lannov Park. It has been open to the public since September 16.



At the center of the site is an approximately 92-meter-long agility course. It includes a tunnel, slalom poles, an A-frame and several jumping obstacles. The playground is freely accessible and does not require prior booking.

“Space in the center of Prague is very limited, so we want to use every suitable location to serve local residents,” said Kateřina Klasnová, Prague 1’s deputy mayor responsible for the environment.

The playground is currently unfenced, meaning dogs can enter and leave the area freely.

Some dog owners raised concerns about the lack of a fence during the opening, and Prague 1 said it would consider adding one.

An information board at the site explains the operating rules and provides instructions for using the agility equipment. The playground also has a waste bin and two dispensers containing bags for dog owners to clean up after their pets.

Responsibility for the site lies with the Prague 1 Department of the Environment. Visitors can report damaged equipment or other defects directly to the municipal district.

World.title: Emeli Sandé to Bring Her Biggest Hits to Prague at O2 universum
World.content:
One of Britain’s most acclaimed contemporary singers, Emeli Sandé, returns to Prague on November 3 for a special live concert at O2 universum.

The singer-songwriter will perform her best-known hits alongside music from her latest album, How Were We to Know.

Tickets are available through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

Select 2 tickets and enter promo code EXPATPRAGUE at checkout. You’ll only pay for 1 ticket. The offer is valid from 14 to 21 September 2026 for tickets in sectors 102-109, subject to availability.

Emeli Sandé’s biggest hits

Sandé became an international star with songs including Next to Me, Heaven, Read All About It, Clown and My Kind of Love, combining soul, pop and powerful vocals with deeply personal songwriting.

Her debut album, Our Version of Events, became one of the most successful British albums of its era and was the UK’s best-selling album of 2012. It also produced several of her biggest hits and established Sandé as one of the country’s leading vocalists.

She further cemented her place in British music history with performances at both the opening and closing ceremonies of the London 2012 Olympic Games.

In Prague, fans can expect a set spanning her career, including songs from her latest album, How Were We to Know. Released as part of a new chapter in her career, the album combines her distinctive soul influences with a contemporary pop sound.

ADONXS joins as special guest

Sandé will be joined by ADONXS, singer, songwriter and one of the newer names on the Czech and Slovak pop scene.

ADONXS represented the Czech Republic at the Eurovision Song Contest 2025, where he performed his song Kiss Kiss Goodbye. He has also released tracks including Wasted and Perfume, while his latest single, Cherry on Your Cake, continues his development as a songwriter and performer.

His appearance at O2 universum will open the evening before Sandé takes the stage.

Emeli Sandé live at O2 universum

The Prague concert will bring together Sandé’s most recognisable songs with material from her more recent work, giving audiences the chance to hear her signature voice in a live setting.

With hits that have become familiar to audiences around the world, the concert offers a chance to revisit songs such as Next to Me, Heaven and Read All About It, while discovering the latest direction of her music.

World.title: EU Citizens Can Vote in Czechia’s October Elections: Here’s How
World.content:
EU citizens living in Czechia can vote in the country’s municipal elections this October, but those who are not already registered will need to take action before election day.

The elections will take place on October 9 and 10, with voters in Prague choosing representatives for both the Prague City Assembly and their local municipal district.

EU citizens aged 18 or over who have permanent or registered temporary residence in Czechia can vote in municipal elections. However, they must be registered in the relevant electoral register.

Registering to vote

The deadline for registration is October 7, but the civic initiative Volby pro všechny recommends registering as soon as possible.

Its EU Voter Registration Tool generates the necessary application form and explains how to submit it to the relevant municipal or district office.

Registering early also means voters should receive their ballot papers at home before election day, giving them time to understand the unfamiliar Czech voting system. Those who register closer to the deadline will receive their ballots at the polling station.

There is also an important option for those who miss the registration deadline. According to Volby pro všechny, EU citizens will have a special possibility this year to register directly at their polling station on election day, provided they bring the required identification and proof of residence.

Find your polling station

Voters cannot simply choose any polling station. Their home address determines where they can vote.

The Polling Station Finder allows residents to enter their address and find the correct polling place. It can also create a calendar reminder for election day.

Voters should bring a valid ID or passport and the relevant Czech residence document.

What will Prague residents vote for?

Prague voters will cast two votes: one for the Prague City Assembly, covering the capital as a whole, and one for the council of their municipal district.

For those unfamiliar with the division of responsibilities, Volby pro všechny has created a “Who Does What?” quiz explaining which level of local government deals with different issues.

The organization has also published an overview of political parties and groups and is preparing a quiz that will allow users to compare their answers on policy questions with the positions of Czech political parties.

A guide in 23 EU languages

Volby pro všechny has also prepared a seven-step checklist for EU citizens, available as a downloadable PDF in 23 EU languages.

For EU citizens who have never voted in Czechia before, the resources provide a straightforward way to check their registration, find their polling station and understand what to expect on election day.

World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: How education is bringing Indonesia and Hungary closer
World.content:
From Indonesian language class in Budapest to gamelan performances and university life from Sumatera to Papua, education is giving Indonesians and Hungarians a chance to meet, learn from one another and build connections that last far beyond graduation.

For decades, educational exchanges have provided one of the most direct ways for Indonesia and Hungary to get to know each other. Indonesian students come to Hungary through programmes such as the Stipendium Hungaricum, while Hungarian students have travelled in the opposite direction through Indonesia’s Darmasiswa Scholarship to study the Indonesian language, arts and culture. The result is more than a scholarship exchange. Students return home carrying new language skills, friendships, professional networks and personal stories about another society.

Darmasiswa: Indonesia beyond Bali

For Hungarian students interested in Indonesia, few programmes offer as immersive an experience as Darmasiswa. The Indonesian government describes it as a non-degree scholarship programme for international students to study Indonesian language, arts and culture at selected institutions across the country for almost a year. The programme was introduced to Hungary in 1991, while the first Hungarian alumni are recorded from 1993.

For Hungarian participants, the attraction is not limited to learning Bahasa Indonesia in a classroom. Depending on their field of study, students can explore traditional dance, gamelan, batik, visual arts, crafts, photography and other forms of Indonesian cultural heritage.

And importantly, they do not have to experience Indonesia only from the perspective of Java or Bali. The alumni records show Hungarian participants studying at institutions in Yogyakarta, Bandung and Surakarta, but also in Denpasar and Singaraja in Bali, Padangpanjang in West Sumatra, Malang in East Java, Mataram in Lombok, Medan in North Sumatra and other parts of the country.

Source: Indonesian embassy in Hungary

This gives students an opportunity to see Indonesia as an archipelago rather than a single destination. Indonesia is not simply Bali, beaches and tropical tourism. A student living in Padangpanjang encounters Minangkabau culture; someone studying in Mataram experiences the warmth of Lombok and West Nusa Tenggara; another student in Medan encounters the cultural landscape of North Sumatra. The experience can turn a distant country into a collection of familiar places, people and stories.

If you missed it: Indonesian Embassy in Budapest celebrates 81st Independence Day with festive bazaar and cultural Performances

From scholarship recipients to diplomats and academics

The long-term impact of Darmasiswa can also be seen in what some alumni went on to do after returning to Hungary.

The list of Darmasiswa alumni in Hungary records Norbert Kiss, a Darmasiswa alumnus who later became a diplomat at Hungary’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Sándor Sipos, another alumnus, is listed as having served as Hungary’s ambassador to Thailand. The same records also include Eszter Tari, associated with the University of Pécs and later as a guest lecturer in Indonesia. These examples show how the impact of an educational exchange can continue long after a student leaves Indonesia. What begins as a scholarship can become part of a diplomatic career, an academic path or a lifelong professional connection.

Another particularly visible example is András Térfy. As a former Darmasiswa participant who studied Balinese karawitan at ISI Denpasar, Térfy later became a member of the Surya Kencana A gamelan group, a band consisting of Darmasiswa alumni who still play gamelan. Hungarian and Indonesian media have highlighted his role in cultural performances, while he has also been involved in translating Hungarian children’s literature into Indonesian.

His story captures something that statistics cannot: the relationship created by Darmasiswa can become part of everyday life in Hungary.

Indonesian language is also finding a place in Budapest

The connection does not stop when Hungarian students leave Indonesia.

In Budapest, Indonesian language learning has also been supported through the Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest. They regularly offers free Indonesian language courses (BIPA – Bahasa Indonesia bagi Penutur Asing) for adult learners. The program also guided by BIPA modules to help Hungarians master Bahasa Indonesia effectively. For Hungarian learners, opportunities like these offer a first step before deciding to spend a longer period in Indonesia. A language class in Budapest may begin with vocabulary and grammar, but it can also lead to curiosity about Indonesian food, music, history, universities and everyday life.

Source: Indonesian embassy in Hungary

Stipendium Hungaricum: the bridge in the other direction

The educational bridge also works from Indonesia towards Hungary.

For Indonesian students, Hungary has become an increasingly familiar destination for higher education, particularly through the Stipendium Hungaricum scholarship programme. The programme has enabled Indonesian students to pursue degrees at universities in Budapest, Debrecen, Szeged, Pécs and other Hungarian cities. For these students, the experience is about more than obtaining a degree. Living in Hungary means navigating a different language, climate, cuisine and social environment while building friendships with Hungarian classmates and other international students.

The same process happens in reverse. Hungarian students living in Indonesia become part of local communities, meet Indonesian students and experience traditions directly rather than encountering them only through news articles or social media.

That is where the people-to-people dimension becomes especially important. Formal diplomatic relations are maintained by governments, but long-term understanding is often built by ordinary people: students sharing a meal, musicians playing together, researchers working on the same project or former scholarship recipients staying in touch years after their programmes have ended.

Two scholarships, one growing connection

Darmasiswa and Stipendium Hungaricum serve different purposes, but together they illustrate how education can work as a two-way bridge. Indonesian students gain access to Hungarian higher education, while Hungarian students can experience Indonesia through language, arts and culture. And the exchange does not necessarily end with graduation. Alumni can become teachers, diplomats, academics, musicians, researchers, businesspeople or simply enthusiastic advocates of the country they once studied in. That is perhaps the most lasting value of educational exchange: a scholarship may fund a student’s journey, but the relationships built along the way can continue for decades.

Source: Indonesian embassy in Hungary

And there is another Indonesian scholarship opportunity worth knowing about. The BSBI (Beasiswa Seni dan Budaya Indonesia/Indonesian Arts and Culture Scholarship) is a cultural programme introducing young people from other countries to Indonesian language, arts, traditions and communities.

For young Hungarians looking beyond the usual study-abroad destinations, these programmes offer something that a degree or a short holiday cannot easily provide: the chance to live another culture, form personal relationships and return home with Indonesia no longer feeling quite so far away.

World.title: Hungary public holidays 2027: six long weekends to plan for
World.content:
Anyone already planning trips, holidays or time off in Hungary next year can start marking their calendar: Hungary public holidays 2027 will produce six guaranteed long weekends, including a four-day Easter break. Several other public holidays, however, will fall on Saturdays or Sundays, while the status of Christmas Eve remains uncertain.

According to Pénzcentrum, the 2027 calendar is relatively straightforward, with no obvious need for the usual Hungarian system of moving working days to Saturdays – although one important question could still change that.

Hungary public holidays 2027: The full list

Hungarian labour law currently provides for 11 public holidays each year. Eight have fixed dates, while Good Friday, Easter Monday and Whit Monday move according to the Christian calendar.

The public holidays in 2027 will fall as follows:

1 January, Friday – New Year’s Day

– New Year’s Day 15 March, Monday – anniversary of the 1848–49 Revolution and War of Independence

– anniversary of the 1848–49 Revolution and War of Independence 26 March, Friday – Good Friday

– Good Friday 29 March, Monday – Easter Monday

– Easter Monday 1 May, Saturday – Labour Day

– Labour Day 17 May, Monday – Whit Monday

– Whit Monday 20 August, Friday – St Stephen’s Day and the foundation of the Hungarian state

– St Stephen’s Day and the foundation of the Hungarian state 23 October, Saturday – anniversary of the 1956 Revolution

– anniversary of the 1956 Revolution 1 November, Monday – All Saints’ Day

– All Saints’ Day 25 December, Saturday – Christmas Day

– Christmas Day 26 December, Sunday – Second Day of Christmas

For foreign visitors, it is worth remembering that public holidays in Hungary can affect shop opening hours, public administration and some services, although restaurants, tourist attractions and transport may operate according to separate holiday schedules.

Six long weekends are already guaranteed

The distribution of Hungary public holidays 2027 creates six long weekends without any additional government intervention.

The year will start with a three-day break from 1–3 January, as New Year’s Day falls on a Friday. Another three-day weekend follows on 13–15 March, with Hungary’s national holiday falling on Monday.

The longest guaranteed break comes at Easter. Good Friday falls on 26 March and Easter Monday on 29 March, creating a four-day weekend from 26–29 March.

Three further three-day weekends will follow: 15–17 May around Pentecost, 20–22 August around St Stephen’s Day, and 30 October–1 November around All Saints’ Day.

Pénzcentrum therefore counts five three-day weekends and one four-day weekend in the calendar as it currently stands.

Not every national holiday will bring additional time off. Labour Day on 1 May and the 23 October national holiday both fall on Saturdays. Christmas is even less favourable in calendar terms, with 25 December falling on Saturday and 26 December on Sunday.

Will Hungary have Saturday working days in 2027?

For many foreigners living in Hungary, one peculiarity of the Hungarian working calendar can be surprising: the government can designate an ordinary weekday as a rest day and compensate for it by making a nearby Saturday a working day.

The final arrangement is set annually by ministerial decree. Under the Labour Code, the responsible minister has until 31 October of the preceding year to determine changes to the standard working schedule.

As of 21 September 2026, the decree setting out the 2027 schedule has not yet been published. Based purely on the calendar, however, there is no Tuesday or Thursday public holiday that would normally create a reason for an additional bridge day and a corresponding working Saturday.

There is one possible exception.

What happens to Christmas Eve?

24 December 2027 falls on a Friday, but under current legislation Christmas Eve itself is not a public holiday.

The government could nevertheless designate it as a rest day in the annual working-time decree, as has happened in previous years. If that happens, employees working a standard Monday-to-Friday schedule could receive a three-day Christmas break from 24 to 26 December, but the extra Friday off could have to be compensated for by working on a Saturday.

There is also a separate debate over whether 24 December should become a permanent statutory public holiday. A nationwide referendum initiative submitted by the Trade Union of Commercial Employees asks precisely that question, and the National Election Office lists the initiative among the 2026 referendum procedures.

Until the government publishes the official 2027 working calendar, travellers and employees should therefore treat the Christmas period as provisional. The six other long weekends, however, already provide several opportunities to plan extended breaks in Hungary throughout 2027.

As we wrote before – Hungary could get a new public holiday: Christmas Eve could become a day off this year!

World.title: Hungary new home VAT 2027: developers and buyers brace for a costly shift
World.content:
Hungary’s reduced VAT rate on most new homes is set to expire at the end of 2026, potentially bringing the standard 27% rate back into play from January. In theory, the Hungary new home VAT 2027 change could add almost 21% to the gross price of an affected property if developers passed the entire tax increase on to buyers. The reality, however, may prove considerably more complicated as Hungary’s housing market is already losing momentum.

Under the current rules, the 5% VAT rate generally remains available until 31 December 2026 for qualifying newly built homes. Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) confirms that the standard 27% rate will apply afterwards unless a development qualifies for transitional protection.

Hungary new home VAT 2027: who can keep the 5% rate?

The crucial date for developers is 31 December 2026.

Projects requiring a building permit can continue using the 5% rate for qualifying sales completed as late as 31 December 2030 if the permit becomes final by the end of 2026. Similar transitional provisions apply to projects using the simple notification system, although the precise deadline depends on which building legislation governs the notification.

“This deadline is particularly important for housing developers. With a permitting procedure starting now, a request for additional documentation or prolonged administration could put meeting the deadline at risk,” Péter Szegő, lead analyst at Duna House, said in a statement.

Developers already appear to be accelerating their pipeline. According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), permits and simple declarations covering 16,588 homes were issued in the first half of 2026, up 29% year on year.

This means Hungary could have a two-tier new-build market for years: protected projects still selling with 5% VAT alongside newer developments subject to 27%.

What would 27% VAT actually do to prices?

The theoretical effect is substantial.

Take a new flat currently priced at HUF 100 million (around EUR 275,000) including 5% VAT. Its pre-tax price is roughly HUF 95.2 million. Applying 27% VAT to the same net amount would produce a gross price of nearly HUF 121 million (EUR 333,000).

That is an increase of almost HUF 21 million (EUR 58,000) without any change in construction costs or the developer’s underlying price.

But this calculation assumes something that cannot be taken for granted: that buyers would accept the full increase.

If you missed it: Hungary’s housing market faces a major shift as government backs social housing

Duna House: slowing market could absorb part of the shock

Duna House argues that developers may have limited room to pass the entire tax burden on to customers because demand is already weakening.

The National Bank of Hungary (MNB) found that housing transactions fell by 18% year on year in the first quarter of 2026.

The slowdown remained visible during the summer. Duna House estimated just 8,077 residential transactions in August, 13.1% fewer than in July and the second-lowest monthly figure of 2026. The company’s August market estimate also put turnover 29% below the level recorded a year earlier.

“The 27% VAT rate would in itself represent a significant cost increase, but in a slowing market this cannot automatically be built into home prices,” Szegő said. “If demand does not accept the higher price, developers will have to absorb part of it.”

Could the VAT increase push up second-hand homes too?

There is nevertheless a less benign scenario.

If the price gap between VAT-protected developments and new projects subject to 27% becomes sufficiently large, higher new-build prices could also affect expectations in the second-hand market. Owners of existing homes may try to raise asking prices as newly built alternatives become more expensive.

That does not mean a market-wide 21% increase would automatically follow. Second-hand homes are not themselves subject to the new-build VAT change, and actual selling prices remain determined by affordability, credit conditions, location and demand.

The risk of a wider knock-on effect nevertheless exists, particularly in areas where buyers directly compare new and recently built properties.

Higher prices could collide with Home Start limits

Even a much smaller price increase could have consequences for buyers using Hungary’s subsidised Home Start (Otthon Start) mortgage programme.

The scheme offers loans of up to HUF 50 million (around EUR 138,000) at a fixed 3% interest rate. Eligible flats can cost no more than HUF 100 million (EUR 275,000), while houses are capped at HUF 150 million (EUR 413,000). The maximum permitted price is HUF 1.5 million per square metre (around EUR 4,130). The limits are detailed on the Hungarian government’s Home Start programme page.

A VAT-driven price rise could therefore push some newly built homes above the programme’s eligibility thresholds even if the increase falls far short of the theoretical 21%.

The end of 2026 is consequently becoming a decisive deadline for Hungary’s residential developers. The return of 27% VAT could place substantial upward pressure on new-build prices, but a weaker and increasingly price-sensitive housing market may prevent developers from simply transferring the entire bill to buyers. What emerges in 2027 is likely to depend as much on demand and financing conditions as on the tax rate itself.

World.title: Russia election 2026: What Putin’s strengthened majority means for Hungary
World.content:
President Vladimir Putin’s ruling United Russia party has strengthened its grip on parliament in the Russia election 2026, securing nearly 58% of the vote and remaining on course for a constitutional majority in the State Duma. For Hungary, the result does not immediately change bilateral relations, but it reinforces an important reality: Budapest will continue dealing with a politically entrenched Kremlin just as the new Hungarian government is moving closer to mainstream EU and NATO positions and redefining its relationship with Moscow.

According to preliminary results reported by Anadolu, United Russia received 57.83% of the vote, up from 49.82% in the 2021 parliamentary election, after 95.18% of ballots had been processed. Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said the party was also leading in 208 of the 225 single-member constituencies and was likely to secure 355 of the State Duma’s 450 seats.

Source: Anadolu

The Communist Party received 13.81%, followed by the LDPR with 8.98% and New People with 7.96%, according to the preliminary figures. A Just Russia stood at 4.96%, just below the 5% threshold for entering parliament through the party-list vote.

The three-day election was Russia’s first parliamentary vote since 2022 and took place while the war in Ukraine continues.

Russia election 2026 reinforces political continuity in Moscow

The result points primarily towards continuity rather than a major change in Russian foreign or economic policy.

That is particularly relevant for Hungary. Since Péter Magyar replaced Viktor Orbán as prime minister following the April election, Budapest has begun recalibrating a relationship with Moscow that had become unusually close by EU standards.

In early September, Hungary expelled ten Russian diplomats for activities deemed incompatible with their diplomatic status. Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed that Budapest was not cutting diplomatic ties with Moscow, but said the decision was necessary to protect Hungary’s security and sovereignty, Anadolu reported.

The Russian election result therefore leaves Budapest facing a familiar counterpart: Putin remains president, United Russia continues to dominate parliament, and Moscow’s political direction shows little sign of changing as a consequence of the vote.

At the same time, the election took place in conditions that make its results difficult to interpret simply as a measure of unrestricted political competition. The Yabloko party was not included on the federal party-list ballot, although some of its candidates were able to contest individual constituencies. More than 111 million people were eligible to vote, with turnout reported at 59.32%, according to the election commission figures cited by Anadolu.

If you missed it: Budapest and Kyiv face sharp criticism from the Russian Embassy over alleged secrecy and unfulfilled promises

EU rejects Russian voting in occupied Ukraine

The European Union’s reaction is particularly important from a Hungarian perspective.

On Monday, the EU rejected Russia’s parliamentary voting conducted in Ukrainian territories under Russian occupation and warned that people involved could face sanctions.

According to Anadolu, the EU condemned what it called “so-called elections” in annexed Crimea and Sevastopol, as well as occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. The bloc said the votes violated international law and Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The EU said it would “never recognise” either the holding of the votes in those territories or their results. It also warned that individuals involved in organising the elections there, as well as people deemed responsible for undermining free and fair elections inside Russia, could be targeted with sanctions.

The bloc also criticised Moscow for restricting political competition, excluding opposition forces and failing to invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

For Hungary, this position is more significant than it would have been under the previous government.

Budapest has recently moved closer to the foreign-policy positions of its EU and NATO partners. In a joint declaration issued on 14 September, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul stated that the two countries continued to support Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. They also reaffirmed their commitment to a rules-based international order and closer cooperation within the EU and NATO.

That does not automatically mean Budapest will adopt every element of Brussels’ Russia policy. However, the new Hungarian government’s publicly stated position on Ukrainian territorial integrity places it considerably closer to the principles underpinning the EU’s rejection of Russia’s voting in occupied Ukrainian territory.

Energy remains Hungary’s biggest Russian connection

Diplomatic repositioning does not mean Hungary can quickly disentangle itself from Russia economically.

Energy remains the most important connection. The European Commission’s 2026 country report found that in 2025 more than 90% of Hungary’s imported oil and 74% of its imported gas originated in Russia. Hungary consequently remained one of the EU member states most dependent on Russian fossil fuels.

This dependence is increasingly at odds with the direction of EU energy policy.

The bloc has already dramatically reduced Russian fossil-fuel imports since 2022. Under the REPowerEU framework, Russian LNG imports are to be fully phased out by the end of 2026, while Russian pipeline gas imports are scheduled to end no later than 30 November 2027, according to the European Commission.

For Budapest, this means that future relations with Moscow will increasingly have to reconcile inherited Russian energy dependence with EU-wide diversification.

Paks II could become another major test

The other major Hungarian-Russian issue is nuclear energy.

Hungary’s planned Paks II nuclear power plant, contracted to Russia’s state-owned Rosatom, remains one of the largest economic links between the two countries. The EUR 12.5 billion project involves two Russian-designed VVER reactors and has suffered years of delays.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar has called for a review of the project, citing its costs and environmental issues surrounding the use of the Danube for cooling. Rosatom said in September that it was ready to discuss the project with the new Hungarian government, but had not yet received concrete proposals, Reuters reported.

The parliamentary election is unlikely on its own to alter Moscow’s position on Paks II. The more important question is how far the new Hungarian government wants to revise an agreement inherited from the Orbán administration. As we wrote earlier, Paks II could be delayed until 2035 as Rosatom schedule reveals setback.

What does the Russian result mean for Hungary?

For Hungary, the most relevant feature of the Russia election 2026 is the contrast between continuity in Moscow and change in Budapest.

United Russia’s strengthened majority gives little indication that Russia’s approach towards Ukraine, Western sanctions or relations with Europe will shift as a result of the election. The EU, meanwhile, has responded by explicitly rejecting the voting organised in occupied Ukrainian territories and signalling further sanctions against those involved.

Hungary now finds itself in a different position than during the later Orbán years. The Magyar government has reaffirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity, expelled Russian diplomats and sought closer cooperation with EU and NATO partners.

At the same time, the country remains heavily dependent on Russian oil and gas and is tied to Moscow through the multibillion-euro Paks II project.

The election therefore does not create a new Hungarian dilemma so much as underline an existing one: Budapest is moving closer to its Western allies politically while still having to manage some of the deepest Russian economic and energy ties within the European Union.

World.title: British tourist says he remembers nothing of brutal Budapest assault – VIDEO
World.content:
A 21-year-old British tourist suspected of brutally attacking a pedestrian in central Budapest has told police that he remembers nothing of the incident because he had been heavily intoxicated. The 43-year-old victim was knocked unconscious in the assault on Szent István körút, while reports suggest the suspect had also chased several other people shortly beforehand.

According to information reported by Hungarian news outlet 24.hu, the suspect was visiting Hungary when the attack took place on Friday evening.

The victim suffered head injuries and was taken to hospital after losing consciousness.

British tourist says he cannot remember Budapest attack

The suspect reportedly told investigators that he could not recall what had happened because he had been heavily intoxicated. His statement represents his account to police and does not establish the circumstances of the incident.

The attack had already attracted widespread attention after video footage appeared online. As we published the video before further information emerged about the alleged attacker.

The footage shows a pedestrian crossing the road when another man suddenly pushes him to the ground. The attacker can then be seen repeatedly striking and kicking the victim while he is lying on the pavement.

Several people eventually approach the suspected attacker. An ambulance happened to be passing the scene and stopped almost immediately beside the injured man.

Witnesses said the victim appeared confused after regaining consciousness and did not know what had happened. He regained consciousness inside the ambulance and was taken to hospital with head injuries that were ultimately classified as minor.

If you missed it: 16-year-old Hungarian boy discussed mass violence with AI chatbot, FBI alerts Hungarian authorities – Video

Suspect reportedly chased three other people

Further details suggest the assault may not have been the first confrontation involving the suspect that evening.

Citing RTL Híradó, 24.hu reported that the 21-year-old had allegedly chased three other people before attacking the pedestrian on Szent István körút.

RTL reported that the suspect was a 21-year-old English man and that the victim was a 43-year-old pedestrian.

The motive for the attack has not been established publicly.

Suspect remains at liberty during investigation

Budapest police told that the suspected attacker had been apprehended and that proceedings had been launched on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm.

The later report said the British man had been questioned as a suspect in connection with grievous bodily harm but was not placed in custody. He is therefore able to defend himself while remaining at liberty.

No court has yet ruled on the case, and the man remains a suspect at this stage.

The investigation is expected to clarify what preceded the assault, why the pedestrian was targeted and whether the reported incidents involving other people form part of the same sequence of events.

World.title: Hungarian intelligence services undergo sweeping reorganisation after Orbán era
World.content:
Hungary’s change of government is increasingly being felt inside the country’s national security apparatus. After the replacement of four intelligence chiefs in June, a new report suggests that the overhaul of the Hungarian intelligence services is reaching deeper into the organisations, including middle-ranking personnel and officers serving abroad. The developments come against the background of years of controversy over political control, surveillance and Hungary’s handling of Russian intelligence activity.

How the Hungarian intelligence services are structured

Hungary has five official national security services, according to the country’s National Security Services Act. The Információs Hivatal (IH) is the civilian foreign intelligence agency, while the Alkotmányvédelmi Hivatal (AH) is primarily responsible for domestic counter-intelligence and identifying foreign intelligence operations.

The Katonai Nemzetbiztonsági Szolgálat (KNBSZ) handles military intelligence and counter-intelligence, while the Nemzetbiztonsági Szakszolgálat (NBSZ) provides specialist technical capabilities used in secret information-gathering. The fifth service, the Nemzeti Információs Központ (NIK), functions primarily as an intelligence fusion and analysis body.

For foreign readers, the system can therefore broadly be understood as a division between foreign intelligence, domestic counter-intelligence, military intelligence, technical surveillance support and central intelligence analysis.

Centralisation and controversies under Orbán

Under Viktor Orbán’s governments, control over the civilian intelligence system became increasingly centralised. After the 2022 election, several services were moved under the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office, headed by Antal Rogán, while the NIK was established to bring together intelligence gathered by different agencies.

An investigation by Direkt36 described this process as a major centralisation of the intelligence apparatus around the prime minister’s political centre.

The period was also marked by the Pegasus spyware scandal. In 2021, the international Pegasus Project found more than 300 Hungarian telephone numbers on a leaked list of possible surveillance targets. Amnesty International said forensic examinations confirmed that Pegasus had successfully infected several devices. Those identified as potential targets included journalists, lawyers, businesspeople and political figures.

Later that year, senior Fidesz politician Lajos Kósa publicly acknowledged that the Hungarian state had acquired Pegasus. He maintained that authorities had used surveillance tools legally and with the necessary authorisations, as Telex reported at the time.

Questions were also raised over the authorities’ response to Russian intelligence operations. According to a 2026 investigation by VSquare, Hungarian counter-intelligence recommended the expulsion of Russian embassy official Artur Sushkov in February after identifying him as an intelligence officer operating under diplomatic cover. VSquare reported that the Orbán government did not approve the move before the April election. Sushkov ultimately left Hungary on 4 May, after the change of government.

If you missed it: Orbán’s Russia scandal continues? Fidesz party director’s son talks with Russian diplomat linked to secret services

Four intelligence chiefs removed within days

The clearest early indication of a large-scale restructuring came in June, when the heads of four major Hungarian intelligence services were removed.

Szabolcs Bárdos left the AH, Krisztián Oláh the IH, Csaba Kiss the NBSZ and Norbert Tajti the KNBSZ. The dismissals were formally published by the government and reported by several Hungarian outlets, including 24.hu.

Appointments and transfers followed. The Interior Ministry announced through Hungary’s national news agency MTI that Zsolt Antal Annus would move from the NIK to head the AH, while Szabolcs Tóth was transferred to lead the NBSZ.

The scale and timing of the dismissals suggested that the new government was pursuing a broader institutional restructuring rather than isolated changes at individual agencies.

Reorganisation reportedly reaches officers serving abroad

The latest indication that the changes are moving beyond senior management came on 21 September from specialist French publication Intelligence Online.

The publication describes what it calls a “radical restructuring” of the Hungarian intelligence apparatus, affecting both agency chiefs and middle-ranking personnel. Its headline also says the process has extended to officers posted abroad.

The full report is available only to subscribers, meaning publicly accessible information does not establish how many officers have been recalled, which agencies are most heavily affected or which foreign postings are involved.

The distinction is important. Personnel changes by themselves do not demonstrate wrongdoing by those removed. They do, however, indicate that the restructuring has moved beyond replacing a handful of directors.

Russia provides another sign of a changed security approach

The internal overhaul has coincided with a notably tougher public response to suspected Russian intelligence activity.

On 8 September, Hungary ordered ten members of Russia’s diplomatic mission to leave the country, saying they had engaged in activities incompatible with diplomatic status. According to Helló Magyar, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán stressed the move did not amount to breaking diplomatic relations with Moscow, while Russia condemned the expulsions and promised retaliation.

Taken together, the replacement of intelligence chiefs, subsequent personnel changes, the reported reshuffling of officers stationed abroad and the tougher approach towards Russian intelligence activity point to a substantial reorganisation of the Hungarian intelligence services.

The longer-term significance will depend on whether the personnel overhaul is followed by changes in institutional oversight, operating practices and cooperation with Hungary’s NATO and EU partners.

World.title: Protesters rally outside Budapest’s House of Terror Museum after director’s dismissal
World.content:
Demonstrators gathered outside Budapest’s House of Terror Museum on Sunday to protest its temporary closure and the dismissal of long-serving director Mária Schmidt. Speakers, including Zsolt Bayer and opposition Fidesz politician Tamás Menczer, accused Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government of targeting the institution, while the authorities have announced that the museum will reopen on Tuesday.

The protest followed an announcement by Zoltán Tarr, the minister responsible for social relations and culture, that the museum would close temporarily while its operations underwent a review. Schmidt’s appointment as director was also terminated.

The government subsequently said the museum would reopen on Tuesday, 22 September, with free admission for one week, according to Hungarian news agency MTI.

Bayer and Fidesz politicians criticise the Tisza government

The demonstration took place on Andrássy Avenue, outside the museum, which documents Hungary’s experiences under Nazi and communist dictatorships.

András Bencsik, editor-in-chief of Demokrata, accused the current government of undermining the memory of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, whose 70th anniversary falls this year. He called on the authorities to keep their hands off the museum.

László Szentesi Zöldi, an editor at Magyar Nemzet, also attacked the government, accusing Magyar of weakening democratic institutions. He claimed the governing Tisza Party would lose public support as the opposition reorganised. These were political allegations made during the demonstration, not findings established by the museum review.

Zsolt Bayer, a columnist who has recently faced scrutiny over state cultural grants, pledged to defend the museum. He also proposed adding a room to its exhibition addressing what he described as the dangerous ideologies of the 21st century.

Zsolt Bayer delivers a speech during the protest outside Budapest’s House of Terror Museum on 20 September 2026. Photo: MTI / Péter Lakatos

If you missed it: Hungarian activist reveals new details of questionable state funding awarded to pro-Orbán commentator – Updated

Former Terror Museum director rejects government review

Schmidt, who had headed the institution for 24 years, addressed the crowd and defended the museum’s work. She argued that its exhibitions had challenged what she described as a monopoly over the interpretation of Hungary’s history.

The former director of House of Terror Museum dismissed the planned examination by independent experts and accused those behind the closure of being unable to accept the museum’s historical perspective. Her remarks reflected her opposition to the government’s decision; the review has not been completed.

According to MTI, demonstrators waved Hungarian national flags, flags with holes recalling the 1956 uprising, and other banners. Participants repeatedly cheered former prime minister Viktor Orbán. Police closed Andrássy Avenue between Oktogon and Izabella Street during the protest, diverting traffic.

When will the House of Terror Museum reopen?

Culture minister Tarr said the review of the museum’s exhibition would be carried out by researchers from the ELTE Research Centre for the Humanities’ Institute of History and independent experts. The exhibition will remain accessible in its current form while the review continues.

The museum’s official visitor information confirms that it is scheduled to reopen at 10 am on Tuesday, 22 September. The government has said admission will be free for the first week.
