World.title: ExxonMobil: Global CO₂ emissions to peak this decade
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Global energy-related CO₂ emissions are projected to peak this decade and then decline by around 20% by 2050, even as the global economy expands and living standards improve, according to ExxonMobil’s latest Global Outlook: Our View to 2050.

ExxonMobil estimates that energy-related CO₂ emissions will peak at approximately 36 billion metric tons per year sometime this decade before falling to around 30 billion metric tons annually by 2050.

The company attributes the projected decline to improvements in energy efficiency and greater use of lower-emissions technologies, including renewable energy, carbon capture and storage (CCS), hydrogen and biofuels, alongside a reduction in coal consumption.

“Efficiency improvements and renewables are necessary but not a complete solution,” ExxonMobil said, arguing that technologies such as hydrogen, CCS and biofuels will be needed to address emissions from sectors that are more difficult to decarbonize.

More action needed to meet climate goals

Despite the projected decline, ExxonMobil said the pace of emissions reduction would remain insufficient to meet climate objectives consistent with limiting global temperature increases to below 2°C.

The company said the average of the IPCC's “Likely Below 2°C” scenarios requires energy-related CO₂ emissions to fall to approximately 11 billion metric tons per year by 2050 — substantially below the roughly 30 billion metric tons projected in ExxonMobil's outlook.

ExxonMobil also noted that global energy demand is expected to increase through 2050 as the world's population grows and economies develop.

According to the company, so-called hard-to-decarbonize sectors, including commercial transportation, manufacturing and industrial production, currently account for approximately 45% of global CO₂ emissions, including process emissions but excluding indirect emissions from electricity use.

The company said these sectors will require a wider range of technologies to reduce emissions, rather than relying solely on efficiency improvements and renewable power.

Global emissions continue to rise

ExxonMobil's outlook notes that global energy-related CO₂ emissions continued to increase by approximately 1% in 2025, broadly in line with the average annual growth rate recorded over the past two decades.

The company argues that this trend highlights the challenge of simultaneously meeting rising energy demand and reducing emissions.

It also points to what it describes as multiple potential pathways for achieving climate objectives, giving policymakers scope to balance emissions reductions with energy affordability and security.

ExxonMobil said that more than two decades after the Kyoto Protocol entered into force and more than a decade after the Paris Agreement, the continued rise in energy-related emissions indicates that additional approaches may be needed to accelerate reductions.

The company also cites IPCC scenarios as highlighting the importance of considering the overall climate impact of policies rather than focusing exclusively on the timing of net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions. According to ExxonMobil, policies that constrain energy supply too quickly could contribute to higher energy prices and economic disruption.

Global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions are taking place against a backdrop of rising energy demand and continued reliance on fossil fuels. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global energy-related CO₂ emissions increased by around 0.4% in 2025, reaching a new record of approximately 38.4 billion metric tons. The increase was slower than in 2024, as stronger growth in renewable power, nuclear generation, electrification and other clean-energy technologies helped limit emissions growth.

The IEA said emissions from coal increased by around 0.5% in 2025, while oil-related emissions rose by approximately 0.4%. At the same time, emissions from natural gas increased by around 0.5%. The agency noted that the expansion of solar PV, wind, nuclear power and electric vehicles helped avoid a significantly larger increase in emissions.

World.title: Electricity demand to rise 65% globally by 2050, ExxonMobil says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Global electricity demand is projected to increase by around 65% by 2050, driven by economic growth, improving living standards and rising electrification, according to ExxonMobil’s latest Global Outlook: Our View to 2050.

The industrial sector is expected to account for approximately 40% of the increase, making it the largest source of additional electricity demand. Growth will be driven both by expanding industrial activity and greater electrification of production, particularly in lower-temperature processes.

Residential and commercial buildings are each projected to account for around 20% of global electricity-demand growth through 2050. In residential buildings, higher demand will be linked to population growth and increased use of cooling and heating, particularly in developing economies, although efficiency improvements in buildings and appliances are expected to moderate consumption.

Commercial electricity demand is also expected to rise alongside economic activity and the expansion of data centers. ExxonMobil said data centers could have a significant impact on individual regions and power grids, although their effect is expected to be more moderate at the national and global levels.

The remaining 20% of global electricity-demand growth is projected to come from transportation, with passenger vehicles representing the largest source of additional electricity consumption, followed by regional trucks and buses.

Solar and wind to lead power-generation growth

Meeting rising electricity demand will require a broad mix of generation technologies, ExxonMobil said.

Solar and wind generation is projected to increase more than fourfold by 2050, accounting for around 85% of global power-demand growth. Natural gas-fired generation is also expected to increase by approximately 25%, with gas playing a growing role in maintaining grid stability as variable renewable generation expands.

“Nuclear power generation is projected to grow ~60% by 2050,” ExxonMobil said, citing increasing demand for firm, low-emission electricity and technological developments such as small modular reactors.

However, the company expects nuclear expansion to be constrained in part by the need to replace or upgrade aging reactors, many of which are approaching or have exceeded 40 years of operation.

ExxonMobil expects electricity to meet nearly all of the growth in end-use energy demand globally through 2050, reflecting the increasing electrification of industry, buildings and transportation.

OECD electricity demand also expected to increase

Electricity demand growth is not expected to be limited to developing economies. ExxonMobil projects electricity consumption in OECD countries to rise by approximately 35% by 2050, following roughly two decades of broadly flat demand.

The company attributes the expected increase to greater electrification of industry and transportation, as well as rising demand from data centers.

In the United States, electricity demand is projected to increase by more than 40% from 2025 levels by 2050, marking a reversal from the period of broadly stable demand seen over the previous two decades.

Industry and transportation are expected to account for around two-thirds of U.S. electricity-demand growth, broadly reflecting the global trend.

ExxonMobil also expects substantial regional differences in power-generation mixes through 2050, influenced by access to domestic gas, renewable resources, economic conditions, government policies and energy-security considerations. While renewables are projected to expand across all regions, gas is expected to retain a larger role in areas with abundant domestic supplies, while regions dependent on imported fuels are projected to see stronger renewable growth alongside continued coal use.

The global power sector is entering a period of accelerating electricity demand growth, with industrial expansion, electrification, cooling, electric vehicles and data centers emerging as major drivers. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electricity demand increased by around 3% in 2025, after rising 4.4% in 2024. The agency expects demand growth to accelerate to an average of 3.6% annually between 2026 and 2030, adding around 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity demand each year, compared with an average of about 700 TWh annually during 2015-2025.

Emerging markets and developing economies are driving much of this expansion. They accounted for around 80% of global electricity-demand growth in 2025, and the IEA expects them to maintain a similar share over the next five years. At the same time, electricity demand is increasing in advanced economies as industrial activity, data centers, electric vehicles and other forms of electrification create new loads on power systems.

The growth in electricity consumption is occurring alongside a rapid expansion of low-emissions generation. The IEA estimates that renewables and nuclear power together accounted for more than the total increase in global electricity generation in 2025, while fossil-fuel generation declined overall. Renewable generation almost matched coal-fired generation globally in 2025.

Looking ahead to 2030, the IEA expects renewable power capacity to expand by around 4,600 GW, with solar PV accounting for almost 80% of the increase. Renewables are forecast to provide more than 90% of global electricity-demand growth through 2030, highlighting the growing role of solar and wind as electricity consumption rises.

World.title: ExxonMobil: Energy use in developing countries to rise 25% by 2050
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. Developing countries are projected to increase their energy consumption by around 25% by 2050 as population growth and economic development drive higher demand, according to ExxonMobil’s latest Global Outlook: Our View to 2050.

The report estimates that more than 4 billion people currently live in countries where access to energy is below the level required to meet basic human development needs.

“Access to sufficient, affordable energy enables economic development,” ExxonMobil said, noting that improvements in technology and energy efficiency are expected to moderate the growth in energy demand as populations and prosperity increase.

According to the outlook, the global population is expected to expand by around 1.5 billion people by 2050, representing an increase of approximately 20% from current levels. Nearly all of the population growth is projected to take place in developing countries.

At the same time, global gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to increase by about 80%. Developing economies are expected to grow at roughly twice the rate of developed economies, raising their share of global GDP to more than 50% by 2050, compared with around 40% today.

The combination of population and economic growth is expected to result in energy consumption in developing countries being approximately 25% higher in 2050 than today, ExxonMobil said.

Energy access linked to living standards

ExxonMobil's analysis highlights a close relationship between energy consumption and living standards. Drawing on data from the United Nations Human Development Index (HDI), the company said countries with higher energy use generally record higher life expectancy, education levels and income per capita.

“Energy use and improved living standards go hand in hand. It is impossible to have one without the other,” the report states.

The company estimates that basic living standards require at least 50 million British thermal units (MMBtu) of energy per person annually. By comparison, developed countries currently consume more than three times that amount on average, at approximately 160 MMBtu per person.

Around 75% of energy consumption in developed economies is associated with manufacturing, business activities and commercial transportation, according to ExxonMobil.

Based on its analysis and UN HDI data, ExxonMobil estimates that more than 4 billion people live in countries where energy access remains below the level required to support basic human development, including housing, infrastructure, employment and mobility.

The report points to household cooking as one example of the consequences of inadequate access to reliable energy. In countries with limited energy access, households often rely on wood, coal or kerosene for cooking, including indoors.

Citing the World Health Organization, ExxonMobil notes that household air pollution is associated with approximately 3 million deaths annually, particularly as a result of the use of polluting fuels and technologies for cooking.

Improved access to reliable and affordable energy can enable households to shift toward cleaner cooking options, including electricity and natural gas, the company said.

Efficiency to curb per capita energy demand

Despite the projected 25% increase in total energy use in developing countries, ExxonMobil expects growth in per capita energy demand to remain limited.

The company attributes this to efficiency gains and technological advances that will reduce the amount of energy required to support economic activity and rising living standards.

ExxonMobil also examined a scenario in which all countries reach its estimated threshold for basic living standards of 50 MMBtu per person by 2050.

Under that scenario, even with significant efficiency improvements, the world would require nearly 20% more energy in 2050 than projected in ExxonMobil's base-case Global Outlook.

The finding underscores the scale of the energy challenge facing developing economies as population growth, industrialization and higher living standards increase demand while technological advances work to contain overall energy consumption.

The global energy-access gap remains a major challenge, particularly in developing economies, where population growth and economic development are expected to drive higher energy demand in the coming decades. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), around 730 million people worldwide still lack access to electricity, while nearly 2 billion people do not have access to clean cooking. The agency says expanding access to modern energy can improve productivity in agriculture and local industry, while also supporting health, education and broader economic development.

The United Nations similarly reports that 666 million people lacked access to electricity in 2023, while around 2.1 billion people continued to rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking. Although global access to electricity has continued to improve, progress remains uneven, with the largest gaps concentrated in developing regions.

At the same time, developing economies are becoming the main source of growth in global electricity demand. The IEA expects emerging and developing economies to account for about 85% of additional global electricity demand through 2027, reflecting economic expansion, industrial activity and rising ownership of appliances and other electricity-consuming technologies.

The growth in energy demand is expected to be partly offset by improvements in energy efficiency. UN data show that global primary energy intensity improved by 1.5% in 2023, although the pace of improvement remains below the level required to meet the UN's 2030 energy-efficiency target.

World.title: Azerbaijani Railways and Hamburg Port sign cooperation agreement (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 21. A memorandum of understanding on the development of cooperation has been signed between CJSC “Azerbaijan Railways” (ADY), a subsidiary of the AZCON holding company, and the Port of Hamburg.

This was announced in a statement published by Azerbaijan Railways following a meeting with the management of the Port of Hamburg as part of a visit to Germany by a delegation led by ADY CJSC Chairman Rovshan Rustamov.

The protocol provides for expanding the exchange of expertise between the parties, implementing joint initiatives, and identifying new areas of cooperation in the field of logistics.

At the meeting, which was also attended by representatives of “Mettrans,” the cargo division of the Port of Hamburg, participants discussed the development of relations between the ports of Hamburg and Baku, the improvement of the port-logistics chain, and the expansion of transit capabilities along the Middle Corridor.

The parties explored opportunities for cooperation in increasing multimodal and container shipments, digitizing logistics processes, and integrating rail and maritime transport.

The meeting highlighted the importance of sharing the Port of Hamburg’s experience in managing port operations, operating logistics centers, and implementing digital solutions.

In addition, it was noted that expanding the use of modern technologies at the Port of Baku and strengthening coordination between rail and port operations will significantly contribute to enhancing the competitiveness of the Middle Corridor.

World.title: 'Clock is ticking' as ASIC warns private credit sector investors could bail
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

ASIC has signalled there is no time to waste in preventing an Australian private credit crisis.

Today, ASIC commissioner Simone Constant will tell a gathering in Sydney hosted by the Commercial and Asset Finance Brokers Association (CAFBA) that the "clock is ticking" on "whether we see broader credit stress or not" in Australia.

The collapse of NSW property developer Bathla has highlighted how private lenders are exposed to financially vulnerable construction companies.

Bathla continued running high-profile promotions during its decline. (Supplied: Instagram)

CVS Lane First Mortgage Fund and CVS Lane Property Finance Fund had exposure to Bathla across nine different loans.

"Our work has shone a light on the weaknesses in private credit, but despite our ongoing calls for uplift across the sector, too many have been too slow to respond," Ms Constant said.

Bathla's collapse exposes housing industry issues The collapse of Bathla is a disaster for the national housing supply and affordability project: its now-stalled pipeline of 14,000 apartments represents about 18.5 per cent of new housing stock to be built in NSW this year.

"And what we're seeing now, as some of those weaknesses are tested at scale for the first time by current conditions, are the first significant cracks — the first stress fractures — beginning to emerge."

Private credit is any lending outside the banking sector.

While returns are relatively high, they come with risk, and it's growing.

One estimate has the sector domestically growing by 500 per cent over the decade, according to ASIC.

"But governance, controls and underwriting standards have not kept pace with this growth," Ms Constant said.

"The collapse of Bathla reinforces why strong governance, effective oversight, clear disclosure and accurate valuations are critical.

" We challenged the sector to lift standards by 2027 — that's three months away. "

ASIC runs ruler over sector

ASIC commissioner Simone Constant, ASIC executive director of markets Calissa Aldridge and ASIC chair Joe Longo. (Supplied:ASIC)

Over the past 18 months, ASIC has intensified its scrutiny of private credit, beginning with its discussion paper on public and private markets.

"It was illuminating," Ms Constant said.

"The poorer practices — opaque remuneration and fee structures, inadequate governance arrangements, poor valuation practices, ineffective disclosure — were concerning and demanded scrutiny.

"That scrutiny came through two ASIC reports," she said,

It painted a seriously concerning picture.

Of the 28 funds we reviewed:

Only four published information about the interest rates or ranges charged to borrowers.

published information about the interest rates or ranges charged to borrowers. Less than half had detailed, written credit or impairment and default management policies in place.

had detailed, written credit or impairment and default management policies in place. Most funds did not have adequate separation between those approving loans and those responsible for independently assessing their ongoing performance and value.

between those approving loans and those responsible for independently assessing their ongoing performance and value. And of the wholesale funds, only two performed stress testing as part of their liquidity risk management.

"These were clearly red flags — particularly when we think about the critical risks to be managed in private credit such as credit and liquidity risk, and the fundamental importance of effective disclosure in such a widespread and growing space," Ms Constant said.

Court's quest for justice on white-collar crime Corporate regulator ASIC, and its new boss, is keeping a close watch on Australia's "permissive investment regime".

The second report assessed private market reporting practices globally.

It found Australia falls well south of the line of information and disclosure of other comparable jurisdictions like Singapore, the US, the UK and even Switzerland.

But Wall Street is ground zero for the alternative investment market and there are fears this massive, risky US private lending ship is sinking and investors are jumping out.

"Globally funds under management have quadrupled in a similar time frame and it's estimated that there are now more private equity funds in the US than McDonald's stores," Ms Constant said.

Global investment bank Morgan Stanley announced late last week it was curbing redemptions at its nearly $US7 billion ($9.5 billion) private credit fund again in the third quarter.

Investors requested more than twice the amount the fund was willing to repurchase.

The Morgan Stanley building in Times Square in New York City. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

The North Haven Private Income Fund capped withdrawals at 5 per cent after investors asked to pull 11.4 per cent of shares, according to a shareholder letter.

'Contagion risk'

But the private credit risks for Australia are growing too, especially in the real estate and construction sectors.

ASIC warns of 'first significant cracks' in Australian private credit The collapse of a large and hugely indebted NSW property developer leaves several private credit lenders and their investors heavily exposed, while other major funds have started restricting withdrawals.

And millions of Australians are exposed to private credit — some through direct fund investment, others through shares in credit fund managers, but many through their superannuation fund.

FinCap executive chairman Christian Ryan told the ABC that a contagion or broad, rapid exit of cash out of the sector was "possible".

"That is why some funds are getting ahead of this given the general negative sentiment in the sector," Mr Ryan said.

That is, Mr Ryan said, some funds locally have begun to limit redemption as a precautionary measure to prevent investor panic.

" If you reflect on the material collapses in the past where retail investors in particular have been caught out with investors directly, this type of mechanism is enacted sometimes too late. "

But, he said, many private credit funds are well run by their managers.

"There are losses from time to time and being a credit manager, it is about limiting this risk as much as possible before investing," he said.

"I do know that many of the fund managers have great people that will be doing whatever they can in the background to look after investor funds."

Speaking at a federal parliamentary hearing on Friday, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock also indicated Australian private credit risks were being contained.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock indicated Australian private credit risks were being contained. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

"Our assessment is that, on the whole, the non-bank lending activity we've observed is helping to, for instance, provide the financing that's important for greenfield construction, but we don't have a strong sense that there's been a systematic weakening of lending standards," Ms Bullock said.

"Our assessment there would be that any weakening in lending standards in that segment are primarily going to be a problem for investors who invested in those funds.

"It doesn't speak to a systemic issue," she said.

ASIC laying down the law

Simone Constant will speak today at a gathering in Sydney hosted by the Commercial and Asset Finance Brokers Association. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

The corporate cop is not taking any chances on private credit and the risks it may pose to the financial system.

"We're now beyond warnings," Ms Constant said.

"The sector should prepare for enforcement action."

" The stress fractures we're starting to see represent a line in the sand for private credit. "

The next step, Ms Constant will tell the gathering today, is for other industry associations to develop and adopt their own compliant, good practice standards and of course for the member funds themselves to sign up to them.

"Even without the associations, our road map is there," she said.

"If you are a private credit fund who hasn't assessed yourself against our ten principles of private credit done well, ask yourselves — why not?

"Before your investors do."

World.title: German leader Merz clings on after election 'disaster'
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz is clinging onto power after his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party tumbled to its worst regional election defeat in post-war Germany, with members of his coalition clashing over his unpopular reform agenda.

Mr Merz himself described Sunday's loss in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania as a "disaster" as his party missed the 5 per cent threshold for entering a state parliament for the first time in a part of the country that was the former stronghold of is predecessor and party rival, Angela Merkel.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) took first place. While the AfD fell well short of a majority, it was the second time the party had topped a state election within a month, which it sees as building momentum towards national power.

Mr Merz's party also bled votes in a second election in the state of Berlin, which could see the far-left Die Linke party, the descendants of the Communist party that once ran East Germany, take power in a coalition after winning most seats.

Officials prepare absentee ballots at state elections in Berlin over the weekend. (Reuters: Fabrizio Bensch)

Sunday's results may not prove a knock-out blow for Mr Merz, but his low approval ratings and the AfD's surge have left his future in the balance.

On Monday, he announced that the centre-left Social Democrats wanted to remain in a coalition with his conservatives.

A 'serious moment in Europe' The weekend win by Alternative for Germany in the state of Saxony-Anhalt has sent shivers across the continent, and could embolden the right across Europe.

"I am grateful that we have heard from the Social Democrats this morning that they intend to remain part of the coalition in Berlin," Mr Merz said.

"That applies to us too, and it applies to me as well. Together, we are determined to rise to the historic challenges facing our country."

'Merz should be more humble'

Earlier, several conservative state premiers met to take stock after publicly backing Mr Merz in an open letter last week.

It said "the chancellor needs to deliver more following the CDU's difficult results in the state elections".

Mr Merz, who has vowed to press on with his reform agenda, says tough measures are vital to revive sluggish growth in Europe's largest economy and keep it globally competitive.

But members of his centre-left coalition partner, the Social Democrats, pushed back.

That includes Manuela Schwesig, the popular incumbent state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, who has sharply criticised the federal government's pension reforms.

Ms Schwesig said she was "very irritated" by Mr Merz's remarks.

"I think more humility is actually called for on the part of the Chancellor," she said.

The left-leaning Die Linke party topped a state election for the first time in Berlin. (Reuters: Liesa Johannssen)

The economy has been struggling since the pandemic to regain momentum, with competition from China as well as higher energy prices challenging its export-driven economic model.

The AfD party leads in national opinion polls but has been kept from power by the other main parties' refusal to work with it, in a policy known as the "firewall" that has been increasingly scrutinised as the AfD gained strength.

US to withdraw 5,000 troops from Germany The United States is withdrawing 5,000 troops from NATO ally Germany amid a growing a rift between the nations' leaders over the Iran war.

Its hardline stance on immigration has left some in Germany of migrant background questioning their future.

"The fact that the AfD is in the lead is quite a bitter pill to swallow," said Yasmin Goudarzi, an educational scientist.

In Berlin, Die Linke topped the polls in a state election for the first time on a campaign to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and put a cap on rents, echoing the rise of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Mr Merz, who was elected last year on a promise to return Germany to growth, has struggled to win over voters.

A stream of communication missteps have served to compound resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Xi Jinping's closest military ally expelled from party, accused of corruption
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

China has expelled two high-ranking military officers from the ruling Communist Party, months after it was announced they were being investigated for "serious violations of the law".

One of them, Zhang Youxia, was widely seen as President Xi Jinping's closest military ally and was the senior of the two vice chairs of the top military body in China.

The second officer, Liu Zhenli, was a Central Military Commission (CMC) member and the chief of staff of its joint staff department.

In January, the defence ministry said Mr Zhang and Mr Liu were "suspected of serious violations of discipline and the law" — a common term for corruption — but did not provide any details of the alleged wrongdoing.

Liu Zhenli was a member of China's Central Military Commission. (Reuters: Florence Lo)

Following a meeting of top officials in Beijing on Monday, top officials "decided to expel" the two men from the Communist Party and transfer their cases to the military's legal organs "for review and prosecution", Chinese state media Xinhua reported.

The Chinese leadership accused Mr Zhang and Mr Liu of disloyalty, corruption, dereliction of duty and other serious disciplinary violations.

An investigation found Mr Zhang and Mr Liu had "become disloyal to the Party … and crossed red lines" by engaging in a list of offences including forming cliques and factions, adding that their "political and economic wrongdoing were intertwined, and corrupt self-enrichment coexisted with dereliction of duty and abuse of office".

"The sums involved were exceptionally large; the nature (of their conduct) was extremely serious and the impact extremely egregious," Xinhua said.

The two men also "used their positions to help others in matters such as job promotion", according to the reports, and their their expulsion would be subject to ratification at a plenary session of the Party's Central Committee.

Last month, Mr Zhang and Mr Liu were stripped of their positions in the state CMC.

Military corruption crackdown continues

Monday's decision "reaffirms the firm position that … there is absolutely no place for corrupt elements to hide within the military", Xinhua said.

How a purge at the top of China's military could impact Taiwan Another two senior generals are under investigation for alleged corruption in China and that has big consequences for President Xi Jinping.

The military has been one of the major targets of a broader corruption crackdown in China ordered by Mr Xi in 2021.

Mr Xi has called the graft "the biggest threat" to the Chinese Communist Party, saying previously: "The fight against corruption remains grave and complex."

But Mr Zhang's fall from grace has shocked observers, given his seniority and the perception he was close to the Chinese leader.

Mr Zhang had also been a member of the elite Politburo of the ruling Communist Party and is one of just a few leading officers with combat experience.

The announcement came days before Mr Xi is due to travel to the US for talks with US President Donald Trump, and weeks before a key October party conclave on internal party governance and discipline.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue over White House ban
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico say they have notified US President Donald Trump's administration that they are filing a lawsuit over being denied White House access.

Reporters from the three major news organisations were blocked from the White House on Saturday, local time, a day after Mr Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be "fake news".

Trump bans outlets from White House Cable networks CNN and MS NOW and newsletter publisher Politico have been banned from the White House, effective immediately, with more to follow, US President Donald Trump says.

"Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," the outlets said in a joint statement posted on X on Monday.

All three had previously hinted at legal action, saying they would vigorously defend their First Amendment rights.

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said.

White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) president Jacqui Heinrich called on the Trump administration to immediately restore access.

"The implications extend beyond these organisations — a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," Ms Heinrich said.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favourably."

Latest escalation in anti-news campaign

MS NOW White House reporter Akayla Gardne, CNN senior White House reporter Betsy Klein and Politico White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett. (AP: Jose Luis Magana)

On Friday, local time, Mr Trump said he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked.

White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — went live to report they had been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House on Saturday.

Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated.

White House turns away CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters The White House has denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, following through with Donald Trump's ban.

The actions were a clear escalation of Mr Trump's long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable and are the latest test of US First Amendment protections.

In his second term, Mr Trump and his Republican administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action.

Mr Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms, insulting them in briefings or in his recent speech at the WHCA dinner.

AP

World.title: Chris Brown among trio replacing Kyle and Jackie O
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Three familiar faces have been picked to fill the gap left in Sydney's radio scene by long-time co-presenters Kyle Sandilands and Jackie O.

Bondi Vet television personality Chris Brown, occasional KIIS fill-in host Amy Gerard and former Nova star Jack Charles will begin broadcasting on November 9.

ARN announced the trio on Monday, seven months after an on-air dispute triggered an acrimonious split between the then-hosts of KIIS FM's breakfast program.

The announcement is the first of two, with another team to be announced soon to replace the outgoing hosts' broadcast in Melbourne.

Gig a 'dream come true' for Bondi Vet star

Chris Brown says getting the job is a "dream come true". (Instagram: drchrisbrown)

ARN chief executive Michael Stephenson said the revamped line-up had been designed to deliver big names and fresh talent.

"We have the biggest radio brand in the country, and we now have a team that is building something very special for listeners," he said.

Brown, who had been touted as a forerunner to join the program, is known to television audiences for programs including Bondi Vet, The Living Room and I'm A Celebrity … Get Me Out Of Here!

"Waking up with the city I love and bringing a huge dose of real life, warmth and (hopefully) humour is truly a dream come true," he said.

Amy Gerard is an occasional KIIS fill-in host. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

Gerard, already familiar to the station's listeners, said the new partnership was off to an auspicious start.

"The chemistry between Chris, Jack and I already feels so natural. It's fun, unpredictable," she said.

"There's a very good chance we'll be completely unhinged before most people have had their first coffee."

Charles said he was "pumped" to be joining the program after announcing his resignation from Nova earlier in September.

ARN still in court over Henderson's exit

ARN and Kyle Sandilands settled their suit in June. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Following their spat in Feebruary, Sandilands and Henderson were let go by ARN after 27 years on the air.

Sandilands and Henderson were the company's best-paid talent, having secured a 10-year contract worth a reported $200 million in 2023.

Both hosts launched lawsuits against their former employers. Henderson's remains before the courts.

KIIS on the slide The KIIS Sydney audience has slipped further in the radio ratings in the latest blow to ARN after the departure of renowned breakfast radio juggernaut Kyle and Jackie O.

ARN and Sandilands settled their suit for $12 million in June.

Sandilands launched a subscription-based program, Kyle Sandilands Live, in August, featuring NSW Premier Chris Minns as his debut guest.

ARN Media operates 58 radio stations across 33 markets, including KIIS, GOLD, CADA and iHeart.

AAP

World.title: Man banned from Oz Comic-Con after allegedly biting artist
World.content:
A man has been banned from Oz Comic-Con after allegedly biting one of the artists on Sunday afternoon.

Police were called to the Brisbane Convention and Exhibition Centre in South Bank.

Loading...

A police spokesperson told 612 ABC no formal complaint was filed, but they were aware of the incident.

"All parties have been banned from the venue and future events," the spokesperson said.

Footage supplied to the ABC shows Zyllion stall-holder Bowie Chong in a heated argument with another vendor, Victoria Manton-Williams at about 2:40pm.

Victoria Manton-Williams described the turn of events as highly unusual. (612 ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato)

Manton-Williams told the ABC she asked Chong whether his art was AI-generated, prompting him to tell her to "f*** off".

Manton-Williams alleged Chong snatched the phone away from her artist friend who was filming the scene.

Manton-Williams said her friend pushed Chong, who then allegedly bit her friend's arm and "latched on".

Manton-Williams said she ran over and tried to pull Chong off of her friend and that she was pushed to the ground and kicked in the arm.

Manton-Williams said her friend went to the hospital to receive antibiotics for the bite, which had turned dark red from bruising.

She said the whole encounter was bizarre.

"I've never actually heard of anyone getting bitten at a convention in general," Manton-Williams said.

"I did not even think it was in the realm of possibility that when I went up to ask this guy a question that he would run out and bite someone.

"It's not normal behaviour — not even cosplayers go around biting each other."

Chong has not responded to the ABC's requests for comment. Zyllion's website and social media pages have been deleted.

The bite was treated with antibiotics. (Supplied: Victoria Manton-Williams)

The incident took place next to the esports gaming booth and the Star Trek fan club booth.

Oz Comic-Con would not say what its policy was on AI-generated art or products at its conventions.

An Oz Comic-Con spokesperson said the matter had been referred to police.

"We are aware of an incident taking place, however it is now a police matter and as such it would be inappropriate to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

A Brisbane Convention and Exhibition Centre spokesperson said Oz Comic-Con was run separately from the centre itself.

"We are aware of an incident that occurred and the matter was responded to at the time in accordance with the Centre's established security procedures," the spokesperson said.

"Oz Comic-Con is an independently organised event."

World.title: Darwin teacher takes registration board to tribunal after her suspension
World.content:
A Darwin teacher has challenged an interim decision by the Northern Territory's Teacher Registration Board (TRB) to suspend her registration while conducting an inquiry into allegations relating to "child welfare, psychological safety, professional judgement and fitness to teach".

According to documents filed with the Northern Territory Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NTCAT), the TRB suspended Bindi Isis's registration in May following a complaint by a school principal.

The teacher of 25 years' experience alleges the board failed to properly assess the reliability and context of the allegations.

In its response filed with NTCAT, the TRB says it "did not make final findings of misconduct before exercising its suspension power" and it assessed whether the information it had was sufficient to "justify interim action in relation to [Ms Isis's] ongoing ability to teach pending the outcome of the Inquiry".

Bindi Isis says she has been working as a teacher for 25 years. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

"The substance of the complaint by [the principal] alleges serious misconduct," the TRB wrote.

" The material provided identified concerns regarding [Ms Isis's] fitness to teach, her professional boundaries, child safety, professional conduct and compliance with the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. "

The TRB said material submitted with the complaint noted Ms Isis's "employment had been terminated" in February this year for "serious misconduct following an investigation by her employer which substantiated all but one of the allegations made against her".

However, Ms Isis noted her final day of teaching students at the school was October 13, 2025.

'Mischaracterisations, exaggerations'

In her initiating application filed with NTCAT, Ms Isis said the TRB relied "wholly upon a notification" made by a principal, which she argued included "significant mischaracterisations, exaggerations, subjective opinions and speculative assertions that were not supported by particulars and/or evidence".

"The allegations within the notification formed the core of a workplace dispute," she wrote.

"Much of the supporting materials represent clear conflicts of interest. This material should not have been accepted without careful scrutiny."

Ms Isis adds that prior to its decision to suspend her registration, she provided a "detailed response" to the TRB in April that included a "timeline of the workplace dispute, evidence of professional competence, letters of support from parents and colleagues and reports confirming the applicant's fitness to teach".

Bindi Isis says the registration board gave too much weight to the allegations and not enough to her supporting evidence. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Ms Isis also says she was "never subject to formal performance management, disciplinary findings, or adverse professional assessments".

"[Ms Isis] was never given opportunity to restore a working relationship with her principal," the documents read.

She also writes that following her leaving the school and "a protracted dispute", she and the school "entered into a settlement deed and the school publicly acknowledged [Ms Isis's] positive contribution and dedicated service".

In its response, the TRB said the complaint it received included "supporting documentary material, evidence of a lengthy performance management history, complaints from parents and staff, incident reports, correspondence, a return-to-work assessment, and [Ms Isis's] written response".

The Teacher Registration Board says the complaints related to multiple incidents. (Supplied: Adobe)

"The allegations made were not isolated or confined to a single event," the TRB wrote.

"They include a pattern of conduct spanning several years and involved concerns raised by multiple sources, including school leadership, staff, parents and external consultants.

"The allegations were not limited to a workplace dispute.

"The board was entitled to consider the cumulative effect of those matters when assessing risk.

"To allow [Ms Isis] to continue to teach pending the outcome of the inquiry would expose children, families and schools to an unacceptable and potentially irreparable risk if the concerns are ultimately established."

A 'fit and proper person' to teach

In the documents, Ms Isis said the suspension had prevented her from "working in her profession, caused significant financial hardship, is disrupting to her studies and damages her professional reputation whilst affecting present and future career prospects".

"[Ms Isis] is a single parent, a full-time student and the primary carer of a son with an intellectual disability," the documents read.

Bindi Isis says the suspension was a "severe and disproportionate" response from the registration board. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"Prior to suspension she had recommenced supporting her family with the income derived from teaching, obtaining work as a relief teacher.

"The consequences of the suspension are severe and disproportionate to the evidence relied upon by the TRB.

"[Ms Isis] remains a fit and proper person to teach, and her continued exclusion from the profession is not necessary for public protection.

"Her work is recognised as having ongoing value to our NT community."

In its response, the TRB argues the decision to suspend Ms Isis's registration was "reasonable, proportionate and consistent with the protective purpose" of the legislation.

"The decision of the board should therefore be affirmed and the notification to interstate registration bodies should remain in place," it said.

The dispute was scheduled for a closed compulsory conference at NTCAT today.

World.title: 'Emaciated' woman never accessed NDIS funding despite approval, inquest told
World.content:
A woman with an intellectual disability who weighed just 40 kilograms at the time of her death never accessed the $75,000 in National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) support she was entitled to, a coronial inquest has heard.

The South Australian inquest into the September 2022 death of Nancy White will explore how the NDIS can improve its systems to make it more accessible to those who have been granted funding.

Deputy State Coroner Emma Roper today opened the inquest into the death of the 50-year-old, who had been under the full-time care of her brother Norman White.

The inquest heard that Ms White had an intellectual disability, limited mobility and minimal verbal communication.

It also heard that Ms White was "emaciated" at the time of her death and weighed 40kg.

The post-mortem examination concluded the cause of death was acute peritonitis caused by a traumatic bowel perforation.

Counsel assisting Laura Crase told the court that Ms White had previously been hospitalised in 2021 with septic shock and intubated for two weeks in the intensive care unit.

She said that during the admission, a social worker at the hospital applied for NDIS funding on Ms White's behalf, which was approved shortly after.

"At the time of her death, Ms White was eligible to access $75,000 in NDIS funding to support her to live in the community. However, she never accessed any of that funding," Ms Crase said.

"Mr Norman White later explained that he did not take the steps necessary to access this funding for Nancy, he just 'took care of everything himself' and he was not very good at reading."

Ms White's niece Rachel Dorsett gave evidence to the inquest. (ABC News: Eva Blandis)

Giving evidence on Monday, Ms White's niece Rachel Dorsett said she had offered to help her uncle complete the NDIS paperwork.

"It just never eventuated," she said.

'Hypothermic' and in 'emaciated condition'

Ms Dorsett said she understood Mr White's reading and writing skills to be limited and felt "in her opinion" that he was reluctant to engage with the NDIS.

"I think it was all too much and too overwhelming," she said.

"[It could have been] because it is a lot of paperwork and it is a lot of reading, and it is a lot of engaging with people you don't know and telling them things … because that doesn't come naturally to everyone.

"It might've been a little bit of a pride thing."

Ms Dorsett added that Mr White and his sister were "pretty close".

"I used to hear him tell her stories … [and] he was always trying to keep her involved, I guess," she said.

"He always called her 'sweetheart' as well."

The inquest is expected to continue into next week. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Ms Crase said the inquest would explore ways to safeguard people in Ms White's situation and ensure they, along with carers, got access to NDIS support they had been granted.

Ms Crase added that it would also investigate the circumstances of Ms White's death.

The court heard that paramedics had been called to a Reynella home on the morning of September 5, 2022, where they found Ms White "in an emaciated condition".

"She was hypothermic, had bruising to her face and abdomen," Ms Crase said.

"The paramedics were concerned that her room was cold and there were insufficient blankets on her bed to keep her warm.

"Her bed linen, pillows and jumper were heavily soiled with vomit."

Ms Crase told the court that Mr White told the paramedics that "he had tried to set up assistance with the NDIS" but that it was "difficult".

The inquest is expected to continue into next week.

World.title: Nickelback, Nickelback, and toilet paper footballs: Nick Daicos’ rise to Brownlow Medal greatness
World.content:
It’s unclear where Nick Daicos ranks in the Australian football pantheon.

At 23, and after five seasons, he’s as accomplished as any midfielder we’ve seen over that period in the national competition, and on track to surpass nearly everyone who isn’t a key-position player.

His impact on the outcome of games is up there with any player since his prodigiously gifted father Peter was testing footy physics.

It’s hard to compare Nick to Wayne Carey, Gary Ablett snr or Tony Lockett, but he’s certainly in the company of Gary Ablett jnr and Chris Judd. At the same age, he’s more impactful.

World.title: The elephant in the room: How Brownlow Medal night handled the suspended Swans
World.content:
SportAFLBrownlow Medal The elephant in the room: How Brownlow Medal night handled the suspended Swans Hannah Kennelly September 21, 2026 — 11:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Whenever any suspended member from the Sydney Swans featured in the 2026 Brownlow Medal count, it attracted the same reaction: complete silence. Isaac Heeney and fellow Swans players Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were stood down for the rest of the AFL season for breaching the club’s standards during a night at the Pullman Hotel last month after their side’s win over Essendon. The scene at Crown Palladium on Monday night. AFL Photos The suspended players were also banned from attending this year’s Brownlow count – even though they were eligible to win it. Heeney collected 26 votes to finish equal eighth on Monday night, despite favourite Nick Daicos winning the prestigious medal by a landslide with a record 47 votes. There was silence followed by murmurs in the room at Crown Palladium when Heeney’s name was first read out during round four, with the Swans vice captain receiving two votes.



Warner, Blakey and Bice also received votes throughout the night. There were notably no camera cuts to the Sydney table whenever a suspended player received a vote. There were also no camera pans to other tables to gauge other guests’ reactions. Instead, whenever a suspended player’s name was read, the camera cut to a wide pan of the room. Sydney Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney and Nick Blakey. The Age There was also minimal to no footage of Heeney or other suspended players during the highlight recap of each round.



A source familiar with the broadcast planning said there was “no intention to exclude any individual player”, noting a “a very small number of key moments are selected to feature each round, and it’s just not possible to include every player/moment”. Andrew Dillon chose to read the Brownlow votes at his normal trademark speedy pace.

However, unlike Daicos and Marcus Bontempelli – who regularly received whoops and cheers during their vote count – Heeney and other Swans players received steely silence, excluding the occasional singular clap. Sydney’s Charlie Curnow and Dane Rampe at the Brownlow Medal count. Getty Images Several Swans players attended the Brownlow ceremony including Charlie Curnow, Dane Rampe, Brodie Grundy, Logan McDonald and Tom McCartin, as well as coach Dean Cox. Each of them did minimal to no media interviews on the red carpet and slipped into the ballroom quickly. It follows a sombre week for the Swans, who looked on track to reach the grand final after reaching a game-high 28-point lead in the third quarter of their preliminary final clash with Fremantle.



View post on X Instead, the Dockers launched the biggest three-quarter-time comeback in their history to snatch their place in the grand final. The Swans are yet to make a call on whether the suspended five will remain eligible for the club’s best-and-fairest award, which will be presented at a function in Sydney on October 1. The Swans’ club-imposed suspensions were separate from a Victoria Police investigation into allegations of sexual assault at the Pullman. No charges have been laid. Swans defender Tom McCartin and his partner Sophie Walker on Brownlow night. Getty Images

World.title: Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making
World.content:
SportAFLBrownlow Medal Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making Marc McGowan September 21, 2026 — 10:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nike was right – it was inevitable. After consecutive runner-up finishes, and a third placing before that, Collingwood champion Nick Daicos is finally a Brownlow medallist. Daicos’ major sponsor Nike boldly took out front-page newspaper ads on Monday featuring a photo of the star Magpie, the famous Nike swoosh logo, and the word “Inevitable”. Nick Daicos (right) with his parents Peter and Colleen. AFL Photos The famous brand’s confidence was vindicated when the 23-year-old midfielder, wearing custom Nike swoosh cufflinks, won in record-breaking style, beating dual winner Patrick Cripps’ extraordinary 2024 tally of 45 votes with a new count-high total (in the 3-2-1 system) of 47.



The shortest-priced favourite in the event’s history also set a new benchmark of 13 best-on-ground performances and polled in 18 of his 22 matches. Related Article Brownlow Medal The elephant in the room: How Brownlow Medal night handled the suspended Swans Daicos’ victory was sealed with three rounds to go – when he was 10 votes clear – and he eventually equalled Richmond legend Dustin Martin’s record winning margin of 11 votes from 2017, ending his multi-year run of being a beaten Brownlow favourite. “I’ve learnt not to trust the betting markets,” Daicos said after receiving his Brownlow Medal from last year’s winner and former Carey Grammar teammate Matt Rowell. “But, no, there is [relief]. It’s a massive award, and I’m so privileged to be up here. I can’t believe I’m a Brownlow medallist.”



Geelong superstar Bailey Smith (36 votes), Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (34), Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), North Melbourne’s Harry Sheezel, Blue Patrick Cripps and Brisbane’s dual North Smith medallist Will Ashcroft (27) finished behind Daicos. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney was a further vote back on 26 with Zak Butters, but was unable to attend the event after his role in the Pullman Hotel saga. Speaking during the count, Bontempelli said Daicos was the AFL’s best player and had changed the sport with his ability to impact the game with pure hard work and his offensive skills. View post on X



Daicos revealed post-count that his brother and teammate Josh and father Peter – one of Collingwood’s all-time greats – were instrumental in him developing his famed work ethic. Nick and Josh spent countless afternoons as teenagers with their dad at Greythorn Junior Football Club honing their skills. “I feel like from a young age, I probably had more talent [than others] and didn’t work as hard, and had some chats with Dad and Josh as I grew up,” he said. “It was a realisation I wanted to play AFL, and that I needed to train harder. I walk into the club every day, and I’m immensely grateful to be an AFL footballer. “I think I owe it to the Collingwood Football Club to train with an intensity, and I feel like as a leader at the club, I can’t ask the bloke next to me to put his backside on the line and train really hard if I’m not doing it myself. I try and lead by example.”



Daicos’ custom Nike cufflinks. AFL Photos Daicos’ Brownlow victory followed him also collecting the AFL Players’ Association’s MVP and AFL Coaches’ Association’s player of the year, becoming the first footballer to claim all three since Lachie Neale six years ago. His latest honour makes him arguably the most accomplished young player ever, swelling a resume that already includes the Magpies’ 2023 premiership and four All-Australian selections. Daicos will almost certainly win a third Copeland Trophy next month as well. He is the 10th Magpie to win a Brownlow Medal and first since Dane Swan 15 years ago, also joining Syd Coventry, brothers Albert and Harry Collier, Marcus Whelan, Des Fothergill, Len Thompson, Peter Moore and Nathan Buckley.



Daicos polled maximum votes in each of his first three games – either side of the Magpies’ round two bye – before he was a late withdrawal with a corked calf against Brisbane. That was the only match he missed all season. Daicos’ streak of maximum votes ended in a round five loss to Fremantle, where he still polled one off a 31-disposal effort, and it was enough to break an early deadlock with fellow great Bontempelli. Zak Butters briefly snatched a one-vote lead in round 10, but Daicos was back on top a round later when he was best afield against West Coast as Scott Pendlebury broke the VFL/AFL games record with his 433rd appearance. Smith drew level with the gun Pie on 23 votes in round 14, with Butters a single vote back, before Daicos shot away again a round later with three votes after a 41-touch masterclass at Port Adelaide’s expense.



Daicos proudly shows off the 2026 Brownlow Medal after a record-breaking night. AFL Photos That was when Daicos made his move, turning an entertaining count with superstars spread across the leaderboard into a demolition, like a Melbourne Cup winner turning for home. The man in the No.35 secured maximum votes in six straight matches between rounds 15 and 20 in an incredible purple patch to kick clear of the field and end any doubt about the result. Daicos polled 11 votes to finish equal 27th in his debut season in 2022; came third with 28 votes in 2023; second with 38 votes in 2024; and second with 32 votes last year. Umpires had access to player statistics for the first time this year to help with voting.

World.title: Albanese takes climate warning to New York, but fossil fuel experts test credibility
World.content:
PoliticsFederalParis Agreement Albanese takes climate warning to New York, but fossil fuel experts test credibility Rob Harris September 21, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The world can no longer rely on adapting to escalating climate catastrophes, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will warn as he opens Climate Week in New York with a warning that Australia is heading into a summer of extreme heat, bushfires and floods. The prime minister will tell a United Nations gathering that Australia’s abundant renewable potential – firmed by gas-powered generation – can help deliver its emissions target while declaring the next devastating fire or flood is becoming a question of when, not if. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will tell world leaders in New York that communities can no longer simply adapt to worsening weather disasters Dominic Lorrimer But as Albanese promotes Australia’s renewable energy gains, scientists say the government faces a credibility test given its continuing support for fossil fuel investment and status as one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters. “We can’t rely on the fortitude of our people alone, as tough as they are,” Albanese will say, according to a draft of his speech. “We need to come together, to meet the problem head on.”



Albanese will point to record-breaking temperatures and unprecedented wildfires across Europe during the northern summer while acknowledging Australia and its Pacific neighbours are bracing for their own difficult months. “With a record-breaking El Nino forecast, Australia and the Pacific nations are preparing for a potential summer of extreme heat, bushfires and floods,” he will say. Australia’s 2035 emissions target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 62 to 70 per cent below 2005 levels will be central to the government’s case as it prepares to lead COP31 negotiations with Turkey. He will acknowledge that not every extreme weather event can be directly attributed to climate change, but argue a warmer world is producing more frequent and intense events. “Unfortunately, without strong action, the science tells us these events will get worse and more intense,” Albanese says. “That’s more communities facing repeated trauma. Knowing the next flood or fire isn’t a matter of if, but when.”



Related Article Extreme weather What flash droughts and a super El Nino will mean for your summer Albanese will argue the 62 to 70 per cent target is “ambitious” but achievable, pointing to the rapid expansion of renewable energy and household batteries. Renewables supplied about half the grid at peak periods last summer, while more than 500,000 household batteries have been installed over the past year. But Australia’s climate credentials will face a tougher test as it takes on the presidency of the COP negotiations. Jennifer Morgan, a senior fellow at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University and former climate envoy for Germany, said Australia and Turkey were both pursuing potential new fossil fuel investments and had no coal phase-out date. “They’ve made progress in renewable energy, but I think their credibility – and their ability to therefore bring momentum and good outcomes to the COP – will depend on their taking further action at home,” Morgan said.



Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said Australia and Turkey needed to provide “clear leadership” on transforming the fossil fuel road map agreed at last year’s COP30 in Brazil into concrete action. “This road map cannot be left in a dusty drawer,” Jones said. She said both countries needed to demonstrate how they would transition away from fossil fuels, noting Australia was the world’s third-largest fossil-fuel exporter. Albanese will argue the clean energy transition can deliver lower emissions and economic growth, with Australia using its solar and wind resources, batteries, critical minerals and rare earths to build new industries. “Electrification is the way to reduce emissions while maintaining economic growth,” he will say.



He will also emphasise Australia’s role in the Pacific, where some of the nations most vulnerable to climate change have contributed the least to global emissions. “Pacific nations have long been the strongest advocates for climate action,” Albanese will say. “And the value of listening to their perspectives has never been clearer.” The climate warning will be followed by a broader argument that the international rule of law itself is under strain when Albanese addresses a summit of the Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace and Prosperity at UN headquarters. The speech comes after Albanese formally launched Australia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-30. Albanese will argue middle powers need to accept greater responsibility for maintaining the international system, with Australia seeking to “listen with respect, partner as equals and protect what matters most – security, safety and prosperity”.



On Monday, Albanese will meet Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale before talks with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. AI will also feature in the diplomatic push, with Australia joining a joint statement at the UN calling for stronger controls over the rapidly developing technology. World.title: Sydney boy fighting for life after ‘tragic’ shooting in luxury apartment complex
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Sydney boy fighting for life after ‘tragic’ shooting in luxury apartment complex Daniel Lo Surdo Updated September 21, 2026 — 9:22pm ,first published 6:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three 18-year-olds are in police custody after a boy, 11, was shot in the face and neck inside a luxury Sydney apartment complex on Monday, leaving a confronting scene for officers who stormed the property to render life-saving treatment to the child. Paramedics rushed through the Moda apartment complex on Fairway Drive, Norwest, about 5pm after reports the child had been shot. The boy was conscious and speaking with paramedics while they administered urgent assistance at the complex where he is believed to live, but his health worsened as he was taken to Westmead Children’s Hospital in a critical condition. Police establish a crime scene where the child was shot on Monday. Wolter Peeters The 11-year-old was in the apartment with four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman, none of whom was injured when the gun was fired. Three of the 18-year-olds were arrested and taken to Castle Hill and Riverstone Police Stations for further questioning. Charges against the three were likely but not certain, two police sources told this masthead, and would be determined by further interviews with the occupants and searches of the scene.



The nature of potential charges will also depend on the condition of the boy. Some occupants were related to the boy, while others were friends of the family. The State Crime Command’s Homicide Squad has been notified of the shooting as the investigation continues. All occupants have been interviewed by police, and are assisting with police inquiries. Hills Police Area Commander Naomi Moore promised a “thorough and expansive” probe, saying the shooting was among the most awful scenes she has encountered. Tactical and general duties officers rushed to the Norwest apartment complex on Monday. Wolter Peeters “It is an absolutely tragic situation, and we’ve seen tragedy across Sydney in the last couple of days, this is not far from the worst that I’ve seen,” she said. Tactical officers and a police helicopter swarmed the complex as they combed the property for the firearm used in the shooting, which had not been found by 10pm on Monday.



Officers searched the park adjacent to the complex, as a large exclusion zone covering much of Fairway Drive was established to assist the search for the gun. Police search a park for the gun used in the shooting of the boy. Wolter Peeters No firearms are registered to the address. The circumstances of the shooting and how the gun came to be in the home are under investigation, as are the events leading to the incident and who pulled the trigger. Detectives do not believe the shooting is linked to organised crime, police sources said, and are treating it as a separate, standalone incident. A large exclusion zone has been established on Fairway Drive. Wolter Peeters



The boy’s mother is with her son in hospital, and was, according to Moore, “as stressed as any parent would be”. Officers are investigating whether the gun was accidentally fired inside the apartment, either by the boy or another occupant. Police are still working to determine who fired the weapon. Tactical officers swarmed the Norwest complex where the boy was shot. Wolter Peeters There are 217 properties in the Moda complex, ranging from one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments, according to developers Arden Group, which said each home delivers a “luxury lifestyle” to residents. It is adjacent to the Castle Hill Country Club and two blocks from Norwest station, and includes an indoor swimming pool, gym and a rooftop entertaining terrace.



The Moda apartment complex offers a “luxury lifestyle” to residents in its 217 homes. Aussie Home Loans Residents were seen filtering through the front of the building as tactical police descended on the building, while paramedics moved into the complex. Others stood on balconies, perplexed about the expanding police operation occurring below. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Springing into step
World.content:
“Now that spring is here, I’ve been keeping track of the various local fêtes and fairs with the allure of trash, treasure and pre loved bric-a-brac,” writes Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “At last count, I can look forward to a nursing home jumble sale, a school white elephant and a church charity bazaar, and the various charity market stalls in carparks across the district. There’s one, though, that has caught my eye - the Ugg Boot Car Boot Sale. I’ll be hotfooting it there!”

“I’ve thought of a way to avoid AI killing us all (C8),” claims Alan Phillips of Mosman. “Simple. Feed it with the last 50 years of Column 8 to train on. That will drive it mad, and it will terminate itself.”

As long as it contains this offering from Merilyn McClung of Forestville: “My young granddaughter asked why, when a building is finished, it is still called a building? She wondered if C8-ers might know.”

“The kids liked the Bee Gees (C8), but I ran across Frank Sinatra in a bar in Honolulu in 1957,” says John Crowe of Cherrybrook. “We shared a couple of beers. He belied his reputation and was happy to yarn with a young unknown Australian.”

“The Mouseketeers were performing at the Sydney Stadium in Rushcutters Bay”, circa 1960, recalls Judy Klein of Double Bay. “At the end of the show, Annette Funicello looked directly at me, smiled and waved. I have never forgotten the thrill.”

World.title: Final design chosen for iconic Nullarbor photo stop
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWARoads Final design chosen for iconic Nullarbor photo stop Sarah Smith September 21, 2026 — 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An iconic photo spot along the Nullarbor is getting a makeover. The Western Australia–South Australia border sign has stood tall for three decades, but it is now set to be replaced. The WA-SA border crossing sign on the Nullarbor is getting a makeover. A public vote between two designs across 14 social media posts weighed up “bush to beach” or “ochre and ocean”. The latter eventually prevailed, receiving 888 votes – almost 80 per cent of the total vote.



It’s a design Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti believes represents “reflects the striking colours of the border landscape”. “The WA-SA border sign is an iconic stop for the thousands of people travelling across the Nullarbor each year,” she said. “It’s great to see the community having their say on the sign design, and I’m looking forward to seeing it in place next year.” The current sign along Eyre Highway will begin being demolished next month. The WA letters were replaced in 2023 after they fell down to corrosion.



The new sign will be installed in early 2027 and is set to cost taxpayers $900,000 – and WA will foot the entire bill. Editor's pick Planning and development Green light for $10 million Fast Eddys replacement, with hopes for a Reuben on the menu “Getting money out of South Australia is pretty hard,” Saffioti said. “They are already bemoaning about our GST deal, so we’ll just pay it.” Meanwhile, the border crossing will be accompanied by a shelter 4½ metres tall and 11 metres long.



Main Roads WA worked with key stakeholders, including the Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission, Shire of Dundas, Tourism WA, the Department for Infrastructure and Transport in South Australia, Tourism SA, and the Mirning Traditional Owners, to finalise design options for the new structure and information panels. Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent said the new sign would be a “fitting entryway to our great state, celebrating the rich colours of our region from the red dirt to the blue sky”.
