Nike was right – it was inevitable. After consecutive runner-up finishes, and a third placing before that, Collingwood champion Nick Daicos is finally a Brownlow medallist. Daicos’ major sponsor Nike boldly took out front-page newspaper ads on Monday featuring a photo of the star Magpie, the famous Nike swoosh logo, and the word “Inevitable”. Nick Daicos (right) with his parents Peter and Colleen. AFL Photos The famous brand’s confidence was vindicated when the 23-year-old midfielder, wearing custom Nike swoosh cufflinks, won in record-breaking style, beating dual winner Patrick Cripps’ extraordinary 2024 tally of 45 votes with a new count-high total (in the 3-2-1 system) of 47.



The shortest-priced favourite in the event’s history also set a new benchmark of 13 best-on-ground performances and polled in 18 of his 22 matches. Related Article Brownlow Medal The elephant in the room: How Brownlow Medal night handled the suspended Swans Daicos’ victory was sealed with three rounds to go – when he was 10 votes clear – and he eventually equalled Richmond legend Dustin Martin’s record winning margin of 11 votes from 2017, ending his multi-year run of being a beaten Brownlow favourite. “I’ve learnt not to trust the betting markets,” Daicos said after receiving his Brownlow Medal from last year’s winner and former Carey Grammar teammate Matt Rowell. “But, no, there is [relief]. It’s a massive award, and I’m so privileged to be up here. I can’t believe I’m a Brownlow medallist.”



Geelong superstar Bailey Smith (36 votes), Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (34), Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), North Melbourne’s Harry Sheezel, Blue Patrick Cripps and Brisbane’s dual North Smith medallist Will Ashcroft (27) finished behind Daicos. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney was a further vote back on 26 with Zak Butters, but was unable to attend the event after his role in the Pullman Hotel saga. Speaking during the count, Bontempelli said Daicos was the AFL’s best player and had changed the sport with his ability to impact the game with pure hard work and his offensive skills. View post on X



Daicos revealed post-count that his brother and teammate Josh and father Peter – one of Collingwood’s all-time greats – were instrumental in him developing his famed work ethic. Nick and Josh spent countless afternoons as teenagers with their dad at Greythorn Junior Football Club honing their skills. “I feel like from a young age, I probably had more talent [than others] and didn’t work as hard, and had some chats with Dad and Josh as I grew up,” he said. “It was a realisation I wanted to play AFL, and that I needed to train harder. I walk into the club every day, and I’m immensely grateful to be an AFL footballer. “I think I owe it to the Collingwood Football Club to train with an intensity, and I feel like as a leader at the club, I can’t ask the bloke next to me to put his backside on the line and train really hard if I’m not doing it myself. I try and lead by example.”



Daicos’ custom Nike cufflinks. AFL Photos Daicos’ Brownlow victory followed him also collecting the AFL Players’ Association’s MVP and AFL Coaches’ Association’s player of the year, becoming the first footballer to claim all three since Lachie Neale six years ago. His latest honour makes him arguably the most accomplished young player ever, swelling a resume that already includes the Magpies’ 2023 premiership and four All-Australian selections. Daicos will almost certainly win a third Copeland Trophy next month as well. He is the 10th Magpie to win a Brownlow Medal and first since Dane Swan 15 years ago, also joining Syd Coventry, brothers Albert and Harry Collier, Marcus Whelan, Des Fothergill, Len Thompson, Peter Moore and Nathan Buckley.



Daicos polled maximum votes in each of his first three games – either side of the Magpies’ round two bye – before he was a late withdrawal with a corked calf against Brisbane. That was the only match he missed all season. Daicos’ streak of maximum votes ended in a round five loss to Fremantle, where he still polled one off a 31-disposal effort, and it was enough to break an early deadlock with fellow great Bontempelli. Zak Butters briefly snatched a one-vote lead in round 10, but Daicos was back on top a round later when he was best afield against West Coast as Scott Pendlebury broke the VFL/AFL games record with his 433rd appearance. Smith drew level with the gun Pie on 23 votes in round 14, with Butters a single vote back, before Daicos shot away again a round later with three votes after a 41-touch masterclass at Port Adelaide’s expense.



Daicos proudly shows off the 2026 Brownlow Medal after a record-breaking night. AFL Photos That was when Daicos made his move, turning an entertaining count with superstars spread across the leaderboard into a demolition, like a Melbourne Cup winner turning for home. The man in the No.35 secured maximum votes in six straight matches between rounds 15 and 20 in an incredible purple patch to kick clear of the field and end any doubt about the result. Daicos polled 11 votes to finish equal 27th in his debut season in 2022; came third with 28 votes in 2023; second with 38 votes in 2024; and second with 32 votes last year. Umpires had access to player statistics for the first time this year to help with voting.

World.title: Albanese takes climate warning to New York, but fossil fuel experts test credibility
World.content:
PoliticsFederalParis Agreement Albanese takes climate warning to New York, but fossil fuel experts test credibility Rob Harris September 21, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The world can no longer rely on adapting to escalating climate catastrophes, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will warn as he opens Climate Week in New York with a warning that Australia is heading into a summer of extreme heat, bushfires and floods. The prime minister will tell a United Nations gathering that Australia’s abundant renewable potential – firmed by gas-powered generation – can help deliver its emissions target while declaring the next devastating fire or flood is becoming a question of when, not if. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will tell world leaders in New York that communities can no longer simply adapt to worsening weather disasters Dominic Lorrimer But as Albanese promotes Australia’s renewable energy gains, scientists say the government faces a credibility test given its continuing support for fossil fuel investment and status as one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters. “We can’t rely on the fortitude of our people alone, as tough as they are,” Albanese will say, according to a draft of his speech. “We need to come together, to meet the problem head on.”



Albanese will point to record-breaking temperatures and unprecedented wildfires across Europe during the northern summer while acknowledging Australia and its Pacific neighbours are bracing for their own difficult months. “With a record-breaking El Nino forecast, Australia and the Pacific nations are preparing for a potential summer of extreme heat, bushfires and floods,” he will say. Australia’s 2035 emissions target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 62 to 70 per cent below 2005 levels will be central to the government’s case as it prepares to lead COP31 negotiations with Turkey. He will acknowledge that not every extreme weather event can be directly attributed to climate change, but argue a warmer world is producing more frequent and intense events. “Unfortunately, without strong action, the science tells us these events will get worse and more intense,” Albanese says. “That’s more communities facing repeated trauma. Knowing the next flood or fire isn’t a matter of if, but when.”



Related Article Extreme weather What flash droughts and a super El Nino will mean for your summer Albanese will argue the 62 to 70 per cent target is “ambitious” but achievable, pointing to the rapid expansion of renewable energy and household batteries. Renewables supplied about half the grid at peak periods last summer, while more than 500,000 household batteries have been installed over the past year. But Australia’s climate credentials will face a tougher test as it takes on the presidency of the COP negotiations. Jennifer Morgan, a senior fellow at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University and former climate envoy for Germany, said Australia and Turkey were both pursuing potential new fossil fuel investments and had no coal phase-out date. “They’ve made progress in renewable energy, but I think their credibility – and their ability to therefore bring momentum and good outcomes to the COP – will depend on their taking further action at home,” Morgan said.



Natalie Jones, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said Australia and Turkey needed to provide “clear leadership” on transforming the fossil fuel road map agreed at last year’s COP30 in Brazil into concrete action. “This road map cannot be left in a dusty drawer,” Jones said. She said both countries needed to demonstrate how they would transition away from fossil fuels, noting Australia was the world’s third-largest fossil-fuel exporter. Albanese will argue the clean energy transition can deliver lower emissions and economic growth, with Australia using its solar and wind resources, batteries, critical minerals and rare earths to build new industries. “Electrification is the way to reduce emissions while maintaining economic growth,” he will say.



He will also emphasise Australia’s role in the Pacific, where some of the nations most vulnerable to climate change have contributed the least to global emissions. “Pacific nations have long been the strongest advocates for climate action,” Albanese will say. “And the value of listening to their perspectives has never been clearer.” The climate warning will be followed by a broader argument that the international rule of law itself is under strain when Albanese addresses a summit of the Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace and Prosperity at UN headquarters. The speech comes after Albanese formally launched Australia’s campaign for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-30. Albanese will argue middle powers need to accept greater responsibility for maintaining the international system, with Australia seeking to “listen with respect, partner as equals and protect what matters most – security, safety and prosperity”.



On Monday, Albanese will meet Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale before talks with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. AI will also feature in the diplomatic push, with Australia joining a joint statement at the UN calling for stronger controls over the rapidly developing technology. World.title: Sydney boy fighting for life after ‘tragic’ shooting in luxury apartment complex
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Sydney boy fighting for life after ‘tragic’ shooting in luxury apartment complex Daniel Lo Surdo Updated September 21, 2026 — 9:22pm ,first published 6:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three 18-year-olds are in police custody after a boy, 11, was shot in the face and neck inside a luxury Sydney apartment complex on Monday, leaving a confronting scene for officers who stormed the property to render life-saving treatment to the child. Paramedics rushed through the Moda apartment complex on Fairway Drive, Norwest, about 5pm after reports the child had been shot. The boy was conscious and speaking with paramedics while they administered urgent assistance at the complex where he is believed to live, but his health worsened as he was taken to Westmead Children’s Hospital in a critical condition. Police establish a crime scene where the child was shot on Monday. Wolter Peeters The 11-year-old was in the apartment with four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman, none of whom was injured when the gun was fired. Three of the 18-year-olds were arrested and taken to Castle Hill and Riverstone Police Stations for further questioning. Charges against the three were likely but not certain, two police sources told this masthead, and would be determined by further interviews with the occupants and searches of the scene.



The nature of potential charges will also depend on the condition of the boy. Some occupants were related to the boy, while others were friends of the family. The State Crime Command’s Homicide Squad has been notified of the shooting as the investigation continues. All occupants have been interviewed by police, and are assisting with police inquiries. Hills Police Area Commander Naomi Moore promised a “thorough and expansive” probe, saying the shooting was among the most awful scenes she has encountered. Tactical and general duties officers rushed to the Norwest apartment complex on Monday. Wolter Peeters “It is an absolutely tragic situation, and we’ve seen tragedy across Sydney in the last couple of days, this is not far from the worst that I’ve seen,” she said. Tactical officers and a police helicopter swarmed the complex as they combed the property for the firearm used in the shooting, which had not been found by 10pm on Monday.



Officers searched the park adjacent to the complex, as a large exclusion zone covering much of Fairway Drive was established to assist the search for the gun. Police search a park for the gun used in the shooting of the boy. Wolter Peeters No firearms are registered to the address. The circumstances of the shooting and how the gun came to be in the home are under investigation, as are the events leading to the incident and who pulled the trigger. Detectives do not believe the shooting is linked to organised crime, police sources said, and are treating it as a separate, standalone incident. A large exclusion zone has been established on Fairway Drive. Wolter Peeters



The boy’s mother is with her son in hospital, and was, according to Moore, “as stressed as any parent would be”. Officers are investigating whether the gun was accidentally fired inside the apartment, either by the boy or another occupant. Police are still working to determine who fired the weapon. Tactical officers swarmed the Norwest complex where the boy was shot. Wolter Peeters There are 217 properties in the Moda complex, ranging from one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments, according to developers Arden Group, which said each home delivers a “luxury lifestyle” to residents. It is adjacent to the Castle Hill Country Club and two blocks from Norwest station, and includes an indoor swimming pool, gym and a rooftop entertaining terrace.



The Moda apartment complex offers a “luxury lifestyle” to residents in its 217 homes. Aussie Home Loans Residents were seen filtering through the front of the building as tactical police descended on the building, while paramedics moved into the complex. Others stood on balconies, perplexed about the expanding police operation occurring below. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Springing into step
World.content:
“Now that spring is here, I’ve been keeping track of the various local fêtes and fairs with the allure of trash, treasure and pre loved bric-a-brac,” writes Paul Taylor of Winston Hills. “At last count, I can look forward to a nursing home jumble sale, a school white elephant and a church charity bazaar, and the various charity market stalls in carparks across the district. There’s one, though, that has caught my eye - the Ugg Boot Car Boot Sale. I’ll be hotfooting it there!”

“I’ve thought of a way to avoid AI killing us all (C8),” claims Alan Phillips of Mosman. “Simple. Feed it with the last 50 years of Column 8 to train on. That will drive it mad, and it will terminate itself.”

As long as it contains this offering from Merilyn McClung of Forestville: “My young granddaughter asked why, when a building is finished, it is still called a building? She wondered if C8-ers might know.”

“The kids liked the Bee Gees (C8), but I ran across Frank Sinatra in a bar in Honolulu in 1957,” says John Crowe of Cherrybrook. “We shared a couple of beers. He belied his reputation and was happy to yarn with a young unknown Australian.”

“The Mouseketeers were performing at the Sydney Stadium in Rushcutters Bay”, circa 1960, recalls Judy Klein of Double Bay. “At the end of the show, Annette Funicello looked directly at me, smiled and waved. I have never forgotten the thrill.”

World.title: Final design chosen for iconic Nullarbor photo stop
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWARoads Final design chosen for iconic Nullarbor photo stop Sarah Smith September 21, 2026 — 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An iconic photo spot along the Nullarbor is getting a makeover. The Western Australia–South Australia border sign has stood tall for three decades, but it is now set to be replaced. The WA-SA border crossing sign on the Nullarbor is getting a makeover. A public vote between two designs across 14 social media posts weighed up “bush to beach” or “ochre and ocean”. The latter eventually prevailed, receiving 888 votes – almost 80 per cent of the total vote.



It’s a design Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti believes represents “reflects the striking colours of the border landscape”. “The WA-SA border sign is an iconic stop for the thousands of people travelling across the Nullarbor each year,” she said. “It’s great to see the community having their say on the sign design, and I’m looking forward to seeing it in place next year.” The current sign along Eyre Highway will begin being demolished next month. The WA letters were replaced in 2023 after they fell down to corrosion.



The new sign will be installed in early 2027 and is set to cost taxpayers $900,000 – and WA will foot the entire bill. Editor's pick Planning and development Green light for $10 million Fast Eddys replacement, with hopes for a Reuben on the menu “Getting money out of South Australia is pretty hard,” Saffioti said. “They are already bemoaning about our GST deal, so we’ll just pay it.” Meanwhile, the border crossing will be accompanied by a shelter 4½ metres tall and 11 metres long.



Main Roads WA worked with key stakeholders, including the Goldfields-Esperance Development Commission, Shire of Dundas, Tourism WA, the Department for Infrastructure and Transport in South Australia, Tourism SA, and the Mirning Traditional Owners, to finalise design options for the new structure and information panels. Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent said the new sign would be a “fitting entryway to our great state, celebrating the rich colours of our region from the red dirt to the blue sky”. World.title: Tairāwhiti's beaches overrun with forestry slash
World.content:
Audio player for " Tairāwhiti's beaches overrun with forestry slash " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/environment/1500603%2Ftairawhiti-s-beaches-overrun-with-forestry-slash

Tairāwhiti's beaches overrun with forestry slash Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Tairāwhiti's beaches are some of the most well-known and loved in New Zealand, only now they're covered in forestry slash. It's so normal that some children have never known the sandy shores in their rōhe without it. Teuila Fuatai reports.

Graeme Atkins lives about 30 minutes from Ruatoria, near the mouth of Waiapu River and Tikapa beach.

The hilly, gravel road to his house runs alongside the Waiapu, and on a clear day, you get a full view of the lower part of the expansive waterway. It's wide and shallow, with the riverbed showing in a lot of places. Steep, stony hillside where the road is cut into run along one side while farmland borders the other.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405351947112

Atkin's house, like all the properties around him, is off the grid. That includes the local marae, which runs on solar and has a chest freezer whānau around the area use for meat.

Being self-sufficient, living off the land, and the moana, is part of life, and it's been that way for generations, Atkins says.

"You don't see any power lines here," he says with a grin.

One of his three mokopuna, one-year-old Te Ahupo, hangs out with us for the afternoon.

Atkins says he'll be the 22nd generation of his family to whakapapa to the area.

"So that's such a comforting thought."

Graeme Atkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Less hopeful, and infinitely more challenging is what's happening with forestry in the region.

We head a couple of hundred metres up the road to look at Tikapa beach.

Like all the beaches we've seen on our trip around the East Cape, it's covered in forestry waste.

The slash and woody debris are washed down from forestry blocks when it rains, and when there's a major weather event - like cyclones Gabrielle and Hale in 2023 - the waterways, rivers and coastline are choked with it.

Atkins shows us pictures and videos of the beach after the storm - at first glance, it looks like someone's emptied dozens of boxes of match sticks onto a surface and taken a photo.

That's what came down the river, he says.

Another video shows kōura and paua littered among the slash and logs.

They are another casualty of what's happening on the forestry blocks, Atkins says, because when there's a storm, along with the trees and waste, huge amounts of soil and sediment go into the waterways and sea.

"I think they just get choked," he says, "it's heartbreaking."

Atkins says they first started to notice the slash on the beaches about 10 years ago.

"Our childhood around here, and the access to the beach - we could go to the beach whenever we wanted to.

"Since about 2014, 2015, once they started harvesting inside those Cyclone Bola forests…we just started noticing more and more forest waste - slash, logs, whatever you want to call it - ending up on our beach."

Cyclone Bola, which devastated the region in 1988, is mentioned in every conversation I have about forestry impacts in Tairāwhiti.

Like Gabrielle and Hale, the weather event had significant and long-lasting impacts on the region.

For hundreds of mana whenua like Atkins, who are shareholders in land blocks across their rōhe through whakapapa, it also triggered a fundamental shift in the use of that land to pine forest plantations.

The pine planting frenzy post-Cyclone Bola

About 40 minutes up the cost from Atkin's place is the Whakaangiangi Valley, near Te Araroa.

We meet Roger Haerewa at his house, which looks out at several forestry blocks dominating the valley. He points to the Awatere block, which he used to be a trustee of, and talks about how things were in the area after Cyclone Bola.

The view from Roger Haerewa's house. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"Bola left a lot of damage on our whenua - huge slips," he says, "and forestry at the time was the way to solve it.

"I was on Awatere and Tarere at the time when we planted it. We thought it was a good idea... for future work."

Haerewa is describing the push into pine plantations the government incentivised at the time.

The policies, implemented through the East Coast Forestry Project, sought to stem erosion across the region, particularly on steep hillsides through the planting of pine. The jobs and industry that would result were promoted as a twin-benefit.

Not only have the benefits not eventuated, but Māori landowners have also been disproportionately affected because of the kind of land that was targeted through incentives.

By the late 1980s, much of the land which remained in Māori ownership in Tairāwhiti was classified as marginal - essentially it was too steep to do much with like farming. Planting it with pine was seen as an investment, Haerewa says.

Roger Haerewa. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Now, it's not just the forestry waste and erosion that's causing harm and concern, there's serious questions over the financial viability of harvesting pine - with the price of logs down over the decades and the costs of transporting them to Gisborne climbing.

"At the moment, we've still got forests that should have been cut, but we can't cut it because the owners would get nothing," he says.

'The messaging I'm receiving now is that we are doing too much'

Gisborne District Council is the regulatory body for the forestry industry. It's trying to forge a path to more sustainable land use across the region with the tools it has under the Resource Management Act.

Mayor Rehette Stoltz admits it's a work-in-progress.

Since cyclones Gabrielle and Hale, the council's taken a tougher approach in its consenting and monitoring processes for the forestry industry. The shift followed a ministerial inquiry into the disasters and damage caused by forestry waste, woody debris and sediment in Tairāwhiti and Wairoa.

It's resulted in the council using enforcement orders - issued by the Environment Court against forestry companies - to target areas like poor harvesting practises and unmanaged slash.

But that hasn't come without setbacks.

It's been nearly a year since the council's land transition business case was shot down by the central government. The council was asking for a $359 million contribution or co-investment over a decade to help stabilise the region's most erosion-prone land.

More recently, Stoltz has been contacted by several government ministers over her council's approach to the forestry industry.

Chris Bishop, the minister responsible for reform of the Resource Manage Act, has also refused to grant the council an exemption to implement a plan change that would've enabled it to use more stringent rules to manage erosion-prone land through its consenting processes.

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"It's tough," Stoltz says.

"After Cyclone Gabrielle, the [Ministerial inquiry] panel recommendations made it clear that we had to step up in the consenting, monitoring, and enforcement area.

"The messaging I'm receiving now is that we are doing too much in that space, and it is tough for us because we do want to do the right thing.

"What that that means for us is that the work that we've done in the last two to three years can't really get traction, because we need a plan change to do that."

The uncertainty looming over its regulatory work has led to the council commissioning an independent review into its own consenting, compliance and enforcement practices. Alongside that, Forestry Minister Todd McClay's appointed facilitator Doug Leeder to advise it on what's happening with forestry in the region.

Leeder's a month into his contract and has met with both Stoltz and the council's chief executive Nedine Thatcher Swann. He's also met with the council's consenting, compliance and enforcement teams.

He told Checkpoint there's been a breakdown in the relationship between the council and the forestry industry.

Audio player for " Diggers needed to clear forestry debris crowding " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/environment/1500603%2Ftairawhiti-s-beaches-overrun-with-forestry-slash

Diggers needed to clear forestry debris crowding Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

"Essentially, there's been a lack of trust. It has broken down between the regulator, being [Gisborne District Council] and the forestry companies.

"But that's just not forestry companies. It's those mum and dad businesses, those family businesses that operate harvesting operations throughout the Gisborne Tairāwhiti area."

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Despite that, he doesn't believe the council are being overzealous in its approach, and says the use of enforcement orders have been justified.

"I think, on balance, enforcement orders have done their job, and it's really brought focus to the forest companies to get their act together and clean up some of the stuff."

Leeder says he's due to report to McClay on his progress by the end of the week.

'The nannies would be shocked at the condition the land's been left in'

Atkins, who's been working with the council on its land transition case, says change has to happen now.

He's a member of Mana Taiao Tairāwhiti, a group pushing for sustainable land use in the region that was established after Gabrielle.

"There's a responsibility on us as kaitiaki to leave it in a better state for the generations to come.

"That's the underlying principles and how it operates around here. Kaitiakitanga is to be able to practice that on your own whenua - it doesn't get any better than that."

He looks at his moko Te Ahupo and says the decisions made around the use of whenua by his predecessors were made with the best intentions. In hindsight, that just hasn't worked out.

"I reckon that the nannies that signed those blocks up, in good will and good faith - that they were going to provide employment and the whenua was going to be cared for - I reckon they'd be shocked if they saw the condition that the land has been left in.

"When you fly around here and see all the damage to our whenua, and a lot of it is permanent damage because the land has gone right down to the base rock. Nothing's going to grow on rock - we don't want that."

RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Now, it's about shifting away from the practises which shouldn't be happening so future generations have a chance to thrive on the land they belong to, Graeme says.

"You know, there's always going to be a place for forestry here, just not on that real steep land. And same with farming.

World.title: 'She was a lost soul' - agencies under microscope at inquest into girls death
World.content:
A father has told an inquest into the suspected suicide of a 12-year-old New Plymouth girl in June 2017 she was a "little angel"' and a "fun loving kid" whose life got more and more difficult.

In a statement read by his counsel Quinn Katene-Rosa, the man - who cannot be identified for legal reasons - said he hoped the inquest before Coroner Heather McKenzie would provide answers about government agencies' response to his daughter's living conditions at the time of her death.

"Her life unfortunately sucked. She was a lost soul who did not receive the care and support she needed from the government and agencies and services that were supposed to be there for her. At times it felt to me like no one really cared or, to put it plainly, gave a shit."

Two years after the girl's death, a drug-addicted Taranaki woman was jailed for four years and three months for the physical and psychological abuse of three children.

The father said he hoped missed opportunities to help his daughter would be identified so other people didn't have to go through what he had.

"My daughter's life had value. She was loved beyond measure, and she deserved the opportunity to live the life she had ahead of her. I'm here today because I want to understand what happened to her, and because she can no longer speak for herself.

"I know that this inquest will not bring her back. What I do hope is that her lived experiences and the pain and distress that her and her two sisters went through can bring about meaningful change to a system so that, where possible, other kids in similar circumstances are supported and have a better outcome."

Coroner McKenzie earlier laid out the parameters of the inquest and apologised for delays to the hearing taking place.

She said it would not revisit the previous criminal case nor investigate the immediate cause of the girl's death, but would instead focus on the role of Oranga Tamariki, police and other agencies in her care.

Coroner McKenzie said it would then move to look what would happen today if a similar case arose and look at what recommendations could be made.

She acknowledged the courage of the girl's whānau in agreeing to be part of proceedings.

Counsel assisting the court Rebekah Jordan opened by saying the 12- year-old had been born in Christchurch, but lived most of her life in Waitara and New Plymouth.

While attending an intermediate school in the city, her appearance and behaviour resulted in staff visiting her home on several occasions and subsequently seeking help from Oranga Tamariki, police and other social agencies.

The key social worker involved in the case in the weeks before the girl's death was questioned at length.

The visibly upset social worker, who cannot be named, said a "report of concern" had been received from the school and she met with the principal and a community constable.

She said a home safety assessment was done and a whānau agreement drawn up which proposed counselling and substance-use support for the mother and individual counselling for the child.

"I advised police that Oranga Tamariki will remain involved under a family whānau agreement. On June 13th, I had communication with Tū Tama Wāhine o Taranaki, confirming via email that the mother presented once to their service but did not attend her next scheduled appointment."

A safety plan involving school staff, an aunt, neighbours, and emergency services was also agreed.

Under questioning from Jordan, the social worker said at the time she hadn't been aware of previous "reports of concern" from 2013 and 2015 involving the girl and admitted "it would've been useful".

She acknowledged a screening test done to assess the mood of the child found she felt "sad" and had "thoughts of ending it all" but didn't have a plan to suicide, although she was self harming.

The plan was to seek counselling for the child but there was little follow up on whether she or her mother were attending.

The social worker was quizzed by Jordan as to whether it was fair to to say that Oranga Tamariki had assessed the child's home as being safe and secure because she was left in the home.

The social worker answered: "I believe so".

She was pushed further to say whether it would be also fair to say that was Oranga Tamariki's conclusion until the girl died, but that changed after her death?

After some reflection she replied: "Yes, it changed, I believe, after that.".

Despite at times struggling to remember events from nine years ago, the social worker was adamant that Oranga Tamariki was unaware of any violence or neglect in the home before the child's death and did not have evidence supporting an application for custody.

A specialist teacher working in the area of student well-being and behaviour also gave evidence.

She had been seeing the child at least once a week before her death.

"My question now as it was back then is, if a 12-year-old child needs a safety plan to be in their home, what are they doing there? Almost 10 years later, I cannot say that I have really seen any changes."

She said the various agencies involved with the child worked in silos and did not collaborate closely enough.

The social worker and the police believed that the child was presenting with challenging behaviours and they were satisfied with supports being put in place for the whānau and that stronger boundaries for her were required.

"No one asked the why behind the actions and only viewed them as the actions of a naughty child.

The specialist teacher said all behaviours were a form of communication.

"When working with people in the way that our agencies do, it is important to understand that and not make judgements about what they see, but to ask what is underneath and to look for the why."

In this case the police looked at the legal side and if any laws had been broken and the social worker only saw the disruptive behaviours being displayed as acts of gaining attention.

"No one asked why or what she was trying to tell everyone. No one saw beyond the scope of their role."

Coroner McKenzie praised the specialist teacher for her efforts to help the girl and asked what her impressions of her were.

Addressing her father directly, she said his daughter was a wonderful young lady with a gift for music that was self-taught.

"When she was happy, when she was within herself, she would light up a room. Her laugh was infectious.

"You know, she had dreams. She wanted to go places and do something. And I was hell-bent on trying to get her there. I gave her a magic wand because I wanted her to have hopes and dreams because she didn't believe she had a right to them.

"She was an amazing young lady, and I enjoyed spending time with her."

Fighting back tears the girl's father stood and thank her for all she had done for his daughter.

"I just wish that the other agencies had listened to you, and maybe if they'd listened to you and the right support was put around her, this lovely girl would still be here today."

World.title: Cashmere Club fights for liquor licence after man's fatal fall while heavy drinking
World.content:
When a Christchurch man fell and hit his head during a heavy drinking session celebrating his 70th birthday at the Cashmere Club, the general manager passed him a glass of wine.

Hours later Colin Hunt, known as Charlie, again fell and hit his head while leaving the club. He died in hospital the following day.

The Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority is hearing an application by police to strip or suspend liquor licences held by the Cashmere Club and the manager at the time, Rebecca Hine. The club argued it would have to close if it could no longer serve alcohol.

Hunt arrived at the club just before 2pm on September 19, 2025 and arranged a $3000 bar tab.

At a hearing on Monday, senior constable Olivia Bensley outlined drinking by Hunt and his group captured on CCTV over several hours that evening, including being served trays of shots.

CCTV of Charlie Hunt and his friends at the club. Supplied

The group included club general manager Murray Davies, who was a close friend of Hunt and was not working that day.

Just before 11.30pm one of the people in the group went to the bar while trying to balance a pint glass on his head.

The glass fell to the ground and smashed and the man was served another beer.

The bar closed just after midnight and the till was put away but Hunt's group stayed on drinking and was joined by staff members, some of whom had been working and some who were off-duty, including Hine who was duty manager until 8.30pm.

The club was not licensed to sell alcohol after 1am but the drinking continued, with more shots including another tray of 11 B52s (Kahlua and Baileys), one Galliano and one Fireball whiskey.

Bensley described signs of intoxication in the CCTV, including people becoming more affectionate towards each other and stumbling.

Senior Constable Olivia Bensley, formerly of the police Alcohol Harm Prevention Unit, gives evidence. The Press / KAI SCHWOERER

Hine pulled down a man's pants and fell to the ground.

The man was later seen with his pants down exposing his genitals and on another occasion, several people including Hunt put their hands on and between his buttocks.

Another woman deliberately bumped into Hunt, knocking him off his stool.

On several occasions Hunt could be seen stumbling and catching himself before he fell.

At 1.30am Hunt fell from his bar stool and whacked his head on the table behind him.

The footage showed friends and staff members going to his aid and offering a bag of ice, but he was also handed a glass of red wine by Davies.

The Cashmere Club sign. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

At 2am another tray of shots was brought out but the group packed up to leave shortly after, with $2300 spent on Hunt's tab, including $182 on three platters.

As they made their way out of the club, Hunt offered his hand to help a woman sitting on the steps but stumbled and fell, hitting his head.

An ambulance was called and Hunt was taken to hospital, where he died on September 21.

Bensely said a toxicology report showed Hunt's blood alcohol reading was 226 m/100 millilitres of blood, which equated to four-and-a-half times over the legal driving limit.

Cashmere Club president Andrew Webster told the authority Hunt had many friends at the club who were devastated by his death.

He said Hine remained employed and disputed the allegations.

Cashmere Club president Andrew Webster. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Davies had resigned as general manager but was still a club member and organised pool tournaments because of his involvement with the sport.

Webster said it was clear the club's compliance culture was not strict enough at the time and the bar had morphed into something akin to drinking at a private house, rather than a licensed premises.

The events of that night were a one-off and would not happen again, Webster said.

He told the authority the whole club was at risk if it lost its liquor licence because alcohol sales were its biggest income stream.

Club lawyer Tim Mackenzie said police told him the club should have made more changes directly after Hunt's death, with "a wholesale investigation and terminations on the spot".

Cashmere Club lawyer Tim Mackenzie. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

He said that was with hindsight, pointing out police took nine months to make an application to the licensing authority even though they had CCTV shortly after Hunt's death.

Police prosecutor Karyn South said the club's breach was one of the most serious, with the most serious of consequences.

"No one in that group on the night appeared the slightest bit concerned that the CCTV would ever be checked to see what time the premises were actually cleared, who drinks on the job, who is pouring drinks and not paying for them, who is going behind the bar, who is flailing around with their genitals exposed until two in the morning," she said.

South said that showed a complete lack of board oversight and control because "here were the general manager and the bar manager fully participating in what was happening".

South said today's board was almost identical to the board that at was in place at the time.

World.title: Flooding occurred five times at Moa Point in months leading to the failure, new report reveals
World.content:
A newly-released report into the Moa Point failure reveals flooding occurred five times at the sewage treatment plant in the months leading up to disaster.

It also raises questions about the plant's alarm systems - including whether alarms were sighted but not acted on, and that others weren't programmed to trigger immediate pagers.

About 16 billion litres of raw sewage had spilled into the city's south coast since Moa Point catastrophically flooded on February 4.

The report from infrastructure consultancy firm AECOM had been withheld until now due to insurance discussions.

Its investigation did not identify a single sole cause of the flooding but found it was caused by a combination of technical and organisation factors.

The plant was undergoing critical upgrades to its ultra-violet disinfection channels at the time of the flooding. This reduced the plant's capacity to treat sewage from the community.

A Moa Point wastewater sign. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

With sewage diverted to a bypass pipe, heavy rain and increased flows on the night caused air bubbles in the bypass pipe choking the wastewater and causing it to flood.

But the report said overflows occurred in one of the UV channels twice in October 2025, twice in January and once on February 3 - the day before the disaster.

While these did not spill into the wider plant, they did flood one of the offline UV pipes.

The report noted by October 22 2025, crews were warned flooding could occur in storm events. In an incident report after the January 15 flooding, Veolia operators warned there was a risk of pumping into the short outfall pipe if flows exceeded 3200 litres per second.

A meeting was held between Wellington Water staff, Veolia and Stantec on February 3 to discuss the flooding incidents, where a Veolia staff member said the bypass pipe being used could only take 1500 litres per second, and there was a risk of overflow to the short pipe at Tarakena Bay if sewage flows passed 3000 litres per second.

Check LAWA signage on Wellington's South Coast. (File photo) Kate Pereyra/RNZ

"Veolia have explored options for ways to mitigate/eliminate this and found limited options", meeting minutes cited in the report said.

People raised the potential to limit flow into the pipe, the report said, but this was not taken up because it would result in discharging sewage into the short pipe close to the shore at Tarakena Bay.

The report said Fire and Emergency staff were the first to alert operations staff flooding had happened, shortly after 1am on February 4.

While two Moa Point alarms appeared to have been sighted by a duty manager at 12.19 am and 12.34 am, the report authors' said they were not aware of staff turning off pumps and equipment remotely.

Additionally, several critical alarms triggered before and during the flooding were not pager alarms, and weren't programmed to require immediate operator action.

A Veolia spokesperson said unlike the Crown Review, the AECOM report was not independent or a "complete view of the situation".

The spokesperson said the report explicitly excluded roles, responsibilities and contractural requirements that Veolia was not the contractor or controller of the UV filtration upgrade.

Untreated wastewater signs at Lyall Bay, Wellington. (File photo) RNZ / Krystal Gibbens

"The area was isolated and roped off. Our role was to provide advice and operate the broader plant. As noted in the Crown Review, Veolia alerted Wellington Water to concerns about the project."

The spokesperson said remote monitoring routines that had worked successfully for 28 years were being followed because the UV upgrade had been classified by Wellington Water as a business-as-usual process.

"On the night of the Moa Point incident, as soon as Veolia staff were onsite they initiated action in response to the emergency."

The AECOM report stated this incident was not the result of a single decision or operational failure, the spokesperson said, but the result of longstanding weaknesses in governance and accountability.

Veolia said the plant was on track to be fully operating by February 2027.

"The well reported underlying issue that led to this event is the chronic underinvestment in water infrastructure that has persisted for up to 30 years."

World.title: 'It's certainly not safe for the patients': Six staff resign from  Pahīatua medical centre
World.content:
Six staff at the Pahīatua Medical Centre have resigned today, amid growing concern around extreme workloads and patient safety.

Almost 5000 patients depend on the clinic in the Tararua district.

But over the past two years, 81 staff have resigned from the Tararua Health Group, alleging unsafe workloads and dangerously long wait times for appointments and tests.

Registered nurse Mark Emmerson resigned along with five of his colleagues today.

He told Checkpoint he was "sick" at the decision, but also "relieved" the matter had come to the nation's attention.

"As nurses, we try. We will run ourselves ragged until to get the job done. But it's certainly not safe for the patients. It's not safe for the staff psychologically."

Audio player for " Six staff resign from Pahiatua Medical Centre over safety concerns " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1498378%2Fit-s-certainly-not-safe-for-the-patients-six-staff-resign-from-pahiatua-medical-centre

Six staff resign from Pahiatua Medical Centre over safety concerns Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

He said the clinic was a "pressure cooker" as there were limited clinicians.

"We have a nurse practitioner that works for us four days a week. We've got a nurse prescriber that is full-time, but she's leaving in two weeks."

He said a lot of experience had left Pahīatua Medical centre today: a phlebotomist of 15 years, an administrator of 21 years, three registered nurses including himself, and a nurse practitioner.

He said the clinic would "certainly not" function without them.

He said an acute clinic had been set up a few months ago, but patients were being seen there when it was not appropriate.

"We're getting ACC, we're getting working income renewals and all of that sort of thing just can't be done in an acute setting."

He stressed that the staff were not leaving the community behind.

"We have put out there that we are willing to work with other providers who recognise the importance of our community, recognise the importance of our staff and are willing to work with us towards providing essential primary health care in the area."

Locals rally outside Pahiatua Medical Centre in support of staff. Supplied

Tony Wai - chief executive of the Primary Health Organisation, which managed the clinic's contract - responded that he felt concerns could be addressed with a plan, but he was not sure what that plan would look like.

However, health advocacy group Patient Voice Aotearoa called for a review into every patient who had a screening test through Tararua Health Group.

Co-founder and spokesperson Malcolm Mulholland said the group serviced 9500 patients in the wider area.

He told Checkpoint a review was important to understand patients' status as a delayed cancer diagnosis resulted in negative outcomes for patients.

Audio player for " Major concerns over state of rural health services " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1498378%2Fit-s-certainly-not-safe-for-the-patients-six-staff-resign-from-pahiatua-medical-centre

Major concerns over state of rural health services Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

He said the health minister and Health NZ were responsible.

"Ultimately it's up to the minister and Health New Zealand to intervene and say 'enough is enough; we're pulling the contract and we're going back to the community to see what best meets their needs'."

Mulholland said other regions were facing similar problems, citing Kirikiri as an example of where there might not be a GP within a couple of years.

In order to retain GPs in rural areas, he argued that Health NZ should hire practitioners directly.

"There's no middleman, there's no PHO, there's no business, there's no practice."

He said the approach would hand doctors more freedom as well.

World.title: Labour rules out changes to interest deductibility settings for landlords if elected
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has ruled out any changes to interest deductibility settings for landlords, if elected.

The coalition government in 2024 reinstated landlords' ability to claim tax deductions for interest on residential investment properties.

Opposition parties decried the government prioritising "tax cuts for landlords" which cost around $2.8 billion over four years.

But Hipkins on Monday confirmed Labour would not change the policy, because it was committed to a capital gains tax instead.

"We did foreshadow when we announced a capital gains tax that that was changing our thinking around how we would look at interest deductibility in the future, and that has now been confirmed," he said.

"[Under Labour] landlords will ultimately be subjected to a capital gains tax when they sell their investment properties.

"If you were to make changes to interest deductibility, it would ultimately change then, potentially, the capital gains tax settings."

Hipkins said he also did not want to risk landlords hiking rents, because people were already struggling to pay them.

National criticises 'rank hypocrisy'

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown questioned how Labour would pay for its policies without the additional revenue.

He said the move demonstrated "rank hypocrisy".

"After three years of attacking 'tax cuts for landlords' and blaming them for the cost-of-living crisis, Chris Hipkins has performed an eleventh-hour u-turn and decided to keep the very policy Labour has spent years condemning," he said.

World.title: Chris Hipkins wants police to 'front up' and explain 'ongoing matter' with Rakesh Naidoo
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins says police need to "front up" and "explain what is going on", following comments by the Police Minister about Labour's top cop candidate Rakesh Naidoo.

It comes after Police Minister Mark Mitchell last week said there was an "ongoing matter" in relation to Naidoo, but would not say what it was.

On Monday, following questions from RNZ, Hipkins said he had "absolute confidence in Rakesh Naidoo".

"He has behaved with absolute integrity throughout this process."

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Hipkins said Mitchell "should not be using his position as minister of police to make unsubstantiated insinuations against the character of a rival political candidate".

"Neither Mr Naidoo nor the Labour Party have any idea what is actually being alleged.

"The police need to front up here and explain what is going on."

In response, Mitchell told RNZ Hipkins "should not be commenting on something that has nothing to do with him".

"As I have said I am unable to comment any further as I am observing the rules around 6c of the Official Information Act.

"That is the response I gave when asked by media about Mr Naidoo. I have nothing further to add."

Naidoo's candidacy - announced in June - prompted public criticism from Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and minister Mark Mitchell, both claiming the superintendent should have declared his intentions earlier.

An internal review later concluded that Naidoo had complied with police policy, though noted it would have been "prudent" for him to have given his superiors more advance warning.

In response to media questions last week Mitchell said there were "two or three different facets to this situation".

"And they have dealt with one of them."

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

After the review's findings were announced, Mitchell confirmed to RNZ he had two phone calls with Chambers on 8 and 9 June.

"[The calls] were to discuss the situation, including the response to media queries, concerns the minister held in relation to the disclosure timeline, including pre-existing concerns regarding a sensitive briefing Mr Naidoo had attended with the minister prior to Mr Naidoo advising anyone at police of his political intentions."

Mitchell declined to release information in relation to the sensitive briefing under section 6 (c) of the Official Information Act.

Section 6 (c) relates to prejudicing the maintenance of the law, including the prevention, investigation, and detection of offences, and the right to a fair trial.

Mitchell's office confirmed to RNZ earlier this month the grounds for withholding under Section 6c of the OIA still applied.

Mitchell referred to the OIA again last week and said "the OIA is very clear it says there's matters that can't be disclosed because there's an ongoing matter".

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He said he was unable to comment further.

Hipkins said last week Mitchell had "crossed a line here".

"He is the minister of police, and he is using that office to spread claims about a Labour candidate who doesn't even know what the specific accusation against him is. You cannot use the power of the police portfolio to invent allegations against political opponents.

"Mark Mitchell should be ashamed of himself. Mark Mitchell should not be commenting, directing or be privy to police employment matters."

Police declined to comment last week.

RNZ earlier asked for comment on whether there was an investigation into Naidoo.

A police spokesperson said "we have no further comment on the matter".

Speaking to RNZ earlier for the first time since being recruited by Labour, Naidoo said he would not do anything differently with hindsight, pointing to a police review which cleared him of any wrongdoing.

In a sit-down interview marking his entry into the election campaign, Naidoo remained diplomatic about the criticism levelled at him by his superiors.

"In my view, they were expressing themselves based on the information that they had," he said.
