World.title: NRL set to axe ref Klein after controversial semifinal ending
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL is reportedly set to axe top referee Ashley Klein for the preliminary finals after admitting the Warriors were wrongly denied a crucial late penalty in their 12-10 semifinal loss to Newcastle.

NRL officials today confirmed the Warriors should have been awarded a penalty for an escort infringement by the Knights' Tyson Frizell with a minute left in yesterday's Eden Park thriller.

Had the penalty been awarded, the Warriors would have had the chance to level at 12-12 via a penalty goal from just to the side of the posts and send the match to extra time.

NRL investigating Eden Park incident The NRL is threatening to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

But the call was instead missed on the field, with the bunker unable to review the play, despite a stoppage for an injury soon afterwards.

A comprehensive NRL review of Newcastle's 12-10 semifinal did, however, back the bunker over two other contentious calls.

First, it was deemed that bunker official Chris Butler was right to rule that Warriors centre Ali Leiataua got a thumb to a ball before it went to ground late in the match.

The NRL also supported the bunker's decision to stick with the on-field call of a strip against Warrior Te Maire Martin.

But it is the non-call on Frizell that will annoy the Warriors most.

The Newcastle veteran appeared to get in the way of Leka Halasima as he chased through on a kick in the Warriors' last attacking raid.

Given the seconds that would have come off the clock while the Warriors lined up the shot, there would probably not have been time for a restart.

"I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us," Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the game.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

"The last one, two points would have drawn the game, he is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball which they've told us you can't do."

AAP understands Klein will pay for the error by losing his spot in the preliminary finals, with Grant Atkins or Gerard Sutton likely to be called up.

Klein has overseen every game of the past five State of Origin series and two of the last four grand finals.

He had been expected to referee last year's decider, before losing out to Atkins following 18 penalties in a Melbourne-Cronulla preliminary final.

Meanwhile, the NRL have threatened bans for fans who threw projectiles at Klein as he walked off Eden Park on Sunday night.

Vision showed a mass of bottles and rubbish being thrown at the long-time official, with Warriors great Shaun Johnson labelling the fans' behaviour "embarrassing".

AAP

World.title: Daicos wins first Brownlow Medal and sets new modern-day voting record
World.content:
Collingwood superstar Nick Daicos has finally claimed his first Brownlow Medal in a runaway victory with a record-breaking 47 votes.

The 23-year-old surged to a perfect nine votes from his first three games, led from round 11, then registered six consecutive best-on-ground performances between rounds 15 and 20 to seal victory by round 21.

Daicos won the AFL's greatest individual honour from Geelong star Bailey Smith (36) and Western Bulldogs champion Marcus Bontempelli (34).

The Magpie had 13 three-vote performances and beat the previous votes record of 45 set by Carlton champion Patrick Cripps in 2024.

Daicos, the son of Magpies great Peter Daicos, conceded he was relieved, having finally prevailed after runner-up finishes in the past two seasons, a third placing in 2023 and an eighth place in his debut year of 2022.

"I've just learned not to trust the the betting markets, to be honest," Daicos said at Monday night's vote count.

"But no, there is (relief).

"It's a massive award, and I'm so privileged to be up here. And yeah, I can't believe I'm a Brownlow medallist, to be honest."

The dynamic midfielder had already snared the AFL Players Association and AFL Coaches Association player-of-the-year awards this season.

It was the fourth consecutive year that Daicos was favourite, and with the umpires able to consult statistics for the first time, the star Magpie was irresistible.

Nick Daicos and partner Arlette Amor. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Daicos averaged 34.9 disposals, 5.7 clearances, 6.7 inside-50s and 1.1 goals.

The brilliant playmaker was edged out by Gold Coast's Matt Rowell last year and Cripps the year before, when Daicos polled 38 votes.

Daicos, the Collingwood vice-captain who's widely expected to be named skipper next season, is the club's first Brownlow medallist since Dane Swan in 2011.

Bontempelli and Smith were the next best performers ahead of Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), Brisbane star Will Ashcroft (27), Carlton's two-time winner Patrick Cripps (27) and North Melbourne's Harry Sheezel (27).

Port Adelaide superstar Zak Butters, set to join Bontempelli at the Bulldogs next season, was among the contenders before his late-season ankle injury and finished on 26.

Sydney's Charlie Curnow, Collingwood's Nick Daicos, Geelong's Bailey Smith and Collingwood's Josh Daicos. (Getty Images: Michael Wilson/AFL Photos)

Banned Sydney stars Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner weren't in the room as they polled 26 and 12 votes respectively.

Brisbane's Conor McKenna won goal of the year while Hawthorn dynamo Nick Watson was awarded mark of the year.

AAP

Look back at how the count unfolded.

World.title: How Freo's former number one ticket holder has helped Brisbane's dynasty
World.content:
If the Brisbane Lions win a third straight AFL premiership on Saturday, they will be thanking a former number one ticketholder for the Fremantle Dockers.

Luc Longley, a three-time NBA champion with the Michael Jordan-led Chicago Bulls, knows what it takes to reach the top and stay there.

Longley, a Fremantle native, was also the Dockers' number one ticketholder in 2006 and 2007.

But a meeting the Olympian had with the Lions in July may be the catalyst for Fremantle's downfall this Saturday.

The Lions are in their fourth consecutive AFL decider, and are trying to complete three premiership triumphs in a row and join the list of all-time great dynasties.

Despite finishing third on the ladder and making it to the final day in September, the Lions' 2026 season has not been smooth sailing.

Brisbane lost their opening two matches of the season, conceded a record 86 points in the third quarter of their loss to GWS, were hammered by 76 points against Carlton, and lost the qualifying final by 53 points to an understrength Sydney.

But they have overcome all obstacles to be in another grand final, with several players telling ABC Sport of a meeting with Longley in July which has spurred them on.

Former NBA champion Luc Longley is from Fremantle, and was once the Dockers' number one ticketholder. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

"The ability he had to share some of that wisdom and talk to us about what he went through, it was awesome," Lions star Cam Rayner said.

"Just being able to compare and bounce ideas off him and learn things from him about the ability to keep turning up and find that motivation again has held us in good stead."

The Lions had six wins and six losses through 12 games, but were on a five-match winning streak before meeting Longley ahead of their round 18 clash against West Coast in July.

Rayner said Longley's discussions with the team about keeping the desire to win, despite already experiencing success, resonated with the team as they strived for a third consecutive flag.

"The hunger to want to win and to continue to have that success. At the start of the year there were times that wasn't really there in our performances," he said.

"We were dropping in and out of games and struggling to really perform to the level that we could.

"You can't really question the hunger after the game last week. It's back to a level that it needs to be and it's exciting to bring it to this week.

"That's one of the messages Luc Longley brought to us, he said, 'If the game's not going to get you up, you're probably playing it for the wrong reasons'. I feel like that really resonated with a lot of the boys."

Longley was an important part of the Bulls' 1996-1998 championship run, without being the star player.

Michael Jordan was the star of the NBA, while Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman and Steve Kerr also enjoyed big-name status.

For experienced Lions' midfielder Jarrod Berry, speaking to a champion who was known for his team-first work ethic was exactly what he believed Brisbane's dynasty has been built on.

"He [Longley] was never the big dog, the star, the whatever. He got more satisfaction out of seeing his teammates succeed," Berry told ABC Sport.

"Our squad is so talented and we've got so many stars and whatever, but it's not necessarily those guys that are making the club so special.

"It's the other guys that are doing all the tough work and hard work and selfless stuff.

"It was really nice to highlight that. It's all about being generous to your teammates and doing it for them."

The Lions are attempting to become the sixth team to win three consecutive V/AFL premierships, and the first since Hawthorn, who did it from 2013-15.

The Lions won three premierships on the bounce in 2001, 2002 and 2003, then lost the 2004 grand final.

The only club to have won three consecutive flags twice is Melbourne, which did it from 1939–1941 and 1955–1957.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

World.title: Wallabies eye Springboks scalp amid Dockers frenzy in Perth
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

This is how Wallabies flanker Carlo Tizzano wants this weekend to pan out: Fremantle saluting in the AFL grand final on Saturday and Australia beating world champions South Africa in front of a rocking Perth Stadium crowd on Sunday night.

Perth is abuzz with Flagmantle fever ahead of the Dockers' date with destiny against Brisbane at the MCG on Saturday.

It's little wonder the Wallabies' arrival in Perth has gone mostly unnoticed.

But rather than feeling a bit miffed, Wallabies players are keen to lap up the Dockers-inspired party atmosphere and hope they can add to the happy vibes.

Petaia in Wallabies squad Precocious outside back Jordan Petaia is back in the Wallabies squad for the first time since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Australia brace for the Springboks.

Perth-born Tizzano is leading that charge.

"We're behind Freo all the way and hopefully they get a good win," he told AAP.

"The atmosphere here is crazy. You saw what Fremantle was like after their preliminary final win, and what a game that was.

"They're the minor premiers, so they've got a lot of momentum, and hopefully they win the grand final for the first time ever, and then we get the win on the weekend as well."

Like Fremantle, the Wallabies will start as underdogs when they face defending World Cup champions South Africa.

The Springboks beat Australia 30-12 in their last visit to Perth in 2024.

Tizzano was playing just his second Test on that wet and wild night, and although his team didn't come away with the win, the 26-year-old lapped up the experience of donning the Wallabies gold in front of family and friends.

Australia have won three and drawn one Test under new coach Les Kiss.

Taking into account the Wallabies' 57-10 win over Italy in Perth in Joe Schmidt's last match in charge in July, Australia are on a five-match unbeaten run.

Tizzano hopes the team can produce something special to take down South Africa, who arrive in Perth full of confidence following a 3-1 series win over New Zealand.

The Wallabies have included uncapped Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips in the 34-man squad.

But the biggest addition was the return of star back Jordan Petaia, who left the Queensland Reds in 2024 to pursue his NFL dream, and hasn't played for the Wallabies since the 2023 World Cup.

The Springboks arrive in Perth without Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende after the veteran duo were released from the squad to spend more time with family.

AAP

World.title: The clause that may save Lions ace for AFL grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL tribunal chairman was blunt: the "good bloke" clause does not exist.

Instead, tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC turned to a fresh provision in the AFL's laws, centred on compelling and exceptional circumstances.

It is the clause that could save Brisbane's Lachie Neale from being suspended for Saturday's grand final.

The Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

On video evidence, Neale is guilty.

"There's no point putting energy into it until we know the result," Neale's teammate Jarrod Berry said today.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Precedents this season have resulted in one-game bans to numerous players. The most recent just last week, when Adelaide's Max Michalanney was suspended for delivering an off-the-ball gut punch.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

But what may allow Neale, a dual Brownlow medallist to play in the premiership decider is the clause that saved Collingwood legend Scott Pendlebury from suspension in March.

"Exceptional and compelling circumstances" is certain to be the anchor of Brisbane's argument at Tuesday night's tribunal hearing.

The Lions will cite Pendlebury's hearing on March 17 this year.

The acts in the cases of Pendlebury and Neale are starkly different.

The Magpie great was charged with rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

His proposed one-match suspension was downgraded to a $3,000 fine with Gleeson enacting the "compelling and exceptional circumstances" clause.

Pendlebury's advocate Myles Tehan successfully argued the ex-Pies captain "stands in a class of his own", having never previously been before the tribunal in a 21-year AFL career.

"It's frankly difficult to imagine how it could not constitute an exceptional and compelling circumstance (to avoid a ban)," Tehan told the hearing.

"I should say this is not by any means a good bloke clause or a get of jail free card or anything of that nature."

Tribunal chair Gleeson then interjected.

"I might add, it never has been. It's misreported as being something to that effect from time to time," Gleeson said.

"But people who read the guidelines and listen to what the tribunal says will understand it's nothing to do with being a good bloke.

"It's to do with whether the circumstances are exceptional and compelling."

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record. However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Neale, a 320-gamer, is a dual Brownlow medallist; a dual premiership captain; a four-time All Australian; a four-time club champion who, like Pendlebury, has never been suspended.

His exemplary history gives the Lions cause to argue, and hope for a reprieve.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Fremantle legend in tears as AFL grand final honour revealed
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Fremantle pioneer Shaun McManus will hand over the AFL premiership cup to captain Alex Pearce if the Dockers break through for their maiden flag.

Part of the inaugural 1995 Dockers squad, McManus has been named as Fremantle's cup presenter ahead of Saturday's grand final against back-to-back reigning premiers Brisbane.

The Lions are yet to name their presenter after three-time premiership player Jonathan Brown did so for last year's decider win over Geelong.

McManus was brought to tears when he was told he was the club's cup presenter during a segment on Perth radio this morning.

Peter Bell was named the club's presenter for the eventual 2013 grand final loss to Hawthorn.

Dockers chief Simon Garlick described McManus as a perfect embodiment of the club's values.

McManus began his AFL career as a 19-year-old, going on to play 228 games across 14 seasons.

He captained the team alongside Adrian Fletcher from 2000 to 2001, and played alongside current coach Justin Longmuir.

"Shaun perfectly sums up what a Fremantle person is," Garlick said in a club statement.

"He had a remarkable career as a Fremantle player, but beyond that he has been a champion of this club since our humble beginnings back in 1995.

"Those early foundation years weren't easy, and as a 19-year-old he came in, showed great qualities which resulted in him being named captain at just 24.

"The courage he showed on field speaks for itself, but ever since retiring he's been a passionate and positive influence, someone who purely lives and breathes Freo.

"If we are good enough to get the job done on Saturday, it will be a great moment to see Shaun present the cup to Alex, and his old teammate Justin."

McManus is the ninth-highest game record holder in the club's history and was the second behind Shane Parker to reach the 200-game milestone.

Retiring after the 2008 season, McManus remained at the club as a player development coach and transitioned through various off-field roles.

The 50-year-old became a Dockers life member in 2004.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL set to act over 'embarrassing' referee abuse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL has threatened to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

Footage from after full-time in Newcastle's 12-10 win over the Warriors at Eden Park showed a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish being thrown at Klein as he walked from the field.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Klein had to be protected by security as fans abused the veteran referee and threw projectiles.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of its spectators' code of conduct.

An integrity unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they [the fans] will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chair Peter V'landys said.

Auckland police have since confirmed no arrests were made.

They said there were "no issues to note", other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors exited the finals following the loss to the Knights. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the largest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the match from Mount Smart Stadium.

The spectator abuse came after two contentious calls went against the Warriors late in the match, including a decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at the response of spectators after the match, labelling it "embarrassing".

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth [after] what has been an unbelievable night with the colours, the energy, the happiness and celebration," Johnson said on Sky NZ's coverage.

"But there is just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein has probably refereed the best game of rugby league I have seen in a long time tonight.

Hawks fans facing bans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

"He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down. He didn't let people approach him whingeing.

"He didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play and they dictated the outcome."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster vented his frustration in the post-match media conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

"The last one, [when] two points would have drawn the game, he [Frizell] is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball, which they've told us you can't do," Webster said.

The incident came after AFL umpires also had bottles and cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG following Hawthorn's nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

AAP

Tech.title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On.

Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons.

It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously.

This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.

Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.

Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.

Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.

There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.

Sure.

Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?

Do I ever get nostalgic?

Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?

Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them.

The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me.

So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.

That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites.

There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.

Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?

I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.

The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making.

John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.

Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint.

Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.

All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things.

Okay, let’s do it.

I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits.

Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.”

There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub.

No, I don’t buy it either.

Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?

Right.

You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time.

I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.

Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.

I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ‘98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.

But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.

The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative.

So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.

Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year... I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.

[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.

Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.

There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence.

So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.

They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now.

Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple.

You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into.

So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.”

That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy.

Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based.

I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me.

I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it.

Dozens? Dozens?

Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out.

And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro.

No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale.

It’s IBM.

Yeah, and in the Jobs era, it was all about really, really innovative new products that redefined categories over and over again. You’re describing a whole bunch of new products that came up in the Cook era that John Ternus is going to launch. How do you expect the culture of Apple to change around its products or its relationship to the culture to change as we go from one CEO to another?

But think about what they did. You’ve got the coolest new iPhone and Apple product in maybe 10, 20 years introduced one week after Tim Cook steps down. And then for the next 12 to 18 months, you’ve got, I don’t know, six or seven new product categories. Maybe you have 25 pretty breakthrough things.

So Tim Cook made a decision that, even though his tenure at a product company was pretty limited in major new things, the Apple Watch turned out to be a success, even though it started as a complete dud, as you remember. The AirPods are a unique beast in that they’re an accessory, but it’s not a platform on its own yet. It’s going to get there. And the Vision Pro is a failure.

Tim Cook could have ended his tenure as CEO with the iPhone Duo. He could have just waited. Typical transitions at Apple happen mid-October or mid-April; they happen on January 1st. It was a specific decision that was made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce the iPhone Duo. It was a specific decision made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce this whole new product roadmap. Even though, as you know, because of the length of hardware development cycles and R&D, these things were in the oven for five to 10 years.

So it’s really interesting that this decision was made to let Ternus be the face of this whole new era of products rather than allow Tim Cook to take the credit for it. And I think that’s to your point where they’re trying to draw the line in the sand of this new era. If Cook is already going to step down in the next three years, let’s just do it now and let Ternus take the credit for everything.

Take me inside that. You’ve obviously done a lot of reporting. I think you were the first to break the news that Cook would be searching for a successor. You were, I think, among the very first to break that it would be Ternus. Tell me about that process.

This is a big decision; Cook is going to play a huge role at the company. He has a massive compensation program tied pretty much to having to talk to Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It seems like that’s his job: to just manage that relationship.

For $47 million a year, I would talk to Trump and Xi Jinping on the phone every day.

[Laughs] I would need at least 50, but that’s just me. That’s his job: to go do politics much the same way that Eric Schmidt at Google was in charge of governments after Larry Page became CEO. There’s a whole pattern here.

Brad Smith at Microsoft, even though he wasn’t CEO, but yeah.

He’s the president of the company. Yeah, there’s a parallel here. Tell me about this decision of Tim Cook wanting to elevate his position to something like that, and of making John Ternus the face of the product side of the company in this new role.

So 2023 rolls around and Tim Cook starts every executive team meeting, all high-level meetings with people at Apple at the executive levels, with, “We need to start taking succession seriously. We need to start thinking about who the next people are.” At that time, there was a really strong realization that many of the people at the top of Apple either had half a billion dollars in the bank or were already billionaires, and that this era would start to age out really quickly.

And so Tim Cook knew that he wanted to take a step back. Jeff Williams, the number two as the COO, knew he wanted to retire. The CFO, Luca Maestri, wanted to retire, too. The general counsel, Kate Adams, also wanted to retire. They were all about the same age, give or take a few years. So they basically came up with this plan that would go one by one over the next few years.

It started with the CFO. Luca retires at the very end of 2024, and he’s replaced by the new CFO, Kevan Parekh. Then 2025 rolls around, and Jeff Williams, the COO, retires and is replaced by his deputy, Sabih Khan. Then in 2026, they had the transition for the general counsel, and they got a great replacement for her from Meta, Jennifer Newstead. And then at the end of 2026, the big one: Tim Cook to John Ternus. So they played this out very, very slowly.

What Tim Cook has done, and I do think this is going to change in the Ternus era as we progress here, is that he came up with this strategy that I call “Hotel California.” You never want to leave. Tim Cook, he’s staying around as executive chairman. The general counsel had her stay around an extra six to nine months to run government affairs. Jeff Williams stayed around three to four months after stepping down as COO to just oversee the design team, the watch team, and the health teams as part of a transition.

For CFO Luca Maestri, the vast majority of his responsibilities went to his successor, but he kept three things. He kept oversight of information systems and technology. It’s basically like your IT department, corporate information security — which is security for the organization — and corporate real estate, so campuses, retail stores, facilities, and whatnot. It was kind of a BS job, I’ll be honest with you.

It was more so keeping him on the payroll and keeping him around in case things hit the fan, they had a financial issue, and they needed the adult or the grandfather in the room to take the bull by the horns and fix things as they transitioned to the new guy. But now Luca, he’s still there, still getting paid, and he’s teaching a class once a week at Apple University. So he’s a professor there now. I’m not sure how much longer that’s going to run for, but he’s still there.

All these old-school Apple guys are either retired or semi-retired or a notch between semi-retirement and retirement. And then we have Phil Schiller. The same week that Ternus took over as CEO, I reported that Schiller is leaving his remaining responsibilities of running the App Store and running Apple Events, and he’s at Apple now for the next little while working on special projects. They’re not saying what that is, but he’s there, reporting to Ternus, and still on the Apple leadership website. He’s around if needed in sort of an advisory capacity, and we’ll see how long that lasts.

But really this is just a gigantic end-to-end change of the guard at Apple. It’s the biggest executive overhaul I’ve certainly seen in my career reporting on Apple. Don’t forget, when Tim Cook took over for Steve Jobs, there was no overhaul. Many of the guys under Cook were the same guys under Jobs. So a lot of them have been there for a while.

This is definitely a new era, a new generation, and you’re going to see more changes. The head of marketing, the head of retail, some of the other people, they’re in their mid-60s, almost. They’ve got hundreds of millions of dollars. They can’t do this forever. They’re talking internally about retirement. So you’re going to see another wave of changes in the next few years as well, I believe.

You mentioned Phil Schiller, who I’ve known for ages at Apple because I’m old. He’s transitioning out of his role running the App Store. And you had a piece of reporting that suggests part of it is because John Ternus and Eddy Cue want to extract even more money from developers. They want to keep that Apple tax high. They want to find more ways to have services revenue, and Schiller wasn’t interested in that.

Schiller has famously always thought that Apple was squeezing its developers too much. There’s reporting; there are emails from some of these lawsuits. What’s going on there?

Yeah, it’s very interesting. I mean, obviously one part of it is that Schiller is 66. He wants to spend more time with his family, but for real, when it comes to him, he wants to do more philanthropy. He’s been involved in all sorts of stuff in that regard. But at the same time, this is a new era for Apple. Eddy Cue has a firm grip over all Apple services now, really for the first time in a while.

John Ternus is very close with Eddy Cue, and they are looking at new ways to make more money on the App Store, whether that’s additional advertising slots or additional subscription opportunities. Obviously, there’s going to be a reinvention of the App Store coming in the next few years to make more use of AI and to fill in to Siri AI as well.

Phil Schiller, according to my reporting, believes regulators are still hot on Apple’s trail. Developers are still unhappy with Apple. All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it?

I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years.

The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal.

Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables?

Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it.

I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy.

That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible.

Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are?

I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook.

But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years.

Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that.

I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV.

Oh, yes.

He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it.

They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years.

That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature.

Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open.

All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance.

Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

Tech.title: iPhone owners can now submit claims in Apple’s $250 million Siri AI settlement
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is paying $250 million to settle claims that it failed to deliver an AI-upgraded Siri — and now, eligible iPhone owners can submit a claim for a payout. If you live in the US and purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10th, 2024, and March 29th, 2025, you can file a claim on the settlement’s website, as reported earlier by MacRumors.

You can receive an estimated $25 per eligible device, but the settlement’s website notes that this can increase to $95 depending on how many people file claims. To file a claim, you’ll need to enter your name, contact information, and iPhone serial number on the settlement’s website before the December 21st, 2026 deadline.

Tech.title: Vivo’s X500 Pro Max has 17 stops of dynamic range and 4K240 slo-mo
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Vivo’s new X500 flagship phones have arrived in China, and as usual the company’s focus is firmly on photography. The X500 Pro Max — a new tier in its lineup — is the first phone to use new sensors and silicon from Sony and MediaTek that enable impressive dynamic range and slow-motion video recording.

The X500 Pro Max uses Sony’s new Lytia L910 image sensor, its first to use LOFIC, a sensor technology that enables expanded dynamic range. The 50-megapixel, 1/1.28-inch-type sensor delivers what Vivo calls “true 17 EV ultra-high dynamic range,” more than the 16.5 stops claimed by the Xiaomi 17 Ultra. The excellent 200-megapixel, 3.7x telephoto from the X300 Ultra returns here too, along with support for that phone’s 400mm teleconverter lens.

The X500 Pro and Pro Max are also the first phones run on MediaTek’s new Dimensity 9600 Pro, with the 9600M found in the base X500. The 2nm Pro chip brings with it the usual performance bumps, but also the ability to record 4K 240fps slow-motion video. 10bit Log recording and new cinematic video styles are included too.

Display sizes range from the compact 6.36-inch Pro to the 6.85-inch Pro Max, with the base X500 in-between. All three phones feature OLED displays, silicon-carbon batteries between 6,510mAh and 8,000mAh in size, and run on Vivo’s OriginOS 7 software. Today’s launch is China-only, but a global launch is coming, though we don’t yet know when.

Tech.title: These are the first five Googlebook laptops
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google and partners are finally announcing the first laptops under the new Googlebook banner. There are five models from Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo to kick things off. They’re available for preorder starting today and arrive in stores on October 4th.

Starting prices range from $899 to $1,299, putting the Googlebooks in the same territory as the MacBook Air and a plethora of Windows laptops. Each Googlebook also comes with 12 months of Google AI Pro with 5TB of cloud storage, along with three-month trials of YouTube Premium, Adobe Photoshop, and CapCut. Google’s also promising up to 10 years of updates.

Here’s a look at the hardware each Googlebook has to offer for those prices, and how they compare to each other.

Acer Googlebook 14

Previous Next





1 / 4 Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

The Acer Googlebook 14 is the only convertible 2-in-1 in the first round of Googlebooks, featuring a design a bit like Acer’s Chromebook Plus Spin 714. Acer says it offers up to 16 hours of battery life. It also currently has the lowest starting price at $899, although that might not last — Acer’s Kelly Odle said in a comment to The Verge that $899 is the laptop’s “initial launch price available for a limited time,” adding that Acer plans to “reevaluate pricing over time based on component supplies and other market pressures.”

Ongoing shortages of RAM and other components have been driving up prices on other laptops, like Apple’s MacBook Neo, and unfortunately it sounds like a price hike isn’t out of the question for the Acer Googlebook 14, either.

16GB of RAM

256 or 512GB of storage

14-inch 2.8K OLED touch display

13.9mm thick, 2.5lbs (1.13kg)

Fingerprint sensor

Asus Googlebook 14

Previous Next



1 / 3 Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Asus’ Googlebook 14 takes after its ExpertBook Ultra with its design, featuring a metallic gray-blue chassis and more ports than most of the other Googlebooks. It’s the lightest of the first five models at 2.2 pounds, although it isn’t the thinnest (that title goes to Dell). The Asus Googlebook 14 is one of only two that come with an HDMI port as well. It’s one of the pricier Googlebooks, starting at $1,299, but it features spec options similar to the others.

Dell’s first Googlebook, starting at $1,199, closely resembles the XPS 13 but with a light gold “shimmer” colorway, the Googlebook glowbar, and Google’s software. Unlike the Windows XPS 13, the XPS Googlebook also has a fingerprint reader. Unfortunately it’s just as sparse on ports as the original, with only two USB-C ports.

Tech.title: The long dream of the Googlebook
Tech.content:
In late 2010, an up-and-coming Google executive named Sundar Pichai took the stage in front of a bunch of reporters and explained that Google had a big new idea about laptops. In the future, he said, the only thing you’d need on your computer was a web browser — that was where all your apps, data, and connections would live going forward. Your computer didn’t need much storage, Pichai explained, or any fancy hardware, because the cloud would do the work. The software designed for these new laptops, Chrome OS, was an enormous bet that the web would eventually overtake everything.

Chrome OS (which eventually became ChromeOS) has been, in many ways, a huge hit. But the computer currently on Rick Osterloh’s desk isn’t a Chromebook. Osterloh is Google’s head of hardware and devices, and the sleek, slim device he’s tapping on as he joins our Google Meet is a 13-inch Dell clamshell with decidedly un-Chromebook specs: 16 gigs of RAM, a cutting-edge Qualcomm processor, a light and thin and MacBook-ish metallic look. It’s called the XPS Googlebook, and it’s one of five new devices running Googlebook OS, Google’s latest big idea about computers.

At first blush, Googlebooks feel like classic Google in a bad way: yet another operating system, yet another brand, yet another thing destined for the Google graveyard. But Osterloh sees it differently. He greenlit the whole project in part because he saw it as “the ultimate focusing move” for Google. For a long time, he says, Google has built, maintained, and shipped two operating systems. ChromeOS stayed on laptops, while Android conquered phones and tablets and TVs and cars and everything else. Slowly but surely, Google has built Android into a familiar interface and a large app ecosystem across all those devices. Except for laptops.

It’s your computer. It’s your phone. It’s your phone-puter!

Meanwhile, Google became convinced that the advent of AI might change the way we use computers forever — but might not need to change the computers themselves. Osterloh says he has tables full of wheel-reinventing prototypes, and of course the company is betting big on things like smart glasses, but high-end PCs, which have the power needed to run AI models for coding, dictation, and more, have been a surprise winner of the AI revolution so far. (Just ask Apple, which has seen AI enthusiasts buy high-end Macs in huge volume.) “I think laptops are one of those resonant form factors,” Osterloh says. “It’s an established category that’s incredibly useful for productivity and apps, and it’s going to be really hard to replace that.”

Those two ideas together — Android’s dominance and the rise of AI — tell the whole story of Googlebook. There are a lot of bets inside of the Googlebook project, both about what we do on computers and how we’ll do it going forward, but maybe the most surprising is Google’s commitment to building kickass laptops. A generation ago, then-CEO Eric Schmidt argued that the future was “disposable” hardware, that devices wouldn’t matter as the internet took over. Googlebooks represent Google’s growing belief that devices matter more than ever. And that a good laptop is worth paying for.

“The key thing that had changed was just the rapid pace of evolution that Android itself has gone under.”

The Googlebook project started in earnest a couple of years ago, but some of the ideas have been floating around much longer. Rumors and reports of a ChromeOS-Android merger have been around for more than a decade, and Google has tried various ways to bring the two operating systems into harmony. The company spent years programming ChromeOS to be able to run Android apps (and even Windows apps), but never nailed the integration. For years, a project called Fuchsia looked like the combination users had been waiting for, but that petered out into a smart home-specific project.

In early 2024, though, a couple of Googlers asked a new question: What if, instead of trying to bring Android apps to ChromeOS, we brought the best of ChromeOS to Android? They weren’t the first people to ask that question, but they were the first to time it right. “The key thing that had changed,” says Prajakta Gudadhe, Google’s VP of engineering for laptops and tablets, “was just the rapid pace of evolution that Android itself has gone under.”

For so many years, Android was a phone operating system that was sometimes hamfistedly shoved into other devices. But Gudadhe felt like Android had finally matured into something truly cross-platform. Developers had begun to embrace multiple screen sizes and orientations, and the Android team at Google had changed the way they built the operating system. “Android at that time was serving multiple form factors, from phones to wearables to TVs to autos,” Gudadhe says, “and because of that they just had to invest in a much more modular stack that could support this diversity.”

Googlebooks will be able to open apps from your Android phone. Image: Google

What that meant in practice was that it might finally be possible to build an Android laptop that could natively run the universe of Android apps, without looking and working like a grossly oversized Android phone. By combining base Android technology with some of the best features of ChromeOS — excellent multitasking and multi-window support, fast boot times, easy software updates — Google could have the best of both worlds.

The idea became a memo proposing a new laptop OS, which was excitedly received by Google leadership, and Project Aluminium was born. (To be clear: It is A-lu-min-i-um, not aluminum, and there was a swear jar in the office for people who dared to pronounce it the American way.)

In addition to the technical underpinnings, the Aluminium pitch included a couple of big ideas about the future of laptops. The first was that more and more users were starting their computing journey with Android devices, and thus were expecting all their other computers to both interact with and even look like their Android phones. They wanted widgets, homescreens, notification shades, and customization options. They also wanted all their apps on their laptop, and their data in perfect sync all the time. That became one of the core tenets of the operating system — perfect integration with Android devices. (iPhone owners were, and are, mostly out of luck on this front.)

The team was also convinced that Gemini and other AI tools were part of the future of computing, and that they should be built into the operating system and not just a separate app. The advent of vibe coding meant people might want to build their own software, in a terminal or with the help of on-device agents, and would surely want easier ways to get it running on their devices. But even little things about computer use felt ripe for AI change. “The mouse pointer? That thing seems pretty stupid,” says Alexander Kuscher, Google’s senior director of product management for laptops and tablets, just naming one example. Your cursor represents your attention, and moves around with your brain and your eyes, so why can’t your computer just see and respond to it? “I’m copying and pasting stuff all over the place, and typing to chatbots that don’t give me the ability to just express my needs with the mouse pointer.” That thinking became one of the most novel features of Googlebook OS, Magic Pointer, which lets you invoke your AI bot just by wiggling your cursor over an image or a bit of text. The idea, Kuscher said, was to “not change the ergonomics [of a laptop], but to make sure we take care of people coming from the ecosystem, living in an AI world.”

Running, and making, Android apps is core to Googlebook.

As the Aluminium team started working on an AI-centric, Android-powered laptop, they began discovering problems — and other teams at Google trying to solve them. “One is Android Automotive, which cares a lot about multi-user,” Kuscher says. “They need fast user switching because different people get in the car. We were like, oh, me too!” They found folks on the Android Wear team working on improving the Bluetooth stack for better accessory connectivity, and people on the XR team thinking about multi-window support for Android.

This is the focusing that gets Osterloh excited. The well-earned stereotype about Google is that nobody ever talks to anybody else, and so the company ships a thousand slightly different messaging apps, reminders systems, and AI subscriptions. In that vein, the Aluminium team could have come up with new ideas about everything and baked them all into ChromeOS; what they did instead was integrate so many disparate ideas about Android into a single platform.

Even the ultimate name of the devices and the software, Googlebook and Googlebook OS, hint at the extent to which Google hopes Aluminium brings everything Google-y together in one place. “We realized pretty quickly that this is about the whole Google experience,” Kuscher says. “If you have a phone that runs Google, and a car, and a laptop, that’s what this is about.”

(The naming here is a delightful bit of Google chaos, by the way. Googlebooks run Googlebook OS, which is mostly Android, but with some ChromeOS trappings thrown in. Get it? Me neither. They’re Android laptops.)

Android phones are treated like another drive in the file system. Image: Google

It became very clear to the Googlebook team that this operating system was going to ask a lot of the hardware it ran on. All the system-level AI would need enough processing power and memory to feel seamless, of course, but it went further than that. “We didn’t want to have Magic Pointer, and then it’s really hard on your trackpad to actually use it,” says Kuscher. “That’s just incongruent.” Likewise, what good is letting you build software with a prompt if the keyboard is awful to type on or the battery dies before it’s done? If the screen is too small, or too low-res, nobody will want to use it instead of their phone. For a Googlebook to be even a little bit worthwhile, the hardware would need to be great.

From the beginning, Osterloh says, Google wanted to build an ecosystem of Googlebooks. The company began reaching out to PC makers, chip companies, and even phone manufacturers, all with roughly the same pitch: You’ve already been making either great laptops, great Android devices, or both, and now we’re putting the whole puzzle together. For a PC industry always looking for Windows competition and increasingly interested in building ecosystems of products to compete with Apple, the pitch worked: Google is starting with five devices from five partners — Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo — and Osterloh says there are many other partners waiting in the wings. Potentially including Google’s own Pixel team. The first five devices, he said, are merely the ones that are ready now. And he says partners are clamoring to be next.

“I still fundamentally believe it will always be your central computer.”

The harder group to convince of this whole thing? Users. For all their success in education and elsewhere, Chromebooks never really caught on as personal computers. That’s largely Google’s fault, and largely for two reasons: because Google never successfully convinced people that all they needed was a web browser, and because Google and its partners spent so many years making and marketing crappy computers. Early Chromebook commercials were, in fact, explicitly anti-hardware: They showed people lighting their laptops on fire and throwing them into rivers, because who cared about the device when everything was in the cloud? As a result, even when Google and its partners have made high-end Chromebooks, like the terrific Pixelbook, they failed to convince anyone that they were worth the money.

The first lineup of Googlebooks will cost between $899 and $1,299, which puts them squarely in competition with devices like the MacBook Air. Osterloh says he thinks Googlebooks will eventually reach other form factors and lower prices, but seems unfazed by the task of convincing people to spend top dollar on a Google laptop. For one thing, he thinks the increasing popularity of AI has made people more willing to buy high-end computers in general, and has maybe even increased the importance of laptops and desktops. “I still fundamentally believe it will always be your central computer,” he says. “The thing that connects you to networks, that has the primary brain, the important screen for entertainment and productivity.” But more than that, he agrees that this kind of hardware, and this kind of price tag, are simply what it requires to do Googlebooks well. And Google definitely won’t get a third chance to convince you it’s right about laptops.

Googlebooks have some fun features like a glowing bar, but mostly they’re laptops.

When Google first announced the Googlebook concept in May, it was heavily focused on AI and Gemini. But the work that led to Googlebooks goes back much further than the company’s current obsession with LLMs, and is about more than Google’s chatbot. In some ways, Osterloh says, the whole history of Android has led up to the launch of Googlebooks. Their first job, as he sees it, is to “run the applications you know how to use and sync really well with all your Android usage and applications and devices that you’ve connected to it. And it just happens to be an awesome laptop.”

Sixteen years ago, Google shipped a laptop for the internet age. Now it’s trying to build one for the mobile era that has already come, and the AI-centric one that’s still forming. Getting it right will require marshaling nearly everything Google does well — and the best devices it has ever made. It will also require proving to users that they need a computer that’s more like their phone, and more connected to their AI ecosystem. None of that is a given; it might be an even bigger leap than trying to move your laptop to the web. But if Google’s bet pays off, our cursors might never wiggle the same way again.

Tech.title: I got to see Google’s wild ideas about the future of laptops
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There are a few things about using a Googlebook that immediately feel just right. The hardware is polished (since it’s based on current laptops). The OS is familiar (if you’ve ever used a Chromebook). But most impressive, it integrates your Android phone with your PC so they feel more like one device. It’s the culmination of a series of new ideas that blur the two devices together. After my first look, I went from doubtful to excited by the prospect of Google pulling it all off.

After an initial barebones announcement in May, Google is finally launching Googlebooks — its new line of Android-based laptops. The initial five Googlebook models from Dell, Lenovo, HP, Acer, and Asus all launch October 4th, with preorders available now and starting prices ranging from $899 to $1,299.

So what are Googlebooks?

In a nutshell, they’re laptops running a new operating system that’s a blend of Chromebooks and Android — with a whole lot of Gemini AI stuff built in. They look quite like Chromebooks, but with Android’s Material Three Expressive UI stylings on the software side and higher-end materials for hardware. There doesn’t seem to be a baseline spec for Googlebooks, but at launch they’re all thin-and-light laptops ranging from 13 inches to 15 inches with 16GB of RAM or more, touchscreen displays (most of them OLED), metal chassis, backlit keyboards, either fingerprint or facial recognition unlocking (or both), and a Google-y Glowbar light strip on their lids.

The launch lineup for Googlebooks. Image: Google

Powering the initial lineup of Googlebooks are Intel Core Ultra Series 3 “Panther Lake” and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chips, with MediaTek options expected to come later. While the first wave of Googlebooks are similarly sized and all have “Googlebook” in their name, there are some variations: haptic or mechanical trackpads, port offerings, even a 2-in-1 convertible. Check out our roundup of all the hardware here.

I spent a bit of time prodding all the Googlebooks during my demos, and each one felt pretty nice. They each have their own unique qualities: the Asus was incredibly lightweight, the Lenovo has plenty of ports and an optional mouse with a matching Glowbar light, the Acer’s convertible form factor allows some tablet-like use (and it’s pretty affordable for a Panther Lake laptop). The HP had a great looking screen and a latticeless keyboard I surprisingly didn’t hate, and the Dell is basically a gold XPS 13 (which is excellent) but with a different chip.

Previous Next







1 / 5 The Asus Googlebook 14.

But everything really special about Googlebooks comes down to software. They run Googlebook OS, which is built with the native Android stack atop a Linux kernel and supports both x86 and Arm architectures (as implied by the chip offerings). It’s an Android desktop interface that runs Android apps and feels much like ChromeOS, but it’s got some handy features when paired with an Android phone.

You can cast apps from an Android phone directly to a Googlebook, even without touching your phone. Googlebooks essentially have two app drawers: a G-logo start menu for installed Googlebook apps and a second one beside it that pulls up mobile apps from your phone. Click a phone app and you can fully use that app with the mouse and keyboard or the Googlebook’s touchscreen. It’s a bit like iPhone Mirroring on macOS, but the apps are individually extracted to the desktop OS instead of showing your whole phone interface.

Previous Next

1 / 2 You can cast any app from your phone via a second app drawer on Googlebook OS. Here you see both drawers open.

Googlebooks also have a nifty feature called Continue On where the icons of apps you’re currently using on your phone appear in the bottom bar — allowing you to click it on the laptop and hand it off to the Googlebook. These app handoffs can transition to a native app or a web app, depending on how developers have programmed it. A Google rep informed me at my in-person briefing that Continue On is fairly simple for Android developers to add to their apps, and casting apps to a Googlebook doesn’t require anything extra.

The other big way Googlebooks interact with an Android phone is Quick Access, allowing you to see and access all the files stored on your phone right in the desktop Files app. The paired Android phone is listed in the sidebar of a Googlebook’s Files window, just like any other drive or home folder, and you can directly search it and share files from it without physically picking up your phone. This is pretty handy stuff, but of course it all requires you running an Android phone. If you have an iPhone then you’re limited to a Link to iOS app that just does some message syncing and replying.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Quick Access treats your paired phone like another local drive. Image: Google

As Google first showed back in May, the Googlebook mouse cursor is called a Magic Pointer — allowing you to wiggle it to summon Gemini. Doing so allows you to ask Gemini questions or have it look at things on your screen to get further info. One of Google’s live demos was asking Gemini “Is this legit?” on a Spotify account authentication email, or adding a multi-week exercise routine for marathon training to a Google Calendar. Some tasks run locally, while many will go up to Gemini in the cloud — and it wasn’t clear when that was happening during any of Google’s demos. Googlebooks also have recent Android features like Create My Widget (for creating custom widgets from natural language prompts) and Rambler (speech transcription that can parse stream of consciousness-like wordiness).

And while thin-and-light laptops aren’t really built for gaming, since Googlebooks run Android they work with 20,000 games at launch. Many of these are free-to-play mobile games with microtransactions, of course, but the Play Store does have many indie titles that should play fine on a laptop. I briefly demoed a Googlebook running Dead Cells and Balatro — indie staples that are well worth playing on any platform. But it was also jarring to see a demo of Asphalt Legends offer me the option to watch a post-race ad for an in-game currency reward. That felt icky and weird on a laptop. But when it comes to mainline gaming, Nvidia’s GeForce Now service is also coming to Googlebooks, and the first year is free with one of Google’s new laptops.

Love me some Dead Cells. Seeing ads after a race in a mobile game? Don’t love that.

A big draw of Googlebooks is that by being Android-based they can follow software developments that move at a much quicker pace than ChromeOS. Chromebooks will continue on, especially for education use where they’re widely adopted, but it’s pretty easy to feel like their days are numbered as the focus shifts to Googlebooks. Just like Chromebooks, Google is promising Googlebooks will get 10 years of OS support.

I kept asking who Googlebooks are for during Google’s media briefing, and Android president Sameer Samat told me they’re aimed at users who own a phone like a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 that don’t particularly want to use Windows or a Mac. Googlebooks’ initial prices completely overlook direct competition with the MacBook Neo (at least, for now) but considering the state of Windows 11 and frequently voiced frustrations with Microsoft (I see you, Verge commenters) another competitor in the space could help mix things up.

Previous Next

1 / 2 It’s not the Lightroom I want, but it’s a Lightroom and it’s “Optimized for desktop.”

One thing I found comforting was the work Google put into flagging apps as desktop-compatible in the Play Store. Kind of like how Valve verifies games for Steam Deck and Steam Machine compatibility, Google has three designations for Play Store apps on Googlebooks: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, or Better on the website. It’s cool to see an “Optimized for desktop” version of Lightroom I can install on a Google laptop, though I know it’s the mobile version and not the Lightroom Classic I regularly use on Windows and macOS.

But while that hints at Google taking this initiative pretty seriously, and all the Android integration tricks seem cool, there are many open questions for Google and its new OS that remain to be answered.

Even if Chromebooks continue on strictly for education, what will happen as that software ages with the development attention turned to Googlebooks?

Do people want to trust Google with their whole computer these days?

Do people want a laptop built with Gemini in mind? There’s an ongoing AI backlash, and Googlebooks puts Gemini at the forefront — even in the cursor.

Will developers like Adobe further optimize its mobile creative apps for desktop use? Or bring desktop-only apps like Lightroom Classic to Android? (Please?)

Are these laptops ready for showtime? Not to get too inside baseball, but Google isn’t sending out review units ahead of the launch. And some OEM reps told me they just got the hardware shortly before our briefing — deferring all software questions to Google. Maybe that’s no big deal, but it doesn’t instill much confidence.

What will future cheaper Googlebooks look and feel like? And just how cheap (or expensive) might they get — especially in the age of RAMageddon?

After seeing what Googlebooks can do I went from having no idea why they even exist to feeling at least adequately whelmed and looking forward to seeing some new ideas and competition in the laptop space (even if it might be just another Trojan Horse for Gemini). It’s not every day we get a new player in the desktop operating system and laptop spaces. There seems to be a higher ceiling of potential with Googlebooks than there was with Chromebooks, along with some cool features, but Google has a lot to prove at higher prices than people are used to paying for its laptops.
