Tech.title: The Mac Mini is still mighty, just not as cheap
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

There are lots of compact desktop computers out there, but none match the Mac Mini’s small size and big power. 2024’s redesign reduced the Mini to 0.82L, a chassis so minimal you can easily mount it behind a monitor or under a desk. I’ve used gaming laptop charging bricks that are nearly as large and definitely heavier than this whole computer. But despite being tiny, the Mini maintains a bunch of speedy ports — even a front-facing headphone jack.

The 2026 Mini is the first Mac to get Apple’s new M6 chip, with more cores — and more kinds of cores — than the outgoing M4 model. Along with that comes another beefier version, replacing the M4 Pro model with an M5 Pro. It’s a chip bump year, and that’s just fine. But it’s also a price bump year: While the M4 Mac Mini started at $599, the new model starts at $899. In spite of that, the Mac Mini remains the best value in the Mac lineup, because just about everything costs more these days.

Since May, the cheapest M4 Mini was the model with 512GB storage, for $799; Apple discontinued the $599 model with 256GB of storage due to supply constraints — in part because of people buying up Mac Minis en masse for use with OpenClaw. So while the base M6 model with 16GB / 256GB is technically only $100 more than the last available M4 Mini, it’s really a $300 increase.

Speakers: D

We have two specced-up units in for review. One is a $1,299 M6 model with a 12-core CPU / 12-core GPU, 24GB of unified memory, 512GB of storage, and 2.5Gb ethernet. The M5 Pro config is a very pricey $2,899 for an 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU, 48GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and 10Gb ethernet. As powerful as the M5 Pro is, this is a bit overkill for a Mac Mini. Spending $2,899 puts you well into M5 Max Mac Studio territory.

Like all the latest M-series Macs, both the M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini are absolute speed demons for raw performance. They even benefit from Apple’s recent push to faster storage, doubling the storage speeds of the M4 / M4 Pro Mac Mini. The M6 is Apple’s newest chip, and it’s now the head of the pack in single-core performance. Not just the Mac pack, either; the entire pack. The M6 chip’s jump to a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU over the M4’s 10-core / 10-core makes it faster on all fronts.

The M6 contains all three of Apple’s current core types: two super, four performance, and six efficiency. (The super cores are the fastest ones, which Apple called performance cores until earlier this year; the performance cores are new and meant for multithreaded work.) The M4 had four of the old performance cores and six efficiency cores. The M5 Pro Mac Mini has six super cores, 12 performance cores, and zero efficiency cores.

In single-threaded work, the M6’s super cores are about 10 percent faster than M5’s performance cores, and a little more than 20 percent faster than the performance cores in the M4. The super and performance cores in the M5 Pro are both slower than the M6’s, and so are the GPU cores, but what they lack in speed they make up for in number, not to mention memory bandwidth. The M5 Pro is 40 to 50 percent faster in multi-threaded CPU and GPU benchmarks than the M6.

It’s just so dang tiny.

Looking at a real-world benchmark like our Adobe Premiere 4K export test, the M6 Mac Mini finishes in 2 minutes and 34 seconds — 40 seconds faster than the M4 we tested in the iMac with the same amount of RAM. The M5 Pro did it in 1:51, almost a third faster than the M6 and even faster than our recent re-test of the 10-core / 32-core M1 Max (which took 2:03).

What does all of this feel like in everyday use? These Mac Minis are more than capable for lots of multitasking and content creation, with the M5 Pro of course having more headroom. I was able to import a batch of 1,253 50-megapixel RAW images (all my recent photos still living on my SD card) from my full-frame Sony camera into Lightroom Classic on the M6 Mac Mini in about 6 minutes and 13 seconds. The same import only went about 30 seconds faster on the M5 Pro Mac Mini. But doing some heavy batch editing with AI subject detection across a selection of 188 photos showed the performance advantage of the M5 Pro. The M6 Mac Mini was decently fast, but even with 24GB of RAM this little torture test hit swap memory and slowed mid-processing. The M5 Pro sailed through and stayed speedier the whole way through.

The M5 Pro model should come in black.

If you’re doing video editing, visual effects, or 3D rendering then you’re best served looking at the M5 Pro Mac Mini — or maybe even the Mac Studio if you have the budget. The M6 Mac Mini is more for generalists who do creative work on the side or want an everyday desktop they could use for a very long time, like up to a decade. When I bought a Mac Mini for myself in 2023 I opted for the cheapest M2 Pro. (Yes, I’m plenty jealous of how small the current models are.) It served me well, but these days I’d probably be fine with an M6 Mac Mini. While I often deal with lots of high-res images in Lightroom Classic, photography isn’t my full-time work. If I were editing thousands of photos for hours a day I’d definitely consider the M5 Pro Mac Mini or M5 Max Mac Studio — and then I’d also get my precious SD card slot.

And yes, the Mac Minis are great for local AI compute, thanks in part to fast unified memory, and Apple’s leaning into that with the new models. The press release announcing the M6 and M5 Pro chips mentions AI capabilities nearly 40 times.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Lots of ports.

Hardware-wise, these Mac Minis are nearly identical to the older ones. They have the same ports as the last-gen model, with two 10Gbps USB-C ports and a headphone jack on the front. On the rear, there are three Thunderbolt ports (TB4 on the M6 model; TB5 on the M5 Pro), plus HDMI 2.1 and an ethernet port. The ethernet has been bumped from 1 gigabit to 2.5Gbps; you can upgrade to 10Gb for $100.

Sure, the power button is still on the bottom, but it remains mostly no big deal since the Mini is designed to sip power when idle; you can just put it to sleep instead of turning it off. Apple even added a software feature to somewhat alleviate this by having the Mac Mini turn itself back on after the power is cut.

The other thing that’s still the same are the Mac Mini’s crummy little speakers. I’ve owned and used the older, larger M2 Pro Mac Mini for years so I know how you can get by with the built-in speakers when you’re too lazy to put on headphones, but they should only be relied on for hearing the beeps, boops, and “knock brushes” of notifications.

There’s now Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support on the 2026 Mac Minis, which is a nice small upgrade. Just like annual phone releases, the new Mac Mini will best serve newcomers and people still running much older models. Do you still have an Intel-based Mac that’s now run out of OS updates with the introduction of macOS 27 Golden Gate? Boy, are you in for a treat.

On the software side, I feel the same way about macOS 27 Golden Gate as I did during the developer beta: the visual refinements that tone down Liquid Glass transparency, increase window sidebar legibility, and fix window corner radii are all welcome changes. Golden Gate is an overall nice improvement over macOS 26 Tahoe, even if Siri AI and Apple Intelligence on the Mac are just kinda Fine.

The bottom power button remains weird, but it’s rarely an issue. It could pose a problem if you mount the Mini somewhere hard to reach.

This is our new normal. The Mac Mini is still a great deal; it just doesn’t feel like the steal it used to be. But with the recent price increases hitting MacBook Airs and MacBook Pros, the new Mac Minis remain much cheaper than getting similar chips in a laptop (especially if you already have a monitor, mouse, and keyboard). The base M6 Mac Mini is $400 cheaper than the cheapest M5 MacBook Air, and the base M5 Pro model is $800 less than the MacBook Pro with the same chip and memory.

Sadly it doesn’t seem likely we’ll ever see a Mac Mini start at a price like $599 ever again. It’s still an easy recommendation if you want a tiny desktop computer that runs circles around comparably priced PCs and will last for years, but it’ll take time to forget the gut punch that is these price increases.

Tech.title: The M5 Ultra Mac Studio tears through our benchmark tests
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The Mac Studio review unit that Apple sent us to test this year is, put simply, kind of outrageous. It has an M5 Ultra chip with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU, 256GB of RAM, and 4TB of storage and costs $12,299. This thing is not for your typical content creation workloads. It’s for AI developers and some of the most demanding 3D visual effects houses out there.

Frankly, our usual benchmarks aren’t cutting it.

The latest version of Apple’s most powerful computer begins shipping today with new chips and prices that extend even further into the stratosphere. The new Mac Studio uses the same design that’s been with us since 2022, replete with ultra-fast ports both front and back, now kitted out with either an M5 Max or M5 Ultra chip, compared to the M4 Max or M3 Ultra of last year’s model.

My precious! (I’m talking about the SD card slot, of course.)

The M5 Max model starts at a relatively modest $2,499 with an 18-core CPU / 32-core GPU, 36GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage. We’ve tested an M5 Max already, in the MacBook Pro, where it starts at $4,099 with the same amount of memory and 2TB of storage (the equivalent Mac Studio costs $3,299). The M5 Ultra is another beast altogether. It starts at $5,499 with 30 CPU cores, 64 GPU cores, 96GB of memory and 1TB of storage.

I’ve only had my hands on the new Mac Studio as well as a pair of the latest Mac Minis for a handful of days. That’s enough time to adequately test the M6 and M5 Pro chips in the Mac Mini, and to run our standard benchmarks on the M5 Ultra — but not enough time to seriously challenge it.

Conveniently, we still have the similarly specced M3 Ultra Mac Studio from last year — though it was only $8,099 at the time. Aside from CPU core count and architecture, they’re nearly the same, which makes them easy to compare.

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is around 30 percent faster than our similarly configured M3 Ultra in both single-core and multicore synthetic CPU tests. It varies more in graphics tests, but some, like the new Geekbench 7 OpenCL test, also saw around a 30 percent uplift. And a heftier GPU rendering test like Cinebench scored 63 percent higher.

I’ve never tested anything this fast before. The storage speeds are off the proverbial charts. It renders the classroom test in Blender faster than I can tie my shoes. Our Premiere 4K video export test, which yields an MP4 file of about 1.7GB, is done in about 40 seconds. I can’t get up from my desk and get a cup of coffee that fast without risking a serious burn.

All ports in a storm.

Apple is talking a big game about the M5 Ultra being “a monumental step for AI.” I don’t normally run local AI stuff (I just don’t find generative AI and LLM stuff very useful for my work — and I’ve tried). But I want to give it a serious go, so I’m open to suggestions. I’ve already reached out to our great Verge audience for ideas, and I appreciate all of you who commented. (Yes, even those of you with the “Can it run DOOM” jokes. I see you, and it never gets old. I mean, it does. But it doesn’t. I love DOOM.)

How long is this going to take me? Hopefully not very long, but it’s going to be a busy couple of months. Google is announcing its whole new line of Googlebook laptops at exactly the same time this article publishes. And there’s a Microsoft event coming up next week that sounds a whole lot like it’ll jumpstart Nvidia’s RTX Spark initiative. There’s never a drought of laptops to test, but this Techtember and Techtober seems like a deluge that’s about to engulf Your Friendly Neighborhood Laptop Reviewer.

I know, I know; “So many cool computers to test, what a burden.” Truly, it is a very exciting time for computers. An expensive one, for sure, but I don’t think the space has ever been this dynamic. So I’ll do my best to get back to you when I’ve got something cool to share about the M5 Ultra Mac Studio. Feel free to drop more ideas and tips in the comments here. Or email me or DM me on Bluesky if you’ve got suggestions you’d like to share. I also accept words of encouragement and compliments. :)

The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is a powerful machine. Let’s see if we can find its limits. Stay tuned.

Tech.title: Corridor raises $25M seed to build a health benefits brokerage for SMBs
Tech.content:
It’s been a while since Jackson Wagner left his job as a product lead at Scale AI in July 2022. Now, he’s building in a new space altogether: The new effort is an AI health benefits brokerage called Corridor that focuses on small businesses, which it says traditional brokerages often overlook because small accounts generate lower commissions even though they take the same amount of time as larger accounts.

Corridor is betting an AI solution may help on that front. On its platform, customers work with human advisors while AI agents do administrative tasks in the background. The company says its agents can handle tedious office work like checking whether a doctor is in a customer’s insurance network, scheduling care, or providing a doctor updated health insurance information.

“We are every single employee and management’s concierge for all things healthcare,” Nikhil Aggarwal, the company’s CEO, told TechCrunch.

On Monday, Corridor said it had raised a $25 million seed round led by Bain Capital Ventures.

Corridor came about after Wagner was in a running accident, and the poor handling of his care led him down a path of “significant, consistent, chronic pain.”

“I developed a long list of complications that needed to be worked through one by one,” he said.

He eventually left Scale AI to get a master’s degree in computer science and electrical engineering at UC Berkeley, before joining Build Robotics in 2023. Later, he teamed up with former Scale AI colleague Eric Qian to work on Capernaum AI, a startup building a clinical agent targeting musculoskeletal care and chronic pain.

The two eventually approached Cold Start to see if they would fund Capernaum, but Aggarwal, who was a partner at Cold Start along with Jason Dong, saw a much larger opportunity. So the four of them took off and launched Corridor together.

“Since health plans are the window through which the vast majority of Americans access health care, it became overwhelmingly clear that one of the highest impact things I could do to improve outcomes for individuals was to create a way for them to access better health plans,” Wagner said.

Other companies in this space include Ignition Benefits and Nava Benefits.

Investors in Corridor’s round include BoxGroup, as well as executives from OpenAI, Scale AI and Ramp. The startup is now preparing for Q4, since “80% of small businesses choose their health plan in Q4,” Aggarwal said.

“Our vision is to build the most trusted healthcare institution in America,” he said. “To earn that, we are laser-focused on a simple promise: doing what we say we’re going to do for the businesses and employees we serve.”

Tech.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
Tech.content:
This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale.

At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence, so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems.

But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.”

To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities.

That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me.

Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out?

No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic.

In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building.

Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario: If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention.

This post was first published on September 18, 2026.

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s latest Boring Company pitch involves a Hyperloop between Austin and San Antonio
Tech.content:
In Brief

Elon Musk recently claimed that his tunneling startup The Boring Company is working on “a simple precursor Hyperloop” between Austin and San Antonio that will reduce the journey between the two cities to less than 30 minutes.

The Boring Company account shared Musk’s statement and said it “would be excited and honored to build this massive infrastructure project.”

Many of The Boring Company’s announced projects — including tunnel systems in Chicago, Los Angeles, and between New York City and Washington, D.C. — have not materialized. However, it does operate a transportation system combining tunnels and surface routes in Las Vegas, and it recently raised a $3 billion round led by the United Arab Emirates.

Musk’s comments about a potential Austin-San Antonio Hyperloop were actually in reply to an AI-generated video depicting a generic science fiction future with human colonies on other worlds. Musk re-posted the video and declared, “This is the future we shall bring into being”.

Musk’s critics have argued that his vision of the future is apparently inspired by pulp science fiction and comic books; historian Jill Lepore recently told me that he seems to favor sci-fi that “completely defeats and defies all of his political beliefs.”

Tech.title: Is the AI industry really ready to slow down?
Tech.content:
We’re seeing a big debate over AI safety and a potential slowdown, as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a plan to “pace the frontier,” while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly echoed President Donald Trump’s claims that the AI backlash is a hoax and regulation is unnecessary.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed whether executives like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are serious about wanting to slow down.

While I was surprised at how many industry leaders seemed to throw their support behind Amodei’s plan, Sean noted that the plan seemed short on details.

And when Kristen asked whether a combination of existing regulation and the workings of the free market could provide enough safeguards on their own, Sean replied, “We have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.”

Plus, he argued, “There does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.”

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Anthony: Sean, what do you think? Are we actually going to ”pace the frontier”?

Sean: That sounds, for some reason, like something from “Point Break.” It’s just a very California statement, like, “We’re gonna pace the frontier, bruh.”

I don’t know. I said on this show last week, I didn’t think we were headed for a slowdown of any kind, in large part because I don’t think these companies are structured in a way where that works.

So this was a pretty immediate flip of what I said a week ago, to hear this from Dario at Anthropic and Sam at OpenAI and even Elon Musk to a certain degree — and we can get into whether we believe that or not. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down.

Anthony, I know you read this stuff pretty closely last weekend as it was all popping off, so I’m curious if you’re maybe more generous than I am, as far as understanding what it is they’re trying to say here.

Anthony: I mean, I also have questions. What really stood out to me is the fact that so many people in the industry seemed to coalesce around this fairly quickly. Even before Amodei published his blog post, I was seeing other people post some version of this [plan,] just in the days leading up to it.

My understanding is, these suggestions that have come out of the AI safety community; these are things that have been percolating for a while. They’re not just things that [Amodei] thought up on his own. But it just seemed like a lot of people were kind of ready to embrace this and in some ways, [it’s] encouraging to see that there’s a consensus. But it also makes me a little skeptical that this would represent genuine, major steps towards a slowdown.

Kirsten: First of all, consensus can be a good thing. Also, it can be the beginnings of forming a cartel. And so, let’s be clear [about] who we’re talking about here. We’re talking about frontier AI labs. and that’s specific and important.

You did say a minute ago that the details aren’t really clear, but we do know that the general idea here is that independent third-party evaluators would come in that would work inside [companies] like Anthropic or OpenAI and monitor AI safety practices and incidents. But there is a lot of vagueness around that.

Then there’s another proposal to have major AI companies in democratic countries coordinate on safety standards and limits. And then this international coordination piece. So those are the general ideas around this.

I’ll also add that there’s been very considerable pushback from very specific people. And surprisingly, some people I didn’t think would push back on this. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. I don’t know what either of you think of […] some of his comments and the call he took from President Trump onstage [at the All-In Summit].

Sean: I think Jensen understands that, to a certain extent, he is seen as the adult in the room here. Which is interesting, because that’s a dynamic that I think has changed. If you were to ask people a year, almost two years ago now, who was playing that role as these AI companies were really starting to blow up in big ways, I think a lot of people would have pointed to Microsoft and Satya Nadella, and I feel like Microsoft has — for a number of reasons that we don’t need to get into right now — lost that grip on being the adult in the room. Certainly in part because Nadella said he was going to make Google dance, and then that never happened. And in fact, the opposite happened, in a lot of ways.

Jensen, I think, understands not only that he needs to be pleasing the most amount of people and so he wants to say the most measured thing, he also is one of the most useful liaisons between this field and this administration, to the point that he’s getting a call from the president while he’s onstage at this very well-attended and high-profile conference that allowed both of them to respond to all this mess.

Kirsten: [To] your point about him being the adult in the room and the liaison, he is in a position where he could do that. But in my view, I would say that [his appearance,] which did feel a little staged, went a step too far and really highlighted the fact that Nvidia greatly benefits from AI moving forward in an unpaced manner.

I hate to be cynical about it, but that was sort of my initial reaction to it.

Anthony: Trump’s and Huang’s interests are aligned, and also [Huang’s] telling [Trump] what he wants to hear.

I did think some of the things he was specifically focusing on are worth unpacking a little bit. First he talked about this idea of, “We are not going to have a slowdown.” It’s interesting, just that phrase “slowdown,” which has come up a lot — but at the same time, both Altman and Amodei [will] use the slowdown language, but the word they like to use more is “pace.” right?

And these three proposals — the ones you just described, Kirsten — in theory, they could result in things slowing down, but they’re not saying that explicitly. It’s saying, “Hey, we’re making some basic safety measures and having some people keep an eye on us.” But none of those things are intrinsically saying that things have to go slower than they are now, at least as I understand it.

Kirsten: So I have a question for Sean. Couldn’t you argue in a free market society, we have existing regulations in place, and also [in] the competitive environment in which there isn’t protectionism, if there is something unsafe that is released by a company, that they would no longer be able to be a viable company? And there are regulators in place today that could go after these companies? Or do you reject that idea?

Sean: In a vacuum, or in a market that is not being distorted by a whole bunch of different external pressures, yeah, I think there’s an element of that. But we have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.

And we’re also in this weird situation where — I don’t really know the right way to put it, but it does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.

Especially now, as they have moved into enterprise and they’re making so much more of their money from selling their services to companies, it’s just naturally harder to vote with your dollars there. Corporations are not going to pack up and move from [OpenAI’s] Codex to [Anthropic’s] Claude Code just because they disagree on principle with something that OpenAI did.

And then they’re also just being floated by so much investment money that it makes it easier for them to absorb any of those losses if they actually do face them. So I think it’s a nice idea in theory, but I feel like in practice, there’s none of that really happening.

Tech.title: Vocci’s ring adds a new form factor to meeting note-taking
Tech.content:
There is no dearth of different forms of hardware for meeting note-taking, including pendants, pins, and credit-card-styled devices. That hasn’t stopped Vocci from releasing a new device for the same use case in a ring form factor, which is convenient but could create some privacy issues.

The ring form factor is one of the easiest for anyone who wants to just press a button and have the device start recording. Pebble’s new Index 01 Ring, which I am testing right now, lets you hold the button and take a note or a reminder. Stream Ring, made by Sandbar, works similarly with a control pad on the top. Vocci’s ring takes a different path, with meeting note-taking as a central function.

The ring has a button, which you can double-tap to start recording and double-tap again to stop. You can tap and hold the button to ask Vocci AI questions, but that only works when you have the app open. There is an indicator light and a haptic motor for recording feedback. The ring is lightweight at under six grams and uses titanium material on the inner and outer surfaces — likely a coating.

The company claims that the Vocci ring can record notes for eight hours on a single charge. The device comes with a chunky plastic case, which can charge the ring up to three times.

Image Credits:Vocci

The device captures meetings very well. I have had conversations spanning more than an hour in loud cafes, and the ring managed to convert most of the chat into accurate transcripts. However, this method of note-taking is not great if you want to take short notes.

The software is the disappointing part of the Vocci ring. The app itself is a bit confusing. Whenever I took shorter notes, I saw AI-generated insights that were longer than the notes themselves. Each recording has Chat, which is the main transcript; Highlights, which are short snippets you can capture by pressing the button while recording a conversation; and Notes, which is a summary and insight of the whole conversation.

In the app, there is a tab called Base where you can find transcripts, recordings, and anything you generate from them, and I found that redundant. I didn’t find a way to directly initiate a chat with AI for session transcripts.

Voice-enabled rings are a great form factor for taking short notes or reminders. The app doesn’t have direct integration with reminder apps, which is a bummer. The feature rollout for its software is also slow. The company informed me that users can use Vocci’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to other assistants, but the option to do that didn’t appear until a few weeks ago in the app. Other meeting notetakers are building their platforms to allow users to automate insights and workflow through AI, and at the moment, Vocci’s platform is not fully built out for that.

There are some privacy concerns with this device because of its form factor. Vocci’s ring looks like a regular piece of jewelry until someone notices the button on it. The ring has a recording indicator, but it faces the user. It’s best practice to let someone know that you are recording a conversation, and it’s also required by law in some countries and regions. But with this kind of device, some miscreants can easily choose not to disclose that information and record the conversation without anyone noticing. The company said it encourages people to disclose that they are recording, but that may not be enough.

At $249, the ring is pricey compared to other note-takers like Plaud or Pocket, and that is due to the device’s lightweight form factor. The ring is for someone who doesn’t want to stick a gadget on the back of their phone, wear a wristband, or wear a pendant. On the hardware layer, a lot of these devices are combinations of some microphones, a battery, and a connection to the phone. We will likely see more variety in hardware meeting note-takers in the coming years, until users pick the specific formats that work for them.

Tech.title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
Tech.content:
Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through?

That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll.

ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end.

“The younger generation is increasingly going short form, vertical feed only (especially the 18 year olds we’ve spoken to!), and this poses challenges for any kind of media that requires depth,” Utsav Gupta, ScrollEd’s co-founder, told TechCrunch in an email. “We want to meet them where they are…We just have to be deliberate about how we use it and choose not to maximize engagement on the platform.”

“A short video can make you curious; following that curiosity can mean searching for another explanation or leaving the app,” Gupta continued. “We wanted going deeper to be as easy as moving to the next video.”

Gupta bootstrapped ScrollEd this year alongside his co-founder and wife Rebecca Neff after the two both noticed feeling dissatisfied after doomscrolling before bed. Both are students — Gupta studies AI and human purpose at Stanford, and Neff studies computer science at the University of Pennsylvania.

The startup is targeting educational institutions, corporate training programs, and individuals who “just want something better to scroll on,” according to Gupta.

ScrollEd is following a freemium model, combining a free consumer feed with a paid ScrollEd Pro subscription and annual institutional licenses. Institutions pay to deliver educational material through the platform, in exchange for reports about engagement, lesson progress, and other data.

In the coming months, ScrollEd intends to focus on its consumer launch, building its lesson library and source-checking workflow, and developing pilots for institutions. (The company will launch its consumer business at Disrupt, in fact. “We’re hoping to ‘disrupt’ social media and short form!” Gupta joked.)

The startup is also building infrastructure that will one day allow educators to assess individual learners and adapt to their needs.

“The ambition is a social network that’s better for you,” Gupta said.

Check out ScrollEd and the other smart startups that TC’s editorial team has vetted and you’ll want to check out at TechCrunch Disrupt, coming up October 13-15 in downtown San Francisco. You can find many more details, and tickets, right here.

Tech.title: Here’s the iFixit Repairability Rating for the iPhone 18 Pro
Tech.content:
iFixit, the company known for completely tearing apart just about every product and device it can, has fully disassembled a brand new iPhone 18 Pro. The goal is to understand how all the parts fit together and find ways to fix anything that might break.

In the company’s post and teardown video, iFixit showed off how it took apart the latest iPhone, and what people who may someday need to fix theirs should look out for.

It gave the iPhone 18 Pro a repair rating of 7/10, citing easy-to-remove camera and battery assemblies. This matches the rating it gave the iPhone 17 Pro in 2025. That doesn’t mean the iPhone repair process is simple.

The Achilles heel of the iPhone 18 Pro may be a new feature: a variable aperture lens in the phone’s main 48-megapixel camera. It is the first variable aperture in an iPhone (though not the first in a smartphone). It uses six rotating aperture blades the width of a human hair to allow for different apertures for photo and video.

Courtesy of iFixit

The problem with the aperture is that Apple is introducing moving parts—therefore more parts that might need repair. Given the size and intricacy of how the blades are positioned, iFixit called trying to fix the individual blades an almost-impossible task. That means if the camera does break, you’d probably have to replace the full camera assembly. That will undoubtedly be pricier than paying for individual pieces. Luckily, the assembly itself proved easy enough to remove.

A stickier situation is repairing the iPhone 18 Pro’s battery, which requires prying open the glued-on screen. Once that is removed, though, the battery isn't glued down but secured by screws, so it’s simpler to extract.

All in all, the iPhone 18 Pro is about as straightforward to repair as it has been for a few years—not a totally easy fix, but one with some tangible improvements. This comes after Apple’s long, contentious relationship with repair advocates, which made it a target of European Union legislation to make its products easier to fix.

Apple introduced a self-repair program in 2021. It got off to a bumpy start as the company withheld or made it difficult to access certain tools. After pressure from US state lawmakers, Apple made it slightly easier to repair its phones and eventually introduced a repair assistant to help guide users through the repair process. Still, just this year, the ownership advocacy group PIRG gave the iPhone 17 a D- rating for its repairability.

Tech.title: Got an Android Phone? Google Thinks You’ll Probably Want a Googlebook Laptop
Tech.content:
There are three ratings for apps on the Google Play Store: Made for Desktop, Optimized for Desktop, and Better on the Website. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

The next tier of Android app is “Optimized for Desktop.” These apps take advantage of the bigger screens with better layouts and a little more functionality. The final tier is “Made for Desktop,” like the desktop versions of Chrome. Google says around 20 or so apps are either optimized for desktop or made for the desktop so far, including CapCut, Adobe Photoshop, Notability, and Fantastical. As the platform grows, Google expects more developers will target Android’s “Made for Desktop” tier and bring their desktop-grade apps from Windows and macOS to Googlebook.

People want to play games on their laptops, and so Google says you’ll be able to access more than 20,000 titles on the Play Store, many of which support cross-device play between mobile, tablets, and laptops. Google says around 50 of the 100 top titles are optimized for keyboard, trackpad, and touchscreen. But since you can’t download AAA games for Googlebooks (yet), especially without a discrete GPU, Google is offering 1 year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now game streaming service, which is optimized for the platform.

New Frontiers

Googlebook is an opportunity for Google to bring artificial intelligence to the forefront of the laptop computing experience, which is why many of the core new features are AI-powered. For example, similar to Android 17, you can generate your own desktop widgets with simple prompts to Gemini.

Magic Pointer is the marquee Gemini feature. Wiggle the mouse pointer over anything, and a Gemini overlay will suggest contextual actions. For example, if you wiggle over an event someone invited you to, you’ll get a prompt to automatically “Create an event” and have it added to your Google Calendar with one tap. Or if you’re wondering what breed of dog you’re looking at (whether it’s a video or photo), wiggle and ask Gemini, “What’s the breed?” If you’re wondering whether an email is a phishing attempt, wiggle over it and ask Gemini.

Tech.title: Apple Mac Mini (M6) Review: For the AI Curious
Tech.content:
Ports remain the same. Two forward-facing USB-C 3 ports (up to 10 gigabytes per second), as well as a headphone jack and a power indicator light. On the back, there are three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI 2.1, an Ethernet jack, and the power adapter port. Using the available USB-C ports and HDMI on the back, you can connect up to two 5K 120-Hz external displays (such as the Studio Display XDR or BenQ 5K MA270S) or three 4K displays.

One controversial design is that the power button is still hidden underneath the back left corner of the computer. If you know where it is, just tilt the Mac Mini to the side and reach your finger back—easy. If you don't know (or keep forgetting, as I do), it means having to flip the thing over entirely, with all your cables attached. It remains a silly design decision in my view, but it's nowhere near as egregious as the Magic Mouse it pairs with (sold separately), which still infamously charges from the bottom. But I digress.

I still wish it had an SD card slot (forward-facing, like the Mac Studio) though. Plenty of photographers and videographers would be well suited for the Mac Mini, and yet they'll need to buy an additional dock or adapter. And yes, some color options, like the iMac, would be nice. But from the outside, it's the same well-built, compact mini PC it's always been. It's the performance under the hood where you'll need to dig in to see the extra value in this latest generation.

AI Gains

Right off the bat, I was eager to test a couple of new components in the M6 Mac Mini. First, there are the advances in the M6 chip itself. This is our first glimpse of the next generation of Apple Silicon, and the first built on a 2-nm process node. It represents a significant step up in transistor count on the die—46 billion in this case. That's around a 35 percent increase in transistor density, which translates to higher efficiency and more performance. In theory.

The M6 Mac Mini also adds two more CPU cores than the M4 model, for a total of 12. That's a 21 percent increase in single-thread performance and a 36 percent improvement in a multi-threaded run. Those numbers sound impressive, but compared to the M5 in the MacBook Air, they're not as substantial. It's only around 10 percent faster than the M5 Pro chip in the MacBook Pro in single-threaded performance (and unsurprisingly, much further behind in multi-threaded). Those two extra CPU cores, though, do prop up the multi-threaded performance, even compared to the base M5 chip. It's hard to do apples-to-apples comparisons to only a laptop.

Like previous Mac Minis, it has a fan inside. And when you get to work on something heavy, you'll definitely hear it start to make some noise. It's not terrible, but if you're coming from a MacBook, you'll definitely notice. That active cooling ensures you get stronger performance from that M6 chip than you would in a MacBook Air (though I won't be able to do a side-by-side comparison until the M6 MacBook Air comes out, presumably in 2027).

Tech.title: US and China Discuss Alerting Each Other to AI National Security Threats
Tech.content:
Talks have begun between US and Chinese officials to propose a mechanism for the two countries to notify each other of artificial intelligence incidents which could threaten national security.

The framework, called the US China AI Dialogue, would also see representatives from both countries meet again to discuss the technology and try to align on common goals and threats, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

“We think that, just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent told reporters on Sunday.

Bessent said the discussions picked up from where they had been left off after US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. Since then, public safety concerns about the technology have grown. Security incidents over the summer, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted the capabilities of frontier models and how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace.

Fears reached a fever pitch earlier this month after Anthropic employees warned AI could be on course to wipe out humanity. In recent weeks, leaders of the biggest frontier laboratories, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk, have called for a slowdown in development of the technology while they set safety standards. In an essay suggesting steps for laboratories and governments to pace the technology’s development, Amodei had asked for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party.

Tech.title: Bambu P2S Combo 3D Printer Review: My Own Little Plastics Factory
Tech.content:
I tested the P2S on the West Coast in late summer, when the humidity was very low, so my filament stayed below 40 percent relative humidity, according to the built-in hygrometer—it didn’t need drying. However, if you live in a humid region, springing for the AMS will be a massive time-saver.

With the P1S, if you needed to swap out a different nozzle, it was something of an ordeal—you basically have to unplug everything and take apart the assembly with screws. On the P2S, the front of the nozzle head is magnetic and pops right off—simply unclip the old nozzle and clip in the new one. Another massive improvement if you find yourself swapping nozzles often.

The P1S’s automatic nozzle cleaning function that “poops” filament blobs out the back of the machine is still in effect on the P2S. I’d been warned, but I was still surprised to see the amount of detritus it left on the floor, especially during multi-color prints. I highly recommend that a “poop chute” or collection basket be one of your first prints. (And there are plenty of fun designs for using the waste filament blobs once they’ve accumulated, from creative games to a “poop Atlas” filament waste world map.)

Do You Really Need One?

Yes, unless you need a dual-nozzle printer or a commercial-grade unit that can also laser cut and engrave—features this printer doesn’t offer. The ability to print and customize useful household and garage objects, art projects, and toys easily and quickly—with minimal fuss—makes the P2S worth every penny. This is doubly so if you have some basic engineering skills, as importing files into Bambu Studio is a cinch.

Bambu Lab-brand filaments start at about $15 a roll with spool. Note that we flagged some app inconsistencies when using non-Bambu filaments with the P1S, but I did not have any non-Bambu filaments on hand to test in the P2S, so I can’t vouch for whether this issue has been fixed.

Tech.title: Justice for CSS
Tech.content:
The first S in CSS stands for “style.” Think colors and fonts, borders and shadows, rows and columns, animations and transitions. CSS is the programming language that makes a website look pretty (or pretty ugly, often). It’s what makes this very webpage look like itself—look WIRED.

One paragraph in, a certain reader will already be smarting at my description of CSS. “It’s a style sheet language,” I can hear them say, “not a programming language.” (The second S indeed stands for “sheets,” and the C, if anyone cares, for “cascading.”) Or, “it’s a domain-specific language, not a general-purpose language.” Also, “it doesn’t execute” and, of course, “it’s not Turing complete” (although … ). Granted, CSS is a little different. There’s no compile step, and it doesn’t throw errors at run time like other languages. But that’s all beside the point.

Machine Readable A regular column about programming. Because if/when the machines take over, we should at least speak their language.

The gatekeeping over whether CSS is a “real” programming language exists partly because it’s so simple to start—anyone can grok “background: red” right away. But simple does not mean easy, as the programmer-writer Jeremy Keith observed, and calling CSS easy or unserious should be tired by now. There were about 50 properties in the initial CSS specification in 1996 (like “color” and “font-size”); today there are at least 10 times as many (get ready for “hanging-punctuation”). The language has changed so much in three decades, and by now it is just so capable. One programmer recently re-created Doom in CSS. Others have used it to build holographic Pokémon cards and 3D-rendering engines. Cassidy Williams, who competed in this year’s inaugural March MadCSS tournament, built an experimental database-query engine entirely in CSS. When she demo’d it at Microsoft Build, even the emcees—seasoned programmers themselves—took a cheap shot at CSS. “You’re one of the people that likes it,” they snarked. “You might be the only one.”

Why is the lore of JavaScript’s creation so famous (Brendan Eich, Netscape, 10 days) and yet hardly any programmer would recognize the name of CSS creator Håkon Wium Lie? It might have something to do with Lie being a Norwegian guy with a diacritic in his name, not an American in Silicon Valley like Eich nor a Brit like Tim Berners-Lee, who invented HTML. And to be fair, JavaScript and HTML each have a chip on their own shoulder to worry about. But in the browser’s holy ternary of JavaScript-​HTML-CSS, people tend to treat CSS as less than or purely decorative. Styling can be decorative—and wonderfully so—but the legibility and rich design it affords are important. People care how things look!

There’s another, uglier explanation for the CSS disrespect: It’s considered a “feminine” language. CSS developers work on the frontend—the part of a website you can actually see. There’s the obvious undertone that dealing with style and beauty is Female Work, along with the recycled joke that a CSS developer is “a freak in the style sheets.” How seriously a language is taken has knock-on effects on programmer salaries, what skills are sought out and tested in job interviews, and how accessible websites are for people with disabilities.

I recently talked to a friend, a talented backend engineer, about this. In college, she got an internship at a reputable software company in San Francisco doing entirely backend work. “I’d never expressed any interest in frontend at all, almost to an extreme extent,” she told me. “I don’t like frontend.” And yet, when she joined the company full-time after graduation, she was immediately assigned … a frontend role. She eventually worked her way back to the backend, and by now she’s used to the skepticism. “I’ve been in a million and one conversations with the classic man engineer who doesn’t think I know what I’m talking about until they work with me for six months and see my first backend project.”

Tech.title: The Search for Silicon Valley’s Most Powerful Woman
Tech.content:
Mira Murati was trying to speak. Women swished around in evening gowns, men in tuxes. Giant piles of carved meat rested like sleeping babies on banquet tables draped in linens as red as a handmaid’s robe. Bartenders served up a cocktail named Zero to One, a nod to the philosophy of Peter Thiel.

It was a recent Saturday night in a converted church in San Francisco, and the Foundation for American Innovation, a center-right think tank, was hosting a black-tie affair to hype the new religion of AI.

Murati, the founder and CEO of Thinking Machines Lab, was talking about the history of revolutions to a crowd of more than 350 people. The Albanian-born executive had for several years kept a relatively low profile as a VP and then CTO of OpenAI before participating in an unsuccessful coup against Sam Altman and then launching her own $12 billion AI startup. Now, with chatter bouncing off the church walls, Murati’s efforts to get her points across were about as successful as that coup: No one seemed to be listening. The woman interviewing Murati asked more than once for people to stop talking or take their conversations outside.

I whispered to the friend sitting next to me that this was the second time in a week that I’d seen a woman getting drowned out. She sighed. Both of us were there to actually hear what Murati had to say. I tried to restrain myself from what I said next, but I sensed my friend was holding back too. “Her hair is amazing, though,” I hissed. “Oh my God, I know,” she replied immediately. Murati’s hair has achieved AGI. Her jaw cuts glass.

Soon after, President Donald Trump’s top science adviser, Michael Kratsios, took the stage. The crowd quieted down. We are all part of the problem.

Tech.title: Women Still Face Too Much Bullshit—in Silicon Valley and Beyond
Tech.content:
It didn’t take more than a few sessions for my new therapist to ask me a delicate question.

“Katie … do you have a problem with men?”

I wanted to say no. After all, brilliant, kind, fantastic men have long surrounded me at home and at work. The therapist in question was himself a man, and one I didn’t think twice about confiding in.

But if I’m being honest with myself, my therapist, and you? I do have a problem with some men. And it started with WIRED. In 2009, I got my first job interning and later reporting for WIRED.com. The publication in that era was enthusiastic about technology, and about the innovators and visionaries defining the future. For decades, WIRED eagerly reinforced the narrative that the vast majority of those geniuses were men: One 2010 analysis found that since its founding in 1993, WIRED had published 70 covers featuring at least one man. In that same span, the magazine published four covers—yes, four—that celebrate women for their professional accomplishments. I can’t remember working with a single female editor during my first stint at WIRED. I do, however, remember a 40-something male editor asking “where’d the legs go?” when I opted to wear pants instead of a skirt to the office.

Photo-illustration: WIRED Staff; Vincent Tullo

It turned out to be just a preview. Off the top of my head, and across a 17-year career: There was the boss who, upon learning that I wanted kids, said that I seemed “too cold” to be a parent. I held my tears long enough to make it to the bathroom. A few years later, I remember being visibly pregnant in another employer’s office, as he joked that a woman as intense as me would probably keep her baby locked in a closet. One boss tried to pay me exponentially less than my male predecessor, because, he said, I was younger and less authoritative. A highly regarded media company enrolled me in its internal program for promising female leaders, which was being run by two male executives. I stood last year among a crowd of my peers at a packed event, listening to a prominent think-tank leader (male) credit WIRED’s previous editor in chief (also male) with the magazine’s successes during my tenure. Let’s not forget the cofounder of this very publication, who suggested via email following the 2024 election that I might “seppuku” myself because he disagreed with an editor’s letter I’d written. And in 2023, The New York Times published a story about my appointment as WIRED’s global editorial director—then had to issue a correction for inaccurately stating that I was the first woman to run the magazine. In fact, Katrina Heron ran WIRED from 1997 to 2001.

WIRED Women Nobody wants to talk about women in tech anymore—not even women in tech. Is that progress?

It’s gotten easier to be an ambitious woman, but if my own personal experience is any indication, not by nearly enough. The steady reminders of sexism and deeply ingrained gender dynamics have had consequences: I wonder, often, if I was granted certain jobs or opportunities for less-than-professional reasons; on the flip side, I also wonder if I got them to fulfill some kind of quota. I second-guess my decisions. I apologize endlessly. For years, I dressed as sloppily as possible—it was easier to show up unprofessionally than risk attracting any attention. In a bid to command the respect at work that a man would, I’ve often felt the need to behave more like a stereotypical one: meaner, louder, less empathetic. I hate that. And I’ve got it relatively easy: If a white, straight woman working in media and technology deals with this much bullshit, imagine the experience of a woman who happens to be a person of color, or gay, or transgender.

WIRED Women started as a joke at our weekly San Francisco happy hour; we laughed at the idea of turning a historically dude-loving publication into a women’s rag, complete with over-the-top pink design and outrageous cover lines—a tongue-in-cheek way to highlight the sorry state of women’s advancement in fields like tech and science. We soon found ourselves inspired, full of ideas, and ultimately pretty damn angry. But could we do it? Should we? Deciding in 2026 to commit an entire issue to all things women might seem regressive, or too obvious, or even unnecessary in an era where many people—and plenty in tech—are happy to wave off the notion that gender is still “a thing” to contend with.

I disagree. A convicted sex predator, after all, is in the White House; the tech industry executives in his ear are virtually all men. Women do wield power in Silicon Valley, but far too many still serve at the pleasure of a man above them. When Mark Zuckerberg bemoans the loss of “masculine energy” in his workforce, and Pete Hegseth says that the military is too “effeminate,” and Elon Musk’s DOGE cuts impact Black female civil servants above all other groups—it can seem like they want to erase women altogether. And it’s infuriating. The world deserves better heroes, women deserve better colleagues, and my daughter—who sleeps in a bed, not a locked closet—deserves to be less furious than I am when she’s 40. My therapist, God bless him, was onto something.

Tech.title: The First Googlebooks Are Here, and They’re Everything I Need in a Laptop
Tech.content:
Google

When it comes to my daily devices, I live in two worlds. For work, I use a MacBook Pro and an iPhone. My personal devices, on the other hand, are a Chromebook and a Pixel phone. Now that I’ve used a Googlebook and seen what it can do, I’ll likely swap out my Chromebook for one. That’s because, much like the MacBook and iPhone work well together, the integration between an Android phone and a Googlebook is absolutely fantastic.

What is a Googlebook?

Essentially, a Googlebook is a premium laptop running on Googlebook OS, which brings together Android, Gemini AI and the desktop functionality and robust security of ChromeOS. While Google Chromebooks and ChromeOS were made for life on the web, Googlebooks are about how we work today. They’ll let you seamlessly move between your phone and your laptop, while also giving you access to powerful AI-based tools. You’ll also have full access to the Google Play Store, including apps and games developed for mobile and desktop use.

When Google announced Googlebooks back in May, it didn’t say much about the actual devices. Mainly, just that they’d be premium laptops — a departure from Chromebooks’ budget-friendly identity. Check out the video below for a better look at the features of Googlebook OS and the laptops. Specs for the first five Googlebooks are also below.

You can order the Googlebooks now, or you can wait until Oct. 4 when they arrive in stores in the US (Oct. 5 for Canada, the UK, Ireland, France, Germany and Australia). Prices start at $899, but these are premium devices, so you’ll find things like high-quality materials, haptic touchpads, backlit keyboards, OLED touchscreens and Intel Panther Lake and Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite processors.

Every purchase also includes 12 months of Google AI Pro, which normally costs $200 and comes with 5TB of cloud storage and Gemini Advanced tools. You’ll also get three months each of YouTube Premium and Adobe Photoshop, plus one year of Nvidia’s GeForce Now cloud gaming service. And, like current Chromebooks, Googlebooks will get new features and OS updates for 10 years.



Dell XPS Googlebook

Josh Goldman/CNET

The smallest of the Googlebooks, the XPS has the same high-end look and feel as the XPS 13 Windows laptop, which is awesome. It’s a great design with a full aluminum body that weighs 2.2 pounds. However, unlike the Windows version, it starts at $1,199, not $799.

Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite

16 or 32GB of memory

512GB of storage

13.4-inch 2.5K-resolution touchscreen, 500-nit brightness

Fingerprint reader

Lenovo Googlebook 15

Josh Goldman/CNET

With a beautiful 15.3-inch OLED touchscreen, the Lenovo is the largest of the launch Googlebooks. Made from magnesium-alloy and carbon fiber, it not only looked and felt good, but it was incredibly light for its size at 2.8 pounds. Pricing starts at $1,299.

Intel Core Ultra 5 Series 3 (Panther Lake)

16GB of memory

256GB of storage

15.3-inch 2.8K-resolution OLED touchscreen

Dolby Atmos

Haptic touchpad

Facial and fingerprint recognition

Acer Googlebook 14

Josh Goldman/CNET

The lone two-in-one in the group, it looks like a sleeker, slimmer version of the company’s Chromebook Plus 714. It’s also the only $899 model, though according to the information Acer supplied, this is a limited-time offer at Best Buy. Made from magnesium and aluminum, it weighs only 2.5 pounds.

Intel Core Ultra 5/7 Series 3 (Panther Lake)

16 GB of memory

256GB of storage

14-inch 2.8K-resolution OLED touchscreen

USI 2.0 pen support

Fingerprint sensor

HP Googlebook 14

Josh Goldman/CNET

Starting at $1,299, the 14-inch laptop has an all-aluminum build and weighs in at 2.7 pounds. It’s certainly nice-looking, with a sturdy build, similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14 — one of our favorite premium Windows laptops.

Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite

16 or 32GB of memory

14-inch 2.8K OLED touchscreen

Fingerprint sensor and Face authentication

Josh Goldman/CNET

Asus’ Googlebook appears to follow the design path of the company’s ExpertBook Ultra, a $3,600 business laptop. It’s a beautiful laptop with a body made from aluminum and magnesium with a ceramic finish that feels incredible and weighs just 2.2 pounds. Like the Lenovo and HP, it starts at $1,299.

Tech.title: M6 Mac Mini First Look: Bigger Power Packed in the Same Small Package
Tech.content:
The M6 update for the Mac Mini arrived not a moment too soon. Not only has it been nearly two years since the last Mac Mini was released, but it’s also become increasingly difficult to find an older M4 Mini for purchase in recent months. In the year of the AI agent, Apple’s Mac Mini has enjoyed a surge in popularity to the point of dwindling supplies and long wait times.

The compact, quiet and affordable Mini with its energy-efficient yet powerful Apple silicon and unified memory has become a popular pick for people looking to run OpenClaw and other local AI agents around the clock. Even at its slightly elevated starting price of $899, the M6 Mini is sure to remain en vogue as a tiny, always-on AI server. The core count ticks up for the CPU, GPU and NPU in going from the M4 to the M6, skipping over the M5 in the process.

If you want to pack more power into the Mac Mini for running demanding creative workloads or larger LLMs, Apple offers two M5 Pro processor upgrades and the ability to stuff the Mini with up to 64GB of RAM. Apple sent me a pair of Mac Minis to test, an M6 model with bumps to the memory and storage and a loaded M5 Pro unit whose price places it in Mac Studio territory.

Apple Mac Mini specs (as tested)

Mac Mini M6 Mac Mini M5 Pro Price as reviewed $1,299 $2,899 CPU M6 12-core CPU M5 Pro 18-core CPU Memory 24GB unified memory 48GB unified memory Graphics Integrated M6 12‑core GPU Integrated M5 Pro 20‑core GPU Storage 512GB SSD 1TB SSD Networking Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 Ports Front: USB-C (x2, up to 10Gbps), 3.5mm headphone jack



Rear: USB-C Thunderbolt 4 (x3, up to 40Gb/s), HDMI out, Gigabit Ethernet, power input Front: USB-C (x2, up to 10Gbps), 3.5mm headphone jack



Rear: USB-C Thunderbolt 4 (x3, up to 40Gb/s), HDMI out, Gigabit Ethernet, power input Operating system MacOS 27.0 Golden Gate MacOS 27.0 Golden Gate

Josh Goldman/CNET

Even before the latest price hike with the M6 model, the Mac Mini lost its standing earlier this year as Apple’s most affordable Mac computer. It debuted two decades ago at $499 and could be had for $599 for most of its tenure before jumping to $799 earlier this year.

Released this spring, the MacBook Neo became the cheapest Mac at just $699, but it’s based on an A18 Pro processor borrowed from the iPhone. So, the Mac Mini still remains the most affordable Mac computer with a proper M-series processor. At $899, it’s still $400 less than the cheapest MacBook Air. And it beat every MacBook in the race to be the first Mac to get Apple’s new M6 processor.

Meet the M6

The M6 processor is the first of Apple’s M series processors to be fabricated with a 2nm process, which allows for denser circuitry in the same size die. The smaller process usually results in greater efficiency and lets you increase the core count and clock speeds without increasing the size of the chip.

And sure enough, the M6 is richer in cores than the previous M4 part. The M6 has 12 CPU cores and 12 GPU cores — up from 10 cores of each type in the M4 chipset. Meanwhile, the core count of the neural processing unit that’s designed to handle the integer math required for AI tasks, including Apple Intelligence, has doubled.

Josh Goldman/CNET

The M6 has a dual 16-core neural engine; its combined 32 cores are double the 16-core NPU of the M4 and M5 Pro. The M6 and M5 Pro also feature the same neural accelerators on the GPU that Apple introduced with the M5 to help boost AI and ray-tracing performance.

For $899, the M6 Mac Mini has 16GB of RAM, a 256GB SSD and a 2.5Gb Ethernet adapter. Offering 256GB of storage on a desktop computer, no matter how small that computer may be, is borderline offensive. You can’t even buy a MacBook Air with a 256GB SSD after Apple jettisoned that undersized option earlier this year. Unfortunately, the cost to double the storage to 512GB is steep at $200, which quickly pushes the price of the Mac Mini over $1,000. Want to double it again to 1TB? That’s another $300. Be prepared to part with another $500 if you want to double it yet again to 2TB.

Memory costs are similarly steep. Each 8GB upgrade adds $200 to the bill, going from 16GB to 24GB and 24GB to 32GB. Choose one of the M5 Pro upgrades, and you can take the memory to 48GB or 64GB and storage up to a whopping 8TB. (I’ll let you discover those upgrade prices on your own; just be sure you’re sitting down when you take a look.)

Pricing for the Mac Mini with an M5 Pro starts at $1,699. For that price, you get an M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, along with 24GB of memory and a 512GB SSD. (Yes, along with you, I was relieved to see the 256GB SSD option disappear with the M5 Pro upgrade.)

Josh Goldman/CNET

Apple sent me the higher of the two M5 Pro offerings. It has an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU. Apple also upped the memory to 48GB and the storage to 1TB while also upgrading the Ethernet adapter to 10Gbps. The cost of this test system is $2,899. That’s $400 more than the entry-level Mac Studio.

Notably, the M5 Pro chips have the same 16-core neural engine as the standard M5 chip and not the M6’s dual 16-core neural engine. No matter the CPU you choose, the Mac Mini comes with Apple’s N1 chip that delivers Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 networking.

The good news and bad news with Apple’s unified memory

Let’s get the bad news (and a couple of acronyms) out of the way first. Apple’s M-series processors have a system-on-a-chip (or SoC) design with a unified memory architecture. The downside of this arrangement is that the RAM cannot be upgraded after purchase. You’re locked into whatever amount you buy. Common on today’s laptops, it’s more of a drag on a desktop computer, even one as compact as the Mac Mini, where space for upgrades is limited.

Now, the good news. The SoC design combines the CPU, GPU and neural engine to remove bottlenecks and speed up both performance and efficiency. And with Apple’s UMA, the system’s memory is shared among the CPU, GPU and neural engine instead of splitting it into separate blocks where most of the RAM is accessed by the CPU and only a smaller amount of video RAM is allocated to the GPU. Running a local LLM is extremely memory-intensive, which is why the affordable Mac Mini, with its unified memory, has become the move for many people looking to run local AI agents.

Josh Goldman/CNET

Memory bandwidth has improved with the new Mini models. The M6 Mac Mini’s memory has a bandwidth of up to 153 GB/s with 16GB of RAM and up to 170 GB/s with 24GB or more, which is an increase from the 120 GB/s of the M4 Mini. The M5 Pro jumps you up to a memory bandwidth of 307 GB/s.

Design stays the same

Apple refreshed the internals but kept the design the same from the M4 model, which introduced a much smaller footprint than the previous M2 model. The M6 Mini has the same 5-by-5-inch box that stands 2 inches tall, with the power button still in the same somewhat strange location. It’s on the bottom panel, which means you’ll need to pick up the Mini to power it on.

The same design means the new Mini has the same port selection, which was strong with the M4 Mini, so it wasn’t begging for a change — unless you were looking for the adapter-free convenience of getting a USB-A port. With all of the USB ports of the Type-C variety, you’ll need an adapter for older USB-A peripherals or a wired mouse. Like the M4 model, the M6 Mini supports up to three external displays.

Josh Goldman/CNET

M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini performance so far

Based on my initial testing, the M6 Mac Mini is looking like it’s going to be an even more popular pick than the M5 Pro Mini or previous M4 Mini for agentic AI workloads. The dual 16-core neural engine, combined with the neural accelerator on each GPU core, helped the M6 rocket ahead of the M4 Mini on our Geekbench AI test, which measures the on-device AI performance of a laptop’s NPU. The M6 also topped the M5 Pro Mini and every M5-based MacBook we’ve tested on this test. The M5 has the GPU neural accelerators of the M6 but not its dual 16-core neural engine.

Still, the Asus Ascent QN10 mini PC based on a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite CPU performed better on this test than the M6 Mini, thanks to its NPU, which is capable of 80 trillion operations per second.

On our application benchmarks, the M6 Mini turned in outstanding single-core performance on the Geekbench 6 and Cinebench 2024 tests, where it again outpaced the M5 Pro and the crop of M5 MacBooks and Windows competitors. The M5 Pro Mini put its extra CPU cores to good use and beat the M6 Mini on the Geekbench 6 multicore test, but surprisingly, it fell short of the M6 Mini on the multicore CPU test of Cinebench 2024.

Where the M5 Pro Mini had its largest advantage over the M6 Mini in graphics performance. It easily outpaced the M6 Mini on our 3DMark Steel Nomad test.

I have more tests to run on these two machines to further investigate their AI and graphics performance. Check out the initial benchmark results below for the M6 and M5 Pro Mini, and check back soon for my full review of Apple’s latest Minis.
